abstract:
Background and purpose

Accurate estimation of relative stopping power (RSP) is essential for proton therapy (PT) treatment planning. Emerging X-ray computed tomography (xCT) technologies are enabling more advanced RSP calibration strategies, but may also introduce greater variability across centers. This study aimed to assess inter-center variability in xCT calibration and RSP estimation for proton treatment planning, using a proton CT (pCT) prototype as reference.

Material and methods

An ex vivo phantom was transported to five European PT centers and one research center, and scanned with both single-energy and dual-energy xCT systems. Acquisitions were performed in three phantom configurations, simulating different anatomical sizes. The reconstructed xCT images were calibrated to RSP according to each center's clinical protocol and compared against the pCT-derived RSP maps.

Results

Voxel-by-voxel comparison between xCT-based and pCT-based RSP maps showed inter-center RSP variability of about 1% in soft tissues and up to 5% in bone, with larger differences observed for larger phantom sizes. The largest discrepancies (up to 5%) relative to pCT were observed in the same configurations. Centers implementing beam-hardening corrections generally showed closer agreement with pCT, whereas the effect of size-specific HLUTs was tissue- and anatomy-dependent. The impact of these RSP variations on water-equivalent thickness in representative clinical scenarios resulted in a 2σ inter-center variability of 1.09% and 1.39% for brain and prostate cases, respectively.

Conclusions

This work presents the first inter-center comparison of xCT-based RSP estimation using an ex vivo phantom and pCT measurements as reference. The observed variability highlights the relevance of a comprehensive and standardized validation of xCT calibration protocols.

abstract: Purpose of Review Imaging-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR) is rapidly evolving beyond conventional computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-based pipelines toward machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and physics-informed approaches that enable fast, wire-free, and scalable functional assessment of coronary artery stenosis. This review synthesizes recent advances in computed tomography (CT)-and angiography-based FFR measurement, with particular emphasis on emerging physics-informed neural networks and neural operators (PINNs and PINOs), as well as key considerations for their clinical translation.Recent Findings ML/DL approaches have markedly improved automation and computational speed, enabling prediction of pressure and FFR from anatomical descriptors or angiographic contrast dynamics. However, their real-world performance and generalizability can remain variable and sensitive to domain shift, due to multi-center heterogeneity, interpretability challenges, and differences in acquisition protocols and image quality. Physics-informed learning introduces conservation structure and boundary-condition consistency into model training, improving generalizability and reducing dependence on dense supervision while maintaining rapid inference. Recent evaluation trends increasingly highlight deployment-oriented metrics, including calibration, uncertainty quantification, and quality-control gatekeeping, as essential for safe clinical use.SummaryThe field is converging toward imaging-derived FFR methods that are faster, more automated, and more reliable. While ML/DL offers substantial efficiency gains, physics-informed frameworks such as PINNs and PINOs may provide a more robust balance between speed and physical consistency. Prospective multi-center validation and standardized evaluation will be critical to support broad and safe clinical adoption.

abstract:
Introduction

In 2020, the American Association of Physicists in Medicine (AAPM) conducted a comprehensive imaging physics workforce survey (2020 Survey) to evaluate staffing needs, validate prior time and effort estimates, and explore workforce satisfaction. This report summarizes key findings, highlighting gaps between training and professional demands, challenges in recruitment, and shifts in workforce demographics and employment patterns.

Methods

The 2020 Survey, administered by the American Institute of Physics (AIP) Statistical Research Center (SRC) to AAPM and Health Physics Society members, had 953 responses from participants who were primarily diagnostic and nuclear medical physicists. The data were analyzed across four key areas: professional task workloads, workforce demographics and retirement outlook, lifestyle factors, and skill gaps.

Results and discussion

The AIP SRC analyzed the results of the 2020 Survey (results archived on the AAPM members-only website). The 2020 Survey validated the relative time required for equipment performance evaluations and the wide range of Level 2 services performed by the imaging physics workforce relative to AAPM Report 301. The 2020 Survey showed that the imaging physics workforce is aging (30% of respondents providing their age stated they were 66 years or older) and that many of these individuals could retire within 5 years of completing the survey. Finally, the 2020 Survey demonstrated that there were gaps between the skills and knowledge employers look for when hiring compared to the same self-identified qualities of the imaging physics workforce.

Conclusions

The 2020 Survey provided insights into the imaging physics workforce that validated prior publications estimating imaging physics workforce activities. The 2020 Survey indicates the imaging physics workforce is aging, with a wave of retirements on the horizon, and that individuals entering the workforce may not possess the skills and knowledge desired by employers. The data from this survey can be used to guide analyses and address future trends of the imaging physics field and workforce.

This study introduces a physics-aware Geometric Deep Learning framework to simultaneously predict quality, safety, and complexity metrics directly from surface topology. abstract: The field of Medical Health Physics (MHP) lies at the intersection of Health Physics (HP) and Medical Physics (MP). The MHP is one of the five subfields identified by the AAPM that in which a Qualified Medical Physicist (QMP) may operate independently to provide clinical professional services. The pathway to become a QMP employed in the field of MHP varies depending on which community an individual originates from (HP or MP). This document aims to identify the minimum educational requirement, appropriate professional certification(s), work experience, and the minimum areas of responsibility (scope of practice) for a QMP working the MHP subfield.

abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as mesh-free approaches for solving partial differential equations, but their learned representations are often difficult to interpret. RBF-kernel-based formulations such as sparse, physics-based, and interpretable neural networks (SPINNs) make the geometry of the physical kernels explicit and show that kernels adapt coherently around dominant solution features, motivating the question of whether all kernel geometries need to remain independent. To investigate this question, we introduce kernel-adaptive physics-informed learning machines (KAPI-LMs), a general framework for solving PDEs with structured RBF representations in which a large physical kernel dictionary is organized through a smaller set of geometric variables while retaining all physical kernels and independent expansion coefficients. The resulting hypothesis class provides explicit control over the degree of geometric sharing and can be combined with different physics-informed learning strategies. To demonstrate this flexibility, we develop compressed SPINN (cSPINN) using joint geometry-coefficient optimization, compressed physics-informed extreme learning machine (cPIELM) using variable projection for coefficient-linear PDEs, and Meta-cSPINN using task-conditioned learning for parametric PDEs. We establish approximation guarantees and quantify the effect of geometric sharing. Numerical studies across linear, nonlinear, parametric, coupled, and multiscale PDEs demonstrate substantial geometric compression at fixed physical basis resolution and reveal problem-dependent limits to sharing. They also show that different optimization strategies can discover markedly different geometries within the same hypothesis class. For parametric PDEs, Meta-cSPINN supports one-shot prediction and suggests additional organization across solution families, while PDE residuals identify where geometric sharing should be released or local resolution added. KAPI-LM thus provides a physics-informed PDE-solving framework in which geometric complexity is explicit and controllable, allowing the solution representation to be interpreted, compressed, and adaptively refined according to the physics.

abstract: Borophene is a compelling 2D material known for its considerable structural diversity, and its lack of a band gap can be overcome by synthesis of hydrogenated borophene, also known as borophane. However, with the realization of semiconductor borophane polymorphs, understanding the mechanisms controlling their band gaps is fundamental, particularly in vertically stacked architectures, where the role of interlayer coupling must be fully elucidated. Here, we investigate the electronic properties of semiconductor borophane bilayers in different stacking arrangements using density functional theory calculations. Our results show weak interlayer binding, with minor effects on bond lengths, low exfoliation energies, and little charge redistribution. In contrast, interlayer coupling of electron states plays an important role in band gaps, mainly by modifying the conduction bands, an effect strongly influenced by the stacking configuration. The linear optical response also depends on the interlayer twist angle and is strongly affected by excitonic effects in this material. These findings establish a fundamental framework for band gap engineering in borophene-based architectures, paving the way for their integration into next-generation nanoelectronic and optoelectronic devices.

abstract: Since its experimental discovery as an intrinsic antiferromagnetic topological insulator in 2019, the MnBi<sub>2</sub>Te<sub>4</sub>family of materials has greatly propelled the development of condensed matter physics over the past several years. This family naturally integrates long-range magnetic order with topological band structure within a two-dimensional van der Waals layered material, providing an unprecedentedly clean platform for exploring quantum phenomena such as axion insulators, the quantum anomalous Hall effect, and the topological magnetoelectric effect. However, the transition from fundamental research to practical applications, particularly the realization of high-temperature quantum effects, is confronted with severe challenges in intrinsic defects, magnetic ground-state tuning, and electronic structure engineering. This article aims to review the current development status of the MnBi<sub>2</sub>Te<sub>4</sub>family, focusing on its core quantum phenomena, recent revolutionary breakthroughs in sample preparation techniques, and diverse tuning methods. On this basis, we outline possible pathways toward high-temperature quantum effects through innovations in material synthesis, interface engineering, and multi-strategy tuning and heterostructure engineering.

abstract: X-ray induced acoustic computed tomography (XACT) enables high-contrast bone imaging but typically relies on dense and expensive transducer arrays. Sparse array sampling introduces severe streak artifacts and loss of fine structural details in conventional reconstruction. This work aims to establish a robust reconstruction framework that achieves high-fidelity structural imaging under sparse sampling, thereby overcoming hardware density limitations and facilitating low-cost, high-resolution skeletal health assessment. We propose a self-supervised, physics-driven framework based on sinusoidal implicit neural representation. The unknown initial pressure distribution is parameterized as a continuous coordinate-to-pressure function via a sinusoidal representation network, and is coupled end-to-end with a differentiable acoustic forward simulator implemented in j‑Wave. Network optimization is performed by minimizing waveform residuals between measured and predicted signals, eliminating the need for paired ground-truth data. To improve training stability and accelerate convergence, an adjoint-based warm start and total variation regularization are employed. In experiments on simulated hand and femoral bone sparse array datasets, the proposed method consistently outperforms conventional approaches under various sparse sampling conditions. Notably, for an osteoporotic femur imaged with only 64 transducer elements, the method effectively suppresses artifacts and faithfully preserves fine trabecular structures, achieving a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 32.43 dB and a root mean square error of 0.0239, surpassing the structural and quantitative accuracy of traditional reconstruction using a full 256‑element array. These results demonstrate that the framework supports stable XACT reconstruction under sparse array conditions and, with its favorable artifact suppression and microstructural preservation capabilities, offers a practical computational pathway toward low-cost, high-quality XACT imaging.

abstract: High-mobility semiconductors that simultaneously host robust valley physics and mechanical compliance are highly sought after for translating valleytronics into flexible device technologies. Using first-principles calculations, we propose monolayer TMX2 (TM = Ti, Zr, Hf; X = N, P, As) as a multifunctional 2D platform for valleytronics and flexible electronics. Crystallizing in a hexagonal P 6m2 lattice, these materials exhibit robust valley-contrasting physics, with opposite spin polarizations and inverted Berry curvatures at K/K ' valleys, and a giant conduction-band spin splitting of up to 316-375 meV in HfX2. Nitride members (ZrN2 and HfN2) achieve high room-temperature electron mobilities of ∼10 3 cm 2 V -1 s -1 , far exceeding most known 2D valleytronic materials. Mechanically, All nine monolayers feature a rare mechanical combination of a Poisson's ratio near 0.6 and low Young's moduli, affording excellent stretchability for deformable devices. Strain engineering enables continuous band-gap tuning while preserving direct-gap character, and vacuum-level alignment shows their heterostructures can realize Type I, II, and III band alignments. These properties position TM2 as a unique multifunctional 2D platform combining fast transport, intrinsic valleytronics, and mechanical compliance for flexible optoelectronic and valleytronic applications.

abstract: Although photodynamic therapy (PDT) has emerged as a promising treatment for unresectable cholangiocarcinoma, the hypoxic tumor microenvironment severely limits oxygen-dependent Type II photochemical processes, resulting in insufficient reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and compromised therapeutic outcomes. Therefore, developing Type I photosensitizers (PSs) with optimized excited-state dynamics and efficient hypoxia-tolerant ROS generation is critical for improving PDT efficacy under hypoxic conditions. Herein, we developed three hemicyanine-based Type I PSs (HCy1-3) and systematically investigated the relationship between molecular structure, TICT-mediated excited-state relaxation, and ROS generation behavior. By modulating the electron-donating capability of donor moieties, the TICT characteristics of the hemicyanine scaffold were precisely tuned, thereby regulating the competition between nonradiative decay and ROS-generating pathways. Among them, HCy3 exhibited enhanced excited-state utilization and the highest Type I ROS generation efficiency under both normoxic and hypoxic conditions. Furthermore, HCy3 efficiently accumulated in mitochondria and induced mitochondrial dysfunction, leading to superior photodynamic cytotoxicity against cholangiocarcinoma cells under hypoxia compared with the clinically used PS HiPorfin. The therapeutic potential of HCy3 was further validated in cholangiocarcinoma organoids. This study establishes a structure-photophysics-photochemistry correlation between TICT regulation and Type I ROS generation, providing a mechanistic strategy for designing high-performance hypoxia-tolerant PSs for PDT.

abstract: Predicting species persistence within ecological communities is a fundamental challenge for both empirical and theoretical ecology. Existing methods span from mechanistic models, whose parameters are difficult to estimate from data, to statistical tools whose context-specific parameters are less interpretable. Here we present a general framework, grounded in the statistical physics of complex systems, that integrates the key processes governing species survival into a single measurable quantity: the competitive balance. This metric quantifies the vulnerability of a focal species to competitive exclusion beyond what is captured by its abundance alone by incorporating the diversity of dispersal strategies and the structure of interspecific interactions within the community. Crucially, the competitive balance can be inferred from spatial abundance data, thus circumventing the need to estimate species traits or dispersal parameters. Our results reveal that greater heterogeneity in dispersal strategies reduces vulnerability to competitive exclusion for a given abundance. We validate the framework using tropical and temperate forest data and discuss how it can be applied to a range of different ecosystems, providing a systemic and interpretable tool for assessing a context-dependent species vulnerability that accounts for its interactions with the entire community.

abstract: Memristors that combine metal-oxide thin films with two-dimensional graphene electrodes hold immense promise for high-density, energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware. Here, we demonstrate a vertical memristor based on a single-crystalline rutile TiO₂ thin film (~150 nm) sandwiched between a chemical-vapor-deposited monolayer graphene bottom electrode and an Ag top electrode. The atomically flat graphene/TiO₂ interface yields exceptional resistive switching uniformity, ultralow leakage currents, and a high resistance ratio. The devices exhibit forming-free bipolar switching with an ultralow set voltage of +0.45 V and reset voltage of -0.35 V, a high ON/OFF resistance ratio exceeding 2 × 10⁵, and a read endurance beyond 10⁷ cycles without degradation. High-temperature retention measurements confirm stable resistance states for over 10⁵ s at 85 °C with an Arrhenius activation energy of 1.1 eV, and cycle-to-cycle and device-todevice variability in both high-and low-resistance states remains below 3.2% (n = 20 devices, 100 cycles each). By precisely controlling the compliance current, we achieve 64 distinct, linearly spaced conductance levels, enabling 6-bit-per-cell multilevel storage. Energy consumption per switching event is calculated as 87 fJ (E = V × I × τ = 0.45 V × 3.9 μA × 50 ns), positioning this platform among the most energy-efficient memristive devices reported. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM) reveals a uniform TiO₂ thin film morphology on graphene, and Xray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirms a Ti:O stoichiometry with 15% oxygen vacancy concentration. The high resistance state (~20 GΩ) is attributed to the atomically flat graphene/TiO₂ interface suppressing leakage, nanoconfinement of the switching volume, and a Schottky barrier at the Ag/TiO₂ interface (εᵣ ≈ 86). These metrics position the TiO₂ thin film/graphene memristor as a robust, scalable building block for next-generation in-memory computing and neuromorphic processors.

abstract: Collaborative robotic welding of dissimilar steel joints involves coupled decisions concerning task assignment, welding sequence, thermal interaction, energy consumption, and production time. Conventional distance-based allocation methods do not explicitly account for the fact that neighboring welding operations may modify the thermal state and mechanical response of subsequent operations. This study proposes a physics-coupled task-allocation framework in which collaborative welding robots are modelled as players of an α-potential game and the thermo-mechanical response is evaluated using a physics-informed neural-network (PINN) surrogate. The α-potential formulation represents the bounded discrepancy between individual utility changes and changes in a common potential function resulting from non-additive thermal interactions. A sufficient equilibrium result is established: under a finite feasible strategy space, a global maximizer of the α-potential is an α-Nash equilibrium. Log-linear learning is employed as a stochastic strategy-update mechanism, while finite-time convergence results from the potential-game literature are invoked only for the exact-potential case and under their stated assumptions. The PINN incorporates the transient heat-conduction and mechanical-equilibrium equations into its training objective and provides a reduced-cost approximation of repeated thermo-mechanical evaluations. In the computational study, the proposed framework reduced normalized makespan and energy consumption relative to the distance-driven allocation strategy while simultaneously accounting for residual stress and carbon redistribution. The results indicate that coupling physical response with distributed task allocation can improve the quality of multi-robot welding decisions. The reported numerical values are computational predictions and should be independently validated experimentally before being generalized to industrial welding applications.

abstract: We investigate the structure of quantum and classical correlations in the generalized off-diagonal Gamma spin chain, focusing on the interplay between interaction range and anisotropy across an interaction-driven quantum phase transition. By combining concurrence, quantum discord, Fermionic Correlation Participation (FCP), entanglement entropy, and central-charge scaling, we develop a unified multiscale characterization that connects two-site correlations, collective fermionic organization, and universal critical behavior. A central finding is the existence of a finite separation between the entanglement-vanishing point and the quantum critical point throughout the XY regime (0 < δ < 1), which collapses continuously as the system approaches the Ising limit. These results demonstrate that bipartite entanglement suppression and criticality are not generically equivalent in anisotropic long-range systems. Anisotropy progressively aligns the entanglement structure with the quantum critical point; however, in weakly anisotropic regimes the system remains in a critical phase with divergent correlations even after pairwise entanglement has vanished. Quantum discord, FCP, and entanglement entropy scaling collectively show that this suppression reflects a redistribution and geometric reorganization of correlations rather than their absence. Our results clarify the nontrivial relationship between entanglement, correlation geometry, and criticality in extended quantum systems, and have direct implications for engineered quantum spin systems with tunable anisotropic exchange couplings.

abstract: Forecasting Uniaxial Compressive Strength (UCS) across geologically varied landscapes poses difficulties, since data-centric models developed on localized datasets often falter when applied to unfamiliar geological areas. This research assesses the cross-geological applicability of UCS predictions via a Leave-One-Country-Out methodology across six nations and 397 rock specimens, contrasting solely data-driven models with a physics-based residual technique among four foundational modules. Zero-shot outcomes indicate a significant compromise: Direct ML attained a slightly reduced initial RMSE (58.5 MPa) compared to Physics-Residual (60.2 MPa), however this benefit concealed significant instability, since single-sample calibration unexpectedly heightened error. Physics anchoring converted extrapolation inaccuracies into systematic, interpretable biases grounded on physical principles. We provide a Calibratability Index (CI) that measures the proportion of the domain gap bridged using five calibration samples; Physics-Residual attained a CI of 0.511 compared to 0.364 for Direct ML. Diversity-oriented active sampling using non-invasive Vp and density assessments decreased RMSE to 37.7 MPa at k = 3 and 36.8 MPa at k = 5, indicating a 17% enhancement compared to random sampling. The Wilcoxon tests validated significance (p < 10⁻⁸) with moderate effect sizes (Cohen's d = − 0.53 to − 0.58). Geological Bias Correction multipliers varied from 0.36 in Turkey to 5.60 in South Africa, indicating that cross-domain error is organized and geologically significant. Feature engineering yielded no enhancement compared to the original predictors, affirming the notion of parsimony for datasets with few samples. The methodology is independent of models and facilitates a decrease of over 90% in destructive testing needs, creating an effective process for dependable UCS forecasting in new geological contexts.

abstract: Altermagnets simultaneously possess momentum-dependent nonrelativistic spin splitting and zero net magnetization (1-6). Their defining crystalline symmetry connects opposite-spin sublattices in real space and imposes alternating spin polarization on the symmetry-related electronic states in momentum space (1-3). Identifying such an order and its associated spin response therefore calls for atomic-scale spin-sensitive measurements in both real and momentum space, an experimental milestone yet to be achieved. Here we show that the helical edge modes of the higher-order topological insulator α-Bi<sub>4</sub>Br<sub>4</sub> can serve as a spin-selective scanning tunnelling microscopy probe of the two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetic order in the surface layer of KV<sub>2</sub>Se<sub>2</sub>O. Atomically registered mapping reveals the spatial relationship between the two V sublattices and a density-wave lattice modulation, as well as real-space patterns consistent with the checkerboard antiferromagnetic order. Field-dependent spectroscopy further finds opposite energy shifts of the unidirectional quasiparticle excitations extending along two orthogonal crystal axes and a predominantly out-of-plane magnetic response. In momentum space, spin-sensitive quasiparticle interference imaging reveals a bias-reversing d-wave anisotropy between the symmetry-paired X and Y valleys. These results provide converging evidence for two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetism on the surface of KV<sub>2</sub>Se<sub>2</sub>O and demonstrate helical-edge-mode tunnelling as a route for atomic-scale spin sensing in quantum materials.

abstract: Background. The graviton, the hypothetical quantum of gravity, is often invoked in speculation about future artificial intelligence (AI) and immersive virtual worlds, yet a single graviton is widely regarded as undetectable and its only quantified observable property is an upper bound on its mass. Whether massive-graviton physics could even be represented inside the computational systems that run virtual worlds and AI has not been tested. Methods. Two computational experiments with known truth were run. Experiment 1 asks whether the Yukawa correction implied by a graviton at the current 90% credibility bound (m g ≤ 2.42 × 10 −23 eV/c 2 ) is representable in six floating-point formats, using a 60-digit reference, a naive in-format evaluation, and a velocity-Verlet orbit integrator of the kind used in physics engines. Experiment 2 injects the massive-graviton dispersion phase into noise-free inspiral waveforms and measures, for each format, the ratio between the time-and-phase-aligned dispersion residual and the rounding error, and the test AUC of a neural-network discriminator trained on rounded inputs (90 training runs). Results. The correction is unrepresentable at every virtual-world scale: it first becomes storable in float64 at 5.4 × 10 8 m and in float32 at 1.25 × 10 13 m (about 84 AU). Naive in-format evaluation manufactures phantom corrections up to 9 × 10 16 times the true value, and a float32 orbit at 1 AU deviates by 834 km where the true effect is 8 m. In AI formats the opposite holds: at the bound every format, including 8-bit FP8, preserves the residual (representational SNR 9.7 to 2 × 10 7 ), with representational floors 3 to 4,500 times below the bound for formats from FP8 to float32; classifier accuracy did not degrade with precision. Conclusions. Precision is the binding constraint for virtual-world engines but not for AI, where noise and learnability bind first. Any claim that a graviton-scale effect appears in a simulated world should be accompanied by an explicit representability check.

abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are emerging as the backbone for latent world models in robotics and autonomous driving, yet injecting domain knowledge (physics, kinematics, geometry) into these models consistently degrades performance—with no theoretical explanation. We resolve this paradox by proving, through six theorems, that the isotropic maximum-entropy embedding is symmetry-stable under sequential prediction losses—no first-order incentive exists to rotate away from it under any Lipschitz, Euclidean-invariant prediction objective—and by validating across a phased empirical protocol that no non-Gaussian alternative outperforms it in practice. This yields a world-model design principle with a provable guarantee: encoder maximum-entropy, predictor dynamics, decoder physics—and explains why prior physics-informed JEPAs failed: they constrained the encoder, where constraints provably destroy the entropy guarantee, instead of the decoder, where they are provably benign. We validate this principle across two domains and two encoder mechanisms through a phased protocol covering measurement artifacts (Proposition 1: the N/K ≥ 5 reliability threshold), powered statistical testing (110 seeded ablation runs across autonomous driving and bimanual robotic manipulation, under both a SIGReg-regularized encoder and a marginal-only VAE-KL encoder—the encoder family of classical world models—with paired Wilcoxon significance and joint Holm correction in every domain×mechanism combination), and a budget replication demonstrating that the encoder-physics violation deepens with training. Phase 3 additionally characterizes an entropy–utility frontier on low-intrinsic-dimension robotics data, discovering that per-dimension variance matching alone produces correlated collapse—a failure mode invisible on high-dimensional data—and that optimization budget, not regularization weight, is the binding entropy constraint. We further show this failure generalizes: a marginal-only VAE-KL encoder collapses identically on the same data, and we introduce a posterior signal-fraction diagnostic revealing that such collapse can hide beneath the encoder’s own sampling-noise floor, invisible to marginal diagnostics. To test whether the placement rule matters beyond representation quality, we further probe its consequence for downstream control: a latent cross-entropy-method (CEM) planner built on the trained Phase 3 models consistently outperforms real-action replay on model-internal cost across ablation conditions and both encoder mechanisms—an impossible result for genuine planning, since replaying the true actions is itself the ground-truth solution. A model-exploitation diagnostic traces this to the planner discovering action sequences roughly a quarter of the action range away from the true trajectory while still lowering the learned decoder’s cost, uniformly regardless of physics placement and encoder choice. We report this transparently as a boundary condition on the practical claim: offline latent planning against a learned decoder is not, by itself, sufficient evidence that a representation supports downstream control, and we identify closed-loop, simulator-verified execution as the necessary next test. The result is the first formal, cross-domain-validated blueprint for physics-informed world models: place physics where the theorem says it is safe, never where intuition suggests—together with a concrete, reproducible cautionary result on how easily offline latent planning can be mistaken for evidence of control competence.

abstract:
Rationale

The molecular anion WF5 - constitutes an isobaric interference for the mass spectrometric detection of the HfF5 - anion. The latter is expected to form an extremely sensitive way of detecting the radionuclide 182Hf at natural levels using, for example, accelerator mass spectrometry.

Methods

Photoinduced detachment of WF5 - molecular anions was studied in the Double ElectroStatic Ion Ring ExpEriment (DESIREE), with the ring cooled to cryogenic temperatures (~13 K). Photon energies from 2.5 to 4.5 eV were applied using an OPO laser system for excitation. This energy range covers the threshold for the removal of an electron from that anion species.

Results

Photoinduced reactions were observed which indicate the existence of an energy threshold for WF5 - anions above which the neutralization yield increases strongly. In that range, the data of the neutral signal could be fitted by a linear function of photon energy E, yielding a threshold energy Eth = 3.13 ± 0.01 eV. This result constitutes a substantial improvement both in the range and the resolution of the photon energy as compared to previous data and provides now a rather precise value for that threshold.

Conclusions

This knowledge is required for any attempts to suppress WF5 - anions by photodetachment in the ultrasensitive detection of the very rare radioisotope 182Hf using the 182HfF5 - analyte anion; for that, the 182WF5 - anion would be a stable isobaric mass interference for analyses by accelerator mass spectrometry. The radionuclide 182Hf is considered of great interest in various astrophysical environments such as nucleosynthetic processes.

abstract: The present review critically examines the application of statistical physics to the development and interpretation of adsorption isotherm models, with particular emphasis on systems relevant to wastewater treatment. Rather than describing adsorption solely through empirical uptake curves, statistical physics provides a molecular-level framework that connects equilibrium adsorption data to descriptors of steric effects, energetic heterogeneity, and thermodynamic behavior. The models reviewed encompass monolayer, multilayer, single-solute, competitive, binary, ternary, and quaternary adsorption configurations. More than fifteen statistical-physics-based formulations are discussed, with particular emphasis on their mathematical expressions and the physicochemical significance of their fitted parameters. Thermodynamic quantities, including adsorption entropy, free enthalpy, internal energy, and adsorption-energy distributions, are considered as complementary tools for improving the mechanistic interpretation of adsorption processes. The review further examines the application of these models to pollutants such as dyes, pharmaceuticals, and heavy metals at adsorbent interfaces. In contrast to classical isotherm equations such as the Langmuir and Freundlich equations, statistical physics models provide access to molecular descriptors, including the aggregation number (n), receptor-site density (NM), adsorption energy, and layer-formation tendency, thereby offering deeper insight into adsorption mechanisms. Models derived from the grand canonical partition function can further account for adsorbate orientation, anchoring modes, interaction types, physisorption or chemisorption, and the number of molecules retained per adsorption site. In addition, they enable the macroscopic evaluation of adsorption through internal energy, entropy, and Gibbs free energy. Overall, this review highlights the potential of statistical physics as a powerful framework for bridging macroscopic adsorption measurements with molecular-level mechanisms and for providing a more comprehensive interpretation of pollutant removal at adsorbent interfaces.

abstract: Higgs inflation, identifying the Standard Model Higgs boson as the inflaton, causes a unitarity issue during the preheating epoch after inflation in its simplest form, calling for a UV completion. Higgs-R 2 inflation serves as a natural candidate for the UV completion of Higgs inflation, providing a consistent framework to describe the inflationary dynamics till the end of the reheating. Higgs-R 2 inflation contains a new scalar degree of freedom, the scalaron, which unitarizes the theory in the same way that the Higgs boson unitarizes the longitudinal electroweak gauge boson scatterings in the Standard Model. In this short review, we will summarize the physics of Higgs-R 2 inflation. A particular emphasis is put on its particle physics aspects, such as the unitarity structure, frame-independence, and the renormalization group evolution.Unitarity violation of Higgs inflationHiggs inflation identifies the unique elementary scalar field in the SM, the Higgs boson, as the inflaton, and is a simple possibility to explore. However, the simplest version of Higgs inflation, in which the Higgs boson has a non-minimal coupling, causes a unitarity issue during the preheating epoch. We therefore need a UV completion of Higgs inflation, and this motivates to consider Higgs-R 2 inflation.

abstract: We present the first study of Leggett-Garg inequality (LGI) violation in polarized muon spin precession. We formulate a procedure to reconstruct temporal correlators of the longitudinal muon polarization from measured time-dependent muon decay spectra and apply it to publicly available Fermilab Muondata corresponding to approximatelybillion muon decays. Using a simplified model of the detector acceptance and efficiency, the LGI is found to be violated with a single-bin significance of, while combining neighboring bins further increases the significance. While our analysis is limited by systematic uncertainties associated with the detector modeling, a dedicated experimental analysis could reduce these uncertainties toward the statistical level,, potentially enabling one of the most precise measurements of temporal quantum correlations.

abstract: Driven by their unique lattice structure, Kagome systems exhibit fascinating properties, prominent among which is the emergence of flat bands. Here we report a scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy study on the lateral finite-size effect of flat-band spectral weight in the Kagome metal CoSn. We identify two distinct cleaved surfaces: Co3Sn and Sn2. On the Co3Sn surface, we detect two electronic peaks located at 70 and 250 mV below the Fermi level, which correspond to the flat bands originating from Codorbitals. Notably, the flat-band intensity exhibits a strong dependence on the lateral size of the Kagome islands. The flat bands start to emerge in Co3Sn islands consisting of only a half-unit-wide Kagome chain. As the island width increases, the flat-band intensity rises exponentially and reaches saturation when the island width reaches four-unit cells or larger. By analyzing the size-dependent intensity data, we extract the characteristic length scale for this saturation behavior. Furthermore, on the large Co3Sn surface, we observe a broad and non-dispersive wavevector with a periodicity close to √3×√3 in the Fourier-transformed differential conductance maps. These results not only reveal the novel lateral finite-size effect of flat-band spectral weight at the atomic scale, but also pave the way for a deeper understanding of the complex electronic structures in Kagome materials.

abstract: Security assessment requires repeated alternating current optimal power flow (AC OPF) solutions under changing injections and line outages. We propose a topology conditioned physics informed graph Fourier neural operator (GFNO PINO) that predicts voltage phasors and dispatch from network and operating data. Chebyshev filters adapt to each topology without eigenvector alignment. Output transformations enforce voltage and generation bounds and the reference angle; power balance, thermal limits, and angle differences remain soft constraints. Supervised initialization is followed by physics fine tuning with adaptive loss balancing. A topology disjoint benchmark covers four IEEE systems from 30 to 300 buses, three unseen outage topologies per system, and five training seeds. Physics fine tuning reduces mean sample maximum balance mismatch by 63.4--89.3\% relative to the data only GFNO\@. However, mismatch remains 0.281--5.959 p.u., with 0\% feasibility at the $10^{-3}$ p.u.\ threshold and no consistent advantage over topology blind or spatial models. CUDA inference medians are 8.3--138.1 times lower than stored IPOPT CPU solve medians, excluding verification and restoration. The model therefore requires independent feasibility checks and correction before operational use.

abstract: For more than two millennia, Archimedean screws have been used for water pumping and, more recently, as turbines in hydroelectric power stations[1]. Their helical-blade structure, essential to their function, is also found in chiral molecules and nanostructures, where injected electric current has been proposed to generate torque-mediated rotation[2,3]. Here, we present a torque-driven molecular machine with a rotor actuated by electric current and conductance enhanced by its rotation. Suspending a helicene molecule between two electrode tips, we show that an applied voltage induces cyclic molecular motion with 100% directional preference that can be inverted by the voltage's polarity. Above a voltage threshold, the current through the rotating molecule is significantly enhanced, and the enhancement onset is tuned by stretching or compressing the helical molecule. Such effects were absent in previous helical molecular junctions, likely due to structural and operational differences[4-6]. Calculations show that molecular rotation by current-induced forces explains both the observed cyclic motion and current enhancement. This mechanism predicts a transition from stepwise to continuous rotation at a threshold voltage, yielding a current increase as rotation allows adopting highly conducting configurations not accessible at rest. Our work introduces a prototype for a new class of torque-driven molecular machines with perfect rotor unidirectionality and significant current modulation.

abstract:
Objective

To develop and evaluate a physics-informed machine-learning framework for rapid organ-dose estimation in fluoroscopically guided interventional procedures without requiring patient-specific imaging. Approach: We used 385 adult radiation dose structured reports from three procedure types-bilateral carotid angiography, percutaneous biliary drainage, and liver chemoembolization-comprising more than 50,000 irradiation events. A body-size-matched computational phantom was selected using patient sex, height, and weight. RDSR-derived beam parameters and engineered descriptors of beam-organ geometry and attenuation were used to train organ-specific XGBoost models for localized organs and a multi-output multilayer perceptron model for four distributed tissues. Monte Carlo-derived dose coefficients from NCIRF3 were used as target values. Main results: In the held-out test set of 12,683 irradiation events, 49.4% and 84.8% of XGBoost-based localized-organ estimates were within ±5% and ±20% of the Monte Carlo-derived values, respectively. The corresponding proportions were 88.2% and 98.0% for the distributed-tissue estimates and 87.6% and 98.3% for detriment-weighted dose. The median relative prediction error across organs and tissues was 0.37% (interquartile range, -3.68% to 4.99%). A reliability score was developed to support uncertainty-aware interpretation. The framework required approximately 0.3 s per irradiation event, corresponding to an approximately 290-fold acceleration relative to conventional Monte Carlo simulation under the benchmark conditions. Significance: The proposed image-free framework enables rapid organ-dose estimation when patient imaging is unavailable and may support large retrospective epidemiological studies and uncertainty-aware dose monitoring. Because development and validation were limited to three procedure types and relied on reconstructed phantom-beam geometry, external validation is required before application to other procedures or high-precision individual clinical decisions.

abstract: Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) offers a powerful means of combining physical knowledge with data-driven models, potentially improving prediction accuracy, robustness, and interpretability. However, its application to condition monitoring and predictive maintenance remains limited. This study investigates a hybrid PIML framework for forecasting future vibration states from current measurements, addressing three key challenges in industrial applications: limited training data, incomplete knowledge of the underlying physics, and the absence of failure examples. The proposed framework combines approximate physical and physics-based surrogate models with Bayesian data-driven parameter correction during operation. A neural operator then forecasts vibration states in the model-parameter space, efficiently integrating physical knowledge and observed data. The approach is evaluated using vibration data from accelerated lifetime tests of self-lubricated hydrodynamic journal bearings. Distinct training and test datasets with no overlapping signals are used to ensure rigorous evaluation. The proposed framework is compared experimentally with conventional physics-informed methods and recent neural network architectures. It achieves forecasting errors below 25% for horizons exceeding 8 hours, while accurately capturing nonlinear vibration dynamics from limited data. It consistently outperforms the reference models and generalizes to operating conditions not represented in the training data. The generic architecture can be applied to systems with unavailable, incomplete, or difficult-to-reconstruct physical descriptions, demonstrating the potential of hybrid PIML for predictive maintenance and condition monitoring of complex engineering systems.

abstract: In this paper, a combined statistical physics and computational modeling framework was used to elucidate the molecular mechanism of olfaction through a putative adsorption process in which coumarin compounds bind to the mouse olfactory receptors Olfr924, Olfr285, and Olfr1016. Adsorption isotherms derived from experimental data were analyzed using both monolayer and double-layer statistical physics models, enabling the quantitative determination of steric and energetic parameters governing odorant-receptor interactions. The steric analysis reveals diverse anchoring behaviors, with coumarin molecules adopting both parallel and non-parallel orientations relative to receptor binding sites, indicative of mixed adsorption configurations. The estimated adsorption energies, ranging from 13.563 to 33.872 kJ/mol, suggest that the coumarin compounds are physically adsorbed onto the receptors, offering insight into the steric and energetic heterogeneity of the receptor. Moreover, the application of statistical physics modeling enabled a detailed steric characterization of the receptor surface through binding site size distributions (BSDs) and an energetic characterization via adsorption energy distributions (AEDs). To complement microscopic analysis, a macroscopic thermodynamic study was also performed, providing further insight into the adsorption behavior of coumarin compounds on the olfactory receptors. To further validate and complement these findings, molecular docking simulations were performed to identify interaction types and binding modes between coumarin ligands and olfactory receptors. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating statistical physics modeling with molecular docking to elucidate mechanisms of olfactory perception at both microscopic and macroscopic scales. The three complexes formed between coumarin and the olfactory receptor sites (Olfr285, Olfr924, and Olfr1016) have been analyzed using molecular docking simulations, molecular dynamics simulations, and free binding energies calculated using the molecular mechanics-Poisson-Boltzmann surface (MM-PBSA) and molecular mechanics-generalized Born surface (MM-GBSA) methods.

abstract: The study of twisted two-dimensional (2D) materials, in which twisting layers create moiré superlattices, has created opportunities for investigating topological phases and strongly correlated physics. The broader potential of a seemingly infinite set of twistable 2D materials remains largely unexplored. Here, we define "theoretically twistable materials" as single- or multilayer structures that allow for the construction of simple continuum models of their moiré structures. Our high-throughput algorithm systematically searches for theoretically twistable semimetals and insulators based on the Topological 2D Materials Database(2D-TQCDB). By analyzing key electronic properties, we identify thousands of candidate materials, propose representative twistable materials, and provide examples of crystal growth and exfoliation for several of them. Our results provide a resource for future experimental and theoretical studies of moiré systems.

abstract:
Objective

Conventional photoacoustic tomography (PAT) reconstruction algorithms often suffer from performance degradation under complex media and non-ideal detection conditions. To tackle these limitations, we propose a novel reconstruction method based on physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). Approach: The network model is optimized with constraints from observational data, wave equation, and initial conditions, to reconstruct the spatial distribution of initial acoustic pressure. The PINN framework further incorporates time reversal method to improve computational efficiency. Main results: Comprehensive PAT simulations demonstrate that the PINN achieves superior reconstruction quality compared with conventional algorithms. The PINN exhibits favorable adaptivity to both heterogeneous and lossy media, and strong robustness against noisy measurements, sparse sensor layouts and limited-view detection geometries. Significance: The PINN integrates the physical interpretability and the powerful capability of neural networks to represent continuous acoustic pressure fields. It eliminates the requirement for training datasets, offering broad application potential for PAT.

abstract: Biological clocks reset and entrain to external cues in a phase-dependent manner. The infinitesimal phase response curve (iPRC) provides the local dynamical rule underlying this process by quantifying how an input changes the instantaneous phase velocity of an oscillator. Inferring iPRCs would make it possible to predict how rhythms respond to new stimulus timings and durations, but existing approaches often require detailed mechanistic models, long perturbation recordings, or specialized population-level resetting experiments. Here we introduce Physics-informed neural network for iPRC inference (PINN-iPRC), a physics-informed neural network framework for inferring iPRCs from standard finite-pulse stimulus-response recordings. PINN-iPRC represents the unknown iPRC as a neural network and embeds the phase equation into the loss function, identifying the iPRC that leads to the observed transient phase trajectory under the known stimulus. In synthetic oscillators, PINN-iPRC accurately recovered iPRCs from finite-pulse recordings, including complex ones that are difficult to capture with simpler parametric reconstructions. Applied to existing experimental Arabidopsis circadian recordings, PINN-iPRC recovered iPRCs comparable to those obtained from specialized population-level resetting experiments, while requiring only conventional stimulus-response trajectories. The inferred iPRCs were further used to predict finite-duration PRCs and circadian peak phases across photoperiods. In particular, the predicted near-invariance of the prr7 peak phase across 8-16 h of darkness was consistent with independently published prr7-11 root recordings. These results support PINN-iPRC as a practical physics-informed approach for extracting interpretable phase-sensitivity functions from routine biological oscillator recordings, with potential applications in experimental design, entrainment prediction, and chronotherapeutic or pharmacological schedule optimization.

The Berry curvature andvalley-resolved topological invariants vary systematically with the applied electric field (upto 1.0 eV/nm) for the twist angles (θ < 2◦), arising from the electronic reconstructionswhile preserving the time reversal symmetry. However, the twist angle governs the valleyband topology leading to the valley based topological phase transition in the moir´eheterostructure. The tuning of valley topological phases with electric field and twist anglescarries potential in valleytronics and nanoelectronics.

abstract: Accurate, real-time knowledge of the forces generated at each tire contact patch is central to electronic stability control, traction control, and learning-based driver-assistance functions in electric vehicles (EVs). Conventional model-based observers assume a single friction coefficient and degrade under the transient, spatially varying friction conditions typical of real roads, while purely data-driven estimators can output forces that violate the friction-ellipse constraint, undermining safety-critical decisions. This paper proposes a physics-informed multimodal learning framework that fuses forward-facing camera imagery with in-vehicle chassis-sensor streams to predict per-wheel longitudinal and lateral tire forces and quantify a grip-utilization ratio for early loss-of-traction warning. A vision branch, calibrated to the reported accuracy of convolutional road-surface classifiers trained on the public Road Surface Classification Dataset (RSCD), supplies a road-friction class posterior; a chassis branch summarizes a 0.8 s sliding window of inertial, wheel-speed, steering and powertrain signals via a time-delay neural network encoding; the two modalities are combined through a lightweight cross-modal feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) fusion gate. Training combines a data-fidelity loss with physics-informed soft constraints derived from a quasi-static load-transfer model and the Pacejka Magic-Formula friction ellipse. Using a hybrid dataset of 9,000 samples from a validated four-wheel vehicle-dynamics simulator spanning five friction classes, from dry asphalt to ice, and five manoeuvres, the proposed model reduces wheel-force RMSE by 22–42 percent relative to chassis-only and naive multimodal baselines on wet, snow-covered and icy surfaces, lowers the deployable friction-ellipse violation rate to 13.5 percent, and improves accuracy under distribution shift to unseen low-friction conditions relative to a non-physics-informed ablation. The complete model contains only 4,200 parameters and executes in under one millisecond per inference, supporting real-time deployment on embedded control units. These results indicate that lightweight cross-modal fusion combined with physics-informed regularization is a practical route to safer, more generalizable grip-utilization estimation in production EVs.

abstract: Wire Electrical Discharge Machining (WEDM) is an important non-conventional machining technique used in the production of precision components with complex geometry. However, corner error is still a major problem in WEDM process due to wire lag, thermal effects, and discharge mechanism. In this paper, a new Physics-Informed Neural Network with Adaptive Path Compensation (PINN-APC) method is proposed to intelligently predict and compensate the corner errors in WEDM process. The physics-informed constraint based on wire deflection mechanics and thermal discharge phenomenon is combined with data-driven neural network for the intelligent prediction and compensation of corner errors. Taguchi L27 design experiments are performed on Stainless Steel 202 material to validate the proposed model. Comparing analysis proves that the proposed PINN-APC model performs much better in corner error prediction (R2=0.96, RMSE=4200 μm2) than the conventional Taguchi additive models (R2=0.72), Response Surface Methodology (R2=0.87) and conventional Artificial Neural Network (R2=0.85). Also, adaptive path compensation can reduce the corner error in 31% when compared with conventional machining process without path compensation. Ablation studies show that physics-informed constraint contributes 6.7% improvement in prediction performance over pure data-driven model.

abstract: Chirality has emerged as a new mechanism for inducing spin and Berry-curvature phenomena in quantum materials and molecular chemistry<sup>1-7</sup>. Collinear antiferromagnets (AFMs) are promising for spintronics and topological magnetism, yet realizing large Berry curvature and spin-split bands remains challenging<sup>8,9</sup>. Here we report a chiral-superlattice route to spin-split topological phenomena from collinear antiferromagnetism. We study the collinear AFM UOTe, in which we show a spontaneous chiral superlattice arising from frozen chiral phonons at a finite wave vector. Without the superlattice, the pristine collinear AFM in UOTe has neither Berry curvature nor spin-split bands. When electrons move through the chiral superlattice, their orbital Bloch wavefunction and quantum geometry are modulated by the strong chiral superlattice potential, generating large Berry curvature, which we detect by the nonlinear Hall effect. At 150 K, the chiral-superlattice-induced Berry curvature couples to the collinear AFM order, leading to an anomalous Hall angle of about 0.14 abruptly near the Néel temperature T<sub>N</sub> which is among the largest in bulk magnets. Moreover, our spin Hanle precession measurement shows that the chiral superlattice also generates spin-polarized current from the collinear AFM, a long-standing goal in spintronics. We shed light on the supermodulation formation mechanism based on chemical ion size and physical interlayer-intralayer energy competitions, which we use to propose a design principle to discover similar bond-mismatch superlattices, providing a chiral superlattice pathway through real-space engineering of quantum geometry<sup>10,11</sup>.

abstract: Controlling hierarchical organization across multiple length scales is a central challenge in materials science. Microspherical architectures offer powerful platforms for addressing this challenge because their confined geometry enables the integration of nanoscale interfaces, internal porosity, and structural hierarchy within a single functional unit. These features have driven extensive exploration of microspheres for applications in biomedicine, catalysis, photonics, and energy systems. However, the mechanistic connections between microsphere formation pathways and emergent functionality remain fragmented, limiting predictive materials design. Here, we present a unified perspective on morphology-controlled microspheres by integrating thermodynamic principles, kinetic processes, and hierarchical materials design. We examine key formation mechanisms, including nucleation, growth dynamics, phase separation, Ostwald ripening, and interfacial energy regulation, and analyze how major fabrication strategies such as sol-gel processing, hydrothermal synthesis, spray assembly, emulsification, and co-precipitation govern nanoscale organization and structural evolution. By linking formation mechanisms with functional outcomes, this Review establishes general design principles and highlights emerging opportunities for predictive nanoarchitectonic engineering of microsphere-based functional materials.

abstract: Coastal aquifer responses to tides can be simulated using coupled groundwater flow and solute transport models, but repeated numerical simulations are computationally costly. We developed a Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) surrogate for an idealized two-dimensional coastal aquifer simulated with SUTRA. The model maps tidal amplitude and landward hydraulic head to transient pressure head and concentration fields. Supervised, physics-regularized, and physics-only training strategies were compared, and the supervised model was evaluated at higher tidal amplitudes using few shot adaptation. On test simulations within source-range, the supervised model achieved pooled RMSEs of 5.87×10−3 m for pressure head and 5.75×10−4 for concentration. Adding continuous physics constraints did not improve agreement with the numerical reference, and lower physics residuals did not necessarily correspond to smaller field errors. Prediction accuracy decreased outside the source range, whereas adaptation with two higher-amplitude simulations reduced pressure-head and concentration RMSEs by 36.8% and 68.5%, respectively. The surrogate reconstructed a complete 72-h response in approximately 0.018 s, compared with approximately 15 s for the numerical simulation. These results demonstrate the potential of DeepONet as a computationally efficient surrogate for tide-driven coastal aquifer simulations while showing the dependence of physics-based regularization and adaptation on training data and forcing-space coverage.

abstract: Two-photon absorption (TPA) combined with thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) molecular systems hold great promise for organic optoelectronics and bioimaging due to their high electroluminescence efficiency and nonlinear optical properties. However, current TPA-TADF emitters suffer from limited two-photon absorption cross sections and low photoluminescence efficiency. Herein, we systematically investigate the photophysical properties of experimentally reported molecules (2PhCzTPN, 2TPATPN, TPCzTPA, TPCz1NP, and TPCz2NP) in toluene based on first-principles calculations combined with the thermal vibration correlation function (TVCF) method. Furthermore, a novel near-infrared TPA-TADF molecule (TPCz2NP-2CN) is theoretically designed through an acceptor fusion strategy, providing insights into the underlying mechanisms of acceptor fusion-mediated regulation of two-photon absorption and delayed fluorescence. Our findings reveal the influence of acceptor modulation on the photophysical properties of TPA-TADF molecules and offer a rational molecular design strategy for the development of high-performance TPA-TADF materials featuring enhanced emission efficiency and two-photon absorption performance.

abstract: Data-driven channel models often require extensive simulation data and capture only limited statistics of the underlying physical process. To address these limitations in diffusion-based particle signaling, we build upon physics-informed machine learning to develop a framework that fuses sparse channel measurements with governing diffusion-reaction laws. This work explores physics-informed operator learning for particle-based communication channels, aiming to bridge mechanistic PDE modeling and data-driven surrogates in this domain. Our method employs a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) to predict the spatiotemporal particle concentration field and generalizes across channel configurations with reduced dependence on explicit geometric parameterization. We further extend the framework to model quorum sensing between bacterial colonies, capturing autoinducer dynamics. Compared with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and Deep Operator Networks (DeepONets), PINO achieves high accuracy and significant computational efficiency: on the nanomachine channel, PINO reduces the relative $\bf{ {\ell}_{2}}$ error from 99.3% to 9.2%; on the quorum sensing model, PINO improves $\bf {R}^{{2}}$ from 0.808 (DeepONet) to 0.999, while multi-resolution inference yields 4-5 $\times $ speed-ups on coarse grids. These results highlight physics-informed operator learning as a promising method for particle-based communication networks.

abstract: The current trend in quantum technologies is deeply rooted in quantum computation, with Majorana fermions and their topological protection believed to play a central role. In this context, topological superconductors (TSCs) offer a promising arena for investigating Majorana modes in the context of topological quantum computation. In dimension d > 1, the spatial localization profile of the topological Majorana modes can be tuned in higher-order TSC extending beyond the realm of conventional first-order topological superconductor (FOTSC). In this review, we systematically survey the zoo of topological superconductivity, ranging from FOTSCs to third-order topological superconductors (TOTSCs), wherein the spatial dimensionality of Majorana zero modes (MZMs) is progressively reduced. We show that periodic driving protocols enable the Floquet engineering of all the above phases, even when the corresponding undriven systems are topologically trivial. We further investigate various driving schemes and the interplay among spinorbit coupling, magnetic fields, magnetic impurities, and symmetry-breaking mass terms to design Floquet higher-order topological superconducting (FHOTSC) phases, which are characterized by appropriate topological invariants. We extensively discuss the development of invariants that are able to distinguish between regular MZMs and anomalous Majorana π-modes, appearing at two distinct energies, where the latter does not exhibit any static analog.

abstract: Altermagnetism defies conventional classifications of collinear magnetic phases, combining compensated magnetization with momentum-dependent, nonrelativistic spin splitting. While altermagnetic band splitting has been established in three-dimensional compounds such as MnTe and CrSb, layered altermagnets remain far less explored spectroscopically. Here, combining termination-resolved micro-ARPES, fine photon-energy mapping, spin-ARPES, and density functional theory, we map the three-dimensional fermiology of the layered g-wave altermagnet CoNb4Se8 , obtained by ordered Co intercalation of 2H- NbSe2 . We resolve the spin-split branches of the altermagnetic pairs directly in the raw photoemission spectra and, with spin-ARPES at these experimentally identified momenta, show the reversal of the spin polarization at opposite momenta and between two regions of the sample, consistent with opposite time-reversal domains, and its absence along the symmetry-protected nodal Γ -K direction. We further report a weak low-temperature anomaly near T<sub>0</sub> ≈ 50-60 K, detected by magnetometry, temperature-dependent micro-ARPES, and ultrafast reflectivity, whose microscopic origin remains open. These results provide a momentum-resolved benchmark of the electronic structure of a layered altermagnet.

abstract: Accurate short-term photovoltaic power forecasting is essential for grid scheduling, reserve allocation, and the reliable integration of renewable energy into power systems. However, many data-driven forecasting models are trained and evaluated at a single photovoltaic plant, which limits their transferability to plants operating under different climatic, geographic, and engineering conditions. This study evaluated a cross-site physics-informed transfer-learning framework for one-hour-ahead photovoltaic power forecasting across six heterogeneous solar plants. The framework integrated a hybrid temporal model with plant-level static descriptors and a physics-based power prior derived from irradiance, module temperature, installed capacity, and grid export limits. The primary experiment used six leave-one-site-out target folds: for each held-out target plant, the other five plants were pooled as the source domain for pretraining. A separate, ordered single-source-to-single-target analysis (30 routes) was used solely to examine pairwise source-target distances and route-dependent transfer behavior. Source-domain and target-domain validation data were kept separate during checkpoint selection. Compared with direct transfer and conventional fine-tuning in the primary held-out-target analysis, the full physics-informed transfer model reduced forecasting error across the evaluated target sites. The study provides a structured framework for cross-site photovoltaic forecasting under heterogeneous environmental and operational conditions. Because inferential comparisons were based on six held-out target sites, they were interpreted as site-level evidence rather than evidence of broad population-level statistical generalizability.

abstract: Large-strain piezoresistive sensors are critical for wearables and soft robotics. Still, conventional hyperelastic materials suffer from a trade-off between sensitivity, linearity, and strain range due to their intrinsic nonlinear electromechanical response. Here, we introduce a new class of aperiodic electromechanical metamaterials, where spatially graded carbon nanotube (CNT)-polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composites are architected into hierarchical networks via direct ink writing (DIW) of adjacent cells with varying filler concentrations. The resulting interdependence among cells gives rise to emergent electromechanical responses that are governed by architectural organization rather than intrinsic material properties, unlocking combinations of sensitivity, linearity, and strain range inaccessible to homogeneous composites and thereby expanding the accessible performance space. A physics-guided framework maps how local cell behavior propagates through the hierarchy, enabling rational inverse design through systematic exploration of this expanded performance space toward targeted electromechanical functionality. This transforms sensor development from costly trial-and-error optimization and data-intensive black-box AI models into an interpretable, physics-guided design process. Experimental validation confirmed metamaterials-based piezoresistors exhibiting a fourfold enhanced sensitivity (gauge factor 1.55) compared to their most linear homogeneous constituent material, while preserving an extreme linearity (R² > 0.98) over a 30% strain range, and tenfold enhanced sensitivity (gauge factor 37.5) compared to the most sensitive constituent material. As proof of concept, these metamaterials served as strain gauges for accurate respiratory monitoring. Most importantly, this physics-guided universal framework introduces a rational inverse-design paradigm for hierarchical nanocomposites, in which tailored electromechanical responses arise from architectural organization rather than from intrinsic material properties, enabling navigation of the expanded performance space toward application-specific functionality. Grounded in fundamental physical interactions, it enables systematic, interpretable design and extends naturally to other electromechanical sensing modes, such as transverse piezoresistivity and piezocapacitance, for potential applications in multi-modal sensing, soft robotics, stretchable transistors, and adaptive structures.

abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are a hybrid modeling approach that integrates physical priors into neural networks. By encoding governing equations as soft constraint terms into the loss function, this method accomplishes organic integration of data-driven approaches with physical laws. PINNs demonstrate significant advantages in complex scenarios including data scarcity, high-dimensional spaces, and multi-physics coupling. However, existing research has identified many challenges that PINNs face when tackling with strongly nonlinear dynamical systems. Specifically, during the numerical prediction of complex systems, the nonlinear interactions between system state variables can lead to error coupling and propagation across the variables, which hinders the effective optimization of physical constraint terms. This accumulation of errors may cause inconsistencies between the gradient directions of data constraints and physical constraints, consequently weakening the actual guiding role of physical constraints in the training process. To mitigate these issues, this paper proposes an Observation-Guided Physics-Informed Neural Networks (OG-PINN). By integrating partial observed data into the physics-driven loss function, this approach effectively reconciles competing optimization objectives between physical constraints and data constraints. This mechanism not only enhances the robustness of physical constraints but also significantly reduces the interference of multivariable forecast errors on physical residual. Consequently, the model captures system dynamics more stably. We applied for the OG-PINN to reconstruct the Lorenz 63 system, a typical nonlinear chaotic system, and conducted a systematic comparison with conventional PINN methods. Results demonstrate that the OG-PINN exhibits superior performance over PINN in multiple training sample experiments, especially in long-term forecasting, reducing errors by up to 60% compared to PINN. These experiments not only validate the effectiveness of the OG-PINN in complex dynamical system modeling but also provide technically feasible pathways for physics-constrained deep learning under data-scarce and strongly nonlinear scenarios. Furthermore, we also analyze the impacts of regularization weight (λ) and training sample size (N) on model convergence and generalization capability.

abstract: Interactions derived from effective field theories of quantum chromodynamics have thus far failed to bind calcium nuclei beyond neutron number N=40, while nuclear density functionals typically place the neutron drip line near ^{70}Ca, at N=50. We present the chiral interaction N^{3}LO_{Texas}, a combination of two- and three-nucleon potentials at fourth and third chiral order, respectively, with low-energy constants optimized using emulator-accelerated fits to few- and many-body data. This interaction accurately reproduces binding energies and charge radii of key nuclei with mass number A=3 to 208, important excited states, and nuclear matter near saturation. Using ab initio methods, coupled cluster and valence-space in-medium similarity renormalization group, we find that the calcium two-neutron drip line extends to ^{71}Ca.

abstract:
The MESSENGER magnetometer data for the years 2011 through 2015 are used to study the presence of mirror modes in Mercury's environment. Using magnetic-field-only-detection of these structures, 13,691 intervals of 20 s and longer are found in the solar wind, and in the magnetosheath and magnetosphere of Mercury. The distribution of mirror modes around the planet is similar to that found at Venus and Mars, however, the occurrence rate of ∼1.0×10-4 per second is up to 2 orders of magnitude smaller than at the other two planets. The mirror modes are more prone to be excited near Mercury's aphelion. A comparison shows that mirror modes and magnetic holes have a similar behaviour around Mercury, and that about 40% of the mirror modes can also be identified as magnetic holes. As ion cyclotron waves can be generated by the same temperature anisotropy, they are also compared with the mirror modes. It is found that the ion cyclotron waves show a lesser dependence on the true anomaly angle.

abstract: Soft manipulators offer a route to safer, more adaptive and physically intelligent robots, but their compliant bodies remain difficult to model, predict and control. Large deformation, distributed actuation, hysteresis, material variability and contact-rich interaction challenge both classical mechanics-based models and purely data-driven approaches. Here, we examine emerging modeling perspectives for soft manipulators through a conceptual progression from sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics to hybrid intelligence. We discuss how sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy), Koopman learning, neural ordinary differential equations, physics-informed neural networks, and hybrid physics machine learning models contribute complementary capabilities, including interpretable reduced-order dynamics, control-ready prediction, continuous-time latent modeling, physics-constrained field reconstruction, and residual correction. We present that no single modeling approach is sufficient for the next generation of soft robotic systems. Instead, progress requires integrated modeling ecosystems that combine mechanical structure, data-driven discovery and task-aware adaptation. Such hybrid-intelligence frameworks can transform models from passive descriptions of deformation into active components of sensing, control, design and decision-making, enabling soft manipulators that are more interpretable, robust and deployable in real-world environments.

abstract: Inverse problems in pharmacometrics and quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) often involve sparse, noisy data, limited measurable states, and complex dynamical systems. Traditional parameter estimation methods can struggle with ill-posed problems, stiffness, discontinuities, and gray-box scenarios where only part of the system dynamics is known or observable. This tutorial provides an end-to-end, reproducible workflow for applying physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to PK/PD/QSP inverse problems and gray-box discovery tasks. We present three worked case studies: (1) constant parameter recovery in a three-state compartmental system, (2) gray-box discovery of an unknown right-hand-side function, and (3) inference of a time-varying chemotherapy efficacy function under partial observation. For each, we provide implementation guidance, validation checks, and practical advice on collocation design, feature expansion, optimizer selection, numerical precision, constraint enforcement, loss weighting, and residual-based attention. We also discuss when to consider newer architectures such as Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs) as drop-in alternatives to standard multilayer perceptrons. All code and notebooks are provided through our PhINs library, short for Pharmacometrics-Informed Networks, and are publicly available at https://github.com/NazAhmadi/PhINs/.

abstract: As a frontier in condensed matter physics, the concept of topological insulators has been successfully extended from electronic systems to photonic systems and even to structured microcavities, where strong photon-exciton coupling gives rise to hybrid part-light, part-matter exciton-polaritons quasiparticles. Polaritons inherit the low-loss, tunable characteristics of photons while retaining strong excitonic nonlinear interactions, offering an ideal nonequilibrium platform for exploring topological states. This review systematically surveys the progress of topological insulators in exciton-polariton systems, with emphasis on their underlying physical mechanisms, exotic quantum phenomena induced by various strategies, and the impact of nonlinear effects on topological states. Finally, we discuss the key challenges currently facing this field and provide an outlook on future research directions.
