abstract: Differences in nuclear charge distributions between isotopes lead to small changes in atomic spectra known as the field shift. While largely proportional to the change in the mean-square nuclear radius, the field shift also contains higher-order contributions with different dependencies on nuclear moments. Their knowledge is required in searches for new physics using King plots, as they can induce deviations from King-plot linearity. We present a systematic expansion of the field-shift energies in terms of nuclear parameters and test its validity against direct numerical calculations for H-like ions. We also compute leading-and higher-order field-shift corrections for alkali-like systems from Li-like to Rb-like ions, and find that their ratio is nearly independent of the ionic charge state, agreeing with the corresponding hydrogenic 1s ratios on a sub-percent level. Motivated by this observation, we introduce an approximation in which these fractional contributions are assumed to be independent of the electronic configuration. We show that within this approximation, higherorder field-shift corrections do not contribute to King-plot nonlinearities.

abstract: The purpose of this work was to evaluate image quality of non-contrast neurological CT scans on a commercially available energy-integrating detector (EID) CT compared to a prototype deep silicon (dSi) photon-counting detector CT (PCCT). A cohort of subjects scanned on the EID-CT (Apex CT, GE HealthCare, Waukesha, WI) was retrospectively recruited. A second cohort of prospectively recruited subjects was scanned on the prototype dSi-PCCT CT using deep learning (DL) recon. Image quality was assessed by four neuroradiologists on a 5-point Likert scale for sharpness, noise, and presence of artifacts, differentiation of gray-white matter, and structural confidence in the lentiform nucleus and insular ribbon. Reader agreement was assessed through a linearly weighted Cohen's kappa. Contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) between gray and white matter was determined. Differences between the median Likert scores and CNRs of the two cohorts were assessed with the Mann-Whitney U test. Reader agreement was fair on average ([Formula: see text]). Median Likert scores of the dSi-PCCT with DL recon cohort were statistically superior compared to the median scores of the EID-CT scores for sharpness, noise, gray-white matter differentiation, and structural confidence of the lentiform nucleus and insular ribbon. No statistical difference was detected in the presence of artifacts between the cohorts. Average CNRs were 1.45±0.14 and 1.53±0.08 for the EID-CT and dSi-PCCT cohorts, respectively, but no significant difference was detected (p = 0.72). Increased sharpness, lower noise, and better ability to differentiate structures demonstrate improved image quality and the potential for utilizing PCCT in non-contrast neurological imaging tasks.

abstract: In conventional antiferromagnets, local electric environments remain equivalent and combined inversion and time-reversal PT symmetry enforces spin-degenerate bands, whereas altermagnets and related compensated phases realize this inequivalence as long-range order electric environments. Materials with zero net magnetization can, nevertheless, exhibit spin-split electronic bands when the local electric environments associated with opposite magnetic moments are inequivalent. Here we this regime in which electric inequivalence arises locally from a polymorphous magnetic configuration, represented by a static, globally compensated arrangement of nonzero local moments with distinct spin neighborhoods. These neighborhoods self-consistently generate site-dependent electric offsets through the exchange-correlation potential. The correlation between these offsets and the local moments produces a finite potential-weighted Néel vector even though the net magnetization vanishes, providing a route to exchange-driven, s-wave-like spin splitting without chemical substitution, structural relaxation, heterostructures, or long-range-ordered electric inequivalence. Using spin-density functional theory for EuB6, for which previous calculations identified spin-polymorphism-induced on-site electric inequivalence, we contrast an electrically homogeneous antiferromagnetic reference with polymorphous representations of the paramagnetic state. The former remains spin degenerate, whereas the polymorphous configurations develop environment-dependent charge redistribution and finite spin splitting in the unfolded spectral function. These results establish magnetic polymorphism as an additional design axis for spin-resolved electronic structures beyond ferromagnetism, ferrimagnetism, and altermagnetism.

abstract: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics provides a powerful tool for the rational design of yeast cell factories. However, the rigid yeast cell wall architecture and the fast-growing scale of strain libraries present certain challenges for efficient protein extraction and high-throughput proteomic profiling. Conventional protein extraction methods either demand lengthy incubation periods or specialized equipment, leading to limited sample throughput and low efficiency. Herein, we report an efficient protein extraction strategy using a solvent combination of ionic liquid, guanidine hydrochloride, and lithium acetate under heat treatment (IGL-H). This method enables rapid protein extraction and is compatible with diverse yeast species across different growth phases. Compared with the classical glass bead grinding method, the IGL-H method affords higher protein yield and comparable or superior proteome coverage, and recovers higher proportions of integral membrane proteins of the endomembrane trafficking system. Furthermore, this method is readily amenable to liquid handling workstations for high-throughput proteome sample preparation by using magnetic solid-phase alkylation (mSPA) materials in less than 1.5 h, achieving Pearson correlation coefficients exceeding 0.97. Applying this pipeline to study proteome dynamics of Candida utilis under different nitrogen sources revealed an adaptive strategy involving carbon flux-specific allocation. These results establish the IGL-H extraction strategy as an effective solution for rapid protein extraction and high-throughput proteomic analysis of yeast strains, advancing rational cell factory design in synthetic biology.

abstract:
Purpose

Traditional Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) methods used in the hydrodynamic design of blood-contacting medical devices create a bottleneck in optimization processes due to their heavy dependence on mesh structure and high computational costs.

Methods

In this study, using a mesh-free Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) approach, complex flow fields and Turbulent Kinetic Energy (TKE) distributions in FDA reference nozzle geometries were mapped with high resolution. Unlike artificial intelligence algorithms that merely fit data, the proposed model directly integrates the axisymmetric mass conservation equation into the loss function as a mathematical constraint. The model was trained on experimental PIV/LDV data over a wide range covering laminar, transitional, and fully turbulent regimes ( Re=500-6500 ).

Results

The model predicted sharp velocity gradients in the shear layers with high accuracy. Additionally, a practical empirical correlation for peak TKE was derived within the investigated conditions, serving as a rapid hydrodynamic indicator.

Conclusion

The findings demonstrate that this physics-constrained approach reduces the need for mesh generation and offers a computationally lightweight framework for the continuity-constrained reconstruction and regularization of complex and inherently noisy experimental flow fields.

abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly disrupting education and the employment prospects for recent university graduates. Thisstudy examines the prevalence, motivations, and perceived effects of AI usage among undergraduate Physics degree studentsat a London research university during Spring 2026. Student voice was sought on the key question of how universities shouldrespond to the changing landscape. Applying a mixed-methods design, data was collected through a survey, analyzed withdescriptive statistics, and semi-structured focus groups, analyzed through a qualitative coding analysis. In general agreementwith a range of recent studies, we find the Physics degree student uptake of AI at a near-universal 90%, motivated by efficiency,conceptual support, and social pressure stemming from perceived peer advantage from using AI. Several students regardedoral examinations as a robust assessment of their learning. A majority of the students displayed an acute awareness of issuessurrounding AI, such as over-reliance, skill erosion, job market displacement, and environmental impact. The nuance found instudents’ in-person discussions, underexplored in previous studies, is highlighted here.

abstract: Two-dimensional rhombohedral boron nitride (rBN) has emerged as a promising sliding ferroelectric material for high-density, fast-speed and non-volatile memories. However, the batch production of ferroelectric rBN wafers has remained a critical challenge due to the thermodynamic instability of the rhombohedral phase and the inherent difficulties in maintaining consistent growth kinetics. Here we report a step-templated interfacial epitaxy strategy that enables the reproducible fabrication of 4-inch rBN wafers from nickel-boron films sputtered on the stepped sapphires. Comprehensive structural characterizations across multiple scales confirm the high phase purity and batch-to-batch consistent quality of produced rBN wafers. The intrinsic sliding ferroelectricity is verified in a unified ferroelectric field-effect transistor (FeFET), which exhibits ultrafast switching speed (at the nanosecond scale), high fatigue resistance (>2 × 10<sup>9</sup> cycles) and long-term non-volatility (10 years). FeFET arrays are also constructed based on rBN wafers, featuring a high integration density with significant on/off ratios (10<sup>6</sup>). Remarkably, the rBN FeFETs can maintain large memory windows (4 V) and excellent thermal stability (>470 K), even at an ultrashort channel length of 30 nm. These results establish rBN as a scalable platform for next-generation sliding ferroelectric memories, facilitating their applications in high-density memory chips and artificial intelligence accelerators.

abstract: Rare-earth-based intermetallic compounds are at the forefront of materials science, providing valuable insights into the interplay among magnetism, topology, and structural correlations. The interesting properties of these materials, driven by localized 4f -electrons, strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC), and crystal electric field (CEF) effect, make them a focal point in solid-state physics for designing advanced functional materials. We have synthesized NdAsTe using the solid-state reaction route and explored the temperature and field-dependent magnetic properties, which demonstrate long-range antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering below T N ≃ 2.4 K. The low-temperature Curie-Weiss temperature θ CW ≃ -1.89 K implies a net AFM interaction between the Nd 3+ ions. Furthermore, the isothermal magnetization data exhibit signatures of spin-reorientation of the AFM-aligned spins at T < T N , corroborated through magnetic entropy studies. The signature of AFM transition is also manifested as a peak at T N in the temperature-dependent specific heat which gradually shifts towards lower temperatures at higher applied fields. The derived parameters from specific heat data suggest the presence of strong electronic correlations in NdAsTe. The magnetic susceptibility and specific heat data suggest that the magnetic ground state is a Kramers' doublet with effective spin J eff = 1/2 at low temperatures. The electrical transport study revealed the semiconducting nature with a band gap of 70 meV. Furthermore, the low temperature (T < 20 K) magnetotransport studies unfold a crossover from positive to negative magnetoresistance behavior.

abstract: Hydropower turbine–generator units operate under strongly coupled hydraulic, mechanical, electrical, and thermal dynamics, making reliable fault diagnosis and predictive maintenance challenging under uncertain and time-varying conditions. This study proposes an uncertainty-aware physics-informed digital twin that integrates a reduced-order multi-physics model, learned residual correction, online state synchronization, ensemble-based uncertainty quantification, out-of-distribution detection, fault classification, severity estimation, and remaining-useful-life prediction within a unified real-time framework. The method was evaluated under healthy operation, load transitions, progressive degradation, multiple fault classes, measurement noise, and unfamiliar operating conditions. Over 10 independent runs, the proposed digital twin achieved a state-reconstruction RMSE of 0.0025±0.0004 and an R2 of 0.997±0.002, while reducing the normalized physics residual to 0.0094±0.0011. Diagnostic performance reached a macro-F1 score of 0.950, an MCC of 0.940, and an AUPRC of 0.970. The calibration strategy reduced the expected calibration error from 0.0947 to 0.0115, while out-of-distribution detection achieved an AUROC of approximately 0.954. The prognostic module produced an RUL RMSE of approximately 2.24 h. End-to-end processing required 21.4 ms per synchronized measurement window, supporting operation within a 100 ms monitoring interval. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework combines high-fidelity reconstruction, physically consistent learning, reliable uncertainty estimation, robust diagnosis, actionable prognostics, and real-time computational feasibility for intelligent hydropower asset management. The framework therefore offers a practical foundation for risk-informed condition monitoring and maintenance decision support in modern hydropower plants.

abstract: Altermagnetism has emerged as a third fundamental magnetic phase, uniquely combining the zero net magnetization and ultrafast dynamics of antiferromagnets with spin splitting typically reserved for ferromagnets(FMs). This review provides a systematic overview of the burgeoning field of altermagnets(AMs) and AM-based devices. We first present the symmetry principles that enable non-relativistic spin splitting. Then we examine representative material candidates-ranging from bulk systems to emergent van der Waals layers and metal-organic frameworks, and evaluate their applications in functional devices. Special focus is given to tunneling junctions, anomalous Hall effect sensors, and terahertz (THz) devices. Finally, we discuss methods for electrical and mechanical control of altermagnetic states and the effects between altermagnetism and superconductivity, offering a perspective on the challenges and opportunities for this new paradigm of energy-efficient spintronics.

abstract: One important electrical quantity in devices is the conductance; for systems on the mesoscopic scale and nanoscale, the conductance is given by the Landauer-Buttiker formalism. In this paper, by using the minimal Weyl Hamiltonian, a theoretical study on the ballistic conductance of two-dimensional (2D) Dirac materials is carried out, with the aim of deriving properties of the ballistic conductance. In addition, formulas for calculating and comparing the ballistic conductance of Dirac materials with diverse cones are given. Our study reveals that the ballistic conductance can be both isotropic and anisotropic, depending on the values of the Dirac cone characteristics (i.e., the anisotropy and tilt). The effects of the anisotropy and tilt of the Dirac cone on the ballistic conductance are investigated in detail. For the right Dirac cone, we show that the ballistic conductance in the x direction does not depend on the strength of the anisotropy of Dirac cone, while the ballistic conductance in the y direction varies inversely with the strength of anisotropy. We find that the ballistic conductance of the oblique Dirac cone is greater than that of the right Dirac cone. Also, when the strength of tilt increases, that is, when the Dirac cone becomes more tilted, the ballistic conductance rises. We also investigate symmetry properties of the ballistic conductance. This paper provides a new and deeper insight into properties of the ballistic conductance from massless Dirac fermions and can be useful for designing electronic devices with desired performance.

abstract: Polymer composites show complex, nonlinear mechanical behaviour. This makes their rational design hard. Running tests or high-fidelity simulations for every candidate design is slow and costly. Purely data-driven models are fast, but they can break basic mechanics outside the training range. Most physics-informed (PI) models, on the other hand, target a single constitutive law or failure mode, and their loss weights are set by hand. This study presents a DBN-GJO-PI-RNN surrogate that links deep feature learning, physics-constrained learning and failure screening in one workflow. A Deep Belief Network (DBN) learns compact latent features from the material and loading inputs. A PI Recurrent Neural Network (PI-RNN) then predicts the mechanical response under a composite loss with data, constitutive, equilibrium and boundary terms. Golden Jackal Optimization (GJO) tunes the network settings and the three loss weights together. Its fitness function rewards both accuracy and physical consistency. The predicted failure index is then checked against the onset criterion (FI ≥ 1). We tested the framework on a public dataset of 5,000 polymer-composite samples with six response targets. On the test set, it reached an MAE of 1.1132, an RMSE of 1.3962 and an R² of 0.9932. Its RMSE was 38.3% lower than that of the best purely data-driven baseline (TCN) and 50.6% lower than that of a standard RNN. The ablation study showed that each module reduced the error. The framework offers a fast, physics-aware surrogate for screening polymer-composite designs before costly tests or simulations.

abstract: The development of blue-green emitting organic chromophores with excellent optoelectronic properties remains an important issue. In this context, the newly synthesized oxadiazole-based blue-green emitting chromophore, 2-(4-(2-(anthracen-10-yl)vinyl)phenyl)-5-(4-tert-butylphenyl)-1,3,4-oxadiazole (AVBO), was accomplished via the donor-π-acceptor (D- π-A) strategy using a Wittig reaction. The integration of aryl-heteroaryl groups and the oxadiazole group was utilized to obtain efficient blue-green emission with excellent optical properties. AVBO exhibited stable and efficient PL in the range of 485-510 nm across diverse solvent environments. Solvatochromic analysis using multiple correlations (Lippert-Mataga, Bakhshiev, Kawski-Chamma-Viallet, and Reichardt) revealed a significantly higher excited-state dipole moment compared to the ground state ([Formula: see text]>[Formula: see text]), with a parallel orientation ([Formula: see text]). The values calculated using these empirical equations were compared with those calculated computationally. Kamlet-Taft and Catalán MLR analyses further identified dominant non-specific solvent interactions ([Formula: see text]) alongside specific hydrogen-bonding donor contributions. To explore its potential in optoelectronic applications, AVBO was integrated into hybrid systems with ZnSe/ZnS core-shell quantum dots (7-8 nm). This assembly functioned as an efficient FRET mechanism, reaching an efficiency of 88% with Förster radii of 6.14-6.16 nm. The quenching kinetics, validated by Stern-Volmer plots, showed both static and dynamic components with super-diffusion-limited rate constants (k<sub>q</sub> ≈ 10<sup>14</sup> /MS). abstract: The bacterial flagellar motor adapts to mechanical load by adding or removing stator units, which can either be inactive in the inner membrane (the stator pool) or attached to the motor in a torque-generating configuration. This adaptation is well understood, but what sets the load range over which the motor responds remains unclear. Building on a previous two-state model of stator binding, we derive how the on-rate depends on the diffusing stator pool and find that it increases in proportion to pool size. The model predicts that pool size governs motor occupancy at low load but not at high load, where the motor saturates regardless of how many stators are available. We confirmed this prediction in Escherichia coli: increasing motAB induction increased swimming speed and single-motor rotation rate at low load. This dependence on induction weakened as load rose and was undetectable at high load. The model further predicts that larger pools make the motor mechanosensitive at lower loads, which our measurements of load-induced occupancy change support. Mechanosensitivity is therefore not fixed by motor architecture alone, but also determined by stator abundance, which cells can set through expression to position their mechanosensory range.

abstract:
Objective

The aim of this paper is to develop a method for region-based post-reconstruction partial-volume correction (PVC) of SPECT images, which explicitly estimates the mean activity concentration in regions without assuming strict intra-regional uniformity.

Approach

Partial-volume correction was applied to177Lu-SPECT images obtained from the simulation of eight anthropomorphic phantoms as well as two example patients. Both sets of data were reconstructed using OS-EM with ten subsets and up to 40 iterations, including compensation for attenuation, scatter, and spatial resolution. Reconstructed images were deconvolved using the van Cittert algorithm and Lucy-Richardson algorithm, both implemented on images represented as standard cuboid voxels or as regional voxels, consisting of regions defined from whole-image segmentation. Methods embedding regional voxels were applied both assuming region-wise uniform activity concentration and incorporating perturbations in the form of cosine series to relax the uniformity assumption. For comparison, images were also processed with the iterative Yang method and MIRD recovery coefficients. Evaluation was performed with respect to the estimated activity concentration for kidneys, spleen, and tumours, as well as the total activity in the images.

Main results

Mean activity-concentration errors prior to PVC were (-22.6±11.5) %, (-13.8±2.1) %, and (-7.4±2.8) % for tumours, kidneys, and spleen, respectively. Region-perturbed van Cittert deconvolution with order 4 reduced these errors to (2.3±7.7) %, (0.3±2.2) %, and (4.0±1.6) % while the errors for region-perturbed Lucy-Richardson deconvolution of order 4 were (0.3±8.0) %, (0.0±1.6) %, (2.6±0.5) %. Corresponding results for the iterative Yang method were (2.8±21) %, (-0.3±2.1) %, and (3.8±2.4) % and using MIRD recovery coefficients (-5.0±14.2) %, (-7.1±1.9) %, and (-0.6±3.1) %.

Significance

Region-based PVC improves the accuracy of quantitative SPECT, and the inclusion of cosine perturbations allows for a gradual relaxation of the uniformity assumption.

abstract: Quality assurance in radiotherapy traditionally relies on pre-treatment measurement-based verification using homogeneous phantoms, which may not fully account for patient-specific heterogeneities. Independent dose calculation (IDC) methods have emerged as an alternative for secondary plan verification, but their accuracy depends on proper modelling of multileaf collimator (MLC) parameters. This work focuses on the efficient and systematic tuning of these parameters. In particular, the MC module of RadCalc® (RCMC, version 7.4) was commissioned for multiple photon beam energies (6X, 6FFF, 10X, 10FFF) for two Varian TrueBeam® linear accelerators, namely TB1 and TB2. An analytical workflow was developed to determine the optimal Additional Radiation to Light Field Offset (ARLFO) value from a linear interpolation of the differences between dose measurements at different MLC-gaps and RCMC calculations, combined with weighting factors reflecting dosimetric sensitivity and clinical MLC-apertures frequencies. The method was validated on an independent clinical set of plans using the Gamma Passing Rate (GPR) evaluation (2%/2 mm local dose criterion, 10% dose threshold), and statistical significance of differences between optimal and default values of ARLFO was assessed via Wilcoxon signed-rank test.The obtained optimal ARLFO values differed between the two linacs, being positive for TB1 and negative for TB2 across all beam energies. The use of the optimized ARLFO led to a systematic increase in median GPRs: for TB1, improvements ranged from +3.8 to +8.4 percentage points (p ≤ 0.028); for TB2, increases ranged from +8.8 to +17 percentage points (p ≤ 0.0020), with no significant change observed for 10X (p = 0.31).The proposed analytical approach enables simple, efficient, and reproducible user-specific parameter tuning in Monte Carlo-based secondary dose verification and is expected to be applicable across different clinical settings.&#xD.

abstract: A study of the dynamical two-dimensional (2D) nonlinear response of the dimerized spin-1/2 chain to external electric fields is presented. The coupling of the spin system to light is set to arise from the inverse Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. In the XY-limit, we provide analytical expressions for the second-order nonlinear dynamical response function. Apart from multi spinon continua, this response displays a strong antidiagonal, i.e. galvanoelectric, feature in the 2D frequency plane. This allows to read off scattering rates of the fractional spinon excitations. For the XXZ-case, we focus on the interaction-driven renormalization of the light-matter coupling by considering vertex corrections which are induced by the zz-exchange. We show this renormalization to modify the spinon joint density of states significantly, potentially allowing for the formation of in-gap bound states. As a result, the vertex corrected light-matter coupling can induce a dramatic spectral weight transfer to lower energies for the dynamical response function within the 2D frequency plane.

abstract: Microbial cell factories have emerged as important platforms for the sustainable production of fuels, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and other value-added bioproducts. Synthetic biology provides a systematic engineering framework for their construction and optimization through standardized biological parts, modular design, and iterative Design-Build-Test-Learn cycles. This chapter summarizes the major tools and strategies for developing microbial cell factories, beginning with the fundamental principles of synthetic biology and the characteristics of representative microbial chassis. Key genetic engineering approaches, including CRISPR-based genome editing, transcriptional and translational regulation, and modular DNA assembly, are discussed together with strategies for metabolic pathway design, enzyme engineering, flux balancing, and dynamic regulation. Genome-scale metabolic modeling, adaptive and directed evolution, and multi-omics analysis are further introduced as systems-level approaches for identifying engineering targets and improving cellular performance. In addition, emerging computational tools, machine learning, artificial intelligence, high-throughput screening, and laboratory automation are highlighted for their roles in accelerating strain development and closing the Design-Build-Test-Learn cycle. Finally, representative applications illustrate the translation of engineered microbial cell factories from laboratory-scale design to industrial biomanufacturing.

abstract: Studying the transcriptome and the proteome of cells is essential for gaining a detailed understanding of cellular behavior, development, drug action, and disease progression. Spatial biology emerges to advance our ability to study the expression of molecules within tissues while preserving their natural spatial context. These cutting-edge technologies enable the mapping of thousands of individual cells in their original environment by detecting the location and biological quantity of cellular contents, such as RNAs and proteins. Here, we present a protocol to combine spatial transcriptomics (Xenium) and spatial proteomics (PhenoCycler-Fusion) within 8 days on the same tissue section to successfully study the expression of hundreds of RNAs and tens of proteins simultaneously. The combination of these two technologies and consequent integration of the two data layers together with high-resolution H&E images allows for the extraction of a maximum of information from a single tissue section. Application of this protocol and the resulting integrated data will help researchers to understand complex biological processes and disease mechanisms, supporting more nuanced research in molecular biology and pathology.

abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has facilitated the studies of cellular heterogeneity in many different biological contexts, including how B cells function and mediate immune responses to infection, malignancies, and autoimmunity. scRNA-seq as applied to B cells requires specific bioinformatics strategies, which consider the distinct biology of B cells and biological processes unique to these cells, such as somatic hypermutation (SHM) and class switch recombination (CSR). We present here a protocol that analyses scRNA-seq alignments and count matrices, as well as B-cell receptor sequencing data obtained in parallel to scRNA-seq. We highlight computational strategies to ensure cell clusters align with biologically relevant B-cell subsets and cell states. We provide practical guidance on how CSR and SHM information can be extracted from the data and utilized to build robust computational models of B-cell maturation.

abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent the first line of host immune defense against a broad spectrum of microorganisms. Whether naturally occurring or synthetically designed, these small peptides can potently inhibit microbial growth and remain stable under diverse conditions. Most AMPs act by directly disrupting fungal or bacterial membranes. In this study, we identified a glycine-rich peptide with strong antifungal activity against Botrytis cinerea. We further investigated its mode of action (MOA) and demonstrated its preventive antifungal activity in plants. Our work focuses primarily on the in vitro characterization of AMP features in the context of plant-Botrytis interactions.

abstract: Cell attachment is the process by which cells interact with their environment, including neighboring cells and the extracellular matrix (ECM). Attachment plays a critical role in maintaining skin integrity, promoting wound healing, and facilitating cellular communication in epidermal cells, such as keratinocytes. However, the many different factors that can influence this mechanism make it challenging to recapitulate in cellular models. The overlap between attachment and adhesion mechanisms both physiologically and methodologically further complicate the production of cellular models. Here, we present a flexible, quantitative, and cost-effective tool for studying epidermal attachment under various conditions. We provide optimized starting conditions for several different adaptations of the core protocol and provide approaches for quantitative, reproducible data that can be performed in most laboratories. This assay enhances experimental reproducibility and enables a targeted approach to studying epidermal biology. This approach offers researchers an improved tool for dissecting the molecular events in cell attachment and advancing skin biology research.

abstract: The plasma membrane (PM) is the primary interface between plant cells and their environment, and its resident proteins mediate key processes such as extracellular signal perception and downstream cellular reprogramming. Yet, PM proteins are typically underrepresented in total protein extracts, and existing enrichment strategies are often laborious and require extensive optimization. Here, a simple and robust workflow is described for enriching PM proteins from Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings using total microsomal membranes obtained by differential centrifugation as starting material. Sequential low- and high-speed spins are used to isolate total microsomal membranes and progressively deplete contaminating organelles, thereby increasing the relative abundance of PM proteins. Coupled with the rich genetic toolkit available in Arabidopsis, this protocol provides an accessible platform for systematic characterization of the PM proteome.

abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are universally conserved and essential players in the communication between cells across nearly all organisms of life. Botrytis cinerea produces and secretes EVs that are critical in its virulence on plants. Numerous studies in various fungal species reveal that EVs are important across different pathosystems to facilitate fungal infection. For characterization of the cargo and role of EVs in fungal growth and communication, it is necessary to carefully and precisely purify fungal EVs from fungal culture or the plant interaction interface. Here, we present a method for the isolation of Botrytis cinerea EVs from culture and the infection site of B. cinerea on Arabidopsis thaliana. Fungal EVs isolated using this method are free from cellular contamination from fungal or plant cells, remain viable in functional assays, and provide high-quality RNA and protein.

abstract: Deep learning has transformed medical image analysis, but progress in cancer and stem cell applications is often constrained by limited access to large, diverse, well-annotated imaging datasets. This bottleneck is especially acute for studies of tumor heterogeneity and cancer stem cell (CSC) biology, where rare phenotypes and dynamic cell-state transitions-frequently linked to stemness-associated transcriptional programs (e.g., OCT4, SOX2, NANOG)-benefit from high-quality imaging across many samples and conditions. At the same time, regulatory and practical barriers (patient privacy, acquisition cost, and uneven institutional data sharing) restrict dataset scale and reuse. Diffusion models offer a practical route to synthetic data expansion by generating high-fidelity synthetic images that retain salient radiologic and pathologic features. In this chapter, we present an end-to-end protocol for adapting latent diffusion (Stable Diffusion) to oncology imaging using DreamBooth fine-tuning with small numbers of representative images, coupled with text-to-image and image-to-image workflows to generate controlled variations across modalities and disease presentations (e.g., brain tumor MRI, breast cancer mammography/CESM). We also describe quantitative and qualitative evaluation strategies, including Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) benchmarking and expert review considerations, to assess realism and diversity. These methods enable cancer and stem cell biologists to augment training data for segmentation and classification, build shareable educational resources, and prototype analyses for rare tumors or stemness-enriched subtypes while potentially reducing reliance on direct sharing of patient images.

abstract: The study of plant organogenesis presents significant challenges due to the small number of cells involved in its initial stages. Observing the initial cell divisions becomes increasingly challenging when transitioning from Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis) to other species. Lateral root (LR) initiation is an essential process for enhancing a plant's ability to access water and nutrients. In most cases, LR formation starts in the pericycle of the parent root, giving rise to a new meristem. Understanding the mechanisms coordinating LR development is important for improving plant resilience to biotic and abiotic stresses. The prediction of the precise timing and location of LR initiation along the root axis remains challenging, even in Arabidopsis. This is magnified when attempting to observe LR development in crops. Brachypodium distachyon (Brachypodium) has emerged as a versatile model for cereal crops. However, studying Brachypodium LR development requires a revision of protocols and methodologies to be applied from seedling growth to root imaging. Here, we present protocols for seed preparation, in vitro growth, and tissue clearing for Brachypodium. Whereas ClearSee appeared to be unsuitable for rendering Brachypodium root tissues transparent after a reasonable incubation period, our modified DEEP-Clear method resulted in improved efficiency in tissue clearing and is compatible with major fluorescent proteins and dyes. Finally, we introduce a simple and straightforward approach to locally synchronize LR development. These tools and methodologies are crucial for advancing our knowledge of plant root system architecture, transitioning from a model plant to agronomically important species.

abstract: Allergenicity is a multifactorial and context-dependent property that emerges from the interaction between intrinsic protein features and host immune mechanisms. Although regulatory frameworks rely primarily on sequence homology to known allergens, increasing numbers of novel and engineered proteins require more comprehensive computational strategies for preclinical assessment. This chapter describes a modular bioinformatic pipeline for the prediction and characterization of potential protein allergens. The workflow integrates FAO/WHO sequence-based criteria for regulatory compliance, structure-informed homology methods, and machine learning-based classifiers. Proteins identified as potential allergens are subsequently subjected to downstream immunological characterization. This stepwise decision framework enables flexible and biologically informed prescreening of candidate proteins, providing a structured approach prior to experimental validation or systems biology-based analyses.

abstract: Microbial genetic resources are a key part of global biodiversity. They are critical for biomedical innovation, environmental sustainability, and industrial biotechnology. In the past 10 years, microbiome research, synthetic biology, and systems biology have expanded how we view microorganisms. Microorganisms are now seen as more than just pathogens or environmental agents. As a result, preserving microbial diversity has become a strategic priority. The microbial resource ensures scientific reproducibility, supports biotechnology, and protects ecosystem services. This chapter gives a broad overview of microorganisms important to biomedicine and the environment. It examines the main principles, methods, and limits of their conservation. The chapter highlights the challenges of maintaining microbes' viability, genetic stability, and functional integrity. It discusses common preservation methods, such as subculturing, refrigeration, ultra-freezing, cryopreservation, and lyophilization. It also reviews which methods fit best based on biology and intended use. Finally, this chapter highlights the need for advanced preservation strategies that combine cryobiology, materials science, and synthetic biology. Microbial conservation is presented as a crucial part of building a sustainable bioeconomy and strong global health systems.

We also summarized approaches for the identification of eRNAs' putative regulatory network, and eRNA-correlated traits and clinical features. This workflow provides guidance for readers to use bioinformatic tools for analyzing eRNA expression and eRNA-associated traits.

abstract: Advances in data acquisition tools, particularly mass spectrometry-based techniques, have made high-throughput methods like proteomics and phosphoproteomics increasingly accessible. However, the volume and complexity of the data require specialized computational tools for analysis and interpretation to extract meaningful insights. Here, we describe the use of rROMA software to analyze pathway and kinase activity in proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets. rROMA is an open-source package available on Github at: www.github.com/sysbio-curie/rROMA . As a case study, we applied rROMA to breast cancer samples from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC), which provides precise relative quantification of proteins and phosphorylation sites of a large cohort of breast cancer samples through Tandem mass tag (TMT)-based mass spectrometry. These analyses illustrate how to identify active pathways and kinase-driven mechanisms potentially involved in disease subtypes, along with their associated proteins and phosphosites.

abstract: Single-cell transcriptomics has revolutionized our understanding of cellular heterogeneity by enabling high-resolution gene expression profiling at the individual cell level. However, traditional single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) lacks direct protein quantification, limiting comprehensive immunophenotyping. Cellular Indexing of Transcriptomes and Epitopes by sequencing (CITE-seq) overcomes this limitation by integrating antibody-derived tag (ADT) quantification with scRNA-seq, allowing simultaneous measurement of surface protein and gene expression from the same cell. This multimodal approach enhances immune cell characterization, revealing new functional states and rare subpopulations in complex biological systems. Here, we provide a detailed protocol for performing CITE-seq, from sample preparation to sequencing and data analysis. We highlight key experimental considerations, discuss challenges related to antibody selection and batch effects, and provide troubleshooting strategies to ensure robust and reproducible results. The integration of transcriptomic and proteomic data through CITE-seq provides unparalleled insights into cellular function, with broad applications in immunology, oncology, and systems biology.

abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) culture systems are powerful in vitro tools that have revolutionized the study of intestinal stem cell biology. These culture systems derived from mouse intestinal and colonic epithelia enable the modeling of tissue architecture, barrier function, and disease mechanisms under physiologically relevant conditions. This protocol details methods for isolating and maintaining mouse intestinal crypts as 2D monolayers. Monolayers are established via enzymatic dissociation and seeding onto ECM-functionalized hydrogels. abstract: Lipids are a fundamental group of biomolecules that play diverse roles in biological systems, including energy storage, membrane architecture, and intra- and extracellular signaling. They are classified into eight major categories, and more than 50 000 distinct lipid structures are currently reported in the Lipid Maps Structure Database (LMSD). Given their importance in cellular metabolism and physiology, accurate identification and quantification of lipids are essential. In ticks, lipid metabolism is closely associated with physiological processes related to survival, pathogen transmission, and host interaction. Tick blood-feeding has also been linked to the development of alpha-gal syndrome (AGS), a delayed allergic reaction to mammalian-derived products, suggesting that characterization of tick lipid and glycolipid composition may provide insights into mechanisms of host sensitization. This chapter describes a protocol for untargeted lipidomic analysis of tick samples using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry (UHPLC-HRMS). The workflow includes rapid sample freezing, tissue homogenization, solvent-based lipid extraction, protein precipitation, and sample reconstitution prior to analysis. Lipid separation is achieved using reverse-phase chromatography on a C18 column, followed by detection with a quadrupole time-of-flight (Q-TOF) mass spectrometer operating under optimized ionization conditions. The use of blanks and pooled quality control (QC) samples ensures analytical stability and reproducibility. The presented method enables comprehensive profiling of lipids in tick tissues and provides a reproducible platform for studies of tick biology, host-tick interactions, and tick-induced sensitization processes, supporting the mechanistic studies and the identification of potential lipid-based biomarkers.

abstract: Fish epidermal keratocytes provide a powerful model system for investigating cell motility due to their rapid, persistent migration and stable morphology. While single-cell dynamics have been extensively characterized, recent studies have increasingly focused on collective migration. Because keratocytes cannot be maintained as continuous cell lines, experiments rely on primary cultures derived from fish scales. This chapter presents optimized protocols for culturing primary keratocytes, transiently introducing fluorescent probes using a custom electroporation system and performing high-resolution three-dimensional time-lapse imaging with confocal microscopy. These procedures enable visualization of dynamic molecular and cellular behaviors in both single-cell and collective migration contexts.

abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a paradigmatic fusion-driven cancer in which oncogenic FET::ETS transcription factor fusions orchestrate complex regulatory, epigenomic, transcriptional, and proteomic programs. Despite extensive molecular profiling, biological insight, and translational progress, EwS are strongly shaped by how data are generated, structured, and shared across heterogeneous initiatives. Fragmented cohorts, uneven molecular depth, and limited longitudinal sampling influence both integrative analyses and systems-level interpretation. This chapter is organized around this structural reality. It first maps the current EwS data landscape, including patient-derived and preclinical omics datasets, profiling initiatives, repositories, and annotation resources, highlighting how their design and governance define the biological questions that can be addressed. It then synthesizes key biological insights derived from genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and single-cell studies, with an emphasis on regulatory logic, transcriptional plasticity, and context-dependent vulnerabilities revealed through integrative analyses. Particular attention is given to the predominance of preclinical approaches in systems-level EwS biology, reflecting the experimental resolution required to interrogate regulatory mechanisms that remain largely inaccessible in most patient cohorts. Finally, the chapter examines how these observations motivate a shift from opportunistic data aggregation toward intentionally designed EwS-specific data ecosystems. It discusses the technical, ethical, and organizational requirements for longitudinal, multilayer profiling and federated data access, and argues that such infrastructures are necessary to support reproducible systems biology and therapeutic translation in EwS.

abstract: Cell migration is a crucial biological process involved in immune responses, early stages of development, metastasis of cancer, and also wound healing. abstract: Apical-basal polarity is essential for gastrointestinal epithelium function, where the apical membrane mediates nutrient absorption, host-microbiota interactions, and pathogen defense. However, conventional intestinal organoid culture displays an "apical-in" topology, limiting functional research with respect to the apical membrane. F-actin labeling with fluorescent phalloidin, a well-established apical marker, is also incompatible with live imaging. To address these limitations, in this chapter we describe an extracellular matrix (ECM) removal protocol to achieve "apical-out" topology in porcine intestinal organoid model and further validated WGA and Nile Red live imaging tracers enabling discrimination between apical-out (AO) and basal-out (BO) organoids. Subsequently, using integrated computational pipelines (automatic nuclei segmentation and single-nucleus phasor-based lifetime analysis), we can quantify organoid proliferative states at single-nucleus resolution following BrdU and Hoechst 33342 staining. Using the analysis of Hoechst 33342 fluorescence lifetime, we demonstrate that both organoid topologies exhibit intrinsic proliferative heterogeneity, but overall proliferative capacity is topology-dependent: apical-out organoids displayed decreased proliferation, whereas basal-out organoids remain highly proliferative.

abstract: Proteomics datasets require detailed and standardized metadata annotation to ensure reproducibility, reusability, and alignment with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles. This chapter presents a practical, hands-on workflow for annotating a label-free proteomics dataset using the Sample and Data Relationship Format for Proteomics (SDRF-Proteomics), a HUPO-PSI and EuBIC-MS standard that has been adopted by major proteomics data repositories. We demonstrate the process on a COVID-19 nasal-swab dataset (PXD020394), showing how to derive sample and assay metadata from the study files, encode them in SDRF with the lesSDRF web application, and validate the result. Although the worked example is label-free, the approach can be generalized to other quantification strategies.

abstract:
Background

Globally in 2024, only 54% of people diagnosed with tuberculosis received an initial WHO-recommended rapid molecular diagnostic test. Pooled testing could expand access to molecular detection using existing laboratory capacity. We aimed to evaluate the performance of pooled tuberculosis testing in a multicentre diagnostic accuracy study.

Methods

In this prospective diagnostic accuracy study, we enrolled individuals with presumptive tuberculosis through facility-based case finding (district hospitals and primary health centres) and community-based case finding in Bangladesh, Brazil, Cameroon, Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria, and Viet Nam between Nov 30, 2023, and Feb 27, 2025. Sputum was tested individually on Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra (Xpert Ultra) and in pools of two, three, or four specimens on Xpert Ultra. Culture was used as the microbiological reference standard. We estimated the sensitivity and specificity of pooled testing versus culture, positive percent agreement (PPA) versus individual Xpert Ultra, and cartridge savings.

Findings

Results were available for 14 040 (95·2%) participants from 3666 pools, including 3195 (87·2%) pools of four. Using culture as the reference standard, sensitivity of pooled testing versus individual Xpert Ultra was 84·9% (95% CI 82·5-87·0) versus 88·0% (85·9-90·0), and specificity was 98·3% (98·0-98·5) versus 97·7% (97·4-97·9). PPA was 90·1% (95% CI 88·4-91·7), remaining above 96% for high (98·1% [96·1-99·2]), medium (98·3% [95·8-99·5]), and low (96·5% [93·8-98·2]) individual Xpert Ultra semiquantitative grades, but lower for very low (86·6% [79·9-91·7]) and trace (55·4% [47·9-62·7]) grades. Pooled testing used 7028 cartridges versus 14 362 for individual testing, a 51·1% reduction.

Interpretation

Pooled testing with Xpert Ultra had slightly higher specificity and a 3·2 percentage points lower sensitivity compared with individual Xpert Ultra, and required half the cartridge use. Scale-up of this approach could facilitate expanded access to molecular testing in low to moderate tuberculosis positivity settings without the need for additional infrastructure.

abstract: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium that infects the columnar epithelium of the human endocervix. While conventional two-dimensional cell cultures and animal models have been instrumental in advancing our understanding of C. trachomatis biology, they are limited in capturing the multicellularity, architecture, and physiological microenvironment of the human cervix. This chapter describes the use of a three-dimensional (3D) microphysiologic model to study Chlamydia trachomatis infection. The model is inexpensively made without specialized equipment and is designed to recreate the epithelial-stromal interface. We outline procedures for coculturing cervical epithelial cells and fibroblasts, infecting epithelial cells with fluorescently labeled C. trachomatis, monitoring infection progression via fluorescent microscopy, and quantifying infectious progeny. The complete developmental cycle of C. trachomatis within this model provides a robust and accessible platform to investigate C. trachomatis-specific host-pathogen interactions, immune responses, and the influence of diverse physiological and environmental stimuli within a relevant cervical context.

abstract: G-quadruplex (G4) nucleic acids have been shown to regulate a wide range of cellular processes, including replication, telomere maintenance, epigenetic landscape, and various aspects of transcription and translation. In this method, we describe an experimental purification procedure for identifying RNA G-quadruplex-binding proteins from nuclear extracts. Using biotinylated oligonucleotides allows immobilization to streptavidin-coated magnetic beads and convenient washing during the pulldown. Importantly, the experimental protocol presented here can distinguish protein interactions with structured and unstructured RNA within the same oligonucleotide by controlling ionic conditions throughout the folding, RNA pulldown, and washing steps. The binding of individual candidate proteins can be determined by western blotting, while mass spectrometry can readily identify the whole RNA G-quadruplex-interacting proteome.

abstract: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) represents a significant global health threat due to its recent resurgence. abstract: The rapid growth of biomedical literature has created an urgent need for computational tools that enable researchers to systematically analyze publication trends, identify emerging research themes, and map the evolution of scientific fields. PubMed Atlas is a command-line and web-enabled workflow for topic-driven bibliometrics and trend intelligence using PubMed E-utilities. The pipeline executes PubMed queries, retrieves matching PMIDs, downloads full metadata records in batches, parses structured information (title, abstract, authors/affiliations, MeSH terms, publication types, grants, keywords, DOI), and stores normalized data in a local SQLite database for rapid querying and visualization. A Streamlit dashboard provides interactive exploration of publication trends, journal distributions, MeSH term summaries, geographic distributions, and recent article browsing with direct PubMed links. This protocol describes the installation, configuration, and operation of PubMed Atlas for cancer stem cell and stem cell transcriptional network research, and other fields, enabling investigators to conduct reproducible bibliometric analyses and identify knowledge gaps in rapidly evolving fields.

abstract: Histopathological analysis of tissues infected with Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), including biopsy and autopsy specimens, can provide valuable insights into the pathogenesis of atypical and fatal cases. By examining tissue architecture and cellular alterations under the microscope, it is possible to identify patterns of injury, inflammation, and cellular degeneration. These morphological findings provide evidence of how the pathogen interacts with host cells and tissues. Moreover, immunohistochemistry may be performed in tissue sections for the detection of viral antigens. Importantly, this technique allows the characterization of diverse biologically relevant targets in tissue samples, such as distinct immune cell subsets, cytokines, and additional molecular markers. This is accomplished by the use of antibodies selected for their specificity toward the antigen of interest. In this chapter, we present a concise overview of how histological analysis and immunohistochemical approaches can enhance the understanding of CHIKV-associated pathological mechanisms.

abstract: Rice is the most important staple food crop cultivated by millions of small-holder farmers. The effective utilization of extensive genetic diversity leads to sustainable rice production. The 3000 Rice Genomes Project is a publicly accessible giga-dataset of genomic sequences with an average coverage depth of 14×, derived from 3000 rice accessions that represent global genetic and functional diversity. Seeds of these accessions are conserved in the International Rice Genebank Collection, and these resources constitute an unprecedented platform for advancing rice science and modern breeding strategies. A key challenge with the available dataset is the need for comprehensive, systematic mining to associate genomic variation with functional traits. SNP discovery from the 3 K rice panel for specific traits provides a robust foundation for dissecting genetic diversity, population structure, and evolutionary relationships in cultivated rice, ultimately enabling the creation of new varieties to support the world population.

abstract: Shoot architecture, mainly determined by tiller angle, is a key agronomic trait affecting crop yield. Winter wheat undergoes dynamic erect-prostrate growth transitions in response to low temperatures during overwintering, yet the coordinated regulation of shoot architecture by temperature and gravity remains elusive. In this study, we identified TaHGH1, an HSFA2 transcription factor, via GWAS and found it positively regulates shoot gravitropism and thereby reduces tiller angle. TaHGH1 promotes amyloplast abundance to enhance gravitropism; heat-induced transcription and cold-induced alternative splicing of TaHGH1 jointly modulate gravitropism and the erect-prostrate-erect growth shift. Mechanistically, TaHGH1 directly activates TaLAX3 and TaARF19, leading to asymmetric auxin distribution and differential cell elongation. Beneficial TaHGH1 haplotypes associated with compact architecture and increased spikelet number have undergone global artificial selection. Our work reveals a molecular module integrating thermal and gravity signals for adaptive shoot architecture, providing valuable targets for high-yield wheat breeding.

abstract: DNA undergoes a wide range of chemical reactions every day, and such DNA lesions might have deleterious consequences as they not only affect cellular components and biological processes but can also accumulate permanently in the genome. Since DNA alterations eventually lead to multiple detrimental consequences, including genomic instability and cancer predisposition, these lesions must be efficiently detected and repaired by tightly regulated mechanisms to maintain genome integrity. Various DNA repair mechanisms contribute to the correction of the alterations that occur every day to prevent genomic instability, providing key insights into genome editing. Genome editing is a significant exogenous mutagen, in which conventional editing strategies cause double-strand breaks, and nickases induce single-strand breaks, albeit base editing depends on the modulation of base excision repair, and prime editing results in mismatches. A comprehensive understanding of DNA repair mechanisms is strategically important for genome editing applications. In this chapter, we discuss the pivotal DNA repair mechanisms to provide a better insight into the role of DNA repair mechanisms in genome editing.

abstract: Cancer cell identity is governed by coordinated transcriptional programs that are frequently rewired during tumorigenesis. Systematic identification of cancer type-specific gene regulatory networks provides a framework for understanding oncogenic state transitions and for prioritizing candidate therapeutic targets. Here, we present a reproducible network-based workflow for reconstructing and analyzing transcriptional regulatory programs across human cancer types using publicly available expression datasets. We describe procedures for curating and preprocessing microarray data from the Gene Expression Omnibus, implementing random forest classification, and reconstructing gene regulatory networks using the CellNet platform. Detailed guidance is provided for evaluating classifier performance, quantifying network influence scores, integrating transcription factor, target interaction resources, and performing functional enrichment analyses. In addition, we outline approaches for comparing cancer-specific networks with corresponding normal tissue profiles to identify candidate drivers of malignant cell identity and potential prognostic biomarkers. Together, these protocols provide investigators with a scalable computational framework for defining cancer type-specific transcriptional states and for systematically interrogating regulatory mechanisms underlying tumor heterogeneity.

abstract:
Objective

Disruption of the circadian clock, such as during ageing, is linked to cartilage degeneration in mice and increased osteoarthritis (OA) risk in humans. This study investigated whether heat pulses can resynchronise dampened circadian rhythms in articular cartilage.

Methods

Femoral head cartilage explants were isolated from PER2::LUC circadian reporter mice. Tissues were exposed to heat shock at various temperatures and durations. Circadian bioluminescence from explants was recorded in real-time over several days. Pharmacological compounds were used to investigate the pathways involved in clock resynchronisation.

Results

We established that a 60-min pulse at 43 °C resynchronises PER2::LUC rhythms in cartilage explants from young and aged mice. The heat shock was able to counteract circadian disruption caused by IL-1α treatment. Mechanistically, inhibition of HSP90 activity or perturbation of F-actin polymerisation markedly attenuated the heat-induced resynchronisation of circadian rhythms.

Conclusion

An acute 43 °C heat pulse enhanced the circadian amplitude and reset the phase of damped PER2::LUC rhythms in ex vivo murine cartilage. Pharmacological sensitivity to 17-DMAG (HSP90 inhibitor) and agents affecting actin/Rho-ROCK signalling implicates these pathways in the response. These findings identify heat as an experimental synchronising cue for cartilage clocks and support further investigations of heating regimens in OA-relevant models.

This method also enables multiplexing such that different species of RNA can be detected at the same time.

abstract: Outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) from different Gram-negative bacteria, including Salmonella spp., have appeared as potential acellular vaccine candidates for their role in host-pathogen interaction by delivering virulence factors and modulating immune response. Given this host-cell contact, it is crucial to assess their genotoxic effects to ensure safety as vaccine candidates. The Comet assay, a sensitive and effective method for detecting single-cell DNA strand breaks, offers an effective approach for evaluating such effects. This study explores the application of the Comet assay as a highly sensitive approach to investigate the potential genotoxicity of Salmonella-derived OMVs in mammalian cells, with important implications for understanding host-pathogen interactions and cellular DNA damage, and providing a reproducible workflow for evaluating minimal DNA strand alterations in vitro as part of Salmonella-OMV safety studies.

abstract: Genetic manipulation of Chlamydia trachomatis is challenging because of its obligate intracellular lifestyle and reduced genome with a high proportion of essential genes. Functional analysis of chlamydial genes often requires alternative genetic strategies such as conditional knockdown rather than gene disruption. This chapter describes the use of an engineered small RNA (sRNA) to achieve inducible protein knockdown in C. trachomatis. This approach utilizes the C. trachomatis sRNA CtrR3 as a scaffold to express a targeting sequence that interferes with a target mRNA by binding its 5' untranslated region (UTR), in the region of the ribosome-binding site (RBS) and start codon. The protocol detailed here covers design of the targeting sequence, bioinformatic analysis to minimize off-target binding, construction of the knockdown sRNA plasmid, generation of a chlamydial transformant expressing the engineered sRNA, induction of protein depletion, assessment of knockdown efficiency and phenotypes, and complementation to demonstrate knockdown specificity.

abstract: The interaction of RNA helicases and non-canonical G-rich quadruplex (G4) structures in all aspects of RNA metabolism is a rapidly expanding field of study. Both cellular and viral RNA helicases dynamically maintain and disrupt G4 RNA structures in multiple compartments of the cell for efficient trafficking, transcription, splicing, translation, and, in the case of viral RNA genomes, replication. The conserved domains shared by diverse members of the helicase superfamilies for RNA binding and ATP-mediated duplex unwinding suggest that quadruplex disruption is a critical activity for many helicases. To probe the conditions and required energetics for quadruplex interaction and unwinding, robust in vitro assays are needed. To overcome the challenges of studying G4 unwinding under optimized conditions, we have adapted standard helicase unwinding assays to closely examine quadruplex dynamics. This chapter provides detailed protocols for describing the capacity for RNA helicases to remodel G4 structures.

abstract: The division of a mother cell into two daughter cells is a fundamental process in biology, involving the transfer of genomic information to the next generation of cells. In plant roots, cell divisions occur in the root apical meristem, a specialized tissue located at the plant's root tip. Cell proliferation rates in the root apical meristem shape root growth, thereby contributing to general development as well as the acclimatization to stressful environmental conditions through phenotypic plasticity. Here, we present a protocol for the microscopical analysis of cell proliferation in Arabidopsis thaliana root meristems by 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) staining. EdU, a thymine-analog, is incorporated into newly synthesized DNA of proliferative cells during the S-phase of the cell cycle. Subsequently, EdU-containing nuclei can be labeled with a fluorophore and detected by confocal laser scanning microscopy. The combination of the EdU assay with cell wall staining enables the quantification of root meristem architecture parameters and cell division activity from microscopic images. Together, this can elucidate how root meristems respond to changes in environmental conditions or address fundamental questions of developmental plant biology.

abstract: Nonhuman primate (NHP) models are important in biomedical research due to their close evolutionary relationship with humans, which provides a high degree of anatomical, genetic, and physiological similarity. This close resemblance is particularly valuable for studying complex biological processes and diseases that are difficult to model in other animals. NHPs have hematopoietic and immune systems that closely mirror those of humans, making them crucial for researching hematopoietic stem cell biology, immunology, infectious diseases, and vaccine development, offering insights that are more likely to translate to human health. With the rapid development of immunotherapy, the NHP model serves as an invaluable tool for preclinical studies of immunotherapy. Immunophenotyping, the process of characterizing and quantifying hematopoietic cell populations and their functional states, is critical in studies related to the hematopoietic and immune system. While the NHP model is the most relevant animal model for human biology, the immunophenotyping methods used may not always align with those employed for human samples. This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of key considerations for conducting immunophenotyping studies using NHP models, particularly in the rhesus macaque model. It covers methodological aspects, including sample preparation, the selection and validation of appropriate antibody clones, the application of flow cytometry techniques, and the data analysis to ensure high-quality and reproducible results. By providing a comprehensive overview of these considerations, this chapter aims to equip researchers with the knowledge needed to effectively utilize rhesus macaque NHP models in immunophenotyping studies, ultimately enhancing the translational impact of their findings on human health.

abstract: Cas9-guide RNA ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are widely used for genome editing because they provide rapid, transient nuclease activity without introducing exogenous DNA into target cells. Efficient RNP delivery requires a highly purified, correctly folded Cas9 protein that is free of contaminating nucleases and small-molecule impurities. This chapter describes the expression of N-terminally His-tagged Cas9 from a pET28b vector in Escherichia coli Rosetta strains, followed by purification using Ni-NTA immobilized metal affinity chromatography (IMAC) and size exclusion chromatography (SEC) on a Superdex 200 Increase column. The protocol covers bacterial fermentation, cell lysis, IMAC with high-salt and graded-imidazole washes, SEC polishing, dialysis into a storage buffer, and concentration to RNP-ready stocks, with quality control by SDS-PAGE and optional western blotting and BCA assay. Finally, a short procedure for assembling Cas9 RNPs with in vitro-transcribed guide RNAs is provided, making the protocol directly applicable to CRISPR RNP delivery in mammalian cells.

abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs), particles released from cells, have the potential to become an important in vivo delivery vehicle for CRISPR machinery. Unlike viral vectors such as Adeno-associated virus (AAV), EVs reduce risks associated with immunogenicity, long-term expression, and potential off-target effects. EVs can efficiently deliver CRISPR/Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes, which provide transient, ready-to-function editing machinery with reduced off-target risk compared with plasmid DNA or mRNA delivery. RNP loading into EVs can occur without specific targeting signals, although strategies such as membrane anchoring, inducible dimerization systems, or fusion with EV-associated proteins can enhance cargo enrichment. EVs are typically produced by transfecting producer cells with plasmids encoding Cas9 and sgRNA, followed by vesicle release into culture media. Purification requires removal of cellular debris and enrichment of vesicles using methods such as ultracentrifugation, ultrafiltration, chromatography, or precipitation. As no single gold-standard purification approach exists, method selection should balance yield and purity, and characterization using vesicle markers and size distribution profiling is recommended.

abstract: This chapter presents a stepwise optimization of a Matrigel<sup>®</sup>-based in vitro angiogenesis assay using human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) to achieve reproducible and quantifiable tube formation. Critical parameters-including culture surface, matrix composition and thickness, coating temperature and incubation time, growth factor-defined serum-free medium, and cell seeding density-were systematically evaluated. Optimal conditions were identified as 3 mg/mL Matrigel (100 μL/well), polymerized at 22 °C for 90 min, with HUVECs seeded at 20,000 cells/cm<sup>2</sup> and cultured in a defined growth factor cocktail. Standardized imaging and ImageJ-based analysis enabled robust quantification of network features. This protocol improves consistency, stability, and comparability across angiogenesis studies.

abstract: Recent advances in mass spectrometry instrumentation and computational analysis have established label-free data-independent acquisition (DIA) as a powerful tool in quantitative proteomics, offering depth, throughput, and reproducibility. These developments now enable large-scale projects with hundreds or even thousands of samples, opening new applications in systems biology and biomedicine. However, large-scale datasets require special consideration during data preprocessing. Here, we present a practical guide for preprocessing large-scale DIA datasets, illustrated using a public dataset. We cover key steps, including database searching, normalization, batch correction, missing value imputation, and evaluation of preprocessing strategies, and provide R code together with practical considerations.

abstract: In plant roots, the diversity of tissues along the radial axis and of developmental stages along the longitudinal axis implies a highly dynamic and heterogeneous gene expression. Many master regulators of gene expression exhibit distinctive temporal expression patterns or are restricted to specific cell types, making whole-root molecular analyses insufficient to resolve their roles in developmental and physiological processes. Here, we report a protocol for fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)-coupled RNA sequencing to analyze, reconstruct, and ultimately dissect the gene regulatory networks (GRNs) involved in root development and physiology, particularly well-suited for genes that are expressed transiently or in rare or restricted cell types. The method relies on selecting an appropriate cell-type-specific reporter line, which enables the isolation of labeled cells with high specificity and minimal contamination. Furthermore, we discuss the relative advantages of FACS-coupled RNA-seq compared with alternative gene-expression methodologies, including quantitative PCR (qPCR), bulk root RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq), and spatial transcriptomics, considering sensitivity, resolution, input requirements, and cost.

abstract: Gap junctions (GJ), formed by connexins (Cx), are mediators of intercellular communication between adjacent cells by allowing the transfer of small molecules. Connexins assemble to form hemichannels, which are then transported to the plasma membrane. There, they can either function independently or dock with adjacent hemichannels to form gap junctions. The epidermis is an avascular tissue and depends on connexin-mediated communication to maintain epidermal cell homeostasis and dysregulation of connexins can lead to human disorders. Keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness (KID) syndrome is caused by mutations in the GJB2 gene, encoding Cx26 protein, and the severity of the phenotypes varies among individuals carrying distinct mutations. The effects of mutations on channel functions can be assessed by various techniques. Here, we describe approaches to assess hemichannel and gap junctional activity in HaCaT cells that constitutively express Cx26 KID syndrome mutations. Ethidium bromide (EtBr) can be used in scrape loading assay to investigate GJ channel activity, and neurobiotin in dye uptake assay can be used to determine hemichannel functionality using fluorescence microscopy.

abstract: Maize is the third most significant cereal crop, and most of its agronomic traits are quantitative in nature. The fine mapping of genes or quantitative trait loci (QTLs) associated with these traits is essential for marker-assisted selection (MAS) in maize breeding. Although significant progress has been made, there remains a lack of high-density, highly polymorphic single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers, especially competitive allele-specific PCR (KASP) SNP markers suitable for automated genotyping. The development of next-generation sequencing (NGS) platforms has generated vast amounts of whole-genome and transcriptome data, providing a valuable resource for identifying SNP loci for marker development. KASP markers, being cost-effective and reliable, provide a trustworthy molecular toolbox for the precise genetic analysis of major key agronomic traits and the rapid improvement of maize using MAS.

abstract: The recent application of experimental and computational drug discovery workflows has identified hundreds of new molecules that display potent, and in some cases highly selective, activity against bacteria of the genus Chlamydia. The full value of these novel antichlamydial molecules, however, depends critically on our ability to determine their molecular targets and modes of action. A particularly powerful and widely applied strategy for identifying candidate targets involves selecting for bacterial mutants that have acquired resistance to a compound's inhibitory activity, followed by determining the mutations responsible for this resistance. Such mutations often pinpoint the compound's direct target or reveal cellular pathways that modulate target engagement. Here, we present a detailed, step-by-step protocol for applying this approach to the clinically important, human-pathogenic species Chlamydia trachomatis. The workflow includes: (1) determining compound potency by quantitative dose-response analysis, (2) generating a resistant C. trachomatis mutant through serial passaging under progressively increasing selective pressure, (3) confirming the resistance phenotype, and (4) isolating bacterial genomic DNA for whole-genome sequencing to identify resistance-associated mutations and facilitate downstream target discovery.

abstract: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) represent the complex interplay of transcription factors, regulatory elements, and target genes that orchestrate cellular identity and function, playing a crucial role in the differentiation and maintenance of stem cells. This chapter provides an overview of experimental and computational methodologies for inferring GRNs, with particular emphasis on single-cell approaches. We first review key experimental techniques for detecting transcription factor binding sites, chromatin accessibility, and DNA motifs, alongside essential databases that support GRN reconstruction. We then introduce computational inference methods that can be categorized into four principal frameworks: correlation-based approaches, regression and machine learning models, probabilistic and deep learning methods, and integrative or message-passing frameworks. To illustrate practical application, we present a case study applying the pySCENIC workflow to a peripheral blood mononuclear cell single-cell RNA sequencing dataset from mouse, demonstrating how regulon-based analysis can reveal cell-type-specific regulatory programs. This chapter aims to serve as a practical guide for researchers seeking to understand and implement GRN inference methodologies in stem cell biology and related fields.
