abstract:
Background

KBG syndrome (OMIM #148050) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by haploinsufficiency of ANKRD11 on chromosome 16q24.3. Populations outside Western Europe and North America remain underrepresented in the literature, and cohorts that comprehensively evaluate both sequence variants and copy-number variants (CNVs) remain limited.

Aims

To characterize the clinical and molecular spectrum of KBG syndrome associated with an identified ANKRD11 alteration in a Turkish multicenter cohort, investigate genotype-phenotype correlations, and assess the contributions of sequence variants and CNVs to disease diagnosis and variant interpretation.

Study design

Multicenter, retrospective cohort study.

Methods

We retrospectively evaluated the clinical, anthropometric, and molecular characteristics of 36 Turkish individuals with KBG syndrome and an identified ANKRD11 alteration (31 pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants and five variants of uncertain significance) who were recruited from multiple pediatric genetics centers. Molecular analyses included whole-exome sequencing, clinical exome sequencing, and chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA). Variants were classified according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics/Association for Molecular Pathology guidelines. An exploratory genotype-phenotype analysis was performed by comparing truncating, non-truncating sequence variant, and CNV/deletion groups using Fisher's exact and Mann-Whitney U tests, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons.

Results

The cohort comprised 22 males and 14 females (male-to-female ratio, 1.57:1). A total of 29 distinct ANKRD11 alterations were identified, including 25 sequence variants and four distinct 16q24.3 deletions. Truncating variants were predominant (n = 25), while 11 sequence variants and four distinct 16q24.3 deletions further expanded the known molecular spectrum of KBG syndrome. The recurrent variant c.1903_1907del (p.Lys635GlnfsTer26) was identified in three unrelated individuals, supporting exon 9 as a major mutational hotspot. All three missense variants were clustered within the C-terminal degron, consistent with the previously reported enrichment of pathogenic missense variants in this functionally important region. 16q24.3 deletions accounted for 19.4% (7/36) of cases, underscoring the diagnostic value of copy-number analysis in patients with suspected KBG syndrome.

Conclusion

This study finding expand the clinical and molecular spectrum associated with ANKRD11, provide further evidence supporting haploinsufficiency as the primary disease mechanism, and underscore the diagnostic importance of CMA in syndromic neurodevelopmental disorders. Furthermore, integrating our cohort data with published findings provides a practical framework for interpreting ANKRD11 variants, particularly those involving the 5' regulatory region and C-terminal missense variants.

abstract: Using technology to radically improve performance or the influence of business, known as digital transformation, could reshape health care by making care more accessible, personalized, and data-driven, leading to improved patient outcomes and more efficient care delivery. Currently, there is no standardized definition of digital transformation specifically within the context of clinical genetics service delivery. Using Walker and Avant's method of concept analysis, a comprehensive overview of digital transformation in clinical genetics is provided through identifying the concept and describing its attributes, antecedents, consequences, and empirical referents. Six key attributes of digital transformation in clinical genetics were identified: technology-driven data integration, efficiency, patient-centeredness, safety and privacy, equitable access, and outcome improvement. The following definition is proposed: digital transformation in clinical genetics is the integration of data-driven advanced technologies, such as artificial intelligence, data analytics, and digital platforms, into the delivery of genetic services to improve efficiency, enhance patient-centered care, ensure equitable access to services, and optimize clinical outcomes, all while prioritizing the safety and privacy of personal, familial, and genetic data through robust data management. A clear and formal definition will assist practitioners in understanding how digital transformation fits into the evolving landscape of clinical genetics.

abstract: Medical genetics serves as a bridge between basic medical science and clinical courses. With its complex curriculum and abstract concepts, traditional lecture-based teaching often leads to difficulties in comprehension, diminishes students' interest in learning, and results in poor teaching outcomes. Incorporating typical case studies into instruction can make genetic theories more tangible, enhance students' intuitive understanding, facilitate their grasp of abstract concepts, and boost their interest in learning. Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is a group of hereditary neurological disorders characterized by progressive spastic paraplegia of both lower limbs. As a monogenic disorder, HSP exhibits high genetic heterogeneity. To date, more than 80 distinct disease-causing genes have been identified, encompassing various inheritance patterns such as autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked recessive inheritance. HSP has been included in China's first batch of rare disease listings, creating a need for genetic counseling. Prenatal diagnosis and differential diagnosis typically require integration with genetic testing. Case-based teaching focused on HSP can comprehensively cover the core concepts of medical genetics and help students develop a complete clinical genetic reasoning process from clinical phenotype to family analysis, genetic diagnosis, and risk assessment. Based on this educational philosophy, members in our teaching team explored teaching materials focusing on the genetic characteristics of HSP, including disease genes, genetic effect of mutation, pathogenesis, inheritance patterns, genetic diagnosis, and clinical treatment to construct a comprehensive, integrated case-based teaching framework and incorporated it throughout the teaching practice of medical genetics. Teachers implemented this instructional design in their medical genetics courses, transforming abstract theoretical instruction into accessible case-based teaching, which stimulated students' interest in learning and enhanced their ability to understand theories related to genetic diseases. This teaching reform facilitated the effective integration of genetic knowledge with clinical applications, fostered the development of clinical reasoning and research literacy among medical students, and provided an innovative method for medical genetics teaching.

abstract:
Background

The integration of genomic medicine into clinical practice has become increasingly important for frontline clinicians. Pediatricians represent a particularly important group, as they routinely encounter patients with suspected genetic conditions. However, data on genomic knowledge among pediatricians in Turkey - a country with unique epidemiological and healthcare characteristics - remain scarce.

Methods

A cross-sectional survey was conducted between February 10 and March 10, 2026 via Google Forms among 266 pediatricians at various career stages (residents, specialists, subspecialty trainees/specialists, and academics). The survey comprised a demographic section, four Likert-type self-assessment items, and 15 objective knowledge questions. Statistical analyses included the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney U tests, chi-square test, one-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD post-hoc analysis, Dunn test with Bonferroni correction for non-parametric comparisons, and Spearman correlation analysis.

Results

The mean knowledge score was 8.67 ± 2.99 out of 15 (57.8%). Mean subscores were 59.8% for basic clinical genetics and 53.8% for advanced genomic therapies, with low-scoring items in both domains. Professional title (H = 34.29, p < 0.001), years of experience (H = 23.70, p < 0.001), and structured genetics training (Mann-Whitney U, p < 0.001) were significantly associated with knowledge scores; in multivariable analysis, title and training, but not experience, remained associated. Overall, 51.5% of participants reported never having received structured genetics education. Knowledge scores did not differ by gender (p = 0.647). Genetics training was associated with genetic test-ordering frequency(χ²=15.46, p = 0.004).

Conclusions

Turkish pediatricians showed moderate knowledge of the genomic topics assessed, with gaps in both basic and advanced topics. Structured genetics education was associated with higher knowledge scores and more frequent genetic test ordering, although the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. These findings support developing and evaluating targeted genomic education for pediatricians.

abstract:
Purpose

Genetic variant reclassification is increasingly common in clinical genomics, yet limited data describe how patients experience re-contact and variant reclassification in routine clinical care.

Methods

We conducted semi-structured qualitative interviews with 20 adult patients who received a variant reclassification following routine clinical genetic testing. Interviews explored emotional responses, communication experiences, and perceived value of genetic testing. Data were analyzed using Template Analysis, a form of thematic analysis.

Results

Three overarching themes were identified. Participants identified a need for improved communication of reclassified results, particularly with respect to timing, modality, and contextualization (Theme 1). Experiences with reclassification also shaped perceptions of the value of genetic testing, with most participants viewing testing as worthwhile despite its evolving nature (Theme 2). Finally, many participants interpreted reclassification as evidence of personalized and ongoing care, reinforcing trust in genetic testing and biomedical research (Theme 3). Participants generally preferred to be informed of reclassified results regardless of reclassification type, although the direction of reclassification influenced emotional responses and preferred modes of communication. Downgrades from variants of uncertain significance to benign or likely benign were widely viewed as meaningful by participants.

Conclusion

Variant reclassification was experienced as a signal of personalized, ongoing care. Timely, contextualized, patient-centered re-contact practices may reduce uncertainty, strengthen trust, and help patients not feel forgotten.

abstract: Traditional in-person consultations for genetic services create access barriers. We hypothesized that the Genetics Adviser platform-a web-based digital platform delivering clinical genomic services-could reduce these barriers. Focusing on pretest education and counseling, we tested a pilot version of the platform in medical genetics and pediatric endocrinology group practices. The multimethod design consisted of quantitative patient and caregiver surveys, Google Analytics data, and qualitative healthcare provider interviews. Surveys included validated measures of acceptability and empowerment. Transcribed interviews were thematically coded and analyzed using NVivo. Of the 102 patients and caregivers targeted for this study, 85/102 (83%) accessed the platform, 71/102 (70%) proceeded beyond the landing page, and 60/102 (59%) completed the post-module survey. Users expressed high confidence in genetic understanding and empowerment (Genomics Outcome Scale [GOS]: 77/100), and providers noted potential benefits and highlighted technological and content-related limitations. Further research is needed to validate effectiveness across diverse populations and to evaluate long-term impacts on patient outcomes and healthcare efficiency.

abstract:
Introduction

Genetic testing benefits individuals and families with inherited eye diseases by facilitating accurate diagnosis, informing prognosis, enabling assessment for at-risk family members, and supporting targeted therapies. This study aimed to characterize the spectrum of inherited eye disorders and evaluate the diagnostic yield of genetic testing at a single tertiary eye care centre over a one-year period.

Methods

A retrospective review of patients attending the ocular genetics service at a tertiary eye care centre in India from January 1 to December 31, 2024, was conducted.

Results

Of 1325 patients evaluated, 862 (65%) underwent genetic testing. Inherited retinal disorders were the most common (n = 440, 51%), followed by cornea and anterior segment disorders (n = 107, 12.4%). Other conditions included hereditary optic nerve disorders (n = 75, 8.7%), glaucoma (n = 70, 8.1%), lenticular disorders (n = 54, 6.3%), phacomatoses (n = 25, 2.9%), ocular tumours (n = 20, 2.3%), strabismus and albinism (n = 19 and 18; ~2% each), MAC spectrum disorders (n = 10, 1.4%), and systemic syndromes (n = 22, 2.5%). Diagnostic yield was achieved in 605 (70%), while 257 (30%) remained inconclusive. Of the 463 untested families, the motivations were unascertained reasons (n = 156, 33%), financial constraints (n = 138, 30%), intent to test later (n = 90, 19%), and belief that no treatment was available (n = 79, 17%).

Discussion

Inherited retinal and anterior segment disorders constitute the most frequent genetic eye diseases. Genetic testing has enabled genotype-phenotype correlation in over two-thirds of cases. Financial constraints and limited availability of disease-modifying treatments remain key barriers for uptake of genetic testing.

abstract:
Purpose

TRranscription EXport (TREX) is an evolutionarily conserved multifunctional complex with essential roles in regulating transcription, mRNA export, genome stability, cell differentiation and survival. We aimed to determine if variation in the TREX subunits, in addition to THOC2 and THOC6 genes, caused Neurodevelopmental Disorders.

Methods

Through international collaboration we aggregated and assessed 40 individuals with high impact variants across four TREX subunit coding genes: THOC2 and THOC6 (known disease genes), and THOC7 and ALYREF (THOC4) (candidate disease genes).

Results

On the background of considerable heterogeneity of neurodevelopmental and clinical outcomes, we noted that all TREX subunit variants impact cognitive functioning and development, speech and the respiratory systems as well as result in recognisable facial dysmorphism. We identified and studied five recurrent THOC2 variants, which give overlapping yet variable clinical presentations, including severe perinatal lethal arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (AMC). Using cells from 13 affected individuals, we show that their TREX subunit variants are generally partial loss of function (LoF), which alter protein localisation, protein stability, protein-protein interactions or delete internal or C-terminal protein functional domains. Cells from affected individuals from across all four TREX subunits studied show consistent, yet variable accumulation of DNA damage.

Conclusion

The molecular, cellular and in silico data with the clinical presentations define a TREX spectrum disorder due to functional variation across multiple TREX subunits.

abstract: The DNA damage response (DDR) pathway has emerged as the central signaling network that preserves genome stability by using sensors to monitor the genome for aberrant structures and establishing signaling centers that promote organismal homeostasis. This review revisits the formative years of DDR research, focusing on the genetic dissection of the pathway in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and its evolution into a broadly conserved eukaryotic signaling system. Early studies of ribonucleotide reductase regulation, replication stress-induced transcription, and cell cycle control identified key regulators, including MEC1, DDC2, TEL1, MRC1, RAD53, DUN1, and RAD9, providing the first evidence that DNA damage signaling is propagated through a protein kinase cascade. This cascade is initiated when RPA binds to ssDNA generated by replication blocks and double-strand DNA breaks, thereby activating the apical MEC1/ATR kinase. These discoveries integrate the contemporaneous cell cycle checkpoint literature into a more comprehensive framework in which the DDR coordinates replication fork stability, replication origin firing, nucleotide metabolism, DNA repair, genome maintenance, and cell cycle control to maintain genomic stability. Parallel studies in Schizosaccharomyces pombe, Xenopus, and mammalian systems revealed the remarkable evolutionary conservation of the pathway and linked DDR dysfunction to a wide spectrum of human diseases, including cancer. In retrospect, the emergence of the DDR field highlights the extraordinary power of classical genetics combined with molecular biology to uncover a complex signaling network that now occupies a central position in chromosome biology, cancer research, aging, immunity, and therapeutic responses.

abstract: Genetic Counselors (GCs) are an integral part of the Canadian health system across clinics, laboratories, and industry. Although most GCs meet educational and certification standards required by professional organizations and workplaces, the profession lacks consistent legal recognition in Canada. As genetic testing options expand, GC practice is extending into novel settings such as primary care and becoming more autonomous to meet growing demand and improve access to service. While GCs are regulated in countries with similar public healthcare systems such as Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom, Canada has yet to establish this critical measure to protect the public against harms such as inaccurate risk assessment, incorrect or inappropriate genetic test ordering, misuse of healthcare resources and undue psychological distress. All national and provincial Canadian GC organizations endorse the need for regulatory oversight across Canadian provinces and territories and recommend that the Canadian Certified Genetic Counsellor (CCGC)/Conseiller(ère) en génétique agréé(e) du Canada (CGAC) credential be adopted as the standard for assessing competence. We call for coordinated action from provincial and territorial governments and Ministries of Health, as well as provincial and national medical and healthcare associations, healthcare providers, employers, patient groups, and our own organizations to advance the implementation of regulation and ultimately improve access to safe genetic healthcare for Canadians.

abstract:
Background

Clonal hematopoiesis (CH), characterized by clonal expansion of hematopoietic stem cells harboring preleukemic mutations, is an emerging cardiovascular disease risk factor. The American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 (LE8) score is the contemporary standard for quantifying cardiovascular health. However, the interplay between this novel genetic risk factor and classical health metrics remains unknown.

Objectives

This study sought to examine the association between LE8 score and CH prevalence, and determine their joint effects on incident coronary artery disease (CAD).

Methods

We analyzed 427,295 UK Biobank participants. Exposures included LE8 score and CH (evaluated as a composite and by common drivers: DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1). Associations with CH prevalence and incident CAD over a median 13.6-year follow-up were evaluated using multivariable regression.

Results

CH prevalence was 3.4%. A higher LE8 score was associated with significantly lower odds of CH and examined driver mutations, strongest for ASXL1 (OR: 0.79; 95% CI: 0.75-0.83; P < 0.001). CH significantly modified the protective effect of LE8 on CAD incidence on multiplicative and additive scales. A 1-SD increase in LE8 yielded an adjusted CAD HR of 0.74 (95% CI: 0.70-0.78) in CH carriers vs 0.68 (95% CI: 0.67-0.69) in noncarriers (Pinteraction = 0.005). Participants with ASXL1 CH subtype and low LE8 scores experienced the highest absolute CAD risk (18.7 vs 2.0 events/1,000 person-years in noncarriers with high LE8).

Conclusions

Optimal cardiovascular health is associated with a lower prevalence of CH. Although maintaining ideal cardiovascular health is associated with lower CAD risk in CH carriers, this protective benefit is attenuated compared with noncarriers.

abstract:
Background

Although genetic diseases cause at least 30% of neuromotor disorders, genome sequencing is not routinely used for diagnosis in such patients. We assessed the diagnostic value in children with complex neuromotor phenotypes.

Methods

We performed trio genome sequencing in 108 children with complex neuromotor phenotypes in 100 families. Genetic disease was diagnosed by a multidisciplinary clinical research team on the basis of each child's complete medical history, clinical course, family history, physical examination, imaging studies, and all other laboratory test results, as well as the findings on genome sequencing. Genetic variants that were suspected of being disease causing were subjected to orthogonal confirmation in a clinically accredited laboratory, which classified the variants it reported according to the ACMG/AMP guidelines.

Findings

We diagnosed genetic diseases that explained the neuromotor phenotype in 53 of the 100 families studied. Almost all of these children had intellectual disability, a seizure disorder, and/or autism spectrum disorder in addition to neuromotor impairment. An important factor contributing to this high diagnostic rate was the use of each patient's complete clinical phenotype, instead of a "molecular diagnosis" based only on the ACMG/AMP variant classification.

Conclusions

Our findings demonstrate that complex neuromotor phenotypes in children are usually manifestations of a more generalized neurodevelopmental disorder and that the ACMG/AMP classification alone is insufficient to establish or exclude a causal relationship between a genomic variant and a suspected genetic disease.

Funding

Canadian Institutes of Health Research, British Columbia Children's Hospital Foundation, and Michael Smith Health Research BC.

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive cancer characterized by profound desmoplasia and cellular heterogeneity, which cannot be fully resolved using traditional bulk sequencing approaches. To understand how this heterogeneity contributes to PDAC biology, we analyzed a large cohort of primary tumors (n = 62) profiled using single-cell RNA sequencing (443,451 single cells), including a subset of 11 tumors with matched spatial transcriptomics (53,236 spots), to map clonal, transcriptional and spatial diversity. Moreover, our sample set includes a unique cohort of matched samples from six tumors collected before and after treatment with chemotherapy. Our analysis revealed notable intratumoral heterogeneity, with multiple genetically distinct neoplastic clones coexisting within individual tumors. We observed clone-specific ligand-receptor programs that are modulated by genomic dosage: amplifications of ligands or receptors enriched corresponding interactions, while deletions suppressed them, with genetically encoded differences supported by spatial transcriptomics and multiplex immunofluorescence. Phylogenetic integration identified focal 8q24 (MYC) amplification as recurrently associated with classical-to-basal transitions occurring within tumor lineages at a frequency above chance; these transitions were accompanied by coordinated depletion of immune-response programs. Functional perturbation experiments in murine and primary human models showed that MYC knockdown reactivates classical transcriptional programs and restores immune-response pathways, supporting a role for MYC in maintaining a basal, immune-depleted state. Spatial analyses further revealed dispersed clones enriched for epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition activity and immune suppression, correlating with metastatic potential and colonization of lymph node niches. These dispersed clones shifted toward a basal phenotype, contributing to disease progression. Our findings highlight the critical role of clonal diversity, transcriptional plasticity and tumor microenvironment interactions in shaping human PDAC biology. This work provides a detailed view of the molecular and spatial heterogeneity of PDAC and offers potential avenues for therapeutic intervention targeting clonal evolution and the mechanisms driving metastasis.

abstract: Interventional genetics (IG) refers to the development of therapies aimed at treating the underlying genetic cause of disease. Diagnostic sequencing has advanced to the point where genetic results can be returned within weeks, meaning that therapeutically actionable variants associated with specific diseases could be developed immediately after diagnosis. Here, we describe 81 probands with a neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and family matched controls with full genotype/phenotype information and biobanked stem cells, most of which are consented for sharing. We outline a rapid and scalable pipeline for induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) generation directly from clinical collection, without the need for peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) storage, paired with induction to neurons. We provide a proof of principle for rapid creation of oligonucleotide therapeutics for Kleefstra syndrome. This work introduces a cohort of individuals with NDDs and an implemental pipeline to integrate IG with clinical diagnostics for NDDs. This information documents our experience and provides useful details for clinical centers interested in integrating IG for NDDs with diagnostic sequencing.

abstract: In certain populations, founder pathogenic variants are a common cause of Lynch syndrome. Here, we report the identification of a novel Portuguese founder variant, NM_000179.3 (MSH6):c.2061 T > G (p.Cys687Trp). Our study examined 14 probands and 19 additional family members who carry this variant. With one exception, haplotype data are consistent with a single origin for all heterozygotes, likely in the Leiria District of Portugal. We investigated the clinicopathological consequences of this variant and found that, as previously reported for MSH6 pathogenic variants, (a) the presence of a pathogenic variant is not reliably associated with loss of MSH6 expression or microsatellite instability and (b) endometrial cancer is the most common associated phenotype. Due to the requirement to apply the BP5 code according to ACMG criteria, the variant is classified as a variant of uncertain significance rather than likely pathogenic. Nevertheless, the balance of evidence we present here suggests that this variant is associated with an increased risk for MSH6-related Lynch syndrome tumors.

abstract: SRSF3 (SRp20), a member of the serine/arginine-rich protein family of splicing factors, plays a central role in constitutive and alternative splicing. The C-terminal arginine/serine-rich domain of SRSF3 undergoes dynamic phosphorylation cycles that regulate its subcellular localization, protein-protein interactions, and nuclear mRNA export while also indirectly modulating the RNA-binding capability. We report nine individuals with variable developmental phenotypes, including developmental delay and/or mild to moderate intellectual disability as the most consistent feature, and de novo SRSF3 variants. These variants comprise c.181G>C (p.Asp61His) and c.242C>G (p.Ser81Trp), affecting highly conserved residues within the RNA recognition motif, c.330_331del (p.Pro111Serfs∗20), c.402_403del (p.Arg137Ilefs∗16), c.477dup (p.Ser160Valfs∗3), and a recurrent nonsense variant c.445C>T (p.Arg149∗). For c.330_331del, nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) was predicted. Qualitative RT-PCR followed by Sanger sequencing and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of fibroblasts from this individual demonstrated NMD of SRSF3 transcripts containing the variant. However, overall SRSF3 mRNA and protein levels were comparable to control cells, suggestive of a compensatory mechanism acting in these cells. Comprehensive functional studies of ectopically expressed SRSF3<sup>Asp61His</sup>, SRSF3<sup>Ser81Trp</sup>, SRSF3<sup>Arg137Ilefs</sup><sup>∗</sup><sup>16</sup>, SRSF3<sup>Arg149</sup><sup>∗</sup>, and SRSF3<sup>Ser160Valfs</sup><sup>∗</sup><sup>3</sup> in HEK293T cells revealed reduced complex formation with polyadenylated RNA as well as intrinsic instability of C-terminally truncated variant proteins, correlating with decreased C-terminal phosphorylation. Complex formation with the nuclear export proteins YTHDC1 and NXF1 was reduced for SRSF3<sup>Arg137Ilefs</sup><sup>∗</sup><sup>16</sup> and SRSF3<sup>Arg149</sup><sup>∗</sup> and increased for SRSF3<sup>Ser81Trp</sup>. Additionally, nucleocytoplasmic shuttling, assessed in HeLa cells, was reduced for the C-terminally truncated SRSF3 variant proteins. Together, our data demonstrate distinct functional defects for the disease-associated SRSF3 variants, which may underlie phenotypic variability in affected individuals.

abstract:
Background

Intellectual disability (ID) is a condition that is disproportionately represented in Low-and-Middle-Income countries (LMICs), including Africa, where socioeconomic and healthcare disparities contribute to a higher burden. Although prevalence estimates suggest a greater impact in African populations than in high-income regions, data remain limited and heterogeneous. ID has a highly diverse etiology driven by a complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors that contributes to significant regional variability in its presentation.

Methods

This review aims to examine the landscape of ID research across Africa, map geographic and infrastructural disparities in publication output, diagnostic capacity, and genomic investigation.

Results

A strong geographical imbalance is noticed, with North African countries accounting for a substantial proportion of publications, while many regions remain underrepresented. Although South Africa leads overall research production, most African countries contribute minimally, and genetic studies are available for only 19 countries, often restricted to case reports. Genetic studies, frequently influenced by high rates of consanguinity in certain populations, have enabled identification of recessive variants. However, reliance on low-throughput diagnostic approaches such as karyotyping, Sanger sequencing, and gene panels limits the ability to capture the full allelic diversity and mutational spectrum of African populations.

Conclusion

Overall, ID research in Africa remains fragmented and uneven, shaped by socio-genomic and structural constraints. Foreign collaboration biases may inflate output without strengthening local capacity. There is a need for African-led, equitable, and decentralized initiatives using advanced genomic technologies to better define the mutational landscape and improve diagnosis, management, and care.

abstract: Fanconi anemia (FA) is a genetic disorder characterized by congenital anomalies, progressive bone marrow failure, and an increased cancer risk. FA patient cells are hypersensitive to DNA interstrand crosslinks (ICLs), which cause chromosomal and genomic instability if left unrepaired. We identified 11 individuals from seven families who are homozygous for one of two C-terminally truncating variants in BRIP1 (previously known as FANCJ), c.2947del (p.Ile983Leufs<sup>∗</sup>2) (n = 3) or c.2992_2995del (p.Lys998Glufs<sup>∗</sup>60) (n = 8). None of them exhibited hematologic manifestations of FA, including bone marrow failure, myelodysplasia, or any FA-associated early-onset cancer types. Patient-derived blood cells showed stable levels of the BRIP1 p.Ile983Leufs<sup>∗</sup>2 variant and were resistant to ICL-inducing agents. In contrast, cells containing the BRIP1 p.Lys998Glufs<sup>∗</sup>60 variant displayed partial BRIP1 degradation and a mild cellular phenotype, evidenced by intermediate ICL sensitivity and a moderately elevated rate of ICL-induced chromosomal breaks. An isogenic BRIP1 knockout cell model expressing either wild-type or variant BRIP1 fully recapitulated these phenotypes. Introducing a stop codon at position 998 (p.Lys998<sup>∗</sup>) resulted in wild-type-like protein stability and ICL resistance, demonstrating that the aberrant frameshift extension, rather than C-terminal truncation, causes the observed cellular ICL sensitivity. Further deletion analyses revealed that the BRIP1 helicase domain (amino acids 1-888) is required and sufficient for cellular ICL resistance. BRCA1 interaction with phosphorylated BRIP1 Ser990 is dispensable for ICL repair. Our findings indicate that FA can result from the loss of the N-terminal helicase domain of BRIP1 but not from the loss of its C-terminal functions.

abstract: Identification of the biological origin of forensic stains provides critical contextual information for crime scene reconstruction and evidence interpretation. Among forensic biological materials, skin/sweat is particularly important for distinguishing intimate from social contact in sexual assault investigations. Although DNA methylation-based body fluid identification has advanced considerably, reliable CpG sites for skin remain scarce. Here, we systematically screened skin/sweat-specific CpG sites using Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC (850 K) array data from five body fluids and developed a multiplex DNA methylation assay for forensic skin/sweat identification. Following site prioritization and assay optimization, a 10-CpG multiplex panel based on amplification refractory mutation system PCR (ARMS-PCR) was established. The assay was comprehensively validated using single-source samples, simulated degraded samples, and mixed body fluid samples representative of forensic casework. The limit of detection of the 10-CpG panel was 0.25 ng. Integration of a random forest classifier enabled robust interpretation of methylation profiles and achieved 100% accuracy in distinguishing skin/sweat-containing from non-skin/sweat samples, including degraded, mixed, and casework specimens. This study represents a promising addition to the forensic epigenetic toolbox for body fluid identification, particularly in cases involving trace or degraded skin/sweat evidence.

abstract:
Background

Cancer Variant Interpretation Group UK (CanVIG-UK) was established in 2017 in response to the publication of the 2015 American College of Medical Genetics/Association for Molecular Pathology (ACMG/AMP) v3 guidance for the interpretation of sequence variants. Its initial purpose was to ensure consistency in the UK clinical-laboratory community implementation of ACMG/AMP v3 guidance for cancer susceptibility genes (CSGs). Still convening for monthly national meetings, the remit of CanVIG-UK now encompasses additional activities delivered under the following objectives: (1) creation of a national multidisciplinary professional network and regular forum, (2) delivery of training and education, (3) establishment of a consensus approach to the fundamentals of variant interpretation in CSGs, (4) development and ratification of gene-specific frameworks for variant interpretation for CSGs, (5) development and maintenance of an online platform to facilitate information sharing and variant interpretation within the UK clinical-laboratory community and (6) facilitation of UK contribution to international variant interpretation endeavours.

Methods

A survey of CanVIG-UK members evaluating the impact of these activities conducted in November 2025 had 163 responses, including 113 clinical scientists/trainees and 27 Clinical Genetics consultants/trainees.

Results

The utility of the CanVIG-UK consensus recommendations for variant interpretation in CSGs was highly rated, with 89/145 (61.4%) of survey respondents reporting using the guidance at least weekly (≥4 times/month) and 124/128 (96.9%) rating it as extremely/very useful. The usage frequency and perceived utility reported for the gene-specific guidance by survey respondents were similar.

Conclusion

Both qualitative and quantitative survey responses clearly demonstrate the value of the CanVIG-UK activities to the clinical-diagnostic community.

abstract:
Purpose

Our study aimed to examine the effect of coverage criteria utilized by payors on the detection of an individual's carrier status.

Methods

We performed a retrospective chart review of patients and their reproductive partners at a single institution who had a positive carrier screening result to collect demographic information, carrier screening results, and family medical history. We estimated the proportion of individuals who would not have met coverage criteria for carrier screening that would detect their full carrier status based on policies used by major healthcare payors in California.

Results

Of the participants with positive carrier screening results, 93% would not have had their full carrier status detected if carrier screening following payor policies was elected instead of expanded carrier screening. The highest proportion of participants who would not have their carrier status detected were of East Asian ethnicity (94%) and White ethnicity (94%), followed by South Asian ethnicity (93%) and Hispanic ethnicity (93%).

Conclusion

Payors generally rely on ethnicity and family history to determine what type of carrier screening a policyholder is eligible for, therefore missing a significant portion of people who are heterozygous for pathogenic variants. These criteria contribute to insufficient, unequal and limited carrier screening strategies.

abstract: MAP2K4 encodes a kinase that activates the c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway, which is essential for human neurodevelopment. While somatic MAP2K4 loss has been observed in cancer, germline variants have not previously been linked to human disease. We describe nine individuals with de novo MAP2K4 variants and one individual with a MAP2K4 variant of unknown inheritance who present with a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder. Shared features include developmental delay or intellectual disability, epilepsy, and variable congenital malformations, most commonly affecting the genitourinary system. To define the mechanism, we generated CRISPR-edited induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons with MAP2K4 deficiency. These neurons showed reduced JNK pathway activation and impaired maturation in the neurogenin 2 (NGN2) system, characterized by persistence of progenitor-like cells and disrupted neurite morphology. Our findings establish MAP2K4 as a Mendelian neurodevelopmental disorder-associated gene and identify impaired JNK signaling as the underlying mechanism. More broadly, this work expands the spectrum of JNK pathway disorders and underscores the critical role of JNK signaling in human brain development.

abstract:
Background

Kenya is at a transitional point in advancing human genomics research and its applications particularly for non-communicable diseases. While there are foundational legal and institutional infrastructures in place there are still significant governance gaps that exist that need to be addressed before large-scale human genomic research, and genomic medicine can be implemented in a responsible manner.

Methods

This is a report on the perspectives gathered from symposium participants attending the 2nd Human Genetics and Genomics Society of Kenya (HGGSK) symposium, held during 16th KEMRI Annual Scientific and Health Conference. It draws on narrative/ descriptive synthesis of expert speaker presentations and a structured survey completed by symposium attendees to provide insight on ethics, equity, and genomic data governance in Kenya.

Results

Most respondents 13/23 (57%) perceived that Kenya is not yet adequately prepared for the implementation of large-scale human genomics research. The primary concerns were the need for stronger genetic privacy protections, robust informed consent processes, and a national genomics policy framework. A large majority of participants 19/23 (83%) emphasized the need to strengthen genetic privacy protection, while 12/23 (52%) preferred study-specific consent over broad consent for the future use of genomic data. Overall, participants identified the development of a national human genomics policy framework as the most urgent priority to support the responsible advancement of human genomics research and its clinical implementation in Kenya.

Conclusions

Kenya has foundational structures for human genomics research but there is a need to develop governance frameworks that will guide responsible scaling.

abstract:
Background

BMI remains the dominant clinical index of obesity, but does not resolve adipose molecular programs that distinguish metabolic resilience from vulnerability.

Methods

Among 1,479 available human visceral adipose RNA-seq profiles, 1,298 samples from individuals with BMI 30-60 were included in the primary modeling cohort. Using BMI as a phenotypic anchor, we fit a LASSO regression model to derive transcriptome-predicted BMI and applied the resulting BMI-anchored transcriptomic model to mouse selection lines with divergent obesity phenotypes. In humans, directional discordance between measured and predicted BMI was used to define transcriptome-derived metabolically healthy obesity-like (MHO-like) and metabolically unhealthy obesity-like (MUO-like) states and to characterize pathophysiologic variation beyond measured BMI.

Results

Model-selected genes converged on immune, metabolic, mitochondrial, growth, structural-remodeling, and proteostasis programs. Cross-species application showed that BMI-anchored transcriptomic scores more closely tracked adipose-tissue content than body-size condition factor, distinguishing lipid-anabolic and inflammatory features of obesity-prone DU6 mice from the oxidative-catabolic phenotype of DU6P mice characterized by increased muscle mass. Gene-level associations with the transcriptomic score mirrored DU6-associated expression changes, linking the cross-species axis to an obesity-vulnerable adipose state. In humans, MHO-like individuals showed enhanced mitochondrial energy-production programs and more favorable glycemic and lipid profiles, whereas MUO-like individuals showed stress-adaptive metabolic remodeling and greater cardiometabolic medication use. In a separate, non-overlapping validation cohort, projection onto the primary-cohort PCA space retained a signal associated with insulin resistance that remained essentially unchanged after adjustment for sex.

Conclusions

These findings support a conserved adipose transcriptomic axis linking oxidative metabolic resilience to healthier obesity and lipid-inflammatory remodeling to metabolic vulnerability.

abstract:
Background

Mainstreaming, in which genetic testing is shifted outside clinical genetics, can improve access to genetic testing. This is being explored in several countries, including Canada, the USA and the UK. However, standardised practice within a jurisdiction helps ensure equitable high-quality access. This study aimed to evaluate consistency in the implementation of cancer genetics mainstreaming across Ontario, Canada.

Methods

Adult cancer genetics centres in Ontario were emailed an online survey in June 2025, which was completed by mainstreaming implementation leads. Results were anonymised and analysed in aggregate.

Results

Of 18 centres contacted, 13 responded; 12/13 reported having implemented cancer genetics mainstreaming. All mainstreaming centres offered pathways for breast, ovarian, prostate and pancreatic cancers, primarily based on personal history criteria. Most centres did not mainstream for other cancer sites but were planning to expand. A 19-gene hereditary breast/ovarian/prostate panel was most commonly ordered. There was variation in the timepoint of genetics service involvement. Turnaround times for expedited results were relatively consistent (median 21 days, IQR 18-22), whereas turnaround times for routine results varied widely (median 50 days, IQR 36-94).

Conclusion

Across Ontario, centres were generally consistent in mainstreaming the most common indications. Opportunities to improve quality and equity include reducing variability in routine turnaround time, standardising management pathways for negative results and streamlining ordering to align with eligibility criteria. Some centres cited limited genetics knowledge as an implementation barrier, though engagement improved over time. Ongoing evaluation of mainstreaming can support consistent access to care.

abstract: Imaging has revolutionized phenotyping analysis by providing accurate documentation and records of observed phenotypes. Analyzing imaging data remains a major bottleneck in root phenotyping analysis. Advances in technology offer a plethora of analysis options at varying automation levels and price points, providing a reliable open-source pipeline for image analysis that delivers stable, reproducible results. Here, we discuss a maize seedling image analysis pipeline powered by open-source tools that enables rapid analysis of seedling root phenotypes. This image analysis pipeline uses Root Painter, an optional AI cleanup step, and RhizoVision Explorer to extract phenotypic data from maize seedlings grown on rolled towel assays, which are commonly used, enabling rapid analysis of these images.

abstract: G-quadruplex (G4) nucleic acids have been shown to regulate a wide range of cellular processes, including replication, telomere maintenance, epigenetic landscape, and various aspects of transcription and translation. In this method, we describe an experimental purification procedure for identifying RNA G-quadruplex-binding proteins from nuclear extracts. Using biotinylated oligonucleotides allows immobilization to streptavidin-coated magnetic beads and convenient washing during the pulldown. Importantly, the experimental protocol presented here can distinguish protein interactions with structured and unstructured RNA within the same oligonucleotide by controlling ionic conditions throughout the folding, RNA pulldown, and washing steps. The binding of individual candidate proteins can be determined by western blotting, while mass spectrometry can readily identify the whole RNA G-quadruplex-interacting proteome.

abstract:
Purpose

CDK19 (HGNC:19338) is a Mediator-associated kinase that regulates transcription during neurodevelopment. Although CDK19 variants have been linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, the full phenotypic spectrum and the underlying pathogenic mechanisms remain incompletely defined. We aimed to further characterize clinical-genetic correlations and to elucidate disease mechanisms through integrative functional and transcriptomic approaches.

Methods

Through an international collaboration, 28 individuals with CDK19 variants (12 newly identified and 16 previously reported) were evaluated using systematic clinical phenotyping. To assess the functional consequences of the variants identified in affected individuals, Drosophila models expressing CDK19 alleles were generated and examined for viability, lifespan, motor behavior, and seizure susceptibility. Protein stability, subcellular localization, tissue morphology, and transcriptomic alterations were assessed by western blot, immunofluorescence, and RNA sequencing of larval brains.

Results

All individuals demonstrated global developmental delay, with speech delay as a consistently prominent feature; 8 of 12 (67%) had epilepsy, most commonly infantile epileptic spasms syndrome. Hypotonia was present in 6 of 12 (50%) individuals, and craniofacial dysmorphisms and abnormal brain magnetic resonance imaging findings were also frequent. Several pathogenic alleles exhibited reduced protein stability, aberrant nuclear localization, and tissue toxicity, with associated structural abnormalities, including elongated mitochondria, thickened myofibrils, and shortened sarcomeres. Behavioral assays revealed motor incoordination and allele-specific seizure susceptibility. RNA sequencing identified consistent downregulation of synaptic and neuromuscular genes, including GluRIIA, VGAT, nAChRβ1, and Syn, implicating disrupted neurotransmission and impaired neuromuscular junction integrity. These findings, obtained in an overexpression-based allele-comparison system, are interpreted as supportive functional evidence of variant pathogenicity.

Conclusion

These findings corroborate and further refine the clinical spectrum of CDK19-related neurodevelopmental disorders and provide in vivo functional evidence that pathogenic CDK19 variants are associated with the disruption of transcriptional programs relevant to synaptic and neuromuscular function, supporting CDK19 dysfunction as part of the emerging spectrum of Mediator complexopathies.

abstract: Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) are widely used to identify genes involved in complex traits and to infer the direction of gene effects on traits. However, despite their popularity, it remains unclear how accurately TWAS recover the true direction of a gene's effect on a trait. Here we estimate the false sign rate of TWAS for plasma proteins, leveraging the expectation that increased gene expression should generally increase protein expression. We then extend this framework to complex traits, where loss-of-function burden tests provide the expected direction of effect. In both analyses, we observe high discordance with expectations, with TWAS showing a false sign rate of 23% for plasma proteins and 33% for complex traits. We propose that much of the sign discordance arises when expression quantitative trait loci in non-trait-relevant tissues tag haplotypes associated with traits in genome-wide association studies via distinct, tightly linked regulatory variants, yielding spurious TWAS associations with the correct genes but with unreliable direction of effect. These findings show that TWAS-based direction-of-effect estimates should be interpreted with caution and raise concerns about the reliability of TWAS more broadly.

abstract: Machine learning approaches have become a powerful alternative to traditional methods in population genetics. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in particular have been successful in inferring natural selection, recombination rates, introgression, dispersal distances, and effective population size changes. One limitation of CNNs and other deep learning methods is that they can be difficult to interpret. When they have been shown to be as or more successful than summary-statistic-based methods, what are they learning? Here, we investigate CNNs from two different methods: the pg-gan discriminator for identifying real vs. simulated data, and two networks trained to detect selective sweeps. We first compute correlations between learned network features and traditional summary statistics, then assess whether summary statistics can be predicted from the learned features. To understand the learned features, we compute feature importance through SHAP values and feature groupings through dimensionality reduction. Finally, we use decision trees and random forests to build an interpretable "model-of-the-model". Our results reveal that some CNN architectures can implicitly compute summary statistics such as pairwise heterozygosity, while statistics such as the site frequency spectrum are less similar to the network's learned features. We find that long-range linkage disequilibrium is readily approximated by the networks and may be more efficiently computed by CNNs than traditional methods (which are quadratic in the number of sites). Overall, this work contributes to the interpretability of deep learning methods in population genetics by clarifying the relationships between model architecture, learned network features, established summary statistics, and predicted evolutionary parameters.

abstract: Bovine coronavirus (BCoV), a primary etiological agent of calf diarrhea, exhibits dual tropism for the respiratory and enteric tracts. However, research on BCoV gene function and pathogenesis has been limited by the lack of convenient and flexible reverse genetics tools. Herein, we report a robust reverse genetics system for BCoV based on an optimized circular polymerase extension reaction (CPER) methodology. We successfully rescued recombinant BCoV (rBCoV) in HRT-18G cells and engineered recombinant BCoV expressing ZsGreen fluorescent protein (rBCoV/Zs-T2A-ns2). Phenotypic analysis demonstrated that both unmodified rBCoV and rBCoV/Zs-T2A-ns2 maintained growth kinetics comparable to the wild-type BCoV. Importantly, the reporter virus demonstrated remarkable genetic stability for over ten passages, identifying the ns2 locus as a suitable insertion site for stable foreign gene expression without compromising viral fitness or sequence integrity. As a proof-of-concept application, the rBCoV/Zs-T2A-ns2 was employed for antiviral compound evaluation, successfully identifying four compounds-camostat, nafamostat, niclosamide, and nelfinavir-capable of effectively inhibiting BCoV replication. Further time-of-addition assays revealed that nelfinavir and niclosamide targeted the BCoV replication stage, while camostat and nafamostat interfered with BCoV internalization. This versatile CPER-based reverse genetics system provides a critical platform for advanced BCoV pathogenesis research and accelerated development of novel vaccines and effective antiviral therapeutics, ultimately contributing to enhanced bovine health and sustainable livestock production.

abstract: Despite a high level of conservation within its core genome, the Chlamydia genus comprises various species that exhibit diverse pathogenic profiles. Genetic engineering techniques employing shuttle vectors are crucial tools for elucidating the pathogenesis of these obligate intracellular bacteria. In recent years, the introduction of calcium chloride-mediated transformation methods has significantly advanced genetic manipulation techniques for Chlamydia trachomatis. However, the efficiency of transformation using shuttle vectors, as well as plasmid maintenance, varies not only between Chlamydia species but also among strains within the same species, necessitating individually optimized protocols. In this chapter, we describe the entire process from vector preparation and transformation procedures to the clonal isolation of transformed Chlamydia species to facilitate future applications in genetic studies.

abstract:
Introduction

Next-generation sequencing performed for therapeutic decision-making in pediatric cancers provides an opportunity to identify germline variants associated with hereditary cancer predisposition and other actionable inherited conditions.

Methods

Germline whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed within the MAPPYACTS (MoleculAr Profiling for Pediatric and Young Adult Cancer Treatment Stratification) trial. Germline data were available for 674 patients with diverse relapsed or refractory malignancies. Families provided informed consent regarding disclosure of actionable germline findings. A multidisciplinary committee established a panel of 184 cancer predisposition genes with established surveillance recommendations and 49 medically actionable noncancer genes from the ACMG SF v3.1 list. Variants were analyzed using bioinformatic pipelines including quality filtering, ClinVar annotation, and computational pathogenicity assessment.

Results

Overall, 98.6% of families consented to the disclosure of actionable genetic findings. Among 674 patients, a total of 148 likely pathogenic or pathogenic variants (LPV/PV) were identified in 130 patients (19.3%) across 53 cancer predisposition genes. Based on inheritance patterns and clinical relevance, genetic counseling was recommended for 58 patients (8.6%). The most frequently altered genes with clinical application were TP53 (n = 17), DICER1 (n = 5), and BRCA1 (n = 4). Predisposition findings corresponded to the expected tumor spectrum in 48% of cases with 35% of them had not been previously recognized. Additionally, 10 patients (1.5%) carried actionable LPV/PV in noncancer genes associated with cardiomyopathies, familial hypercholesterolemia, or transthyretin amyloidosis.

Discussion

Systematic germline WES integrated into theranostic profiling may provide additional clinical value through the identification of actionable cancer predispositions and other inherited conditions. We propose recommendations for a structured, multidisciplinary framework to support clinical decision-making.

abstract: Barcoded Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains enable pooled genetic analyses across many genotypes. Here, we describe a protocol for generating stable barcoded haploid strains from natural diploid isolates. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Strauss et al.<sup>1</sup>.

abstract: Short tandem repeats (STRs) are highly polymorphic markers essential for forensic science, population genetics, and clinical diagnostics. We developed a 15-locus autosomal STR panel targeting chromosomes 13, 18, and 21 for multipurpose genetic applications. Fluorescent-labelled primers were designed, and PCR products were analysed via capillary electrophoresis and sequencing. Population genetics evaluation using 127 distinct alleles from unrelated Iraqi Hawrami individuals showed that all markers remained in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium after Bonferroni correction, and linkage disequilibrium analysis confirmed their independence. Preliminary forensic analysis indicated that all loci had a polymorphism information content (PIC) value greater than 0.5, demonstrating discriminatory capability, with D13S258 achieving the highest level of discrimination. Combined power of discrimination reached greater than 0.999999, with a match probability of 6.82 × 10<sup>-16</sup>. The clinical assessment effectively identified trisomy 13, 18, and 21 by analysing characteristic peak height ratios and tri-allelic patterns in confirmed cases. This cost-effective STR panel suits population genetics studies, preliminary forensic evaluations, and rapid diagnostic testing, offering a versatile alternative to commercial kits. The panel's robust performance across multiple applications establishes its value for genetic research in Middle Eastern populations and as a screening assay. Complementary analysis using CODIS core loci for phylogenetic construction revealed that the Iraqi Hawrami population is most closely related to Armenian groups (Ararat and Lake Valley) and populations from southwestern Iran. These groups form a distinct Caucasus-Zagros subclade. Non-negative Matrix Factorisation of genetic structure showed clear clustering patterns, illustrating genetic transitions among Levantine, Mesopotamian, and Central Asian populations.

abstract: Whole-exome sequencing (WES) has greatly expanded the identification of rare germline variants in hereditary cancer predisposition. However, the interpretation of variants of uncertain significance (VUS), particularly in novel candidate genes, remains a major challenge in lung cancer genetics. To functionally characterize selected germline variants identified by WES in patients with familial or suspected hereditary lung cancer and provide evidence for their prioritization. Three splicing variants in HGS, CDK12, and CEACAM5 genes were investigated by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing to assess their effect on splicing. Candidate missense variants were analyzed through protein-protein interaction network analysis, gene expression profiling, and structure-based computational modeling to evaluate their potential impact on protein stability and molecular interactions. RNA analysis confirmed that the CDK12 variant produced the previously reported in-frame one amino acid deletion, whereas the HGS variant activated a cryptic splice acceptor site, resulting in an in-frame deletion affecting a region containing a known ubiquitination site. No aberrant splicing was detected for CEACAM5. Network analyses highlighted convergence of three candidate genes (ERBB3, MAP2K1 and RASA2) on receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and the RAS/MAPK pathway. Structural analyses predicted local perturbations affecting membrane interactions, residue interaction networks, or protein stability for variants in the three previous genes and in USP4, supporting their functional relevance. Integrating RNA-based functional assays with network and structural analyses provides a practical framework for interpreting and prioritizing rare germline VUS identified by WES, supporting the identification of candidate lung cancer susceptibility genes and improving genetic risk assessment.

abstract: Zygote electroporation (EP) is a widely used technique for the delivery of targeting constructs into the embryos and has become very popular in the last few years in transgenic facilities all over the world. Zygote electroporation is technically simple, as it does not require equipment for microinjection. Moreover, zygote electroporation is less invasive, resulting in higher survival rates in comparison to pronuclear microinjection, leading to a reduction in the number of animals needed. Another advantage of zygote electroporation is a higher number of zygotes that can be targeted simultaneously, which minimizes the time required for zygote manipulation. abstract: Birt-Hogg-Dubé (BHD) and Tuberous Sclerosis (TSC) are inherited cancer syndromes associated with kidney cystogenesis and tumorigenesis and caused by mutations of the folliculin (FLCN) and TSC1/2 genes, respectively. We and others previously showed that Transcription Factors EB (TFEB) and E3 (TFE3) are the main drivers of the kidney phenotypes observed in mouse models of these conditions. These transcription factors are also responsible for the feedback hyperactivation of the mechanistic Target of Rapamycin Complex 1 (mTORC1), a known tumorigenic factor. This raises the question of whether TFEB/TFE3 exert their oncogenic activity by inducing mTORC1 or by mTORC1-independent pathways. To address this question, we generated kidney-specific mouse models in which we knocked out factors that differentially control mTORC1 and TFEB/TFE3, thus uncoupling their activities. Specifically, we generated three kidney-specific conditional knockout lines: (1) Depdc5-KO mice in which loss of GATOR1 activity leads to mTORC1 hyperactivation and TFEB/TFE3 inhibition, (2) RagC-KO mice in which TFEB/TFE3 are constitutively active and mTORC1 activity is partially inhibited due to impaired Rag heterodimer formation, and (3) Flcn/RagC double KO mice to test whether mTORC1 inhibition induced by RagC loss ameliorates the aggressive kidney phenotype of FLCN KO mice. Comparison between these models revealed that mTORC1 hyperactivation is a key driver of cystogenesis and tumorigenesis, while TFEB/TFE3 constitutive activation further enhances and accelerates pathology by establishing a transcriptional program that integrates metabolic and stress-response pathways. Together, our findings define an oncogenic mechanism by which both mTORC1 and TFEB/TFE3 hyperactivation cooperate in kidney tumorigenesis.

abstract:
Introduction

Primary mitochondrial diseases (PMtD) are increasingly recognized to involve clinically meaningful immune dysregulation in addition to bioenergetic failure. Hyperinflammatory syndromes, including secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and related cytokine-mediated inflammatory states, remain underrecognized complications of PMtD, and the mechanisms linking mitochondrial dysfunction to pathologic inflammation are incompletely understood.

Methods

We report three individuals with genetically confirmed PMtD evaluated at three academic medical centers who developed severe hyperinflammatory syndromes. Clinical, laboratory, treatment, and outcome data were retrospectively abstracted from the medical record using a standardized framework. We also performed a focused narrative review of the literature on hyperinflammation in mitochondrial disease.

Results

Individual 1 had pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency (PDCD), due to a PDHA1 variant and developed infection-associated HLH at age 9 years, with ferritin 17,203 ng/mL and bone marrow hemophagocytosis. He met 6 of 8 HLH-2004 criteria and had an HScore of 303 (>99% probability of HLH). He survived the index episode with corticosteroid-based therapy but experienced recurrent inflammatory decompensations and later died. Individual 2 had POLG-related mitochondrial disease and developed HLH at age 8 years during presumed viral-triggered neurologic deterioration in the setting of pre-existing hepatic vulnerability. He met 6 of 8 HLH-2004 criteria, had an HScore of 233 (>98% probability of HLH), and showed an initial biomarker response to emapalumab, but ultimately died of multiorgan failure. Individual 3 had MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes; due to an m.3243 A>G variant in MT-TL1 and developed a sterile interferon (IFN)-driven hyperinflammatory syndrome during a stroke-like episode (SLE), with markedly elevated serum soluble interleukin (IL)-2 receptor (sIL-2R), IL-6, IL-10, C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 9 (CXCL9), and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) neopterin, without meeting full HLH-2004 criteria (fulfilling only 2/8 criteria). He had minimal response to intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) but showed sustained clinical and biomarker improvement with anakinra and is alive, age 15 years at the time of this publication.

Conclusions

PMtD may be associated with a predisposition to a spectrum of hyperinflammatory syndromes ranging from classic secondary HLH to noncanonical sterile cytokine-mediated inflammation that falls below formal HLH thresholds. These complications may reflect mitochondrial danger signaling, inflammasome activation, engagement of the IFN pathway, and defective immunometabolic regulation. Early recognition and targeted immunomodulatory therapy may be critical to improving outcomes.

abstract: We provide a comprehensive phenotypic characterization of loss-of-function (LoF) variants in WDFY3 based on the largest cohort reported to date (n = 32). Our findings define a monogenic disorder marked by neuropsychiatric features (including autism and ADHD), mild to moderate neurodevelopmental delay, and variable brain growth - most commonly macrocephaly and in one case reduced head circumference. To investigate the effect of WDFY3 LoF we performed knockdown (KD) in the human neuroblastoma cell line SH-SY5Y and used a Wdfy3-haploinsufficient mouse model. WDFY3 KD impaired clearance of protein aggregates and decreased protein levels of the ubiquitin-binding protein p62. Transcriptomic analyses identified dysregulation in gene networks that are primarily involved in nervous system development, neuron projection, MAPK/ERK1/2, and WNT/β-catenin signaling. This was confirmed at protein level. Neuronal cell proliferation was increased, as evidenced by elevated cell counts and proliferation markers Ki-67 and PCNA. Conversely, neuronal cell differentiation was impaired, as indicated by reduced neurite outgrowth. We show that β-catenin is downregulated, while GSK3B is upregulated. LiCl activates WNT/β-catenin signaling by inhibiting GSK3B. We thus tested LiCl treatment, which significantly increased WDFY3 expression. Moreover, in vitro treatment improved the neurite branching capacity of Wdfy3-haploinsufficient neurons above the level of the wild type, although this specific effect appeared independent of WNT/β-catenin signaling. In sum, we expand on the phenotype related to WDFY3 LoF and provide insights into the pathophysiology using in vitro human and murine neuronal models. Our findings suggest that LiCl may serve as a potential therapeutic strategy for patients with WDFY3 LoF variants.

abstract: Effective panicle number (EPN) is a major determinant of rice yield and is strongly influenced by nitrogen (N) availability. Identifying genes that maintain EPN under low-N conditions is therefore important for improving nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) in rice. In this study, bulked segregant analysis by sequencing (BSA-seq) of a recombinant inbred line (RIL) population comprising 1128 individuals identified a novel NUE-related quantitative trait locus, qNUE6. The locus was initially mapped to a 1.93 Mb interval on chromosome 6 and was subsequently narrowed to a 61.8 kb region through fine mapping of backcross-derived populations. Among the four annotated genes within the final interval, OsNRT1.2, which encodes a nitrate transporter, exhibited the strongest response to low-N treatment and was identified as the most likely candidate gene. Sequence comparison between the parental lines revealed one InDel and several SNPs, including promoter polymorphisms that may contribute to differential responses to low-N conditions. Functional analyses of overexpression and knockout lines demonstrated that OsNRT1.2 positively regulates nitrogen uptake, effective panicle number, grain yield, and overall NUE. Taken together, these results identify OsNRT1.2 as a strong candidate gene underlying qNUE6 and provide a useful molecular target for improving NUE in rice. However, broader validation across diverse germplasm and direct testing of the causal promoter variants is necessary to fully resolve the underlying mechanism.

abstract:
Objective

To examine willingness to donate DNA for multiple sclerosis (MS) research, with particular attention to uncertainty versus unwillingness, and perceived learning during completion of a questionnaire on MS genetics.

Methods

An online cross-sectional survey was conducted in Serbia. Regression analyses focused on the non-professional subsample. Multinomial logistic regression examined willing, unwilling, and insufficient-information responses to DNA donation, while multivariable linear regression examined perceived learning, measured by "I know now" responses to seven informational items.

Results

Among 1075 valid DNA-donation responses, 49.8% were willing, 22.9% lacked sufficient information to decide, and 27.3% were unwilling. In adjusted analyses, not wanting personal genetic risk information was more strongly associated with unwillingness than with uncertainty, while prior awareness of genetic data protection was associated with less uncertainty relative to both willingness and unwillingness. Respondents reported a median perceived-learning score of 5 out of 7. Greater objective knowledge and familiarity with MS were associated with higher perceived-learning scores, whereas male sex and age ≤ 20 years were associated with lower scores.

Conclusion

Respondents who lacked sufficient information to decide about DNA donation differed from those who were unwilling to participate, supporting the treatment of uncertainty as a distinct response. The reported perceived learning also suggests that questionnaires incorporating informational content may provide an opportunity to support awareness alongside data collection.

Practice implications

Research communication should distinguish insufficient information from refusal and clearly address personal genetic risk information and data protection. Informational questionnaires may complement these efforts, although their educational effects require objective evaluation.

abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a rare bone or soft tissue tumor that occurs early in life, suggesting genetic variation is likely a major contributor to EwS risk. To date, genetic investigations have identified key somatic mutations and germline variants of importance for EwS risk. While substantial progress has been made in uncovering the genetic etiology of EwS, considerable gaps in knowledge remain. Herein, we provide a summary of methodological approaches for future genomic investigations of EwS. We anticipate that this recommended analytical framework for germline and somatic investigations, along with genomic data from growing EwS case series, will aid in accelerating new genomic discoveries in EwS and expand knowledge of the genetic architecture of this aggressive sarcoma.

abstract: RNA N<sup>6</sup>-methyladenosine (m<sup>6</sup>A) modifications dynamically modulate RNA stability, splicing, and translation in plants, influencing developmental and stress response processes. In this review, we provide an overview of the key protein complexes involved in RNA m<sup>6</sup>A modification, including methyltransferases, demethylases, and m<sup>6</sup>A-binding proteins. We then demonstrate that m<sup>6</sup>A modulates vegetative growth, reproductive processes, responses to stresses, and hormone signaling. In agronomically important crops, RNA m<sup>6</sup>A modifications affect stress resilience, developmental timing, and quality traits, such as drought tolerance, salt resistance, male fertility, pollen viability, and fruit maturation. Furthermore, we elucidate the molecular mechanisms of RNA m<sup>6</sup>A. Finally, we explore advancements in m<sup>6</sup>A detection technologies, highlighting emerging trends and future directions. These strategies provide a conceptual framework for moving plant m<sup>6</sup>A research from descriptive epitranscriptomics toward trait-oriented crop and forest tree improvement.

abstract: Galactose-1-phosphate (Gal-1-P) is an important biomarker for diagnosis and therapeutic monitoring of classic galactosemia and related disorders. Measurement is traditionally performed in erythrocytes, requiring relatively large blood volumes and labor-intensive specimen processing. We developed and validated a liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) assay for quantitation of Gal-1-P from dried blood spots (DBS). Analytical validation included evaluation of linearity, precision, stability, limit of detection (LOD), limit of quantitation (LOQ), and reference interval determination. DBS and erythrocyte specimens from patients undergoing routine galactosemia monitoring were analyzed in parallel to compare performance characteristics and establish a DBS-specific therapeutic range. The LOD and LOQ were 0.11 mg/dL and 0.17 mg/dL, respectively. The reference interval was established as ≤1.0 mg/dL. Comparison of paired DBS and erythrocyte samples demonstrated good correlation (R<sup>2</sup> = 0.86) with an approximately 20% negative bias in DBS specimens. Based on 65 paired samples from treated individuals with galactosemia, a DBS therapeutic target of <4 mg/dL was established, which is lower than the therapeutic target of <5 mg/dL in erythrocytes. DBS-based measurement of Gal-1-P by LC-MS/MS provides a clinically reliable alternative to erythrocyte analysis with advantages including less blood volume required, simplified collection and shipping, and improved specimen stability. A DBS-specific therapeutic range is required because of systematic bias relative to erythrocyte measurements.

abstract:
Unlabelled

Over the last 2 decades, a large global marketplace has emerged in which businesses use direct-to-consumer advertising to sell putative stem cell treatments that are unsupported by convincing scientific evidence of safety and efficacy. It is common for such purported stem cell therapies not to have been reviewed and approved by national regulatory authorities, even though they are supposed to undergo rigorous premarketing review by regulatory bodies responsible for evaluating such medical products and determining whether they are backed by sufficient evidence to warrant approval. The marketing claims, commercial activities, and clinical practices of such businesses have resulted in patients experiencing serious harms, including loss of life, physical injuries, financial losses, and avoidable delays in accessing evidence-based treatments. Such businesses are also responsible for collective harms, including diverting patients from participating in legitimate stem cell clinical studies, damaging the field of credible stem cell research, and contributing to public confusion and misunderstandings about how to distinguish evidence-based stem cell therapies from stem cell interventions that are not backed by robust data. Researchers in bioethics, health law, the social sciences, and other academic fields have made important contributions to the critical analysis of direct-to-consumer digital marketing claims made by businesses selling unproven and unapproved stem cell interventions. Scholars studying such marketing representations have documented the use of persuasive "tokens of legitimacy" to make advertised stem cell interventions seem credible, trustworthy, and backed by current scientific evidence. Acknowledging the value of such scholarship, there is a growing need for the development of best practices in research methods and data-archiving practices. In particular, there is a need for increased digital archiving of online marketing claims made by businesses selling supposed stem cell treatments. Numerous parties can benefit from increased digital archiving of such problematic marketing representations. However, analyzing, archiving, and critiquing the marketing claims, business operations, and clinical practices of such businesses must be done in a careful, rigorous, and evidence-based manner that is attentive to the intimidating tactics some of these businesses use when responding to public criticism. Researchers need to document the marketing representations made by businesses selling unapproved and unproven stem cell interventions in ways that minimize exposure to legal threats and other efforts to suppress critical analysis. Using the Wayback Machine or other comparable archiving tools to create digital repositories of such marketing representations is one way to mitigate such threats, by capturing the exact claims such businesses make when promoting putative stem cell therapies. Archiving such digital marketing representations is important for academic research and can play a valuable role in other contexts, such as in legal actions taken against businesses using purportedly deceptive marketing claims to sell unproven and unapproved stem cell-based interventions.
