abstract: The article presents results of comprehensive analysis of step-by-step implementation of mandatory marking of medical articles as key mechanism of ensuring traceability of their turnover. the particular attention is paid to consideration of transition to per copy accounting significantly transforming activities of all participants of turnover: manufacturers, importers, distributors, pharmacies and, most importantly, medical and preventive treatment facilities. The minute analysis was applied to organizational and technological difficulties occurring under implementation of the given system: necessity in total transition to electronic circulation of documents using universal transfer documents, requirements for integration of medical informational systems into state informational system of monitoring "Honest Sign", risks of errors under verification of marking codes, problem of "double remainders" under separation of flow of commodities by date of putting into circulation, as well as increased load of medical personnel in conditions of staff shortage. The research established steady trend towards toughening of requirements to traceability of medical articles, confirmed by establishment of prompt deadlines for completion of transition periods and introduction of total per copy accounting from September 1, 2025 with subsequent spreading to gloves from March 1, 2026. It is substantiated that mentioned system, being effective tool of state control that ensure transparency of public purchases, control of counterfeit and possibility to track movement of goods from manufacturer to specific patient, requires in its current implementation further optimization of processes. The conclusion is made that key factors of successful practical implementation of system of per copy accounting are thorough integration of accounting systems with operators of circulation of electronic documents, transition from hand scanning to aggregated accounting, as well as division of responsibility between medical and administrative personnel. The participants capable to build the given processes receive not only protection from financial sanctions and reputational losses, but also real tool to increase operational efficiency in conditions of transparent digital environment.

abstract: This study examines the impact of digital transformation (DT) on three non-financial management accounting outcomes: accounting information quality, cost reduction, and decision-making effectiveness in Saudi Arabian companies. Drawing on Organizational Information Processing Theory, the study investigates whether digital transformation enhances management accounting performance by strengthening organizations' ability to process and use information effectively. Data were collected from 150 accounting professionals through a structured survey and analyzed using multiple linear regression after confirming the reliability of the measurement scales, with Cronbach's alpha values ranging from 0.81 to 0.90. The findings indicate that digital transformation has a significant positive effect on accounting information quality, cost reduction, and decision-making effectiveness, with the strongest impact observed for decision-making effectiveness. These relationships remained significant after controlling for company size. The study contributes to the digital transformation and management accounting literature by providing integrated empirical evidence from Saudi Arabia and offers practical implications for organizations seeking to improve management accounting performance and support the objectives of Saudi Vision 2030.

abstract: Accounting firms are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) quickly, but the way they plan and price engagements has changed much more slowly. This paper reviews research from four areas that rarely meet: the pricing of accounting and audit services, the productivity effects of AI on knowledge work, the use of AI in accounting and auditing, and activity-based costing and project control. The review finds that AI's effects on accounting work are large but uneven across tasks, that new review and oversight work appears alongside time savings, and that hours freed by AI are often absorbed by other work rather than appearing as lower recorded effort. Firm-level studies link AI investment to lower audit fees and to changes in staff mix, but almost no research examines how firms adjust the internal, hours-based plans on which fees are set. I identify six gaps: the measurement of activity-level AI effects, the cost of oversight, the fate of freed capacity, in-engagement monitoring, the sharing of AI gains with clients, and the position of small and mid-sized practices. I then propose a research agenda of seven questions with suggested methods and data. The paper aims to help researchers and practitioners study and manage AI-enabled engagements on the basis of evidence rather than general efficiency assumptions.

abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has transformed the operational and strategic landscape of Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs), creating opportunities to improve organisational performance through digitally enabled Strategic Management Accounting (SMA). While traditional management accounting primarily supports operational control and historical financial reporting, SMA extends this role by integrating financial and non-financial information to facilitate strategic planning, competitive positioning, and long-term decision-making. The emergence of cloud computing, artificial intelligence, enterprise resource planning systems, big data analytics, blockchain, and mobile accounting has significantly enhanced the ability of SMEs to generate timely, accurate, and strategic information. Despite these opportunities, the adoption of digitally enabled SMA remains uneven, particularly among township-based SMEs operating in resource-constrained environments such as Soweto, South Africa. Existing literature indicates that organisational limitations, technological barriers, infrastructural deficiencies, regulatory uncertainty, and inadequate managerial capabilities continue to constrain digital transformation within SMEs. Furthermore, much of the existing research has focused on large organisations and developed economies, resulting in limited understanding of how digital transformation influences SMA adoption within township businesses. This literature review critically synthesises current scholarly evidence regarding Strategic Management Accounting, digital transformation, theoretical explanations for technology adoption, and the organisational factors influencing digitally enabled SMA implementation among SMEs. The review further identifies major research gaps and proposes future research directions that contribute to both theory and practice by providing a context-specific understanding of digital transformation and strategic accounting within South African township economies.

abstract:
Background Accounting literacy is increasingly framed as a capacity to understand, interpret and apply financial information rather than merely reproduce procedural bookkeeping routines. The supplied evidence includes studies of simplified accounting templates, educational software, active learning, case-based teaching, experiential learning, digital tools and accounting instruction that moves beyond conventional debits-and-credits explanations. However, the evidence base is incomplete: databases, search dates, screening procedures, data-extraction procedures and synthesis methods were not recorded, and many included records contain incomplete methodological or bibliographic information. Several records also appear to concern accounting majors, secondary education, non-empirical chapters or topics only indirectly related to accounting literacy among non-financial higher education students. Aim This draft systematic review examines which alternative pedagogical models are reported for developing accounting literacy among non-financial higher education students, how those models relate to conceptual understanding and engagement, what implementation barriers and ethical considerations are reported, which contextual factors shape adoption, and where the evidence remains insufficient. Methods The review was designated a Systematic Review and used the supplied Boolean search strategy concerning non-financial students, pedagogical models and accounting or financial literacy, while excluding primary and secondary schooling, professional accountants and related terms. The recorded PRISMA workflow identified 281 records, removed 1 duplicate, screened 205 records, assessed 141 full texts, excluded 7 at full-text stage and retained 134 studies. CASP was used for critical appraisal, with 134 of 134 currently included studies appraised and a reported mean score of 14.9. Because the CASP workspace records conservative text-evidence appraisals and many criteria as requiring verification, scores are not treated as unquestioned total-quality measures. Bibliometric intelligence was used descriptively alongside methodological appraisal, not as a substitute for it.

Findings:

The directly relevant evidence suggests that structured alternatives to purely procedural instruction can support understanding or engagement when they make accounting information visual, applied, interactive or connected to authentic decisions. SATA was specifically developed to help non-accounting students prepare financial-statement components within a business plan, while educational authoring software was used with computer-engineering students studying financial analysis and ClassPoint was associated with engagement-focused teaching among engineering students (Shamsudin et al., 2020; Popgeorgiev et al., 2023; Arshad et al., 2023). Evidence concerning non-financial university students remains thinner than the numerical size of the included set suggests. Many studies use single-site, questionnaire-based, purposive or convenience samples, and outcome measures frequently concern perceptions, financial behaviour or general literacy rather than validated conceptual accounting understanding. Evidence on implementation barriers, ethics and institutional adoption is fragmented and cannot support strong comparative conclusions. Conclusion Alternative pedagogical models appear promising, particularly when they connect accounting concepts to practical tasks, technology-supported representation and active participation. Nevertheless, the present manuscript is not a final review. The evidence base is incomplete and heterogeneous, and the confidence of conclusions is limited by unclear eligibility alignment, incomplete extraction and substantial methodological uncertainty. A verified and better-documented review is required before claims about the superiority of any specific model can be made.

abstract:
Introduction:

Small and medium enterprises may struggle to adopt digital technologies that support Strategic Management Accounting (SMA), while weak accounting information can contribute to financing constraints. The supplied evidence suggests that digital accounting, performance measurement and strategic information systems can improve reporting usefulness, but implementation is conditioned by resources, skills, readiness and organisational support.

Methods:

The researcher-selected databases and information sources were Google Scholar, ERIC. The eligibility protocol restricted publication years to 2020–2026. The exact calendar date of search execution was not recorded in the verified identification provenance; this is distinct from the publication-year eligibility range. A Systematic Review searched Google Scholar and ERIC using the verified Boolean strategy, with publication eligibility restricted to 2020–2026.

Results:

The five analytical themes were: SME adoption is limited by resource, capability and change-readiness constraints; digital transformation requires strategic purpose and sociotechnical alignment; data-enabled SMA can improve the quality and usefulness of financial information; improved information may support funding access, but creditworthiness is only indirectly evidenced; and a practical framework should be staged, measurable and locally supportable. One study reported a negative association between digital accounting and financial performance, indicating that implementation quality matters. Discussion/Conclusion: The evidence supports a readiness-based, strategically aligned and incremental framework linking affordable digital accounting, data governance, employee capability, SMA practices, performance indicators and funding transparency. abstract: This qualitative study explores perspectives of pre-service accounting teachers about their remote learning experiences and what this means for preparing them professionally. Using technological pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPCK), and the theory of Reflective Practice, this study seeks to address a gap in our knowledge base regarding how future educators, who are simultaneously learners and aspiring professionals, understand the transition to emergency remote teaching. Twenty students enrolled in a Bachelor of Education (Accounting) program at a South African university participated in the research, submitting reflective essay responses, participating in focus group interviews and were analysed using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis. Findings revealed two competing realities. While remote learning provided flexibility and opportunities for the participants to pace themselves when mastering accounting concepts; participants lost many of the opportunities for spontaneous dialogue and immediate feedback they needed to develop procedural and professional judgment. More critically, participants functioned as reflective observers of instructional practices, identified a lack of congruence between available technologies and effective pedagogies and used this insight to develop a digital pedagogical mind-set. Participants articulated intentional strategies including content chunking and structured collaborative activities they would use in their future classrooms. Ultimately, the remote learning experience created a hybrid practitioner identity, positioning these future educators as analytical co-designers of learning rather than simply survivors of a crisis. Therefore, teacher education should intentionally include reflective, technology-enabled experiences so that they can produce confident, pedagogically competent accounting educators who can effectively integrate digital tools into meaningful social interactions in a variety of learning contexts.

abstract: This study aims to develop an integrated material flow cost accounting (MFCA) model that goes beyond the traditional one-size-fits-all framework and extends to complete supply chains under the requirements of a closed carbon economy (CCE). The proposed model is based on three core pillars: first, integrating the dimensions of physical mass and carbon density into a unified unit of measurement; The applied study is conducted on an integrated supply chain in the agrobiochemical sector that includes five Quantities (QC) centers, through three methodological stages: building the theoretical model, applying it to case data, and then analyzing the scenarios. The results showed that the total material waste was 5,478 tonnes (19.3% of the inputs), and the cost of carbon waste was US$187,260, while the average carbon cycle closure index was 0.79, indicating measurable improvement potential. The study makes a theoretical and practical contribution, filling a gap in the accounting literature related to the integration of MFCA with chain-level carbon disclosure requirements, and provides a framework that is actually applicable in enterprises operating under mandatory carbon pricing systems. By bridging material flow cost accounting with circular carbon economy metrics across supply chain stages, this study provides an actionable accounting tool to advance Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) and SDG 13 (Climate Action), through quantifiable waste reduction and decarbonization incentives.

abstract: This study examines accounting connectivity between FY2024 sustainability statements prepared under the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) and corresponding IFRS financial statements. Using the full eligible population of 22 Portuguese companies listed on the Euronext Lisbon regulated market, it develops and applies a 26-item Accounting Connectivity Index (ACI) across four dimensions: Referential, Quantitative, Methodological, and Accounting Consequence Connectivity. The analysis combines structured content analysis with qualitative assessment of sustainability-to-accounting pathways. ACI scores range from 17.1 to 94.8, with a population mean of 57.1. Quantitative Connectivity is the strongest and most widespread dimension, largely reflecting traceable relationships between EU Taxonomy metrics and financial-statement amounts. Accounting Consequence Connectivity, by contrast, is concentrated in seven companies. The results show that quantitative traceability does not necessarily imply substantive accounting connectivity and support a distinction between disclosure connectivity and integration into accounting assumptions, estimates, measurement, and financial-statement outcomes. Connectivity pathways also differ across business models. The findings remain stable under alternative population definitions, item specifications, and weighting approaches. The study contributes a replicable, sector-neutral framework for evaluating the nature and depth of connectivity between sustainability and financial reporting.

abstract: Consumption-based and territorial emissions accounting could operate side by side, as has been proposed by a few countries. However, how such dual accounting affects assessments of national mitigation ambition remains unclear. Here, we derive national carbon budgets and implied net-zero emission years under hypothetical net-zero targets that cover both territorial and consumption-based emissions within a dual accounting framework. We apply three effort-sharing approaches for 91 countries plus the European Union. Our results show that the derived national mitigation ambitions are sensitive not only to the effort-sharing approach used but also to the weight given to territorial versus consumption-based emissions when assigning responsibility to individual countries. The impact is strongest for countries with historically large net emissions embodied in trade. Under a dual accounting framework, the weight given to territorial versus consumption-based emissions when assigning responsibility to individual countries cannot be determined empirically and constitutes another inherently normative component.

abstract: Enterprise risk management (ERM) and risk governance require organizations to connect risk identification, assessment, monitoring, and response with planning, performance evaluation, accountability, and organizational resilience. This study examines the development and intellectual structure of research at the intersection of ERM, risk governance, management accounting, and management control systems. A bibliometric analysis was conducted on 1,042 Scopus-indexed publications using Bibliometrix, Biblioshiny, and VOSviewer. The findings show sustained growth in the field and identify risk management, management control systems, and performance management as its principal motor theme. Management accounting occupies a central position in the keyword network and is closely connected with risk assessment, enterprise risk management, and performance measurement. However, the literature remains fragmented across risk governance, corporate governance, resilience, and sector-specific applications. The study therefore positions ERM and risk governance as the primary framework and interprets management accounting, control mechanisms, and information systems as enabling infrastructures through which risk information is translated into responsibilities, limits, resource-allocation decisions, corrective action, and organizational learning. The resulting framework clarifies how organizations can embed enterprise and financial risk considerations in established managerial routines rather than treating risk management as a separate reporting exercise.

abstract: When accounting firms build artificial intelligence (AI) efficiency assumptions into engagement budgets, they need a way to check during delivery whether those assumptions hold. Monthly estimate-to-complete (ETC) reviews provide such a check, but the choice of forecasting method matters. This paper uses a Monte Carlo simulation of 10,000 recurring accounting engagements per scenario to compare six ETC methods under uncertain AI efficiency, uncertain review effort, staff learning and changes in work volume. Three findings stand out. First, re-forecasting during delivery clearly outperforms relying on the original plan: by month 6, the best methods roughly halve the forecast error of the plan alone. Second, the best method depends on learning: when staff are still learning to use AI, a 50/50 blend of plan and latest-month performance is most accurate early in the engagement (mean absolute error 2.37% at month 3), whereas a cumulative average is best when performance is stable. Third, activity-level forecasting matters most when the mix of work changes: after a shift in volumes, an activity-level latest-month forecast had a mean error of 1.55% at month 6, compared with 3.52% for an engagement-level forecast. The simulation also shows that optimistic AI plans are likely to miss their target margin in most cases, which underlines the need for in-flight monitoring. The paper offers practical guidance on which ETC method to use at each stage of an engagement. JEL classification: M41; C63; L84; O33

abstract: This study investigates the relationship between the use of Business Intelligence capabilities and accounting decision quality mediated by accounting information quality and moderated by technology investment readiness. The study emphasizes three aspects of Business Intelligence capabilities: data management capability, data analytics capability, and reporting and visualization capability. A quantitative design was used and data were gathered using a structured questionnaire from 300 Accounting, Financial, Auditor, IS and managerial employees in Jordanian organizations. The measurement model was evaluated and the direct, mediating, and moderating relationships were tested using SmartPLS 4. The results show that capability in data management has a positive and significant impact on accounting information quality as well as data analytics capability and reporting and visualization capability. The results also indicated that the accounting information quality significantly and positively affects the accounting decision quality. Additionally, the relationships between Business Intelligence capabilities and accounting decision quality were greatly mediated by the accounting information quality. The results also confirmed the positive moderation between Business Intelligence capabilities and accounting information quality. The study extends the body of knowledge by expanding the view about the BI capabilities in the accounting decision-making context and the importance of the quality of the accounting information as a key mechanism by which those capabilities enhance decision quality. From a practical perspective, the study recommends that an organization must institute efforts to invest in data management, data analytic tools, reports, employee training and digital infrastructure to increase accounting information quality and to increase the quality outcomes of accounting decision making.

abstract: Unlike living organisms, which persist by balancing energy intake, expenditure, and maintenance, embodied robots are often evaluated primarily by task performance, even when morphology, control, and environment jointly determine what can be sustained over time. This task-centered evaluation supports engineering benchmarks but can obscure embodied costs, limit comparability across heterogeneous embodiments, and weaken biological interpretation when robots and simulations are used as model systems. This Review synthesizes biological energetics and biomechanics to argue that open-system energy accounting provides a common currency for embodied evolution. Under this framing, adaptive success (fitness) is interpreted as persistence under energetic constraint, enabling commensurate comparison of regulation, structural adaptation, and structural plasticity across environments with different energetic structure. A minimal accounting framework and an illustrative experimental paradigm are presented to show how shared accounting yields interpretable differences between adaptive responses beyond task semantics. This paper concludes by discussing implications for interpreting morphological and control complexity and by outlining open challenges and future directions for energy-aware embodied evolution using robots as controlled platforms for biology-facing hypothesis testing.

abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping accounting, auditing, and financial reporting, yet the literature remains fragmented across outlets, disciplines, and methodological traditions. This study systematically reviews 47 publications from 2023 to 2026 drawn from an initial pool of 49 records. Each study was coded on publication year, research topic, and research method, and a full coding protocol is specified for country, research subject, theory, variables, and findings. The results show rapid growth: 34 of the 47 studies (72%) were published in 2025–2026. Nearly two-thirds of the studies address accounting and auditing in general terms or fraud detection and auditing. Fewer than one in five uses a method that can be identified as a systematic or bibliometric review. Theory use, country coverage, and empirical designs cannot be established from bibliographic data alone and are treated as priorities for full-text coding. The study concludes with a research agenda emphasizing theory-driven, context-specific, and empirically grounded work.

abstract: Whether a monetary anchor independent of discretionary issuance can remain stable at the macro level is the central open problem identified by the first paper of this program (Cheng and Cheng 2026a). The present paper takes up that problem under the program’s normative premises and develops a conditional reconstruction of inflation and macrostability. We first specify the complete life cycle of the currency: issuance and extinction are mirror images of the creation and consumption of value. Consumption events trigger the cancellation of the corresponding money at the platform clearing node; durable value is extinguished on an amortization schedule that tracks physical depreciation; money issued against non-rival knowledge persists. The money stock thereby corresponds to the surviving value stock at every instant, M(t) ≡ ks·V(t). On this basis we identify five mechanisms through which inflation is structurally precluded rather than suppressed — temporal synchrony, the quantity identity, channel excision, expectation self-stabilization, and the separation of relative prices from the price level — and we state the structural price-stability proposition with its scope made explicit: the accounting unit, the money price of a unit of negentropic value, satisfies P(t) ≡ ks as a matter of accounting construction, while the consumer price level experienced by households is governed by the dual-price band analyzed in Section 4.7. Inflation is then rediagnosed as the relative deviation produced by four identifiable integrity failures: accounting falsification, consensus distortion, issuance corruption, and extinction failure. The zero-inflation condition, the monotonic structure of consensus distortion, and the existence of a buffering bound for the stability coefficient ks are stated as propositions, together with a viability condition for the metabolism backstop, a composition bound on experienced inflation, an optimal buffering rule under stochastic shocks, and a tipping condition for the transition window. Four embedded stabilizers — the objectivity anchor of accounting, the procedural anchor of consensus revision, the functional anchor of countercyclical public investment, and the social anchor of unconditional basic income — replace interest-rate policy, and a technology–consensus co-evolution cycle replaces the financial–debt cycle as the dominant form of fluctuation. The framework is applied to three contemporary monetary problems, and historical episodes are mapped as illustrations rather than tests. Falsifiable hypotheses with explicit verification designs are stated, and the limitations include, with emphasis, the gap between the constructed accounting unit and the experienced price level.

abstract: This exploratory qualitative study investigates how using active learning techniques impacts Grade 11 learners' ability to retain financial accounting concepts. Specifically, the study compares active learning methods to the traditional rote memorization approach typically employed by the educators. It will explore the effectiveness of various interactive methods for teaching financial accounting, including collaborative projects, case studies, peer-to-peer tutoring, project-based assessments, and other related strategies. Active learning increases student engagement and promotes deeper conceptual understanding. Additionally, this type of learning fosters a shift toward a learner-centred Smodel of education, enabling students to translate theoretical concepts into real-world applications such as bank reconciliations and financial statements. Overall, the study demonstrates that incorporating active pedagogy leads to better long-term memory retention and more effectively develops students' critical thinking and problem-solving abilities. Therefore, it recommends that educators include active learning techniques across all aspects of their curriculum to create authentic, long-lasting learning outcomes.

abstract: A recent paper by Arencibia-Albite presents an analytical proof that the Energy Balance Model (EBM) is internally inconsistent when obligatory non-urinary nitrogen losses are explicitly accounted for. The proof derives a negative protein balance and persistent carbohydrate accumulation under simultaneous energy balance and body weight stability. This commentary identifies a specific thermodynamic accounting issue in the proof: absorbed protein intake is credited with the full oxidative energy density on the intake side of the energy balance equation, while the chemical bond enthalpy carried out of the body by unoxidized nitrogen-containing material is omitted from the outflow side. When this enthalpy is explicitly included, consistent with the First Law of Thermodynamics for an open system, the contradiction resolves. The resolution is not a refutation of the paper's broader project. It is a refinement that strengthens the case for the Mass Balance Model (MBM) by showing that the EBM, when corrected, requires a mass-based term.

abstract: Carbonation curing can store CO₂ in cementitious materials, but its net carbon benefit depends on the emissions associated with CO₂ supply and curing. We manually compiled and curated a literature database, harmonised uptake to an original-material mass basis including aggregates, and coupled machine learning with process carbon accounting. Using 461 records and eight material and curing descriptors, we compared eight regressors and evaluated uptake responses alongside supply, transport and curing emissions. This framework connects experimental uptake data to the conditions under which the assessed process yields a net carbon benefit. At an illustrative predicted uptake of 0.231 kg CO₂/kg original material and an assumed material mass of 2400 kg/m³, all five supply scenarios yield net benefits of 0.189–0.219 kg CO₂/kg original material with electricity at 0.05 kg CO₂/kWh. Two scenarios become net emitters at 0.40 kg CO₂/kWh. Calculated break-even electricity intensities range from 0.314 to 2.047 kg CO₂/kWh, demonstrating how supply assumptions change the conditions for a positive balance. The curated database and coupled analysis provide a basis for comparing these conditions; limited cross-study predictive performance confines the numerical results to conditional scenarios.

abstract:
Purpose:

This study aims to examine the impact of integrating artificial intelligence techniques with management accounting methods on the financial reporting quality in Iraqi government banks. It also examines the impact of the Financial reporting quality on stakeholder confidence, and tests the mediating role of financial reporting quality in the relationship between the integration of artificial intelligence and management accounting and stakeholder confidence. Design/Methodology/Approach A structured questionnaire was used to survey 100 employees working in banks such Accountants, bankers, and specialized academics regarding AI and managerial accounting practices, and reporting quality. Quantitative models using structural equation modeling (SEM) were employed to analyze the direct and indirect relationships between the variables. Results The results indicate that integrating AI technologies with management accounting does not necessarily lead to a direct increase in trust in banks. Rather, this is achieved through high-quality financial reporting, which acts as an intermediary between technological advancement and trust building. While banks strive to generate strong internal key performance indicators (KPIs) and functional accuracy, these should be disseminated clearly to gain the trust of customers and investors. Practical Implications The researchers’ findings, which focus on integrating artificial intelligence with management accounting, do not directly increase trust in banks. Rather, this effect is mediated by high-quality financial reporting. Therefore, it is essential for the studied government banks to focus on producing accurate and clear performance indicators and publishing them transparently to enhance their credibility and gain the trust of customers and investors. Originality/Value This study makes a pivotal contribution to academic literature and adds to the limited body of research on the integration of artificial intelligence, management accounting, financial reporting, and trust in banks.

abstract: This paper proposes an integrated Blue Economy Accounting (BEA) framework that combines Blue Accounting, the Underwater Domain Awareness (UDA) framework, and Modelling and Simulation-based Marine Spatial Planning (M&S-MSP) to support sustainable ocean governance in tropical countries. Marine and coastal ecosystems provide essential ecological, economic, and social benefits through fisheries, aquaculture, tourism, coastal protection, transportation, and other ocean-based activities. However, these systems face increasing pressures from climate change, pollution, overexploitation, habitat degradation, and competing uses of marine space. The proposed framework enables systematic assessment and dynamic valuation of marine natural capital and ecosystem services, while integrating ecological conditions, economic activities, and human pressures into decision-making. Blue Accounting provides the basis for tracking changes in marine assets and ecosystem values, while UDA strengthens situational awareness by integrating ecological, oceanographic, technological, and human-activity data. M&S-MSP supports scenario-based planning by enabling policymakers to evaluate the ecological, economic, and social implications of alternative marine-use strategies. By integrating accounting, underwater awareness, and predictive modelling, the framework promotes evidence-based policymaking, adaptive resource management, conflict reduction, and resilient blue economy development. It provides a foundation for balancing economic growth with ecological integrity and the regenerative capacity of marine ecosystems, thereby supporting sustainable and climate-resilient ocean governance in tropical regions.

abstract:
Introduction

Mass chest X-ray formed a routine part of induction processes to the US armed forces in the 1940-1950s for tuberculosis screening. Today, the skeletal structure recorded in these medical miniature films serves to identify these same soldiers. In the US military's accounting/repatriation setting, chest radiograph comparisons have grown to be a primary identification mechanism alongside DNA and dental records. Identifications are now routinely conducted with contributions from miniature radiographic films. This article reviews the miniature radiographic film as an identification tool and provides the first evaluation of findings (180 cases) against gold standards of DNA and dental analyses for the very same cases.

Materials and methods

This article reviews both miniature film photofluorographs and the standardized chest radiograph comparison (CXR) protocol employed by the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA) for identification. Additionally, all DPAA cases (2010-2025) where radiographic CXR resulted in a match result (280) were reviewed for additional DNA and/or dental record findings, providing 180 cases where dual-modality result existed to cross-validation test the radiographic analyses.

Results

For 172 DNA cases, there was no instance of disagreement between the chest radiograph result and the independently acquired Armed Forces DNA Identification Laboratory's DNA result. For 8 dental cases reporting a positive match result, the CXR identity finding was identical (both evidence lines identified the same person). To be conservative, we assume that the next future CXR case to be conducted using miniature films will yield an erroneous result, thereby setting a positive predictive value for radiographic comparison of 99.4% (=180 correct results/181 total decisions).

Conclusions

Miniature chest radiographs provide useful identification-relevant information. DPAA casework provides a rare circumstance to evaluate the accuracy of miniature film radiograph comparisons across a large sample, as multiple independent and parallel lines of analysis exist for single cases. Evaluation of these cases (180 in total) reveals that the military miniature films supply the same name associations that DNA and forensic odontology provide. The positive predictive value is high (99.4%), conservatively assuming the next case to be an incorrect one. This confirms the value of the miniature chest film and CXR methods, when DNA and dental records alone are unable to provide definitive answers.

abstract: China's sport industry expanded while its composition shifted toward services during 2018-2024, but both the accounting mechanisms behind this change and the robustness of the pattern to the COVID-19 disruption and relative-price movements require careful qualification. We analyze annual national sport-industry accounts published by the National Bureau of Statistics of China and the General Administration of Sport. The analysis combines value-added shares, value-added intensity, a descriptive service-to-manufacturing value-added ratio, shift-share decompositions, alternative time windows, a proxy-based price sensitivity analysis, and crisis-recovery indicators. The service share of sport-industry value added increased from 64.8% in 2018 to 72.0% in 2024, while the manufacturing share declined from 33.7% to 26.5%. Aggregate value-added intensity rose from 37.9% to 41.7%. For 2018-2024, the decomposition assigns +2.50 percentage points to changes in category output weights, + 1.44 points to within-category intensity changes, and -0.13 points to their interaction. The between-category contribution remained positive in all alternative multi-year windows, although it was not always larger than the within-category contribution. Under the specified price-proxy scenario, the between-category contribution remained positive. Co-located services fell by 16.2% in value added in 2020 and rebounded by 24.6% in 2021, ending 4.4% above their 2019 level; education/training and media/information services did not contract in 2020. The published accounts therefore document a service-oriented reallocation over the observed period, alongside substantial post-shock within-category change and heterogeneous exposure across service activities. Because the series uses current-price data and crosses a 2023 census-benchmark break, the results should be interpreted as descriptive accounting patterns rather than causal estimates of productivity, policy effects, or pandemic mechanisms.

abstract: Nutrient trading between point and diffuse sources of nutrients offers an integrated watershed nutrient management approach to achieve nutrient reduction goals that benefit both the terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. This market-based approach requires quantification of the environmental impacts of nutrients derived from different sources. This environmental impact depends on the forms, concentrations, loads, transport, and processing of nutrients within waterways. However, the impacts of source-specific nutrient characteristics in different point and diffuse nutrient sources have not been accounted for in nutrient trading schemes. Here, we explored an accounting method for nitrogen trading that accounts for different aquatic environmental impacts of point and diffuse sources. This environmental impact quantification is based on model fittings of a published dataset on algal photosynthetic responses to the key nitrogen form, i.e., total dissolved nitrogen rather than total nitrogen, from three sources: point source discharge from tertiary-treated sewage and aquaculture ponds, and diffuse watershed erosion runoff. We explored a method for decomposing trading ratios into environmental equivalency, delivery ratio, and uncertainty component for different sources, and considering the co-benefits of watershed mitigation. Our results demonstrate that prioritizing diffuse nitrogen sources with a greater aquatic environmental impact and co-benefits can significantly reduce the watershed mitigation requirements for offsetting the environmental impacts of point-source nitrogen loads. This study presents an exploratory accounting approach for nitrogen trading that incorporates the differential environmental impacts of point and diffuse nutrient sources on aquatic ecosystems. Alternative approaches to equating environmental impacts across sources with different nutrient characteristics also warrant further investigation.

abstract:
Background

Blue carbon has become an important component of climate mitigation policy, integrating selected coastal ecosystems into greenhouse gas accounting frameworks. With their high productivity and large spatial extent, seaweed ecosystems have recently entered this debate, particularly in Europe where interest in seaweed-based climate strategies is expanding. However, it remains uncertain whether the evidence currently available for wild seaweed ecosystems meets the standards required for inclusion in formal blue carbon accounting.

Scope

This review systematically assesses empirical evidence from European wild seaweed ecosystems. Sixteen empirical studies were evaluated using a structured classification framework based on three accounting-relevant pillars: permanence, defined as carbon storage exceeding 100 years; the feasibility of monitoring, reporting, and verification; and demonstrable net climate benefit after accounting for losses and variability. Review and policy literature were examined to contextualise these findings.

Conclusions

No current wild seaweed ecosystem evidence consistently satisfied all three pillars for policy-grade accounting. Evidence for durable carbon storage was limited and highly context-specific. Monitoring approaches were generally site-based and not readily scalable to inventory-level reporting, while net climate benefit was frequently reduced or offset by greenhouse gas emissions and temporal variability. These findings highlight a mismatch between seaweed carbon dynamics, the current evidence base, and accounting requirements. The findings support a precautionary policy approach that prioritises conservation-led management of wild seaweed ecosystems. Current evidence does not yet support their inclusion in blue carbon accounting frameworks and indicates that future research should address permanence, monitoring, reporting and verification feasibility, and net climate benefit.

abstract: Constructivist learning theory emphasises that learners actively construct knowledge, while posthumanist philosophy highlights the interconnectedness between human and ecological systems. In accounting education, these perspectives offer a foundation for advancing socially responsible and sustainability-oriented practices. However, limited research has examined how their integration can enhance ethical sensitivity and sustainable competencies in Further Education and Training (FET) colleges, particularly within resource-constrained contexts in South Africa. This study addresses this gap through a qualitative multiple case study conducted at two FET colleges (urban and rural). Data were collected from 31 participants including educators, students, managers, and community partners using semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and document analysis. Thematic analysis was employed to analyse the data. The findings reveal that project-based learning initiatives, such as sustainability reporting, enhance students’ critical thinking and environmental awareness, while community-based activities, including financial literacy workshops, strengthen practical skills and social responsibility. However, the implementation of these pedagogies is highly context-dependent, with urban institutions benefiting from greater access to technological resources and partnerships, while rural institutions face persistent structural constraints. These findings contribute directly to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 4 (Quality Education) by promoting inclusive and equitable learning, SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) by enhancing employability and professional readiness, and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) by fostering sustainability-oriented accounting competencies. Overall, integrating constructivist and posthumanist approaches provides a valuable framework for advancing sustainable accounting education, although systemic support, curriculum reform, and targeted resource allocation remain essential for long-term impact.

abstract: How much poverty leverage is embedded in U.S. state minimum-wage increases? I combine a month-specific schedule of regular state and federal minimum-wage floors for 2006--2019 with Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement records to trace mechanically predicted wage resources to workers' official families. The accounting separates population reach, poverty targeting, and gap-closing conversion, and compares the resulting allocation with objective-specific benchmarks that reallocate the same predicted resources within each state--reform-year. In pooled reform-exposure records, 14.1 percent of workers in the primary regular-statewide-floor wage interval are linked to poor families, while 11.6 percent of predicted resources accrue to those families. The predicted allocation attains 1.0 percent of the same-resource benchmark for reducing the official poverty headcount and 6.8 percent of the corresponding benchmark for reducing poverty depth. An inclusive incremental-gap diagnostic yields larger placement ratios, but 88.9 percent of its predicted resource total originates below the Consumer Price Index-aligned no-state-reform floor. The analysis is noncausal: annual work inputs, nonwage resources, and the interview-year official-family roster are held fixed throughout. JEL Classification: J38, I32, J31

abstract: The inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IP<sub>3</sub>R) channel is an important calcium channel involved in calcium-induced calcium release, playing a prominent role in intracellular calcium signaling. However, accurately characterizing its gating behavior remains a challenge, particularly because the temporal resolution of patch-clamp techniques is not large enough to detect all short-lived events. This limitation can significantly bias the inference of kinetic models describing the receptor activity. To address this issue, we focused on quantitative analysis of IP<sub>3</sub>R2 gating behavior using patch-clamp data, with particular attention to missed events. We modeled IP<sub>3</sub>R2 channel gating using hierarchical Markov chains and used a Bayesian approach that integrates missed-event correction directly into the likelihood function, enabling more accurate parameter inference and model evaluation. We show that accounting for missed events deeply clarifies the multimodal model that emerges from model selection. In this new model, the park and drive modes both consist of the same 3-state Markov model, with mode-dependent kinetic parameters: the drive mode stabilizes the closed state directly connected to the open one, whereas the park mode stabilizes the other closed state, which is not connected to the open one. Intermediate Ca<sup>2+</sup> concentrations are found to strongly depress the drive-to-park transition rate, so that the IP<sub>3</sub>R2 channel undergoes frequent transitions to the park mode only for <50 nM or micromolar Ca<sup>2+</sup> concentrations. Overall, our approach provides a refined perspective on IP<sub>3</sub>R2 channel modeling and highlights the critical importance of accounting for missed events upon model selection based on single-channel recordings.

abstract: Following the changes in the conditions of water resources and the challenges of water shortage, water resources management is considered more important. Accordingly, the use of the traditional water balance approach that focuses on the balance of water input and output in a system has been replaced with newer methods such as water accounting. Providing a more comprehensive and accurate picture of water flows and uses, water accounting enables more efficient management of water resources. Doing water accounting manually can be associated with many challenges. One of the challenges is the need for computer knowledge to download satellite images. Additionally, the large amount of calculations needed for water accounting usually leads to calculation errors, affecting negatively the validity of the results. Model calibration is also a time-consuming process that requires a lot of concentration and precision. Moreover, analyzing satellite images for water accounting purposes through common software such as ArcGIS1 can be very difficult and time-consuming. Although these software are powerful, they are not developed 1Geographic Information System specifically for water accounting. Therefore, it is necessary to provide dedicated software that facilitates the water accounting process. The present paper introduces the water accounting plus software called Aquametrics Plus. This software has been provided to improve the capabilities of users who face the mentioned challenges when using the WA+ framework. To investigate the performance and accuracy of the software, a case study has been conducted on the Zayandehrood basin. In this research, the results indicated that the use of software increased the speed of calculations, saved time, reduced calculation errors, and increased the precision of calibration and calculations.

abstract: The accounting profession is undergoing a widely documented shift from a compliance-centred, transaction-processing function toward a strategic advisory role embedded in organisational decision-making. In this conceptual paper, an attempt has been made to investigate the way the transition is taking place in two different structural contexts in one national economy, the world of commercial banking and public universities in Ghana. Using the theoretical bases of institutional theory, structuration theory, and the management accounting literature of business partnering, a conceptual framework has been developed for the re-definition of the role of the accountant from watchdog through hybrid to strategic business partner. The framework further proposes that sectoral context, specifically the profit orientation and competitive exposure of banking relative to the budget-constrained, multi-stakeholder governance of public universities, moderates the pace and form of this transition. Unlike much of the existing business-partner literature, the framework explicitly incorporates the possibility that observed role change is partly symbolic: drawing on the institutional concept of decoupling, it distinguishes genuine advisory capability from the ceremonial adoption of business-partner language and job titles without corresponding change in practice. Six research propositions are advanced, five concerning the pace and outcomes of role redefinition and a sixth addressing the conditions under which decoupling is more or less likely. The paper contributes to the literature by extending role-transition theorising, developed predominantly in Western corporate settings, to a dual-sector emerging-market context, by explicitly engaging contested and null findings rather than only confirmatory evidence, and by offering a competency-oriented agenda for professional accounting bodies, employers, and accounting educators in Ghana and comparable Sub-Saharan African economies. Practical implications are outlined separately for industry and academia, and the paper concludes with a research design, including proposed measurement approaches for each construct, for the mixed-methods study needed to test the propositions empirically. abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming accounting systems through automation, predictive analytics, intelligent auditing, and financial decision-support systems. While scholarly and professional debates frequently address whether AI may substitute human accountants, empirical evidence examining actual substitution remains limited. Existing studies have primarily focused on technological efficiency and adoption intentions, with insufficient attention given to the psychological factors shaping professionals' perceptions of AI's substitutive potential. This study therefore investigates how psychological trust, AI anxiety, and cognitive adaptability influence accounting professionals' perceptions regarding AI's potential to substitute selected accounting tasks within future accounting frameworks in China. A mixed-method research design integrating quantitative and qualitative approaches was employed. Primary data were collected from 512 accounting professionals across major Chinese cities using structured questionnaires. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to test the proposed relationships. Additionally, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 25 accounting professionals to contextualize and enrich the quantitative findings. The results indicate that psychological trust positively influences perceived AI task substitution, whereas AI anxiety negatively affects such perceptions. Cognitive adaptability emerged as a significant positive predictor and mediated the relationship between psychological trust and perceived AI substitution. Qualitative findings revealed that although participants perceived AI as having substantial potential to automate repetitive and analytical accounting activities, they consistently emphasized the continuing importance of human judgment, ethical reasoning, strategic interpretation, and interpersonal communication. The study contributes to AI-accounting and psychology literature by integrating psychological dimensions into understanding perceived AI substitution and suggests that future accounting frameworks are more likely to reflect human-AI complementarity rather than complete occupational replacement. These findings reflect accounting professionals' perceptions and expectations regarding AI substitution and can't be interpreted as evidence of AI's actual capability to perform accounting tasks or replace professional judgment.

abstract: Technology transfer enables small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to access external technological knowledge, yet the organisational information-processing capabilities that help firms convert such knowledge into transfer activity remain underexplored. This study examines whether digital management accounting capability (DMAC) promotes technology transfer intensity through absorptive capacity (ACAP) and whether financial slack strengthens the ACAP–technology transfer relationship. Using a two-wave firm-level survey of technology-engaged Malaysian SMEs, 400 usable Wave 1 responses were obtained and 381 firms were successfully matched at Wave 2. Confirmatory factor analysis supported higher-order representations of DMAC and ACAP. Structural equation modelling showed that DMAC positively predicts ACAP (β = .787, p < .001), ACAP positively predicts technology transfer intensity (β = .391, p < .001), and the direct DMAC–technology transfer path remains significant (β = .297, p = .001). The bootstrapped indirect effect is also significant (β = .309, 95% bias-corrected CI [.177, .455]), indicating partial mediation. Financial slack has a positive main effect on technology transfer intensity but does not significantly moderate the ACAP–technology transfer relationship (β = −.056, p = .182). The study positions digital management accounting capability as part of the organisational infrastructure of technology transfer and distinguishes knowledge-processing capability from financial-resource availability.

abstract: This study examines whether firm-level climate risk exposure is associated with accounting transparency using a global panel of firm-year observations spanning 91 countries. Corporate climate risk exposure is measured using earnings-call text-based indicators developed by Sautner et al. (2023), while accounting transparency is captured through three proxies: absolute accruals, earnings smoothing ratio, and earnings smoothing correlation. The results show that climate risk exposure is negatively and significantly associated with absolute accruals, indicating that climate-exposed firms exhibit lower accrual-based opacity and therefore higher accrual-based accounting transparency. The effect is economically meaningful: a one-standard-deviation increase in climate risk exposure is associated with a 13.2% decline in absolute accruals relative to the sample mean. This finding is robust to entropy balancing, dynamic system generalized method of moments (GMM) estimation, and an alternative climate exposure proxy. Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) channel analyses further show that the negative association between climate risk exposure and absolute accruals is stronger among firms with above-median social, environmental, and governance scores, suggesting that ESG performance strengthens the transparency response to climate-related uncertainty. By contrast, climate risk exposure is not significantly associated with earnings smoothing ratio or earnings smoothing correlation across ESG groups, indicating that the effect is concentrated in the accrual-based channel rather than in smoothing-based reporting behaviour. The study contributes to the climate-finance literature and the accounting literature by linking firm-level climate risk exposure to financial reporting quality and by identifying ESG performance as an important conditioning mechanism. The findings are consistent with information asymmetry and signalling perspectives and carry practical implications for regulators, standard-setters, auditors, boards, and investors.

abstract: Social isolation is a major public health concern, yet census-tract-level indicators often exhibit spatial autocorrelation that violates standard regression assumptions. We evaluated geographic patterns and urban-suburban-rural gradients of perceived social isolation across 5,122 Florida census tracts using 2024 CDC PLACES crude prevalence estimates, controlling for spatial dependence. Spatial structure was assessed via global Moran’s I and Anselin’s Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA). Tracts were classified as urban, suburban, or rural by population density. Population-weighted linear regression was used to compare ordinary least squares (OLS) with Conley spatial heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) standard errors. Perceived social isolation showed substantial positive spatial clustering across Florida (Moran’s I = 0.67, p < 0.001). LISA mapping revealed high-high hotspots in urban metropolitan belts and rural interior areas, whereas low-low cold spots clustered along coastal regions. Conventional population-weighted OLS models suggested small, statistically significant reductions in isolation for suburban areas (-1.37 percentage points; 95% CI: -1.61, -1.13) and rural tracts (-1.28 percentage points; 95% CI: -1.54,-1.02) relative to urban areas. However, accounting for spatial autocorrelation with Conley spatial HAC standard errors expanded the standard errors sixfold, making the urban-suburban and urban-rural differences statistically nonsignificant. Compared with regional spatial clustering, broad urbanicity categories explain little geographic variation in social isolation in Florida. Public health strategies and resource allocation should focus on localized spatial hotspots rather than broad administrative classifications.

abstract: Meta-analyses, like primary studies, are affected by researcher degrees of freedom: researchers must decide which studies to include, how to compute effect sizes, and which statistical models to use. Different reasonable choices can lead to different results, making multiverse meta-analysis a useful tool for assessing robustness across alternative specifications. However, multiverse meta-analysis also introduces a multiple-testing problem. Current inferential approaches mainly provide a global test, which can establish that at least one specification differs from the null but cannot identify which individual specifications do so while accounting for multiplicity across the full multiverse. We introduce Post-selection Inference in Multiverse Meta-Analysis (PIMMA), which allows inference on individual specifications while controlling the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER) and accounting for their dependence. In practical terms, PIMMA shows which results remain statistically significant after accounting for multiplicity across all reasonable analytical choices. In simulations, the specification-level test adequately controlled Type I error, with power comparable to robust variance estimation in scenarios where both methods maintained appropriate Type I error control. In an application to meta-analyses of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy efficacy for adult depression, 297 of 336 unique meta-analytic analyses remained significant after step-down max-T adjustment for multiple testing, accounting for dependence among analyses. PIMMA therefore extends multiverse meta-analysis from a global assessment of whether any effect is present to specification-level inference, allowing researchers to evaluate robustness across specifications and identify which individual results remain significant under appropriate error control.

abstract: International climate policy increasingly pressures companies to demonstrate credible greenhouse gas (GHG) emission accounting. While various frameworks exist, firms struggle with system boundaries in complex industrial operations. This study addresses this challenge by developing an emissions calculation grounded in real field conditions and offering strategic insights for Indonesia’s oil and gas sector using Pertamina as a case study particularly regarding future carbon-tax exposure. The research introduces a high-resolution accounting approach for the CPP Gundih gas processing facility in Central Java, correcting a long-standing source of uncertainty where Pertamina assumed the entire 13 MMSCFD of Acid Gas Removal Unit off gas was combusted, inflating annual emissions to 250 ktCO₂. Field inspections revealed that 10–13 MMSCFD is diverted to a Biological Sulfur Recovery Unit. Using an IPCC Tier 3 carbon-content method anchored to real routing data, this study establishes a corrected baseline of 38 ktCO₂ per year. Under Indonesia’s carbon levy of IDR 30,000/ton, this revision reduces annual tax liability from IDR 7.5 billion to IDR 1.15 billion, preventing a four-to-sixfold overpayment. The economic analysis further examines how this compliance costs interact with two upstream fiscal regimes: PSC Cost Recovery and PSC Gross Split. The Gross Split model consistently delivers contractor margins roughly four times higher than Cost Recovery and shows stronger resilience to carbon-policy fluctuations. Integrating Tier 3 accounting with the Gross Split structure outlines a practical pathway to reduce long-term climate liabilities while keeping assets aligned with Indonesia’s Net Zero 2060 ambitions.

abstract: Governments around the world have recently adopted policy support programs for hydrogen, tying the level of support to the assessed carbon intensity of the hydrogen produced. Here we compare alternative carbon accounting rules for determining the policy support available for hydrogen in terms of the resulting financial and carbon emissions performance of Power-to-Gas systems. We calibrate our model to reference plants eligible for the production tax credit available under the Inflation Reduction Act in the United States. Contrary to frequently articulated views, more stringent accounting rules generally provide investors with sufficient incentives to invest in Power-to-Gas systems. Nonetheless, even more stringent rules can lead to carbon intensity levels close to those for hydrogen produced from natural gas with carbon capture. Less stringent rules generally entail stronger investment incentives due to higher profitability, but also significantly higher emissions as investors procure more carbon-intensive electricity from the general grid.

abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping accounting work by accelerating task cycles, expanding exception monitoring, and increasing reliance on automated recommendations. In accounting and auditing, these changes are consequential because work quality depends not only on efficient task completion, but also on ethical vigilance, professional skepticism, and careful evaluation of AI assisted outputs. This study introduces the numb efficiency paradox, a process in which accounting professionals may continue to meet work demands while becoming less affectively responsive to pressure, warning signs, and professional consequences. Using a single three wave longitudinal panel of accounting and auditing professionals recruited through occupation based prescreening and study specific eligibility screeners (T1, n = 512; T2, n = 417; T3, n = 361), the study examines AI related work pressure, occupational resilience, affective numbing, sustained work efficiency, ethical vigilance, and professional skepticism. The declining wave-specific sample sizes reflect panel attrition and quality screening rather than separate studies or newly recruited respondents. The results show that AI related work pressure was prospectively associated with both occupational resilience and affective numbing. Occupational resilience was prospectively associated with later sustained work efficiency. Affective numbing was not significantly associated with sustained work efficiency, but it was negatively associated with ethical vigilance and professional skepticism. AI autonomy and supervisor support showed beneficial direct associations with higher resilience and lower affective numbing, whereas the hypothesized interaction effects were not supported. These findings distinguish resilient efficiency from detached persistence and suggest that AI implementation should be evaluated not only by whether accounting work remains efficient, but also by whether professionals remain ethically vigilant and professionally skeptical when using AI supported systems.

abstract: A prominent developmental plasticity theory proposes that early life adversity accelerates life history trajectories so organisms can maximize fitness in challenging environments. Standard tests of this hypothesis rely on empirical predictions about observable life history variables (e.g., age at first birth), because the proposed internal processes cannot be directly measured. However, the observable proxies are themselves mechanically linked, and regressions that ignore this may conflate causal effects with mechanical relationships among proxies. Here, we develop theory that explicitly justifies some existing empirical tests but rejects others. We integrate an accounting model that incorporates age at first birth, interbirth intervals, and lifespan with an optimization model, to derive the mathematical form that tests of the hypothesis should take. We apply these tests to data from wild female baboons, using early life rainfall as an exogenous proxy for early adversity so that estimates can plausibly be interpreted causally. The accounting model explains >98% of the variation in lifetime reproductive success among females that reproduced. However, our theory-derived tests find no evidence for the reproductive acceleration hypothesis. Our study illustrates the value of formal theory for causal inference in developmental plasticity research, where intertwined measurable variables may be obscured by strictly verbal hypotheses.

abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has emerged as a response to the need to understand and make transparent the decisions of machine learning models, particularly in sensitive contexts such as accounting and financial auditing. In this domain, XAI enables the interpretation of results generated by automated systems applied to fraud detection, risk management, financial analysis, and regulatory compliance, thereby strengthening the trust of auditors and regulators. The objective of this study was to systematically analyze the literature on XAI in accounting and financial auditing in order to identify its application domains, the methods employed, and the main challenges reported. The research was conducted through a systematic literature review following the PRISMA protocol, based on studies retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science. The selected works were organized and synthesized using an analysis matrix, resulting in 85 primary studies. The findings indicate that XAI is mainly applied to fraud detection, credit assessment, financial auditing, and decision-support processes, with a predominance of techniques such as SHAP and LIME. Although these tools enhance transparency, limitations related to computational cost, data quality, explanation stability, and regulatory adaptation persist, highlighting the need to strengthen their integration into auditing processes. abstract: This paper proposes Accounting-State Agent-Based Modeling (AS-ABM), a framework in which each agent maintains a double-entry bookkeeping state space formalized through Exchange Algebra and interacts with other agents through stage-ordered transactions. Because double-entry consistency constraints are inherently entity-specific, the agent-based architecture enforces them by construction at the transaction level rather than through ex post aggregate checks. As a minimal demonstration, we construct an input–output (IO) transaction network using synthetic input-coefficient matrices, treating the IO coefficients as controlled experimental parameters. We show that the framework exactly reproduces the Leontief multiplier-effect benchmark under unconstrained conditions, thereby establishing the equivalence of our dynamic cumulative-difference measure with the static multiplier. When inventory dynamics and input constraints are introduced, the cumulative multiplier becomes inventory-dependent: binding input constraints suppress propagation, and larger safety stocks relax these constraints so that the multiplier recovers toward—but does not exceed—the unconstrained benchmark. The replenishment rule generates overshoot–undershoot dynamics mechanically related to the bullwhip effect; however, across 99 independently generated IO structures these dynamics are highly seed-dependent, and we find no statistically significant amplification of fluctuations with system size. The results suggest that accounting state space provides a workable foundation for constructing dynamic economic models that are simultaneously accounting-consistent, mechanism-based, and extensible.

abstract: At large scales, our ability to compare genetic diversity across species is ofien challenged by the difficulty of extracting range-wide sequence data from online databases. Using mitochondrial DNA from amphibians and reptiles spanning across six regions: Brazilian Atlantic Forest, Iberian Peninsula, northwestern Africa, Arabian Peninsula, Madagascar and Australian Monsoonal Tropics, we develop and implement a framework to overcome common limitations in macrogenetics. We compiled and manually curated a spatially explicit genetic dataset from public repositories, quantified the spatial representativeness of genetic sampling across species’ ranges and developed a novel interpolation framework to estimate and map species-specific patterns of intraspecific genetic diversity (ISD) while accounting for heterogeneous spatial sampling. We estimated mean nucleotide diversity across species to produce regional maps for each genetic marker. Our final dataset comprised 182 amphibian and 239 reptile species, encompassing 184 genera from 54 families. Range representativeness of genetic sampling was generally high, despite some variation across study regions. Spatial patterns of ISD revealed geographic heterogeneity, and were consistent across the best-sampled mitochondrial markers. By combining automated and manual georeferencing, quantifying range representativeness, and accounting for bias in spatial interpolations, our pipeline is marker-agnostic and directly applicable to nuclear and genomic data as they become available.

abstract: The growing need to mitigate anthropogenic CO<sub>2</sub> emissions is driving the development of low-energy carbon capture and utilization technologies. Hardened ready-mix concrete waste represents an underexplored alkaline feedstock for direct aqueous mineral carbonation, offering opportunities for simultaneous CO<sub>2</sub> sequestration and waste valorisation. This study investigates direct aqueous mineral carbonation of concrete fines derived from hardened ready-mix concrete waste under ambient conditions using a CO<sub>2</sub> gas blend representative of cement plant flue gas. The influence of solid-to-liquid (S/L) ratio on dissolved Ca evolution, CO<sub>2</sub> uptake, CaCO<sub>3</sub> production, and degree of carbonation was evaluated, while a gate-to-gate carbon accounting framework assessed the environmental performance of the process. Geochemical equilibrium modelling was used to elucidate the mechanisms governing dissolved Ca evolution during carbonation. Feedstock and carbonation products were characterised. Surface morphology, thermogravimetric, and phase analyses confirmed successful carbonation and the formation of crystalline calcite. An S/L ratio of 1:10 achieved the highest total CO<sub>2</sub> uptake of 100.9 g-CO<sub>2</sub>/kg-concrete fines (20.2 g CO<sub>2</sub> per 2 L batch), with 84.5 g-CO<sub>2</sub>/kg-concrete fines permanently fixed as crystalline calcite. The modelling attributed the observed Ca rebound to continued decalcification of Ca-bearing phases coupled with evolving carbonate speciation. Carbon accounting indicated a net-positive footprint under laboratory conditions; however, substituting technical gases with industrial waste flue gas shifted the process toward a near net-zero carbon footprint. These findings establish hardened ready-mix concrete waste as a promising feedstock for direct aqueous mineral carbonation and highlight process integration with industrial flue gas and product valorisation as key pathways towards industrial implementation.

abstract: Cananguchales, forested wetlands dominated by Mauritia flexuosa, are strategic ecosystems in the Amazonian foothills due to their contribution to ecosystem goods and services. However, their high vulnerability to climate variability and the progressive degradation caused by the global crisis demand new tools for their valuation and sustainable management. This study evaluated the ecological sustainability of Cananguchales through emergy indicators that allow biocountable monitoring of the efficiency and performance of their ecological wealth. Indicators of Ecological Loading, Sustainable Emergy, Investment, Yield, and Renewability were applied within a non-experimental design using a quantitative, applied, and deductive-projective approach. Using ecological data and energy flow equations, values were estimated in joules, later transformed into solar emergy joules and emergy-based US dollars using standardized factors. The results showed a high proportion of renewable energy inputs (>99%) over five consecutive years, demonstrating high energy efficiency and ecological stability. A unified biocountable structure was established for these wetlands. The emergy indicators applied here are established tools; the contribution of the study lies at the level of accounting recognition, namely the integration of emergy synthesis into a formal double-entry biocountable structure in which ecological flows are recognised as debit assets and credit liabilities and closed into an ecological equity balance. It is concluded that this accounting-recognition structure provides an operational route for objectively valuing strategic ecosystems and guiding decisions towards their conservation and sustainability in the Amazonian context.
