abstract: Au carrefour de la philosophie, de la sociologie et de la psychologie, attentif aux conséquences pratiques de tout savoir théorique avec la pédagogie et la praxéologie, Alfred Espinas est l'un des grands acteurs de l'émergence des sciences humaines et sociales à la fin du XIXe siècle. Ce grand acquis de la sociologie, d'après lequel le cœur de la vie sociale est constitué de représentations, se trouve déjà chez lui. C'est sur cette notion de représentations collectives (et plus généralement de représentation), facteur théorico-pratique de cohésion sociale, que cet article se concentre. Après avoir retracé le rôle de la représentation dans la structure même et dans la progression des Sociétés animales, l'article se concentre plus spécifiquement sur la genèse et la nature des représentations collectives, entre psychologie individuelle et conscience sociale, avant d'interroger les effets qu'elles sont susceptibles d'exercer, à partir d'un ensemble d'écrits repré-sentatifs du sociologue.Alfred Espinas was a key figure in the emergence of the human and social sciences at the end of the nineteenth century. At the crossroads of philosophy, sociology, and psychology, he also considered the practical implications of theoretical knowledge through pedagogy and praxeology. Before Durkheim, he identified an important milestone for sociology: the idea that the core of social life consists in representations. This article focuses on the notions of representation and collective representations as theoretical and practical factors of social cohesion. After examining the role of the notion of representation in the very structure and progression of Des Sociétés animales (On Animal Societies), the article more specifically addresses the genesis and nature of collective representations, between individual psychology and social consciousness. Lastly, drawing on a large set of Espinas’ writings, the paper addresses the potential effects of collective representations.

abstract:
Introduction

This study presents a PRISMA-guided scoping review of global research trends in the sociology of development during the period 2020-2025, with particular emphasis on the emerging intersection between development studies and Artificial Intelligence (AI).

Methods

Thirty-five peer-reviewed studies were systematically selected from the Scopus, SAGE, Wiley, and JSTOR databases. A systematic search strategy and qualitative content analysis were employed to identify the dominant thematic areas, theoretical frameworks, and methodological approaches in the reviewed literature.

Results

Social development emerged as the most prominent research theme, accounting for 28.6% of the reviewed studies, followed by social justice (17.1%), social policy (14.3%), and sustainable development (11.4%). Explicit engagement with AI-related perspectives remained limited. Qualitative approaches constituted the dominant methodological paradigm (60%), with case studies and participatory research being the most frequently employed methods, whereas quantitative and computational approaches remained comparatively limited.

Discussion

The reviewed literature revealed limited theoretical and methodological integration of AI within development sociology, highlighting the need for innovative interdisciplinary approaches. The study concludes that the sociology of development is moving toward greater theoretical pluralism and methodological diversity; however, stronger integration with digital transformation and AI-enabled development research remains necessary.

abstract: Despite being admitted to Canada as "the best and the brightest," immigrants often face underemployment and poverty. Few studies on immigrant labour market integration consider the role of local policy actors such as human resource management (HRM) professionals, who make and influence hiring decisions. Drawing on interviews and Relational Inequality Theory, this paper examines how HRM professionals in Alberta categorically define and evaluate immigrant candidates. Findings reveal that HRM professionals fail to recognize immigrants as legally entitled and preferred workers based on their permanent residency, instead treating them as temporary migrants who are administrative burdens or financial risks. Strategic HRM logics provide non-racial justifications for exclusion, yet evaluations are guided by cultural fit criteria that serve as proxies for Whiteness. These insights reframe the problem as also a recognition of legal status, showing how immigration categories and cultural racism intersect to reproduce inequality in Canada's labour market.

abstract:
Objectives

This study examines the momentary associations between intellectual, physical, and social activities and high- and low-arousal positive and negative affect (HPA, LPA, HNA, and LNA), and how social and physical contexts moderate these associations.

Methods

Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) was conducted over 7 consecutive days, with 153 middle-aged and older adults completing 6,102 surveys in China. Two-level linear mixed-effects models with a CAR(1) correlation structure were used for the analyses.

Results

Associations between physical activity and affective states varied across social contexts: compared with being alone, being with a spouse or other social partners was associated with higher HPA and lower LPA, being with a spouse or other family members with lower HNA, being with a spouse with lower LNA. The association between social activity and HPA was lower when participants were with other family members or other social partners than when alone. Compared with being at home, being outdoors moderated several leisure activity-affect associations, whereas being indoors showed no significant moderation.

Conclusion

This study provides a more nuanced understanding of the associations between leisure activities and momentary affective experiences and how these associations vary across social and physical contexts, with implications for psychological health promotion programs and interventions.

abstract:
Background

China's fertility rate has dropped sharply despite policy relaxations, suggesting that subjective cognitive factors-beyond objective socioeconomic conditions-matter for reproductive decisions. However, the distinct roles of current class perception versus future mobility expectations remain unclear.

Objective

This study examines how subjective class perception and class mobility expectations differentially associate with fertility intentions, childbearing behaviors, and the intention-behavior gap, and explores mediating mechanisms.

Methods

Using CGSS2023 data (N = 6073, aged 18-49), we employed ordinal logistic regression, KHB mediation, and propensity score matching.

Results

Subjective class perception positively predicted intentions (OR = 1.125, p < 0.001) but not behaviors, and significantly widened the intention-behavior gap (B = 0.045, p < 0.001). Class mobility expectations positively predicted both intentions (OR = 1.140) and behaviors (OR = 1.129, both p < 0.001), without increasing the gap. Mediation showed subjective class perception worked through traditional gender-role attitudes (indirect effect = 0.0045, 3.81%), while mobility expectations operated via happiness (0.0118, 8.83%) and health (0.0062, 5.14%). Results were robust to alternative models and PSM.

Conclusion

Static status evaluation shapes aspirations but fails to translate into actual fertility, whereas upward mobility beliefs facilitate intention realization by reducing uncertainty and psychological costs. Extending the Intergenerational Investment Utility Framework, our findings suggest that strengthening perceived mobility prospects may be a more effective policy lever than altering current class perceptions alone.

abstract: As governments respond to fertility decline with pronatalist policies centered on economic and childcare support, childbirth itself remains undertheorized as an embodied and gendered experience. This study contributes to fertility research and maternal health scholarship by documenting unmet demand for labor pain relief in China and examining how access to pain management shapes women's evaluations of whether conditions are favorable for having a child. We draw on an original study of 2866 women of reproductive age that combines a conjoint experiment with survey questions on childbirth experiences and attitudes. To our knowledge, this is the first large-sample study to examine labor pain relief and evaluations of childbearing conditions together. We estimate the causal effects of epidural access and family support for its use alongside commonly studied factors such as household income and childcare support. Results show substantial unmet demand: most respondents regard childbirth pain as important for fertility decision-making, yet nearly half of those with recent vaginal delivery experience did not receive epidural analgesia during labor. Experimental results further suggest that, compared with sometimes-available access, always-available epidural access improves these evaluations by approximately 70% of the effect of receiving childcare support, while family support for epidural use increases these evaluations by an amount comparable to that of moving from sufficient to comfortable household income. These findings underscore the importance of integrating maternal health and childbirth experiences into theories of fertility decision-making and reproductive policy debates.

abstract:
Background

Excessive intake of exogenous vitamin A during pregnancy has been associated with congenital malformations. This experimental study aimed to evaluate whether vitamin B12, folic acid, and L-carnitine exert a protective or contributory effect on malformations induced by hypervitaminosis A.

Methods

Thirty-five healthy adult female Wistar albino rats and seven male rats were used. Pregnant rats received vitamin A alone or in combination with vitamin B12, folic acid, or L-carnitine for 21 consecutive days (GD 0-21). At the end of gestation, neonates were evaluated for gross congenital malformations. Brain, liver, and eye tissues were excised and processed for histopathological and morphometric analyses.

Results

No gross external malformations were observed in any group; however, significant growth restriction and multi-organ histopathological alterations were detected in the offspring. Histological examination revealed interstitial edema in brain tissue and retinal detachment in the eye. Hepatic alterations included sinusoidal dilatation, hyperchromatic nuclei, necrotic cells, and cytoplasmic degenerative changes; these lesions remained mild. Somatic and organ morphometry showed that vitamin B12 supplementation partially alleviated retinoid-induced somatic growth retardation.

Conclusion

Although maternal hypervitaminosis A did not cause overt external malformations under the tested regimen, it induced multi-organ histopathological damage and severe fetal growth restriction. Adjuvant supplementation, particularly with vitamin B12, demonstrated modulatory effects against retinoid-induced developmental suppression.

abstract:
Objectives

This study examines associations between completed parity, including childlessness (zero parity), and a range of medical conditions (individually and cumulatively) and self-rated health, including differences associated with race/ethnicity-related factors.

Methods

We conduct correlational and multivariable regression analyses using a historical HRS/AHEAD sample of ever-married, non-Hispanic Black and White women born between 1920 and 1941. Multivariable models adjust for early-life-course social determinants of health, including contextual birthplace exposure to Jim Crow-era structural racial inequalities. We focus on childlessness/zero parity by using zero-inflated count regression methods that statistically identify women with zero probability of having had a live birth (a latent "always-zero" group).

Results

Black women had three times the odds of "always-zero" group membership and, if not in that group, an expected parity 11% higher than White women. In correlational analyses, the predicted probability of "always-zero" group membership (Predicted Infecundity Probability or PIP)-rather than reported childlessness status-and high parity were associated with high-fatality medical conditions and self-rated fair/poor health. In multivariable models, PIP and high parity were positively associated with number of conditions, while PIP and number of conditions were positively associated with self-rated fair/poor health. Net of parity, consistent with weathering, younger Black women had a higher-than-expected number of medical conditions relative to all women.

Discussion

In the context of historical structural racial inequality, race/ethnicity-related differences in childlessness and high parity were strongly associated with later-life, post-reproductive health disparities. Women's number of births was associated with the accumulation of medical conditions in a U-shaped pattern.

abstract: This paper argues to understand racially minoritised people's experiences of mental illness and mental healthcare, we must expand the focus from inpatient stays to understanding a series of interactions with state institutions. We extend Goffman's concept of mortification beyond the inpatient unit to demonstrate how carceral practices are routinely used by state institutions, contributing to the worsening of racially minoritised people's mental health. Drawing upon 22 in-depth interviews from participatory action research (PAR) with racially minoritised people diagnosed with severe mental illness in the UK, we show mortification and carceral practices experienced by racially minoritised patients are related to their racialised identities. This is shown in our data by: institutions' failure to act on reported incidents of racism; controlling and withholding information and services related to patients' mental healthcare; and the assumed criminality and threat of racially minoritised people, often resulting in increased police involvement and surveillance. Specifically, we show (1) mortification is not a process that happens solely inside the physical psychiatric hospital. It happens in a series of interactions with state institutions with harmful effects and (2) mortification is not a discrete event that takes place within one period, in one type of institution. Instead, degrading, racist experiences are interspersed throughout the life course compounding the feelings of identity loss and erosion. We conclude it is vital to bring together the concepts of racism, carcerality and mortification to develop a thorough understanding of the experiences of racially minoritised people diagnosed with severe mental illness.

abstract: Studies of professionalisation, oligarchy and expertise have asked how expertise affects democratic representation in professionalised membership organisations. This article approaches that problem from the other direction by examining the role of representation in the production of expert knowledge. Drawing on interviews, participant observation and document analysis at LO, the Swedish confederation of blue-collar trade unions, I argue that union researchers build expertise through representation. Researchers claim an epistemic standpoint-by-proxy through representative mandates, and experiential knowledge is treated as an epistemic resource accessible through the representative apparatus of the organisation. The case complicates accounts that treat expertise and representation as independent or opposed: expert staff can incorporate representation into their work rather than act upon it as an external force. This suggests that whether expertise displaces or facilitates member influence depends partly on whether and how representation enters their work.

abstract: Public sharing of data and analysis code enables independent verification of published findings. While audit studies have examined data and code sharing in psychology, economics, and political science, comparable evidence for sociology remains limited. We examine 730 empirical articles published between January 2019 and June 2024 in three leading general-interest journals: American Sociological Review, American Journal of Sociology, and Social Forces. For each article, we record whether a publicly accessible replication package is available and, when materials are shared, attempt to computationally reproduce the main-text tables and figures. Overall, 9.9% of articles provide replication packages (12.2% among quantitative articles), with substantial variation across journals (5.2% to 22.9%) and research types (0% for qualitative studies, 30% for experiments). These rates fall well below those reported for political science and economics. Of the 72 packages examined in detail, more than half cannot be verified due to missing or incomplete materials. At the same time, no article is wholly non-reproducible, and 22% are fully or largely reproducible. Sociology is not unusually prone to errors when materials are shared and runnable - it simply shares them far less often. We discuss implications for journal policies and transparency standards that reflect the field's methodological diversity.

abstract: Building on the stress process model, this study examines whether religiosity moderates the mental health consequences of higher-status work among American workers. Drawing on the stress of higher status (SHS) framework and job demands-resources (JD-R) theory, we analyze data from the 2023 Measuring Employment Sentiments and Social Inequality survey (MESSI; N = 1744), a nationally representative survey of American workers. We focus on three work-related stressors central to the stress of higher status-job authority, long work hours, and work-family conflict-and three dimensions of religion/spirituality: prayer, religious service attendance, and beliefs in divine control. Regression results show that divine control operates as a domain-specific moderator. It buffers the positive association between work-family conflict and psychological distress but shows a stress-exacerbation pattern in contexts of high job authority. In contrast, prayer and attendance exhibit modest main effects with psychological distress but do not significantly moderate stressor-distress associations. No patterns of moderation emerge for long work hours. Taken together, our findings highlight religion as a multidimensional and status-contingent resource, underscoring the importance of matching specific religious dimensions to particular stress processes in shaping mental health. We also propose several future directions to integrate religion with research on work and mental health within the SHS framework.

abstract:
Introduction

Subjective class identity is shaped not only by objective socioeconomic resources, but also by everyday experiences through which individuals evaluate their bodies, lives, and social relations. Although physical activity is often studied as a health behavior, leisure-time exercise, sports, and fitness may also function as socially meaningful lifestyle practices.

Methods

Using data from the 2021 China General Social Survey, this study examines the association between regular leisure-time physical activity and subjective class identity among Chinese residents, and further assesses whether self-rated health, subjective well-being, and social interaction help account for this association. The baseline analytical sample includes 5,688 respondents, while pathway analyses use 3,802 respondents with complete information on self-rated health, subjective well-being, social interaction, and all covariates.

Results

Ordered logit models show that regular physical activity is positively associated with higher subjective class identity after adjustment for demographic and socioeconomic covariates, including gender, age, marital status, household registration, ethnicity, region, education, political status, and personal income (b = 0.231, robust SE = 0.052, p < 0.001; OR = 1.26). The association remains stable across alternative measurements of subjective class identity and physical activity, ordered probit models, generalized ordered logit diagnostics, survey-weighted models, province fixed effects, clustered standard errors, propensity-score weighting, entropy balancing, and income-coding sensitivity analyses. Pathway models and Karlson-Holm-Breen decomposition indicate that self-rated health, subjective well-being, and social interaction jointly account for 73.20% of the total association in the pathway sample, with subjective well-being contributing the largest share. Heterogeneity analysis shows broadly positive associations across social groups, with the clearest subgroup difference appearing by marital status.

Discussion

Given the cross-sectional design, the findings should be interpreted as robust associations and statistical pathways rather than causal effects. The study contributes to social stratification and health sociology by showing that subjective class identity is connected to embodied health, affective evaluation, and relational experiences embedded in everyday lifestyle practices.

abstract: Patterns of volunteering have predominantly been explained by focusing on the supply side in terms of volunteers' resources and motivations. We shift the focus to the demand side of volunteering and develop the concept of demand networks. We argue that experienced demand for help in one's personal network is important to explain why individuals engage in informally organized voluntary help and support: the amount of demand for help a person experiences in their network influences the likelihood that the person helps. To explain why individuals who perceive similar levels of demand do not all volunteer to the same extent, we theorize how demand networks are mediated by the institutional factors of social values and gender roles. We hypothesize that altruistic values and gendered social roles dispose individuals to respond differently to demands for help, with women and those holding stronger altruistic values being more likely to act on the needs they perceive. We examine the hypotheses using a cross-sectional survey inquiring about informally organized volunteering during COVID-19. The results clearly indicate the importance of the demand side to adequately explain informal volunteering. We argue that our findings imply that sociologists should reconceptualise social connections not only as providing access to resources but also as a source of demands on individuals. In doing so attention should be paid to gender roles which the results suggest function as an amplifier of demand networks association with informal volunteering. We further discuss how the results have implications for building social capital and societal resilience in times of crisis.

abstract: Cet article examine la place structurante de Rousseau dans l'itinéraire intellectuel d'Alfred Espinas. Loin de relever d'un intérêt circonstanciel, la lecture espinassienne de Rousseau constitue un « antagonisme constitutif » à partir duquel Espinas élabore une sociologie fondée sur le caractère naturel de la vie sociale et sur l'organicité des sociétés. De Des Sociétés animales aux écrits des années 1890, le contractualisme rousseauiste s'impose ainsi comme un véritable contre-modèle théorique, associé à l'artificialisme, à l'abstraction et à une « morale et une politique régressives ». Cette confrontation éclaire, en retour, les conditions de légitimation de la sociologie naissante.This article examines the structuring role Rousseau occupies in Alfred Espinas’s intellectual trajectory. Far from being a mere incidental topic of interest, Espinas’s interpretation of Rousseau embodies a “constitutive antagonism”, upon which Espinas builds a sociology based on the natural character of social life and the organic nature of societies. From Des Sociétés animales to his writings of the 1890s, Rousseau’s contractualism becomes a genuine theoretical counter-model associated with artificiality, abstraction and ‘regressive morality and politics’. This confrontation, in turn, sheds light on the conditions under which nascent sociology gained legitimacy.

abstract: The North American Free Trade Agreement, now the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, has increased semi-truck and vehicular traffic at international ports-of-entry, raising air pollution concerns in the US-Mexico border region. Studying the border county of El Paso, Texas, a central hub for Mexican imports, we extend the literature by examining the prevalence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) across census tracts with varying proximities to the port-of-entry, PM<sub>2.5</sub> exposure, and percent immigrant. We accomplish this objective by merging NASA PM<sub>2.5</sub> measurements with health data from the US Centers for Disease Control and social vulnerability indicators from the US Census' American Community Survey. We also use ArcGIS Pro to determine each census tract's proximity to a port-of-entry. Using Generalized Linear Models, we found that PM<sub>2.5</sub> and the percent foreign-born noncitizens are positively associated with COPD prevalence. Census tracts close to a port-of-entry, compared with those more than three miles away, have higher COPD prevalence. Moreover, COPD prevalence in immigrant communities and the effects of PM<sub>2.5</sub> are stratified across census tracts by proximity to ports-of-entry.

abstract: Contemporary society faces the ubiquitous proliferation of algorithmic systems that structure social life, from intimate subjective modulation to planetary crisis management. This conceptual paper therefore proposes the analytical category of vigitalization. Rooted in relational sociology, vigitalization is defined as a co-constitutive sociotechnical configuration that fuses datafication with structural surveillance to interpret the autonomization of algorithmic governance. Employing a multilevel theoretical framework bridging the macro (systematicity), meso (grouping), and micro (interaction) dimensions, the study dissects the relational interdependencies between technological infrastructures, political economy, and algocratic bureaucracies. Vigitalization operates under a strict recursive logic: digitizing to monitor and monitoring to digitize, naturalizing behavioral extraction across all institutional boundaries. Crucially, this framework positions vigitalization as the primary sociotechnical matrix governing the ASAM Nexus (Agency-Structure-Algorithm-Matter). By doing so, it equips sociology with the critical apparatus required to address the existential macro-risks, biopolitical subsumption, and biometric enclosures intrinsic to the Digital Anthropocene.

abstract: Aksoy et al. (2026) propose three standards for sociology, the integration of theory and empirics, open science, and a careful relation between scholarship and political action. In this comment, we endorse these standards and argue that two developments, the uneven geography of sociological knowledge and the disciplinary reach of artificial intelligence, call for a wider frame. We propose reciprocal collaboration with researchers in the Global South as a single move that absorbs the disruption from AI, corrects an empirical deficit, and narrows the methodological gap, while extending rather than diluting the standards the statement defends.

abstract:
Background

Wellbeing has become an increasingly important focus of disability research as the field has shifted from deficit-oriented biomedical models toward multidimensional, biopsychosocial, and health equity frameworks. However, the rapid growth of disability wellbeing research makes it increasingly difficult to identify dominant themes, emerging priorities, and knowledge gaps.

Objective

This study aimed to analyse global scientific production on wellbeing among people with disabilities between 2019 and 2025.

Methods

A bibliometric analysis was conducted using the Web of Science Core Collection (SCIE, SSCI, ESCI). Publications were identified through a structured search strategy combining disability-related terms in the Title field and wellbeing-related terms in the Topic field. Bibliometric performance analysis and science mapping were conducted using Bibliometrix (R). Analyses included publication trends, leading journals, countries, institutions, collaboration networks, author keyword co-occurrence, strategic thematic mapping, and Bradford's and Lotka's distributions.

Results

A total of 8944 publications were identified, with an annual growth rate of 12.91%. Scientific production was concentrated in high-income countries, particularly the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada. Quality of life emerged as the dominant conceptual theme, accompanied by mental health, rehabilitation, and participation, while social inclusion, digital health, and health equity represented emerging research topics. Important gaps remained regarding Global South representation, intersectionality, and policy-oriented disability research.

Conclusions

Disability wellbeing research is characterised by sustained scientific growth and increasing conceptual diversification. Nevertheless, persistent geographic and conceptual imbalances highlight the need for more globally representative, inclusive, and policy-oriented research to advance disability health equity.

abstract: Women's family-career conflict (WFCC) has received growing attention, yet evidence on its implications for women's job performance remains fragmented, particularly in the South African public sector. This study systematically reviews existing literature to examine the factors associated with WFCC, its implications for job performance, the role of organisational support and workplace policies, and the contextual conditions shaping these relationships. A systematic literature review was conducted using secondary scholarly literature, with the study-selection and reporting process informed by PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The literature was analysed thematically. The findings show that WFCC does not have a uniform effect on job performance. While some studies associate higher levels of conflict with reduced performance and employee engagement, others report weak, mixed or context-dependent relationships. The review further shows that organisational support, flexible working arrangements, supportive leadership and family-friendly policies can reduce the pressures associated with competing family and career responsibilities. However, their effectiveness depends on organisational culture and how policies are implemented. The study highlights the need for South African public-sector organisations to strengthen supportive workplace and performance-management practises that recognise employees' family responsibilities.

abstract: Supporters of a recently announced normative turn in sociology acknowledge that what they recommend is by no means entirely new. However, they have given little attention to an early precursor: the British sociologist Leonard Hobhouse. He focussed on the role of the normative in social life and insisted that sociology could, and must, play an active role in realising progressive values. Furthermore, like some more recent advocates of normative sociology, he insisted on the key role that philosophy plays in grounding the values underpinning it. In fact, he developed an elaborate philosophical system, one which illustrates the challenging requirements that any normative sociology must satisfy, and the problems it faces in doing this. I argue that, despite the encyclopaedic knowledge and extraordinary ingenuity displayed in Hobhouse's work, he fails to provide a sound basis for a normative sociology and that his work raises questions about the likely success of any such project.

abstract: Urban waste management increasingly relies on hybrid collection systems based on controlled-access smart bins. Their implicit promise is to strengthen compliance by increasing behavioural control while reducing the organisational costs associated with door-to-door collection. This article tests this premise through a survey of 502 users involved in a large-scale Italian pilot project. Integrating analytical sociology, social norms theory, and Science and Technology Studies, we identify three interrelated mechanisms underlying the system's ambivalent outcomes: limited norm internalisation, ineffective sanctions, and the increased visibility of non-compliant behaviour. We argue that smart bins reshape users' empirical expectations and may thereby contribute to the progressive erosion of compliance with waste separation norms.

abstract: This article examines the emergence and legitimation of medical social work (MSW) within China's recently marketised healthcare system, building on longstanding sociological debates about professional formation and authority. Drawing from qualitative interviews with medical social workers, doctors and patients across diverse hospital settings, the study compares two organisational models-internal embedding of MSW within hospitals and external collaboration via government agencies-to analyse strategies for gaining professional legitimacy. Three key strategies are identified: external manifestation through symbolic markers (white coat, blue vest), alignment with political imperatives for mediating doctor-patient disputes and resource mobilisation to support vulnerable patients. Findings consider how these three legitimation strategies are enacted in the two organisational contexts and infrastructural access, while externally affiliated strategies enable flexibility, perceived independence and community linkage. The article argues that MSW legitimacy in China emerges not from seeking exclusive control of specialised knowledge but through dynamic negotiation of identity, symbolic authority and responsiveness to policy priorities, providing an empirical case of post-professionalism under conditions of market reform. These insights contribute to the sociology of health and illness by highlighting context-sensitive processes of professional formation in transitional healthcare systems in the Global South.

abstract: Computerised organ-allocation systems are designed to standardise clinical criteria, reduce discretionary intervention, and improve traceability. However, matching begins only after potential donors have been identified, referred, authorised, medically maintained, routed through institutions, and entered into the allocation system. Drawing on seven months of multi-sited qualitative fieldwork in China (2017-2018), this article examines how organisational processes upstream of matching shaped allocation pathways during system-building. Participant observation, interviews with 17 professionals, field conversations and documents inform four proposed mechanisms: relational donor visibility, informal referral brokerage, monetised organisational routing, and potential loss of organisational provenance at formal system entry. These mechanisms concern which donations reach matching, through which institutions and jurisdictions, and whether their histories remain traceable; they need not alter algorithmic rankings. From this historical case, the article develops upstream pathway inequality and algorithmic input blindness, and proposes pathway justice as a framework linking entry conditions, routing and matching fairness. The contribution is a conditional proposition: consistent ranking alone cannot secure procedural fairness where upstream pathways remain opaque or unevenly governed. It does not establish the persistence of the reported practices.

abstract: Mathematical sociology has developed through partially independent programs concerned with exchange, status, mobility, organizations, social influence, collective action, and institutional trust. These traditions often share matrices, hazard rates, games, and differential equations while representing non-equivalent social objects. This survey reconstructs four foundational programs by substantive mechanism. Each model is written as a tuple comprising units, a state space with its social semantics, a structure, a transition law, an observation operator, parameters, and a source of identifying variation. The central result is a mechanism indistinguishability theorem: two transition laws are locally indistinguishable to first order at a common latent state exactly when their difference lies in the kernel of the differential of the observation operator, while equality of whole observed paths requires projectability. No increase in sample size under one observation design removes such non-identification. A corollary on aggregation explains why the mean of a population of logistic actors is not logistic, and a worked example shows that founding counts cannot separate organizational legitimation from competition. A worked cross-scale case study carries one chain from discrete adoption through continuum propagation to a first-passage reduction, with the status of every claim stated explicitly.

abstract:
Objective

The Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas study was designed to examine cognitive health disparities in later life. It gathers data on access to social resources, engagement in cognitively stimulating interactions, and exposure to activity spaces.

Methods

We enrolled 510 participants from 41 Indiana counties during baseline data collection in Fall 2023. All participants completed a computer-assisted personal interview survey that collected data on their cognitive, mental, and physical health, personal networks, sociodemographic attributes, occupational history, lifestyle activities, and social support. Two hundred and seventy-three participants completed a follow-up module in which they used a smartphone to record ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) that were administered four times per day for seven days.

Results

The mean age was 69.9 years. Most participants were women (64.5%), White (90.2%), and retired (54.5%). The average participant named 5.38 network members. Participants were at home (70.7%) and alone (60.2%) for the majority of their EMAs. Approximately one third of the sample scored below a recommended cutoff for mild cognitive impairment on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment.

Discussion

We conclude by outlining a research agenda that (1) characterizes the social networks, interactions, and place-based activities of participants across geographic contexts, and (2) assesses the potential pathways between a combination of networks, interactions, and activities and cognitive function.

abstract: Advantaged young people may engage in transgressive or non-conformist subcultural practices usually associated with disadvantaged youth. When undertaken from privileged positions, however, these practices can carry markedly different meanings, costs and rewards. Sociological research on youth subcultures has illuminated the marginalised side of this dynamic, analysing deviant and oppositional practices as collective responses to blocked opportunities and exclusion from mainstream recognition. However, why young people with more secure and legitimate routes to recognition and success may nonetheless be drawn to risk-bearing subcultural practices remains under-theorised. This article addresses this asymmetry by reframing advantaged youths' subcultural participation as a specific, transgressive form of boundary-crossing cultural omnivorousness, and by analysing advantaged and disadvantaged youth within a field-oriented framework. Extending Bourdieu's logic of condescension into the domain of risk-bearing participation, it proposes the concept of transgressive condescension, to capture how privileged actors can convert visible transgression into recognition and advantage. This reveals a double misrecognition: the visibility of privileged transgression obscures the capital buffers that make such risk-taking manageable, while the absence of such buffers, which renders similar practices acutely costly for disadvantaged youth, is also obscured. The article thus develops the Bourdieusian turn in subcultural studies towards a more symmetrical analysis of participation across social positions, and extends cultural omnivore research beyond taste and consumption by treating transgressive boundary-crossing as a risk-bearing practice, whose authenticity effects, costs and convertibility are unequally structured by class position and capital configuration.

abstract: Inpatient psychiatric nurses practice in environments where therapeutic care, safety monitoring, patient agency, behavioral containment, and institutional order are deeply intertwined. Although psychiatric nursing is often described through clinical tasks, risk management, or therapeutic relationships, less attention has been given to its sociological complexity as socially organized boundary work. This discussion article uses a sociology-of-nursing lens to examine how inpatient psychiatric nurses practice at the boundary of care and control. Nurses are expected to build trust, preserve dignity, monitor risk, maintain the milieu, redirect behavior, set limits, support patient agency, document clinical concerns, and coordinate with broader institutional demands. These responsibilities are not simply technical tasks; they are forms of relational, ethical, and organizational labor that shape professional identity under constraint. Making this labor visible can clarify how psychiatric nurses preserve care and compassion within regulated, risk-oriented settings. The paper concludes with implications for nursing practice, education, leadership, policy, and research.

abstract: Online gambling is a growing public health concern whose harms extend to the family, yet its familial consequences remain underexplored in contexts where gambling is illegal and extended-family ties are strong. This study examined how men who gamble online perceive gambling to affect their families in Siirt, Türkiye. Using a qualitative exploratory design, in-person semi-structured interviews with nine married or previously married men who currently or formerly gambled online (recruited via purposive and snowball sampling) were analyzed with a hybrid deductive-inductive, codebook thematic analysis (Fereday & Muir-Cochrane, 2006), informed by the six phases of Braun and Clarke (2006). Four themes were identified: entry into online gambling and the experience of addiction; the internal disintegration of the nuclear family; the household's economic collapse and drift into crime; and the extended family, stigmatization, and the cultural framing of harm. Participants perceived gambling to erode communication and trust, dispossess the household, and displace men from the provider role, while family responses followed conventional gendered lines-disrupting the material division of roles while reactivating a traditional gender order. Distinctive contextual mechanisms emerged, including the extended family's collective debt-clearing in exchange for religious oaths and the operation of stigma through kinship networks that threatened collective family honor. Because all participants were gamblers, the findings reflect their perceptions of family impact rather than the direct experiences of affected others. The results extend a predominantly Western evidence base and underscore the need for culturally sensitive, family-inclusive support that works with existing kinship structures while protecting those most burdened.

abstract: This article develops a cultural and relational model of political polarisation that integrates insights from currently disconnected streams of scholarship to conceive polarisation as a discursive and performative struggle over sacred meanings. Rather than treating polarisation as mere attitudinal divergence, we frame it as the symbolic organization of political antagonism. We identify three interrelated cultural dimensions and one social dimension. These are (1) ideological divergence as bifurcating responses to contested issues, conceptualized as morally and emotionally charged signifiers; (2) the ideological consistency of these divergent issues, enabling chains of signification held together by what we call 'linking signifiers' that mark group identity; (3) the mutual constitution of opposing semiotic chains and identities, which describes how antagonistic groups performatively mobilise opposing discourses to co-constitutively define themselves in relation to one another; and (4) social polarisation, which is based in for example, inequalities, segregations, or violent conflicts. We then present a pathway model which expresses how cultural and social polarisation drive or diminish one another over time. This model thereby offers a sociological theory of polarisation and depolarisation as interlinked processes rather than as separate phenomena requiring separate theories. This paper also maps out the implications of our model for empirical polarisation and depolarisation research.

abstract: Migrant parents of children and young people (CYP) living with sickle cell disease (SCD) must manage complex care needs within unfamiliar healthcare systems. Drawing on qualitative interviews with migrant parents in England, this study examines how migration reshapes healthcare navigation. Using navigation as an analytical lens, the findings show that parents act as de facto navigators, coordinating services across healthcare, education and welfare domains without structured support. Beyond practical coordination, navigation involved sustained relational, emotional and identity work. Parents described learning to interpret new institutional rules, (re)negotiating expectations of 'good' parenting in a different national context and managing stigma linked to illness, ethnicity and immigration status. Migration intensified caregiving responsibilities through disrupted support networks, legal and economic constraints and uneven access to resources. Although UK services were valued for specialist expertise, parents reported the need for continual self-advocacy within fragmented systems. The study extends navigation scholarship by foregrounding migrant parents' unpaid and often unrecognised labour and demonstrates how healthcare navigation is shaped by intersecting migration, policy and racialised contexts. The findings highlight the importance of embedding condition-specific navigation support within existing specialist services.

abstract: Belonging is a key aspect of human experience. This qualitative study examined where diverse people with learning disabilities feel belonging, what shapes belonging and how it affects their health. Focus groups were held with people with learning disabilities across England who identified as women, LGBTQ+, and from Black and ethnically minoritised backgrounds. Twelve participants also took part in an additional data collection activity: a go-along interview, ethnographic observation and/or photovoice. Our findings demonstrate shared themes and intersectional differences in participants' experiences of belonging. We emphasise belonging as embodied and as felt in diverse places and across time. It is also relational, open-ended and facilitated by several actors and factors, which reflect the multiple social identities of participants. Experiences of nonbelonging are grounded in ableism, which, in turn, is compounded by and cannot be separated from racism, sexism and homo-, bi- and transphobia. Through empirical examples, we highlight the relationship between belonging and health as bi-directional and mutually reinforcing. To belong, people need to feel themselves authentically and valued in their complexity and uniqueness.

abstract: Gender visibility days aim to mark and correct the underrepresentation of women in specific institutions and fields. This article argues that the empowerment-versus-ritual debate in gender visibility scholarship is missing a conceptual distinction already present in the sociology of tokenism and institutional diversity work: the difference between being recognized and being granted authority. Drawing on sociological theories of tokenism, institutional non-performativity, and intersectionality, this article proposes "recognition without authority" as an analytic category for evaluating gender-focused observances. It illustrates the category through a single case: Cormac McCarthy's novel Stella Maris (2022), whose protagonist is watched, examined, and discussed at length within institutions dominated by men, yet whose testimony is never treated as credible on its own terms. The case serves as a practical example of a dynamic that future sociological research on visibility days can test more systematically across different institutional settings.

abstract:
Objectives

Rural residents are believed to experience greater social isolation than their urban counterparts. This isolation is typically attributed to the structural conditions that distinguish rural communities from urban communities. In the present study, we direct attention to the everyday places that older adults visit across the rural-urban context and the implications this has for direct and indirect social exposure.

Methods

We leverage ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data from the Social Environment and Cognitive Health in Urban and Rural Areas study. Two hundred and forty-eight participants recorded 4,906 valid EMAs. We explore the probability of EMAs being recorded outside the home and how far each EMA was recorded from home based on driving distance and time.

Results

There were no rural-urban differences in the probability of participants being away from home during their EMAs. However, rural participants were located farther from home than urban participants during their non-home EMAs. These latter differences were largely explained by trips to restaurants, stores, and healthcare facilities. There were no observed differences in the time separating participants from their workplaces, other people's homes, religious centers, or other outdoor spaces.

Discussion

Although rural and urban older adults visit the same types of places at remarkably similar rates, rural residents face greater travel burdens when accessing commercial places (e.g., restaurants, stores, and healthcare facilities). These findings suggest that the rural disadvantage is concentrated in commercial activity and carries implications for the types of social exposures that residents are likely to encounter depending on where they live.

abstract: Social isolation is a major public health crisis with particularly deleterious consequences for vulnerable populations including incarcerated people. Theoretically, visitation from family should reduce social isolation and improve outcomes among incarcerated people, but existing quasi-experimental research provides limited support for the relationship between visitation and in-custody outcomes. We revisit the effect of visitation on in-custody misconduct-an important but administratively defined measure of institutional safety-by exploiting the fact that fluctuations in gasoline prices create unanticipated shifts in visitation uncorrelated with other factors associated with misconduct. We combine this quasi-experimental variation with smartphone mobility data identifying prison visits from cell phone pings and administrative data on misconduct in California prisons. We find that increases in visits induced by changes in transportation costs are negatively related to misconduct (particularly use-of-force events and personal battery), with effects concentrated immediately after visitation. Although the policy implications are subtle, these findings suggest that some strategies that reduce visitation barriers could be cost-effective ways to reduce prison violence. More broadly, they suggest that social connections have causal repercussions for violence and safety in extreme institutional environments.

abstract: "Trauma" has become a widely circulating cultural framework for making suffering intelligible. Sociological research has documented its institutional expansion but paid less attention to how people use it to organize experiences that disrupt orientation to body, self, and world. This article examines that situated process in non-clinical psychedelic contexts. Drawing on 48 in-depth interviews with people who defined their psychedelic experiences as challenging, we trace how participants mobilized trauma discourse in response to ontological rupture. The analysis identifies five configurations of therapeutic sense-making: somatic discovery of trauma, embodied re-experiencing, the experience as healing instruction, the recursive healing project, and the limits of therapeutic sense-making. Across the first four, trauma discourse condensed diverse suffering into an authoritative category and supplied vocabularies for sequencing experience and directing action; we use personalization to describe how this shared framework becomes biographically meaningful. The fifth captures the cases where personalization broke down: the framework felt imposed, became a performance for others, or disclosed memories and revelations participants could not hold as real. Our abductive analysis of these cases generated three dimensions of authenticity: subjective ownership, non-performance, and realness. The findings point to a structural tension: we suggest that circulating trauma discourse beyond credentialed clinical and ritual authorities both expands the framework's flexibility and leaves personalization vulnerable to social pressure, unaccountable authority, and unresolved epistemic uncertainty. This study extends sociological critiques of therapeutization by shifting attention from the diffusion of therapeutic frameworks to the conditions of their uptake.

abstract: Loneliness is a growing concern among aging migrant populations, with significant implications for their well-being and social integration. This study examines how first-generation Turkish labor migrants in Germany engage with third places such as parks, religious sites, neighborhood centers, and cafés, and how these everyday settings shape their experiences of social connection and loneliness in later life. Drawing on mobile ethnography and go-along interviews with 27 older adults in the Nuremberg metropolitan region in Germany, the study explores how third places are used, adapted, or withdrawn over time. While many participants found comfort and continuity in culturally familiar environments, their use of third places was shaped by gender, age, health, economic constraints, and changing neighborhood dynamics. Rather than serving as universally inclusive settings, third places often mirror broader social divisions, with limited intergenerational or cross-cultural interaction. The findings contribute to scholarship on aging, migration, and urban sociology by showing that third places are not only physical locations but social settings whose meaning, accessibility, and emotional significance shift over time and across contexts.

abstract: This article examines how Chinese migrant entrepreneurs in Prato engage with the contested meaning of the Made in Italy production label. As Chinese-run fashion firms have become central to Italy's fast fashion sector, their growing visibility has raised public concerns about authenticity, national identity, and the perceived erosion of cultural heritage. Drawing on 35 semi-structured interviews and ethnographic fieldwork, the study explores how commercial nationalism shapes both the marginalisation and the legitimisation of migrant-led production. It argues that the controversy surrounding Made in Italy reflects broader struggles over symbolic legitimacy and participation in national production in a globalised economy. The findings show that Chinese entrepreneurs rely on distinct forms of social capital to establish credibility, respond to exclusion, and reinterpret the meaning of national branding. By foregrounding the role of producers, the article contributes to debates on migrant entrepreneurship, nationhood, and the social foundations of economic legitimacy.

abstract: Are members of the public still committed to democracy? Existing studies often ask whether members of the public sanction political actors who break institutional or procedural norms. In contrast, we study a shared cultural horizon, which grounds democracy as a way of living. Drawing on Civil Sphere Theory and the sociology of culture and cognition, we conceptualise the horizon as a binary discourse, which can be internalised as a cultural schema by individuals. Through a concept association task administered to a representative sample of the US public, we uncover a widely internalised democratic schema, which is shared across partisan divides and predicts evaluations of political actors. We temper fears of democratic decline, at least at the level of a shared cultural horizon in the United States, provide an individual-level perspective on Civil Sphere Theory, and bridge two sometimes conflicting traditions in cultural sociology.

abstract: Health sociologists conceptualise the medicalisation of birth and breastfeeding within broader socio-cultural frameworks of fear and antagonism toward the female body. While birth emotions shape breastfeeding initiation, their longer-term implications and the role of emotional support during childbirth remain less clear. We use survey data from the Hampton Roads Infant Feeding Study (N = 1,360), collected among mothers who gave birth between 2020 and 2024, to estimate a generalised structural equation model linking medical interventions, relational care, emotional responses, and exclusive breastfeeding at six months. Building on Hochschild's theory of emotion work and recent literature on emotional geography and emotional resistance, we show that medicalised birth is associated with breastfeeding partly through negative emotional pathways, while doula and midwife support are associated with positive emotional experiences and higher odds of exclusive breastfeeding. We argue that relational care can function as emotional resistance by supporting embodied confidence and mother-infant connection across birth and infant feeding. Relational care during childbirth may therefore extend beyond the birthing space, not only shaping the emotional conditions for breastfeeding, but potentially also transforming more general normative constructions of womanhood.

abstract: As global aging accelerates, culturally competent gerontology education, particularly instruction that cultivates cultural awareness - has become increasingly critical. However, current pedagogical approaches face notable limitations. While effective, study abroad programs remain inaccessible to most students. Conversely, classroom-based global aging content frequently relies on country-level data and macro-level theories, resulting in abstracted and decontextualized learning. To bridge this gap, we propose an instructor-driven narrative pedagogical approach as a feasible and sustainable alternative. Grounded in Narrative Gerontology and Critical Gerontology, this method encourages instructors to integrate their own international fieldwork experiences into their teaching, bringing authentic, lived stories directly into the classroom. Drawing on site visits to Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan, we offer a conceptual exploration alongside illustrative examples of how to develop instructor-led narratives that illuminate sociocultural variations in global aging. We also provide brief instructor guides to serve as templates for applying these narratives in the classroom and for structuring future narrative development during international fieldwork. Instructor narratives offer a unique opportunity to enrich student learning by connecting global theories with local, lived experiences, thereby increasing student engagement and enhancing cultural relevance. Ultimately, this approach presents an accessible, high-impact strategy for integrating global gerontology narratives into higher education curricula.

abstract: Simulated interaction is a common healthcare training tool and is increasingly technologically mediated. Although the need for clinical realism or authenticity of simulated interactions is commonly understood, less attention has been paid to their interactional realism. However, research beyond healthcare suggests that participants interact differently in simulated scenarios. This paper examines simulations conducted through the MetaHuman Live platform, where a human tutor is live-linked to an avatar using the tutor's voice and mapping their gaze and facial expressions. We use conversation analysis (CA) to analyse student nurses' interactions with this platform, identifying key areas where they differ from 'real' interactions. These are openings, closings, establishing shared knowledge, interactional progressivity and orientation to simulation platforms as an assessment tool. We suggest that features of a hybrid platform which aim to increase realism can also make interaction more complicated for learners trying to navigate between 'the person' and 'the system'. We conclude that, although our analysis suggests ways forward for the more effective integration of simulation technologies in training communication skills in healthcare, it also points to our continued need for a better sociological understanding of how interaction itself works in practice, to provide an evidential basis for design and evaluation of such simulations.

abstract: The internet allows patients to take a more active role in the diagnostic process, as the interactivity of "Dr. Google" and other online symptom-checkers demonstrates. Social media has emerged as a locus where (self-)diagnoses can be made through social interaction with others who identify as holding diagnostic identities. This paper builds on a foundation of research analyzing TikToks about ADHD and autism and the platform's content recommendation algorithm to examine how users are served content that implies that they occupy a given diagnosis, representing a distinct iteration of Dr. Google. The algorithm, not the user, could trigger the diagnostic process by labeling the user with a diagnosis or other pathologizing characteristics. I analyze how the TikTok algorithm encourages content themes and forms that may alter public perception of the boundaries, characteristics, and prevalence of ADHD and autism, as well as their entanglement with each other and the label of neurodivergence. I engage with the TikTok algorithm using digital ethnographic and discourse analysis approaches to understand "Dr. TikTok" as an example of how diagnostic pathways may be becoming increasingly mediated by AI systems. I find that the TikTok algorithm shapes TikToks about ADHD and autism by encouraging creators to engage in practices like speaking in second-person to the viewer and positioning relatable experiences as a form of subjective diagnostic expertise, situating these videos as paradoxically hyperpersonalized, yet inclusive. This study contributes to the sociology of medicine by showing how AI systems could intervene in and reorder the traditional diagnostic process.

abstract:
Background

Positive future orientations are increasingly recognized as both a health-promoting resource and an intrinsic aspect of human well-being, while dampened outlooks represent a form of deprivation. This article considers whether pain-a defining corollary of contemporary collective despair-has implications for how people imagine their futures in the short- and longer-term.

Methods

We use daily diary and survey data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study to consider two distinct time horizons: expectations for tomorrow and decade-out life trajectories. Study 1 assesses whether number of daily pain sites is linked to expectations for positive and stressful next-day experiences, while Study 2 uses conventional survey data to examine how chronic pain interference relates to future expectations across multiple domains of life. Both studies employ hybrid between-within panel models to decompose within-person variance at each time scale alongside more stable between-person differences.

Results

Day-to-day occurrences of pain are associated with more pessimistic next-day anticipations, as reflected by within-person increases predicting higher odds of expected stress and lower odds of uplifts (Study 1). Chronic pain interference, meanwhile, modestly dampens decade-out expectations (Study 2), with work, financial, and health outlooks most discernibly susceptible.

Conclusion

Our two-study design provides novel evidence that pain does indeed "cast a shadow" over both short-term and longer-term future orientations. In this sense, pain constitutes not only a biopsychosocial clinical symptom but also a threat to how people are able to inhabit time.

abstract: How credibility is constructed under conditions of epistemic uncertainty is a central question in the sociology of knowledge. Telepathic animal communication (TAC) represents a field in which knowledge claims are inherently non-verifiable, yet services are actively marketed and consumed. This study examines how TAC practitioners construct credibility on their websites. Drawing on Grounded Theory, websites offering TAC services in Germany were qualitatively analyzed. Findings identify three central mechanisms of credibility construction. First, practitioners employ professionalized presentations, including structured services, therapeutic terminology, and biographical self-legitimation. Second, credibility is reinforced through emotional and relational appeal, including personalized communication, expressions of care, and perceived closeness between practitioner and client. Third, strategic non-verifiability emerges as a distinctive mechanism: the inherent unverifiability of TAC is actively mobilized to protect claims from falsification through interpretative flexibility. The findings show how credibility can be stabilized through professional, relational, and epistemic strategies despite the absence of empirical validation.

abstract: Screen time guidelines for preschoolers have heavily relied on duration controls. Recently, guidelines have evolved to focus on the content and context of use; however, digital health impacts are still widely measured against guideline targets that apply a one-size-fits-all assumption. Despite these recommendations, a global meta-analysis shows that only 35.6% of children under age five adhere to these guidelines. This low compliance is driven by contemporary lifestyle demands, busy parental schedules, and constrained urban spaces. Compounded by socioeconomic disparities and a lack of practical ideas for alternative activities, screens have become a default domestic childcare arrangement, escalating passive, isolated consumption. This paper introduces a three-layered ecological framework that bridges the gap between the targets of institutional guidelines and the diverse ground realities of managing digital engagement across different socioeconomic statuses. It lays out a practical blueprint to operationalize these objectives through a protocol that integrates screen awareness, meaningful alternatives, active engagement, responsive caregiving, and traditional games. This framework provides actionable guidance to help families transition from digital silos to interactive, shared spaces, aiming to alleviate parental stress and support the parent-child relationship.

abstract: In settler-colonial societies, indigenous children exhibit elevated risk of CPS involvement, but little is known about the comparative dynamics of indigenous disadvantage. We calculated the cumulative incidence of CPS involvement before age 18 years among indigenous and nonindigenous children in Australia and the United States in 2019. We applied period life-table methods to linked administrative records. Among indigenous children, the cumulative incidences of maltreatment investigation and of out-of-home placement were higher in the U.S. than in Australia, but investigations confirming maltreatment were more common in Australia than in the U.S. Indigenous-nonindigenous disparities in CPS involvement were larger in Australia than in the U.S. In both countries, indigenous-nonindigenous disparities decreased with age and were larger at later stages of CPS involvement. Comparative findings contextualize indigenous children's CPS involvement in settler-colonial societies, informing research into its causes and prevention.

abstract:
Objectives

Homebound status refers to needing assistance or an assistive device to leave home, being normally unable to leave home, or experiencing leaving home as a major effort. This study examines transitions into and out of homeboundness and whether family structure is associated with these transitions, with attention to gender differences.

Methods

Using National Health and Aging Trends Study data from 2011-2024, transition probabilities across four states-independent, homebound, nursing home residence, and deceased-were estimated using an unadjusted continuous-time homogeneous Markov model. Multinomial logistic regression models then assessed associations between family structure and subsequent transitions, including gender interactions.

Results

Among respondents who were independent, 84.6% remained independent, and 12.2% became homebound by the next wave. Among those who were homebound, 23.6% returned to independence, 60.1% remained homebound, 2.4% entered nursing home residence, and 13.9% died. Unpartnered older adults had higher risks of transitioning from independence to nursing home (RRR = 1.752, p <.01) and death (RRR = 1.265, p <.01). Parents had lower risks than childless older adults of transitioning from independence to nursing home (RRR = 0.523, p <.01) and death (RRR = 0.735, p <.01), and from homeboundness to nursing home (RRR = 0.574, p <.001). The association between being unpartnered and becoming homebound was significantly stronger among men than women.

Discussion

: Homeboundness as a dynamic and socially structured process. Family structure may shape pathways into homeboundness, institutional care, and death, with implications for aging in place.

abstract: Culture significantly influences human psychology, making it essential for psychological research, particularly in social psychology, to acknowledge its importance. However, the majority of psychological research ignores or marginalises culture and context. This is problematic because, despite representing a small portion of humanity (specifically Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich and Democratic (WEIRD) populations) mainstream psychology is published as if it represented the whole humanity. Among the subfields of psychology, social psychology is arguably the one in which this issue should be least prevalent. To investigate this, we conducted a study on titles and abstracts of articles from 69 social psychology journals published between 1990 and 2020, examining how cultural diversity and awareness of its importance changed over time. The results indicate that cultural awareness is more prominent in journals focused on culture, international or local issues; while remaining almost entirely absent in journals focused on theory, reviews and business. Furthermore, cultural awareness displays an imbalance regarding culture: while WEIRD mentions remain most common, mentions of other regions appear to be disproportionately represented or 'inflated' in specific contexts. The generalizability of psychological theories will remain impossible if culture is not integrated as a central factor in research.

abstract: The experimental laboratory and the Institute of Psychology and Psychotechnics at the University of San Marcos, which housed it, were inaugurated on November 14, 1935. German professor Walter Blumenfeld (1887-1967), who was in charge of this establishment, assumed the chair of Experimental Psychology, was responsible for designing exams for university applicants and conducted psychotechnical research. This article aims to reconstruct the equipment and daily work of this first laboratory at the university. Blumenfeld's work and the establishment of this laboratory are credited with making the academic study of psychology possible in Peru-a field previously regarded as unknowable-and paving the way for psychology to become a university degree in 1955. abstract: In this study, the trajectories of depressive symptoms and the role of resilience were examined during the transition to high school. A five-wave longitudinal survey, with 1-month intervals, was conducted during the first semester of Grade 10 among 639 Chinese students (M<sub>age</sub> = 15.88; SD = 0.63; 52.2% females) from four high schools. Latent growth modelling was employed to analyse the data. Results indicated that a quadratic growth model adequately fit the data, showing a quadratic trajectory characterised by an initial rapid increase in depressive symptoms followed by gradual deceleration. Sex significantly predicted initial symptom levels, with females reporting higher symptoms than males, but did not predict rates of change. Higher resilience was associated with lower initial depressive symptoms and a decelerated trajectory over time. These findings suggest that resilience could be a valuable target for depressive symptom prevention and intervention programmes during the transition to high school.

abstract: Theories of cognitive development propose that cultural values shape metacognitive skills. However, cross-cultural research on metacognition remains limited and often relies on verbal assessments that may lack validity across cultural contexts. The present study examined metacognitive monitoring in Kenyan, Chinese, and U.S. children (N = 95; 6-10-year-olds; 46% female) using a non-verbal problem-solving task in which children assembled objects according to a model. Across all three cultural contexts, children exhibited various monitoring behaviors (e.g., checking the model), and the frequency of these behaviors increased with age. Cross-cultural differences emerged in the specific monitoring strategies children used: Chinese children engaged in more thorough monitoring than Kenyan and U.S. children. These findings highlight both culturally-recurrent and culturally-variable patterns in children's metacognitive monitoring.

abstract:
Background

Healthcare systems face growing pressure from rising costs, workforce shortages, chronic disease burden, and increasing mental health needs. At the same time, many health outcomes depend on behavioural and psychosocial factors that remain insufficiently integrated into healthcare delivery. Although health psychology provides evidence-based approaches to prevention, behaviour change, and patient-centred care, its contribution often remains fragmented rather than structurally embedded within healthcare systems. This policy-oriented conceptual perspective aims to fill this gap and inform stakeholders about how the discipline can contribute to more sustainable healthcare systems through the integration of behavioural and psychosocial expertise.

Method

This perspective and framework was developed through iterative discussions among the authors, experts from health psychology academia and practice, informed by established health psychology theories and selected interdisciplinary literature, with an emphasis on systematic reviews, large-scale studies, and authoritative policy sources.

Results

We identified three interrelated domains of contribution of health psychology: (1) research, education, and policy support; (2) health promotion and prevention in schools, workplaces, and communities; and (3) interprofessional clinical integration in hospitals and primary care.

Conclusions

Coordinated psychosocial integration across prevention and care pathways may strengthen health promotion and prevention, improve care coordination, and reduce avoidable healthcare costs and burden.

abstract: Toomela (2025) have provided a useful constructive critique of why Cultural Psychology has not yet succeeded in becoming a "general human psychology". This commentary includes a summary of the points Aaro Toomela states in his article and moves further into the discussion and balance between understanding Cultural Psychology as a system, in terms of Luria, Vygotsky and Anokin, as Toomela suggests, and suggesting importance of "bricoleurs" in terms of Smedslund (2012) in flexible and improvising manners. The main content of Aaro Toomela´s article includes (1) clear definitions on culture and psyche (2) scientific explanations and its limits (3) methodology (4) approaches (5) research questions (6) from theory to practice. What follows, is further elaborations of three main themes including improvisation through Smedslunds Bricoleur model, places for psychology and roles for psychologists. This opens up for discussions on the contributions for cultural psychology and limitations to be overcome for the future.

abstract: Interpersonal contact is essential for cooperation and care, but it also provides a route for pathogen transmission between individuals. Hence, a key challenge for social organisms involves maintaining beneficial social contact while also limiting exposure to infection risks. Existing proposals suggest that this trade-off is guided by the interpersonal value of specific social targets. In addition, ecological and cultural factors, including historical pathogen prevalence, individualism-collectivism, tightness-looseness, and relational mobility, might also shape how people avoid pathogens. To test whether and how infection-risky social contact varies with individual-level interpersonal value and these societal-level factors, we collected data from 47,756 participants across 61 societies. Participants were randomly assigned to picture a social target - either a friend, acquaintance, stranger, or enemy. They then rated their comfort with infection-risky contact with that target (e.g., drinking from the same water bottle) and whether they would touch the target when greeting them. In all societies, participants were more comfortable with infection-risky contact and more likely to engage in physical contact during greetings with targets of higher interpersonal value. Such associations varied only modestly across societies. Notably, the associations between infection-risky contact and societal-level factors depended on target interpersonal value and were concentrated among high-value targets-contact was lower where historical pathogen prevalence and tightness were greater and higher where individualism and relational mobility were greater. These findings suggest that infection-risky contact is primarily guided by the value of social targets, with ecological and cultural factors playing a lesser role.
