abstract: Post-COVID-19 condition (PCC) is frequently associated with cognitive impairments, but the integrity of long-term episodic memory remains poorly understood. This study examined immediate, short-term, and very long-term episodic memory in individuals with PCC and evaluated whether emotional disturbances predict long-term recognition outcomes. Forty-one participants (30 PCC; 11 non-PCC) completed a verbal cued-recall task and an immersive virtual reality free-recall object-location memory (OLM) task immediately after learning and the following day. Nine months later, three recognition tasks (verbal, word-list of objects, and visuospatial recognition) and questionnaires assessing anxiety, depression, and perceived stress were administered. PCC participants required significantly longer retrieval times than non-PCC participants in the immediate and delayed OLM trials. Nine months later, PCC participants exhibited significant impairments in verbal cued-recall compared to the immediate and one-day recall trials. Performance on the word-list task was poorer in the PCC group, whereas scores in verbal and visuospatial recognition tasks remained comparable between groups. Emotional symptoms were significantly higher in the PCC group. Exploratory regression analyses suggested a negative association between perceived stress and nine-month visuospatial recognition performance in PCC participants. These preliminary findings suggest a potential vulnerability of very long-term verbal episodic memory in PCC, alongside slowed retrieval processes and heightened emotional distress. The observed association between chronic perceived stress and visuospatial recognition suggests a potential role of stress in very long-term memory performance. Overall, the results highlight the need for long-term cognitive follow-up in PCC and identify perceived stress as a potential factor relevant for long-term recognition of visuospatial information.

abstract: Individuals from regions affected by infectious disease outbreaks may be stigmatized because others hold negative mental images-or mental representations-of them. This study investigated whether such outbreaks lead to the formation of negative mental representations of residents in affected areas and explored the role of disease severity in this process. Study 1 revealed that during the early stages of the COVID-19 epidemic, the public's mental representations of residents from Wuhan were perceived as less attractive than those of Chengdu residents and associated with disgust and behavioural avoidance. However, differences disappeared after the restrictions of the epidemic were lifted. The results indicate that the COVID-19 outbreak triggered stigmatization of residents in Wuhan. In Study 2, disease severity and perceived threat were manipulated, and results show that participants formed less attractive face representations of residents from areas where severe infectious diseases broke out than those from areas affected by mild infectious diseases. This proved that the severity of infectious diseases affected the extent of stigmatization towards residents in outbreak areas. These results further our understanding of the mechanisms and factors underlying stigmatization associated with affected regions and may inform effective public health strategies to mitigate stigma and support disease control efforts.

abstract:
Objectives: The psychology literature is occasionally quoted as being in a replication crisis due to the inability to replicate key findings caused by either integrity issues, or weak scientific protocols. This paper focuses on an unexplored topic in psychological science, ‘tortured phrases’, first to appreciate whether any psychology literature might contain such ambiguous terms, even if they are not related to psychology per se.

Methods and Results:

The Tortured Phrases Detector (TPD) of the Problematic Paper Screener revealed 36 journal articles (including one proceedings paper) with tortured phrases, 14 of which have been retracted to date (10 October 2025). We then induced, using a free online paraphraser, a novel methodology for detecting ‘tortured phrases’, by converting 50 standard psychological terms that started with the letter “A” into purposefully created ‘tortured phrases’. We employed Google Scholar to detect whether any of these created ‘tortured phrases’ might actually exist in published literature. The second method, with only 50 terms, was able to detect at least one potential ‘tortured phrase’ (“evaluation utensil” used to represent “assessment instrument”).

Conclusions:

The exploratory nature of the methodology was prone to false positives but had success. It is our hope that this study will inspire further attempts to detect tortured phrases in psychology literature in order to further increase the scientific and ethical rigor in the field of psychology.

abstract: Human gaze is a potent social signal; it communicates attention, intention and social engagement, and allows observers to infer not only where others are attending but also how they are socially related. Although gaze has been extensively studied in direct social interaction, far less is known about how it shapes the perceptions and actions of uninvolved observers in shared environments. Here, we investigate whether mutual gaze creates an 'attentional territory' that third parties implicitly respect. In a large-scale field study across four university campuses in Europe and Canada (N = 4680 pedestrians), two confederates stood facing one another in a public space. We manipulated gaze direction and reciprocity (mutual, unilateral or no interaction) as well as interpersonal distance (2-6 metres), holding body orientation and spatial arrangement constant. Pedestrians were less likely to cross between individuals engaged in mutual gaze. This effect weakened with increasing distance, but was robust across all locations. Together, the findings demonstrate that gaze does not merely coordinate interaction between individuals but also shapes how uninvolved others perceive and move through shared environments. By isolating gaze reciprocity from spatial arrangement, we demonstrate that mutual gaze functions as a dynamic social boundary organizing the permeability of public space.

abstract: Positive psychology interventions (PPI) have been applied and demonstrated evidence in various population groups. The present systematic review focused on the types and influence of PPI on the physical and psychological health of pregnant women. Studies that matched the selection criteria were identified on EBSCOhost, PsychINFO, Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus and four positive psychology journals. From the 2528 records identified, finally eight studies were included in the review. PPI in this review were delivered utilising various positive psychology components such as hope, gratitude and optimism based on existing theories, for example, the strengths theory, broaden-and-build theory, and hope theory. Most interventions were conducted from 14 gestational weeks onwards and were delivered via virtual platforms or mobile applications. As a result of this systematic review, it was identified that PPIs for maternal well-being were aimed at improving (1) physical health, including labour pain, nausea and vomiting; (2) psychological health, including stress, emotions, anxiety and depression; and (3) subjective health, including life satisfaction, perceived social support and quality of life. Most of the selected studies provided significant evidence towards improvement of well-being outcomes from administering PPI. For future studies, in-depth PPI integrated coping and support approaches should be further evidenced among diverse pregnant populations.

abstract:
Objective

Racial microaggressions are subtle, everyday expressions that communicate derogatory or exclusionary messages toward members of marginalised racial groups and are associated with adverse psychological outcomes. Evaluations of racial microaggressions may vary according to how individuals define and interpret racism. This study examined whether white fragility was associated with how white Australian psychology students evaluated vignettes reflecting the experiences of Aboriginal teenagers, focusing on the extent to which participants considered actor intentions, target experiences, and perceived social acceptability.

Method

White Australian psychology students (N = 130) completed a vignette-based survey assessing their racism evaluations, attributional focus (actor intentions, target experiences, and social acceptability), and white fragility.

Results

Higher white fragility was associated with lower racism evaluations and, after demographic adjustment, modestly lower target focus. There was insufficient evidence for associations between white fragility and either actor focus or reliance on perceived social acceptability.

Conclusions

Higher white fragility may represent a barrier to recognising racially harmful behaviour. Findings regarding target focus provide preliminary support for attentional processes proposed by the Emotion Regulation Model of White Fragility. Implications for professional training in psychology are discussed, particularly for supporting the development of culturally safe and responsive practice when working with Aboriginal clients.

abstract: A growing body of research has aimed to map the characteristics of extraordinary altruists-such as those who have donated a kidney to a stranger. However, this research has primarily focused on adults, and we know little about the development of extraordinary altruism. While children cannot donate their organs to strangers nor large portions of their income to charity, they can choose not to eat animals. In this study we examine independent vegetarians (i.e., children who become vegetarian while being raised in meat eating families) as a potential case-study of extraordinarily altruistic motivation. In retrospective adult (Study 1) and developmental samples (Study 2) of American participants, we compare independently vegetarian children to family vegetarians and non-vegetarians on measures of empathy/compassion, disgust sensitivity, cognitive reflection, fearful facial recognition, social dominance orientation, and speciesism. We find that both independent and family vegetarians were lower in speciesism and SDO, and higher in disgust sensitivity and empathy/compassion, with these differences emerging almost exclusively in the retrospective adult sample. Crucially, and contrary to our hypotheses, we find no differences between independent and family vegetarians, and discuss potential interpretations of this null result. These data offer new insight into a small body of literature about independent vegetarians and show that similar traits are associated with both family and independent vegetarianism.

abstract: Prediction error (PE) signals support feedback evaluation and adaptive updating, and are closely linked to medial frontal theta dynamics, particularly within dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC)-centered networks. However, evidence linking these oscillatory mechanisms to the modulation of PE encoding remains limited. Here, we tested whether theta-band modulation of a dACC-centered medial frontal network altered trial-level PE encoding during food-reward processing. In a single-blind, sham-controlled pre-post design, individuals with elevated food addiction symptoms performed a food incentive-delay task while undergoing electroencephalographic recordings combined with theta-band temporal interference stimulation. Single-trial analyses revealed that feedback-related negativity (FRN) amplitudes varied as a function of both behavioral and model-derived prediction errors. Critically, theta-band modulation altered FRN-PE coupling, with the effect most pronounced for unfavorable outcomes, whereas anticipatory activity remained unchanged. These findings support the hypothesis that theta-band modulation can alter feedback-related PE encoding within this population and task context.

abstract: Contemporary public health challenges, including non-communicable diseases, persistent inequalities, misinformation, and complex organisational systems, are fundamentally shaped by behavioural, social, and psychological processes. Although this is increasingly recognised, psychological science remains unevenly integrated into public health and is often confined to individual-level interventions rather than embedded in system design, governance, and policy. A more fundamental shift is required. Psychology should be understood not as an adjunct to public health but as one of its foundational disciplines. Drawing on behavioural science, social identity research, and systems thinking, this commentary argues that psychological processes operate across multiple levels, from individual behaviour and community participation to organisational practice, leadership, implementation, and collective action. The COVID-19 pandemic illustrated this clearly: psychologically informed approaches supported public adherence, effective communication, trust, and community resilience. However, a broader conception of psychology, encompassing social identity, organisational behaviour, implementation, and structural pathways, is needed. Psychology should be recognised as a foundational contributor within the wider public health sciences ecosystem. Embedding psychological insight within the infrastructure of public health is essential if public health systems are to address the growing complexity of protecting and improving population health. A mature partnership between psychology and public health requires the systematic integration of psychological expertise into the design, implementation and governance of public health systems if they are to respond effectively to the complexity of twenty-first century population health challenges.

abstract: While trait adjectives may be regarded as convenient summary labels for varieties of behavioral expressions with common themes and outcomes, in turn, behaviors typical of a person may be considered as expressions of personality dispositions. In fact, in daily life, behavioral descriptions are way more frequent than the more abstract adjectival descriptors. For the present study, behavioral, verb-based data sets collected in four languages were used for comparison. The data sets each consisted of ratings from 400 participants on 543 Dutch personality verbs, 1,247 participants on 414 Polish personality verbs, 951 participants on 289 Czech personality verbs, and 512 participants on 319 Serbian personality verbs. Principal component analysis-based structures (of different dimensionalities) were compared pairwise across the languages, making use of congruence coefficients. Moreover, using simultaneous component analysis, the verb-based structure common to the four languages, based on a shared data set with ratings from 3,110 participants on 324 personality verbs, was analyzed. Three- and six-component structures based on the common set are discussed in some detail, both showing portions of the Big Five but with no reference to the Intellect-Imagination factor. It is concluded that verb-based behavioral items, in comparison to adjective- and noun-based items, give rise to a diluted and reduced trait-semantic space. To arrive at a full trait-semantic representation, all linguistic categories should be exploited in a joint operation. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

abstract: There is a need to improve the effectiveness of youth mental health services and address health disparities within them. Measurement-based care (MBC), which uses ongoing assessment to support communication and decision-making during psychosocial treatment, holds promise for helping the field reach these goals. However, MBC is not routinely used in youth psychosocial treatment, and research on its effectiveness in youth is limited and mixed, in part due to variation in implementation across studies. In this Future Directions paper, we highlight the need for theory-informed research, grounded in rigorous fidelity measurement, to identify influential MBC practices that engage target mechanisms and predict clinical outcomes. We detail a framework for this research that outlines potential MBC target mechanisms, describes MBC practices, and discusses potential measurement strategies. This framework can guide an experimental therapeutics approach to studying MBC, enabling the reverse-engineering of an MBC protocol based on a clear definition of MBC fidelity. This research can also refine our understanding of what effective MBC entails, which, in turn, can inform the development of implementation strategies to support the successful and sustained implementation of MBC.

abstract:
Introduction

Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) is a widely used intervention for depression and anxiety. However, its effectiveness is typically evaluated using subjective self-report symptom scales, which are susceptible to bias. It is hypothesised that improvements in clinical symptoms following CBT may be accompanied by improvements in physiological regulation, particularly heart rate variability (HRV), which has been proposed as a marker of emotion regulation. We conducted a systematic review with meta-analysis to examine the effects of CBT on HRV in adults with depression and/or anxiety disorders.

Methods

Following a pre-registered protocol (PROSPERO: CRD420251040957), we searched Embase, PsycINFO, PubMed, and Web of Science for randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomised interventional studies involving adults with depression and/or anxiety in CBT, and reporting HRV before and after the intervention. Random-effects meta-analyses in R estimated pooled effect sizes (Hedges' g).

Results

After screening 9713 records, we identified 12 studies; 5 RCTs were included in the meta-analysis, and the remaining 7 in the narrative review because they did not provide calculable effect sizes. Meta-analysis results found that adults randomised to CBT had significantly greater pre-to-post intervention increases in HF-HRV, LF-HRV, and SDNN-HRV. No significant changes were observed for the LF/HF ratio, RMSSD-HRV, and the HRV Triangular Index.

Conclusion

Our meta-analysis provides emerging evidence that CBT might significantly increase selected HRV indices, suggesting that physiological changes may accompany improvements in psychological symptoms. However, further high-quality research is needed to determine the clinical utility of HRV as a predictor of treatment response and a biomarker for treatment effectiveness.

abstract: The present article reconstructs the scientific career of the psychologist Kurt Gottschaldt (1902-1991) in the context of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Anthropology, Human Heredity, and Eugenics (Kaiser-Wilhelm-Institut für Anthropologie, menschliche Erblehre und Eugenik [KWI-A]) in Berlin, Germany. Against this background, it aims to analyze the scope and characteristics of the German-Japanese knowledge transfer during National Socialism and the postwar period. Drawing on Gottschaldt's profile as a Gestalt psychologist, the article establishes that his work at the KWI-A marked a programmatic reorientation toward hereditary psychology and twin research. The twin method functioned as an empirical instrument for quantifying the relationship between "heredity" and "environment" and was embedded within the institute's racial-scientific research program. The transnational dimension of this research is reconstructed for the first time through the cases of the Japanese visiting scholars Takagi Masataka (1913-1962?) and Kamitake Masaji (1909-1983). Their work documents both their institutional integration into the KWI-A as well as the lasting influence of the theoretical and methodological concepts developed there on Japanese psychology after 1945. The article demonstrates that key personnel networks, methodological approaches, and epistemological principles persisted despite the political rupture. In doing so, the study contributes to a nuanced examination of the entanglement of science, politics, and international exchange in the 20th century. abstract:
Objective

The current study aimed to refine and validate a novel model of rural psychology practice in Australia to better support and develop the rural psychology workforce. A secondary aim was to explore participants' perspectives of the need and utility of the proposed model in practice.

Method

A two-round Delphi survey was conducted, via Qualtrics, with Australian psychologists experienced in rural practice. A total of 28 participants completed Round 1 and 22 participants participated in Round 2. Reflexive content analysis was used to explore Round 1 participants' textual responses related to model utility.

Results

Consensus was reached after two rounds, resulting in a validated model of rural psychology practice containing nine domains of competence. An overarching domain of The Rural Context was foundational to the remaining eight domains: Clinical Skills, Networking, Cultural Responsiveness, Practitioner Wellbeing, Ethics, Risk, Professional Development and Digital Adaptations. Participants endorsed the need for a model and provided various uses for implementation.

Conclusions

The current study provides an empirically validated model of rural psychology practice. Utility and clinical implications are discussed, and the model aims to improve mental health service development for rural Australians. International implications are discussed.

abstract: Mice and rats emit ultrasonic vocalizations (USV) above the human hearing range. Such USV are widely regarded as reliable indicators of the animal's affective state. Moreover, USV serve important communicative functions. Given their prominent role in social communication, this review adopts a reciprocal framework that considers both sender and receiver, with particular emphasis on the production and perception of USV. The review focuses on sex differences and subtype variations in the sender, and explores the communicative value of USV through playback studies, revealing their role in regulating social interactions from the receiver's perspective. It also examines recent applications, including the use of isolation-induced USV during the homing test, USV as measures of expectation, and their relevance in modeling mania and emotional contagion. Furthermore, this review takes into account advancements in sender identification and live tracking in semi-natural environments, which have enhanced our understanding of USV. These insights offer valuable perspectives on rodent social communication and emotional processes, with implications for studying human disorders.

abstract: Visual statistical learning enables individuals to extract regularities from the environment, thereby optimizing attentional allocation. Previous research has mainly focused on unidimensional location or feature probability learning, leaving unclear whether individuals can acquire multidimensional mappings between target features and high-probability spatial locations, and how cue-induced expectations modulate the neural expression of such mappings. We employed a location probability paradigm combined with multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and recorded EEG. Reaction times showed a significant gradient from the feature-matched high-probability location to the low-probability location, indicating successful acquisition of feature-spatial mappings under both cue conditions. The N2pc did not reliably differentiate the two high-probability location conditions, providing no detectable evidence of feature-dependent modulation of early lateralized selection. Predictive cues elicited brief pretarget alpha lateralization toward the cue-associated HPTL. Search-array-locked MVPA discriminated feature-matched from feature-mismatched HPTL trials under both cue conditions, with stronger decoding under predictive cueing. These findings show that learned feature-spatial regularities were expressed behaviorally and in distributed neural activity, and that predictive cues modulated their neural expression before and after search-array onset.

abstract: Questionable research practices (QRPs) may inflate false-positive rates and have been surveyed in psychology, ecology, and education, but not in music psychology. In a survey, 198 researchers who had authored empirical music-psychology work reported how often they had used 22 practices and estimated how many colleagues had used each. Three quarters (75.1%) reported at least one of the 18 practices bearing on false-positive risk, and 82.8% at least one of all 22. The most common were citing irrelevant work to satisfy a reviewer (46.9%) and selecting the most favourable analysis after seeing the results (43.5%). Respondents estimated that colleagues used 20 of the 22 practices more than they did themselves, but this gap is largely produced by the response scale in the survey and is not evidence of under-reporting. Researchers who thought practices were more widespread reported more of them between persons (OR = 2.16, 95% CI [1.74, 2.68]) and within them (OR = 2.62, [2.32, 2.96]), consistent with false consensus as well as descriptive norms. Music-specific practices were reported less often than reporting and analysis practices, though this depended partly on item wording and on whether a practice applied at all. Career stage showed no detectable association with admissions. Researchers reporting more open research practices reported more QRPs, not fewer (OR = 1.28, [1.14, 1.44]), which may indicate differences in disclosure as much as in behaviour. These results provide a first baseline for the field.

abstract: Meta-analyses have become foundational tools for evidence synthesis and are receiving increasing attention across research disciplines, including fear conditioning - a central paradigm in affective, behavioral, and clinical neuroscience and psychology - where the number of meta-analyses has notably increased in recent years. However, substantial methodological heterogeneity among these meta-analyses complicates their interpretation and comparability. This review systematically summarizes existing meta-analyses in fear conditioning (n = 26), with particular emphasis on methodological choices and reporting standards. Our findings indicate substantial variability in reporting practices, particularly regarding review processes, applied methodological models, and the operationalization of certain variables, which may challenge reproducibility and interpretability. Most meta-analyses used aggregate data and random-effects models, while moderator analyses were frequently conducted but yielded few significant moderators. Outcome measures were frequently aggregated (e.g., skin conductance, startle responses, ratings) without a clear theoretical rationale. We discuss the implications of moderator analyses, the limited attention to temporal dynamics, and the aggregation of diverse outcome measures. We argue that the field would benefit from more precise reporting, theory-driven analytical decisions, and increased data sharing at both the primary and meta-analytic levels. Such improvements would facilitate individual participant data meta-analyses, which preserve within-study variability, enhance moderator analyses, and address challenges inherent to aggregate-level data synthesis. Establishing and expanding shared infrastructures represents a necessary step toward cumulative, reproducible, and clinically informative work in the future.

abstract: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is central to regulating intrusive thoughts and worry, yet the lateralization and neurophysiological mechanisms underlying these processes remain unclear. Parasympathetic cardiac control, indexed by heart rate variability (HRV), has been proposed to correlate with prefrontal control over brain regions involved in emotional, cognitive, and autonomic regulation, but empirical evidence linking these domains is mixed. In this preregistered, single-blind, sham-controlled, within-subject study, we examined the effects of high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (HF-rTMS) over the left and right DLPFC on parasympathetic cardiac control, worry, and intrusive thoughts in 31 healthy participants. HRV was assessed at rest and during a breathing focus task, a validated paradigm that measures attentional focus, spontaneous intrusive thoughts, and worry. Contrary to predictions, active stimulation did not differ from sham in modulating HRV, intrusive thoughts, or worry. However, right compared with left DLPFC stimulation was associated with higher self-reported worry and lower RMSSD. Exploratory analyses suggested that the differences in RMSSD were not present at baseline and were observed following stimulation. Notably, changes in HRV were not associated with changes in worry, indicating that the effects of HF-rTMS on worry co-occur with, though are not directly explained by, changes in parasympathetic cardiac control, challenging straightforward interpretations of HRV as a correlate of prefrontal regulatory control. Together, these findings provide evidence for hemispheric asymmetries in prefrontal contributions to autonomic and worry-related processes and may inform understanding of the effects of inhibitory right- or excitatory left-DLPFC stimulation protocols on worry-related symptoms.

abstract: Digital assistance systems based on artificial intelligence are increasingly discussed as tools to address growing demands in mental health care. However, their acceptance among future and practising psychotherapists remains insufficiently understood. In a pre-post online survey, N = 317 participants (predominantly psychology students, with smaller groups of trainee psychotherapists and licensed psychotherapists) completed questionnaires assessing perceived usefulness (PU), work-related stress, technological affinity, professional self-efficacy, data protection concerns and prior knowledge. Between assessments, participants watched a video demonstrating a digital assistance system. An open-ended item captured perceived barriers. PU increased significantly after the video (p < 0.001, d = 0.29), with subgroup differences across professional groups. Effects were largest among trainee psychotherapists (d = 0.59) and negligible among licensed psychotherapists (d = 0.06). Work-related stress was positively associated with PU, whereas age was negatively associated. Technological affinity, prior knowledge, professional self-efficacy and data protection concerns showed no significant associations with PU. Open-ended responses highlighted concerns regarding data protection, usability, time demands and professional autonomy. Brief, targeted demonstrations may increase PU of digital assistance systems among psychology students, although effects appear minimal in licensed psychotherapists. The mechanisms underlying the video effect and the positive association between stress and PU warrant further investigation.

abstract:
Objectives

People with chronic pain often experience symptoms of pain-related distress (eg, kinesiophobia, catastrophizing) and general distress (eg, depression, anxiety). Identifying distinct profiles of distress among patients seeking pain psychology treatment can inform personalized pain psychology interventions. Among adults seeking pain psychology treatment, the current study applied latent profile analysis (LPA) to (1) identify distinct patient symptom profiles (based on kinesiophobia, catastrophizing, depression, and anxiety) and (2) characterize pain-related symptoms and demographics of each profile.

Methods

Adults scheduled for a pain psychology evaluation who completed a clinical battery of patient-reported outcome measures were included. LPA was applied to identify distinct subgroups of patients based on psychological symptoms. The resulting groups were compared on pain-related and demographic factors.

Results

Participants were 548 adults (mean age=51.1; predominantly white [66.6%] and female [67.5%]). Two profiles were identified: "global distress" (67.2%, elevated clinical symptoms in all domains) and "localized and mild kinesiophobia" (32.8%, subclinical symptoms in all domains, except mild kinesiophobia). The "global distress" group was younger ( d =0.23) and had higher levels of area deprivation ( d =0.23). They had higher pain intensity ( d =0.76), functional disability ( d =0.72), and opioid misuse risk ( d =1.21).

Discussion

Among adults seeking pain psychology treatment, most experienced elevated distress across pain-specific and general domains. A minority experienced subclinical symptoms, with focal and mild kinesiophobia. The findings highlight a wide range of pain psychology needs among adults with chronic pain seeking psychology treatment, and highlight the value in treatment options that span intensity and breadth.

abstract: Interpersonal neural synchrony (INS), defined as the temporal alignment of neural activity between socially interacting individuals, has been proposed as an index of parent-child interaction quality. However, its relationship with moment-to-moment adjustment of parent-child behavior remains insufficiently understood. This systematic review examined associations between INS and observable behavior during naturalistic parent-child interactions, the factors influencing these associations, and the methods used to investigate them. Following PRISMA guidelines, systematic searches of Scopus, PubMed, and ScienceDirect identified 15 peer-reviewed empirical studies involving children from preschool age to early adolescence. INS-behavior associations were heterogeneous across studies. Higher INS was most consistently associated with mutual engagement, shared positive affect, and supportive parenting, whereas findings concerning reciprocity, responsiveness, and child agency were more context-dependent. Time-resolved analyses further indicated that INS fluctuated in relation to specific behavioral events and revealed temporally asymmetric patterns in which parent or child neural activity preceded that of the interaction partner. However, these patterns do not establish causal directionality and may partly reflect shared exposure to task-related or interactional inputs. Task structure and the availability of direct social cues appeared to shape INS-behavior associations, while parental stress and child social functioning emerged as potential sources of variability in INS. Methodologically, the findings highlight the value of combining micro- and macro-level behavioral coding with time-resolved and directionality-sensitive analyses, alongside stronger controls for spurious synchrony and common inputs. Given the limited number and methodological heterogeneity of available studies, the findings should be regarded as preliminary and primarily hypothesis-generating.

abstract: Students identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or otherwise non-heterosexual or non-cisgender (LGBTQ+) are increasingly represented. However, they still face additional challenges in educational settings, so Educational Psychology needs to research these issues. In this preregistered systematic scientometric literature review, we investigate (a) the extent of LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology journals, (b) common themes and trends, and discuss systematic gaps for future research. After searching all 41,992 articles on ERIC, published in the most impactful (Q1 and Q2) Educational Psychology journals, we combined scientometric-quantitative and qualitative methods to review 68 eligible articles. We found a surge in publications from 2000 onward, driven by special issues. For almost half of these high-impact journals, we found no published articles on LGBTQ+ issues on ERIC; most publish only a few per thousand, even though this topic falls within their scope. Most often, these articles were empirical, correlational, and US-based, with inconsistent measures of LGBTQ+ identities. Through qualitative thematic analysis, we identified seven research themes and highlighted pertinent research gaps. To strengthen the evidence base in the field, future research should conduct rigorous longitudinal and intervention studies with culturally diverse samples and adhere to open science standards.

abstract: Mindfulness-based interventions have shown promise in supporting psychological well-being in children. However, mindfulness is commonly measured using self-report questionnaires, a method that might be problematic due to its reliance on children's accurate self-perceptions of their own mindfulness and the potential influence of social desirability bias. In the current study, we examined the convergent validity, the predictive validity, and the influence of social desirability bias on three mindfulness self-report measures for children ages 9-13  years (N = 109). Results showed that children's self-reported mindfulness demonstrated good convergent validity and predictive validity, as higher levels of self-reported mindfulness were positively associated with higher levels of parent-reported executive functioning. Self-reported mindfulness also covaried with social desirability bias. However, controlling for this bias did not substantively affect the convergent validity nor the predictive validity of self-reported mindfulness. These findings suggest that children's self-reported mindfulness also captures social desirability bias, but this bias may not affect conclusions about mindfulness when assessed as a latent factor across multiple measures. Future work measuring children's mindfulness with self-reports should account for social desirability bias when possible, as well as explore objective methods of assessing mindfulness in children.

abstract: Body appreciation has received a good deal of research attention due to its role in the promotion of well-being and adaptive eating. Prior meta-analytic evidence has pointed to small gender differences in body appreciation (favoring men), but the rapidly expanding literature and growing recognition of gender diversity require an updated synthesis. Accordingly, this account provides the first preregistered meta-analysis and systematic review of gender differences in body appreciation that extends beyond binary gender comparisons, synthesizing 349 samples from 75 nations (N = 204,315), with body appreciation instruments administered in 51 languages and including nonbinary (n = 743) and transgender (n = 540) individuals. Using multivariate 4-level meta-analytic modeling, relevant group differences (women vs. men, nonbinary vs. binary, and transgender vs. cisgender individuals) were examined. Men reported slightly higher body appreciation than women (g = 0.21). Larger differences emerged between binary and nonbinary individuals (g = 0.65 and 0.55 for men and women, respectively, vs. nonbinary individuals). Transgender individuals reported lower body appreciation than cisgender individuals, although estimates were imprecise. For all group comparisons, prediction intervals included both negative and positive effect values, thus indicating substantial uncertainty about the direction and magnitude of these effects in future studies, likely due to effect heterogeneity observed at the study and sample levels, which was partly accounted by sample type, study instrumentation, publication status, nation-level gender equality, and sexual orientation. Overall, findings indicate a graded pattern of body appreciation across gender identities, highlighting the importance of extending body image research beyond binary perspectives.

abstract: Task switching is fundamental to everyday behavior and language use but can elicit more negative experiences than those elicited by task repetition, defined as affective costs. However, whether affective costs differ between switches to dominant and non-dominant tasks remains unclear. Examining this question can help determine whether affective costs reflect general transition demands alone or also direction-specific control processes. We addressed this issue in three progressively designed experiments. Experiments 1 and 2 combined task switching and affective priming paradigms to examine general task switching and language task switching, respectively, whereas Experiment 3 used event-related potentials (ERPs) to probe the electrophysiological underpinnings. Across all experiments, switching to non-dominant tasks produced greater affective costs than switching to dominant tasks, demonstrating affective cost asymmetry. Non-dominant switches elicited larger EPN and LPP amplitudes, suggesting that early attentional capture accompanies this asymmetry and that sustained emotional processing may contribute to its formation. Together, these findings suggest that affective costs may be jointly shaped by general transition demands and direction-specific control processes, supporting a direction-sensitive account of the affective consequences of task switching.

abstract:
Background

Preventing repeated relapse remains a central challenge in drug prevention and rehabilitation. The abstinence violation effect (AVE) highlights the importance of attribution in relapse, suggesting that when individuals misinterpret a transient lapse triggered by external circumstances as a personal failure of self-control, they may become more vulnerable to further relapse. However, the behavioral signatures and computational mechanisms of attributional reasoning under uncertainty in addiction remain poorly understood.

Methods

We recruited 26 individuals with Methamphetamine Use Disorder (MUD) and 40 demographically matched healthy controls to perform an environment reasoning task (ERT), in which motion coherence manipulated confidence in perceptual decisions, allowing us to test whether negative feedback was attributed to internal perceptual errors or external environmental changes.

Results

Following negative feedback, individuals with MUD were less likely to use confidence-related perceptual evidence and accumulated negative feedback to update beliefs about external environment changes. Computational modeling further revealed individuals with MUD exhibited deficits in tracking and maintaining evidence for dynamic environmental changes. Importantly, the ability to maintain such evidence was significantly associated with abstinence duration. These findings provide process-level evidence relevant to the attributional component of AVE.

Conclusions

Atypical causal reasoning under uncertainty may constitute a key cognitive mechanism underlying relapse, offering a computational account of how individuals respond to abstinence violations. This work provides a theoretical foundation for developing targeted cognitive-behavioral interventions aimed at reducing relapse risk.

abstract: Parent-adolescent discrepancies in perceptions of parenting may provide important insight into adolescent adjustment. This study examined how consistency and discrepancy in perceived parental overparenting across parent-adolescent and father-mother dyads were associated with adolescent mental health problems in Chinese families. Participants were 860 adolescents (417 boys; M<sub>age</sub> = 10.17, SD = 1.54) and their mothers and fathers. Results showed that adolescents reported higher levels of anxiety/depressive symptoms, withdrawal, and somatic complaints when both parents and adolescents perceived high levels of overparenting. Discrepancies between adolescents and parents were also associated with poorer adjustment: adolescents reported more anxiety/depressive symptoms and withdrawal when they perceived higher paternal overparenting than their fathers did, and more anxiety/depressive symptoms when they perceived higher maternal overparenting than their mothers did. In father-mother dyads, adolescents showed more anxiety/depressive symptoms, withdrawal, and somatic complaints when both parents reported high overparenting, whereas interparental discrepancies were not significant. These patterns were consistent across boys and girls. Findings highlight the value of considering adolescents', mothers', and fathers' perspectives simultaneously when examining overparenting and adolescent mental health.

abstract: Greater attachment anxiety and avoidance are linked to more depressive symptoms. However, this association may present differently based on one's country of membership and expression of pride. In contrast to the Eurocentric definition of pride in the United States, pride means both pleasant and unpleasant/disengagement emotions in Chinese culture. This cross-cultural study aimed to examine the moderating effect of pride in the association between attachment anxiety/avoidance and depressive symptoms in both the United States and China. Adults (N = 770) from China (n = 410) and the United States (n = 360) completed self-report measures. The results of moderation analyses (PROCESS Model 1) indicated a marginally significant interaction effect of attachment insecurity × pride in predicting depressive symptoms among Chinese individuals, but not among US individuals. Specifically, greater attachment insecurity significantly exacerbated depressive symptoms for Chinese individuals who expressed heightened levels of pride. The role of attachment on depressive symptoms may vary significantly by levels of pride among Chinese individuals. This study highlights the importance of considering culturally congruent emotions such as pride when examining attachment-based mental health.

abstract: Experimental studies of primarily Western participants have suggested that musical synchrony facilitates social bonding. However, critics question the validity and cross-cultural generality of synchrony-bonding relationships, as well as the causal role of music. Drawing on recent data from large-scale Registered Reports co-designed and implemented with over 100 collaborators ("Many Voices"), we show that group singing enhances social bonding significantly more than speaking, across 901 participants speaking 30 languages. We share lessons from this collaboration regarding evolutionary hypotheses about the origins of music and language, as well as the importance of collaborating with Indigenous and non-Western researchers. By making the psychology of music research more inclusive, we may broaden our understanding of music and social bonding in humans and beyond. Indigenous knowledge does not oppose science: it improves science.

abstract:
Background

Performance anxiety and resilience are critical determinants of surgical trainee performance.

Aims

To evaluate the feasibility and preliminary impact of a brief performance psychology intervention, combining individual self-regulation with team-based performance strategies, on performance anxiety and mental toughness in surgical trainees.

Methods

In a prospective single-arm pilot and feasibility study in a university teaching hospital, nine surgical trainees from various subspecialities enrolled, with eight completing follow-up assessments. The intervention comprised two immersive workshops over two weeks, integrating individual and team-based psychological skills grounded in the biopsychosocial model of stress, challenge-threat appraisal, and high performance principles. Participants completed the Sport Anxiety Scale-2 and the Mental Toughness Evaluation Questionnaire-2 (MTE-2) at baseline (T0), three weeks (T1), and three months (T2).

Results

Eight of nine trainees (89%) completed all follow-up assessments, and the programme was delivered as planned. Mental toughness (MTE-2) improved over time (p = 0.002), and a median improvement of 580 points (95% CI 200 to 880) was sustained at three months. Most marked improvement seen in pre-performance distraction control. Anxiety (SAS-2) showed a short-term reduction, clearest for the worry subscale, though returned to baseline at three months. Frequency of technique use did not correlate with outcomes.

Conclusions

This brief high-performance psychology intervention was feasible and acceptable and was associated with short-term reductions in performance anxiety and sustained improvements in mental toughness in surgical trainees. These findings support the feasibility of integrating time-efficient psychological training in surgical education. Larger, controlled studies are required to confirm efficacy and mechanisms.

abstract: Youth represents a critical transitional phase from adolescence to adulthood, characterized by significant psychological changes and challenges. Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), defined as the intentional harm to one's body tissue without suicidal intent, is increasingly conceptualized as a transdiagnostic entity that often emerges during this period. This study examines the combined effects of impulsivity and depression on NSSI in youths from both variable-centered and person-centered approaches. A total of 2,292 university students were recruited for this study, in which we performed moderation and latent profile analyses. The results indicated that impulsivity and depression interact to significantly influence NSSI. Specifically, high levels of impulsivity and depression were associated with elevated NSSI scores. Furthermore, latent profile analysis identified four subtypes of impulsivity-depression, with the "high impulsivity-high depression" type exhibiting the most severe NSSI. These findings highlight the importance of considering both impulsivity and depression in understanding and preventing NSSI among youths.

abstract: In speeded grammaticality decision tasks, the transposed-word effect occurs when ungrammatical word sequences created by swapping adjacent words in an otherwise grammatical sentence are harder to reject than control sequences derived from ungrammatical base sentences, providing evidence for flexible word-order processing during reading. Previous research shows that this effect is often attenuated in atypical display formats, including serial word presentation and backward text, especially in RTs. Some accounts interpret this pattern as a shift from parallel processing, in which multiple words are recognised simultaneously, towards more serial word recognition. However, atypical formats may also disrupt component processes supporting reading, including eye guidance, spatial attention, and parafoveal processing, thereby reducing the uptake of information from adjacent words. We extended this work to Chinese, a script that can be read in horizontal and vertical orientations while individual characters remain upright. Two hundred native Chinese readers made speeded grammaticality decisions to five-word sequences presented left-to-right, top-to-bottom, right-to-left, or bottom-to-top. Robust transposed-word effects occurred in both accuracy and RTs across all orientations. Effects were largest for conventional left-to-right text and smaller in all three atypical orientations. Thus, attenuation occurred even though all words remained simultaneously visible. It was therefore not confined to formats that physically enforce serial presentation. Although attenuation may reflect a shift towards more serial word recognition, it could also arise because difficulty processing atypically oriented text narrows spatial attention and reduces parafoveal information uptake. These component-process changes can occur under either parallel or serial accounts, making the findings compatible with both.

abstract: Almost since the term "empathy" was coined, there has been scholarly disagreement about its meaning. Today it can best be viewed as an umbrella term encompassing a host of more specific constructs, almost all of which are regularly referred to as "empathy" in some form or fashion. Promiscuous use of this global label to denote very different constructs has impaired communication among and between scholars, practitioners, and the general public. A team of 15 empathy scholars assessed this issue and created a lexicon for these specific lower-order constructs. In this article we report the result of this effort. The lower-order constructs making up this lexicon are vicarious affect, emotional contagion, emotion co-sharing, sympathy/compassion, personal distress, perspective taking, accurate inference, mimicry, synchrony, projection, and transportation. We recommend that this more specific language be used more frequently and that the umbrella term "empathy" be used more sparingly.

abstract: Whether developmental prosopagnosia is specific to faces is an ongoing controversy. One difficulty that may contribute to discrepant results is differences in tests used to assess face and object processing. Here, we devised a search test to measure the efficiency of processing for faces, cars, and words. We had 14 subjects with developmental prosopagnosia and 26 controls perform three search tests. For face-search, subjects saw an array ranging from three to seven faces and had to answer whether all depicted the same person or if one was a different person. Similar tests were constructed for cars and words. The main variables were response time and the set-size effect, which refers to the additional time required for every additional stimulus in the array. At the group level, the prosopagnosic subjects were impaired in face search but no different from controls on car or word search. However, at a single-subject level, only 20% had evidence of a putative classical dissociation to support claims that their recognition disorder is face-specific, while 30% had abnormally prolonged car-search times, and 50% had indeterminate results. The results align with a meta-analysis that concluded there was heterogeneity in object recognition in developmental prosopagnosia.

abstract: The purpose of this article was to define and describe impairment from the perspective of the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP). This work is intended to establish a foundation for the development of a system for assessing impairment to complement HiTOP measures of psychopathology. We define impairment as the direct or indirect impact of psychopathology that is not itself part of psychopathology, involving (a) difficulty achieving important and reasonable personal goals and/or (b) direct or indirect interference with the goals of others. We articulate seven specific assessment features of a HiTOP-optimal impairment measurement approach and, having found no existing measures with all seven features in a review of the literature, sketch a prototype approach using a case example and outline a plan for generating a suite of tools for assessing impairment from a HiTOP perspective. abstract:
Objective

This study aimed to map and evaluate specialist psychological and neuropsychological care provision within ALS/MND multidisciplinary teams across the UK.

Methods

A cross-sectional, mixed-methods online survey was circulated to ALS/MND specialist services across England, Wales, Northern Ireland, and Scotland. The survey evaluated service demographics, specialist psychological staffing models, referral pathways, perceived adequacy of care, and access to other wellbeing support.

Results

Responses were received from 25/36 services (69% response rate), representing an estimated 3,500 patients. Access to specialist care was highly variable, with 24% of services lacking an established referral pathway and 20% having a referral pathway for patients living in some parts of their service area but not others. Importantly, even for those services with access to specialist psychology, nearly all reported that the specialist psychology provision was insufficient to meet the needs of their service users and the service; 80% of these services reported insufficient capacity to deliver direct assessments and interventions. Qualitative data highlighted inequitable and insufficient provision, the fragmented nature of current psychological care, and the need for sufficient and stable funding for specialist psychology provision in ALS/MND.

Conclusions

Despite international guidelines recognizing the necessity of specialist psychological and neuropsychological care in ALS/MND, access across the UK remains highly inequitable and under-resourced. To meet UK national standards (NICE) and prevent the negative impacts of untreated psychological distress and inequitable access, more resource allocation is required to integrate specialist psychology as a core component of ALS/MND care.

abstract: Prosocial behaviours, central to human social life, are actions that benefit others. Two key domains are harm aversion, where individuals forgo personal gains to prevent harming others, and prosocial effort, which involves exerting effort to benefit others. Although previous studies suggest a relationship between these behaviours, it remains unclear whether neural responses in one domain can predict prosocial motivation in another. Here, we tested whether neural sensitivity to morally salient information in harm aversion could predict prosocial effort later. Participants (n = 66) completed two tasks: a harm aversion task during fMRI, in which they traded off monetary profit against delivering electric shocks to another person; and, one week later, a prosocial effort task outside the scanner, in which they decided whether rewards for others were worth the required physical effort. We focused on three regions implicated in cost-benefit decision-making and social cognition: the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), anterior insula (AI), and temporoparietal junction (TPJ). Behaviourally, greater harm aversion was associated with increased prosocial effort. Neurally, AI responses to others' harm predicted sensitivity to others' rewards in the effort task, consistent with a role in representing others' outcomes across positive and negative valences. By contrast, TPJ responses to profit from harming others predicted decreased sensitivity to others' rewards, suggesting a role in context-dependent valuation that may constrain prosocial behaviour. These findings reveal that neural responses to morally salient information in one context correlate with prosocial motivation in another, suggesting mechanisms that bridge moral sensitivity and effortful prosociality.

abstract: Social learning, such as learning through verbal instruction, has been proposed to play a crucial role in the development pathological fear of bodily sensations. Despite the ubiquity of verbal information in daily life, the effects of verbal information on subsequent interoceptive fear learning remain empirically untested. Therefore, we aimed to examine how verbal information about the threatening vs. benign nature of bodily sensations influences subsequent interoceptive fear conditioning. 77 healthy participants were randomly assigned to receive either threat- or safety-enhancing information about bodily sensations before completing an interoceptive fear acquisition and extinction task. Two geometric symbols served as CSs and temporary dyspnea (inspiratory load) as the US. Verbal reports indicated successful differential learning in both groups, with no modulation of information type. However, participants of the threat information group showed no differential response in startle response magnitudes towards CS + relative to CS-, indexing that the activation of brain defensive networks, that did not differ between CS+ and CS-. This pattern might suggest a generalization of, or failure to inhibit defensive activation toward the safety stimulus. In contrast, the safety information group exhibited significantly smaller startle response magnitudes towards CS- vs. CS+, indicating preserved differentiation between threat and safety. No group differences emerged during the extinction phase. Despite the preliminary nature of our findings, the pattern of results demonstrates interaction of different fear learning pathways in shaping the risk for the development of pathological fear and anxiety.

abstract: The cerebellum (CE) supports the encoding of the precise sensory event timing and the generation of temporal predictions. Here we investigated whether focal CE lesions impact temporal predictions in a cross-modal context. Individuals with CE lesion (n = 9) and healthy-matched controls (HC) were presented with visuo-auditory stimulus pairs, presented in a temporally regular (predictable) or irregular (unpredictable) manner while EEG was recorded. We hypothesized cross-modal temporal predictions to be mediated by pre-stimulus cerebello-cortical beta-band (12-25 Hz) activity. In turn, we expected HC, but not CE patients, to show a modulation of pre-stimulus beta power as a function of temporal prediction. HC showed greater pre-stimulus beta-band suppression presumably related to anticipation of sound onsets, and stronger post-stimulus delta-band (1-4 Hz) power in the predictable than unpredictable condition. Furthermore, they displayed a significant modulation of pre-stimulus delta-beta cross-frequency coupling as a function of temporal predictability. These effects were not observed in the CE group, suggesting a deficit in temporal predictions. These results extend the role of cerebellar predictive timing from sensorimotor to motor-independent cross-modal temporal predictions.

abstract: Measurement in psychology is often associated with psychometrics. Despite the theoretical insights afforded by psychometric methods, they represent only a restricted range of possible measurement approaches in the social sciences. Representational measurement theory (RMT) generalizes the logic of measurement developed in the physical sciences to domains where direct concatenation is not available, making it particularly relevant for psychological research. However, RMT remains unfamiliar to many researchers, largely because of its abstract mathematical formulation and the gap between its formal results and applied practice. This paper provides an accessible introduction to RMT that emphasizes intuitive understanding while offering a structured pathway for quantitatively inclined readers to engage with its technical foundations. We first present a general description of RMT, followed by its four central problems: representation, uniqueness, scaling and meaningfulness. Finally, we discuss recent developments, including probabilistic extensions of RMT, their relationship to statistical modelling and their implications for the coordination between theoretical constructs and observed behaviour.

abstract: Min et al. (2026) provide a timely checklist for improving the transparency and trust of supervised machine learning (ML) research in psychology. I strongly endorse this goal and recognize that their focus on retrospective reporting is both valuable and the appropriate scope for an article. However, I suggest that two related issues warrant greater emphasis in their framework: information leakage and procedural overfitting. Both can produce optimistic estimates of model performance despite apparently transparent reporting. I propose two extensions to the checklist: reporting requirements that make information leakage auditable and prospective specification of key analytical decisions through preregistration. I argue that these additions would further strengthen the ability of readers and reviewers to evaluate the trustworthiness of supervised ML analyses in psychology. Moreover, comprehensive guidelines that do not sufficiently emphasize these issues may create unwarranted confidence that threats to valid model evaluation have been ruled out, allowing information leakage or procedural overfitting to remain undetected.

abstract:
Background

The psychosis continuum conceptualises psychotic phenomena as existing on a spectrum from subclinical experiences to psychotic disorders. Despite epidemiological and clinical evidence in support of this model, few studies have examined polygenic liability across the severity continuum: from subclinical experiences to first-episode psychosis (FEP).

Aims

To map polygenic liability for schizophrenia (SCZ), bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder (MDD) across the psychosis continuum. We hypothesised that schizophrenia polygenic scores (SCZ-PGS) would track phenotypic severity most closely across this continuum.

Method

We harmonised data from 5 south-east London cohorts (N = 1315; 860 European, 455 African ancestries) across 4 ordered groups indicative of different levels of phenotypic severity: controls (n = 647), individuals with self-reported psychotic experiences (n = 89), individuals at clinical high risk (CHR) that did not convert to psychosis (n = 124) and individuals with FEP (n = 455). We computed ancestry-specific PGS for SCZ, bipolar disorder and MDD and compared these across groups using ordinal logistic regression.

Results

In European ancestry participants, elevated SCZ-PGS (odds ratio 1.72, p = 4.57 × 10-15), bipolar disorder-PGS (odds ratio 1.56, p = 1.03 × 10-10) and MDD-PGS (odds ratio 1.44, p = 4.86 × 10-8) were individually associated with increasing phenotypic severity. SCZ-PGS explained the largest variance (R2 = 0.084) across the psychosis continuum and showed pairwise differences between CHR and controls (β = 0.32, p = 0.027), and between FEP and CHR (β = 0.38, p = 0.017). Multivariable models, combining three PGS, outperformed univariable models (R2 = 0.105). Similar trends in SCZ-PGS across the psychosis continuum phenotype were seen in African ancestry participants, but only controls and FEP groups differed significantly (β = 0.27, p = 0.037).

Conclusions

Our findings provide biological evidence supporting the psychosis continuum framework. In European ancestry, SCZ-PGS differences suggest that CHR who do not transition to psychosis have intermediate genetic vulnerability. Multivariable models, utilising all three PGS, explained additional variance compared with univariable ones, supporting transdiagnostic genetic liability. Improving PGS predictive power in African ancestry remains a priority.

abstract: Contemporary research on digital labor confronts a methodological tension: while mainstream occupational health psychology offers rich empirical evidence on the psychological distress of digital workers, it fails to capture the more fundamental predicament of subjectivity underlying this distress-namely, Why, When formal autonomy has been elevated to an unprecedented height, does workers' inner experience become increasingly passive? We argue that this explanatory gap stems from implicit theoretical assumptions in mainstream psychology, which treats psychological needs as ahistorical, universal constants and presupposes the individual as a rational actor who calculates gains and losses in response to external pressures and resources. Fromm' s psychoanalytic social psychology provides an alternative theoretical paradigm. Through the core concept of "social character," Fromm reveals how socioeconomic structures operate on individuals not as external variables, but by shaping their deepest need structures and affective orientations, so that individuals "voluntarily" come to feel, think, and act in the manner required by the system. This article systematically elaborates the epistemological implications and methodological value of three core Frommian concepts-alienation, social character, and escape from freedom-and proposes that contemporary digital labor cultivates a "digital marketing character": in the process of continuous self-curation, self-quantification, and self-commodification, workers experience alienation as self-realization. The psychological effect of this character structure is a diffuse state of "psycho-emotional deficitization"-a deep-seated experience of constantly feeling insufficiently productive and valuable regardless of objective performance. We critically examine Fromm's own framework, acknowledging its limitations regarding universalist assumptions, normative presuppositions, and historical boundedness. We also situate this intervention within the broader landscape of critical traditions-including Foucauldian, psychosocial, psychodynamic, posthumanist, and platform capitalism scholarship-and explicitly delimit the contribution as a strategic bridge between critical theory and empirical work psychology. To move beyond theoretical speculation, we provide a systematic methodological roadmap with explicit, testable hypotheses, scale development strategies, and multiple research designs spanning qualitative, psychometric, longitudinal, SEM, mixed-methods, and comparative approaches. The contribution of this article is twofold: it furnishes psychology with a set of historically informed and incisive conceptual tools for understanding the subjectivity predicament in digital labor, and it builds a theoretical bridge between mainstream psychology and psychoanalytic social psychology.

abstract: Social media use has been widely linked to sexual attitudes, yet it remains unclear whether its association with openness to sugar relationships is uniform across countries or contingent on country-level normative contexts. In the present study, we examined whether country-level cultural tightness-looseness moderated the relationship between social media use and openness to sugar relationships across 22 countries. Openness to sugar relationships was conceptualized as a manifestation of a broader orientation toward sexual-economic exchange. Using data from 22,292 adult women drawn from a large cross-national dataset, we tested this framework with Bayesian multilevel modeling. Measurement invariance of the openness construct was assessed, and alignment procedures were applied to address cross-country non-invariance prior to analysis. Cultural tightness-looseness was modeled as a country-level moderator of the individual-level association between social media use and openness to sugar relationships, while age was included as a control variable. Results revealed a positive association between social media use and openness to sugar relationships. In addition, this association was modestly stronger in countries characterized by lower normative constraint, suggesting that country-level norm strength may shape the attitudinal relevance of digital exposure. Models including this interaction outperformed alternative specifications that incorporated a range of theoretically plausible country-level covariates, including indicators of digital infrastructure, socioeconomic structure, and internet freedom. Although the interaction effect size was modest, the findings suggest that the attitudinal correlates of social media use vary systematically across countries and highlight the importance of country-level normative contexts in research on sexual-economic openness.

abstract: The present study proposes a framework of critical ethnic-racial socialization. A pilot study with 74 parents (32% Latinx; 27% Black; 19% White; 11% Asian; 8% Multiracial; 3% indigenous) and their 3- to 7-year-old children (57% girls) conducted in 2024-2025 was used to instantiate the framework. Specifically, behavioral observations of parent-child play served to establish proof of concept. Data were consistent with the ethnic-racial socialization literature (i.e., ethnic-racial heritage, ethnic-racial pride, preparation for bias) and the critical consciousness literature (i.e., critical awareness, critical action). Data further suggested messages about ethnic-racial diversity, acceptance and inclusion, and appreciation of diversity. Findings show that even in early childhood, parents engage in strategies to promote children's ethnic-racial identity and critical consciousness.

abstract: Despite growing recognition that parental behavior shapes athlete outcomes, evidence on whether structured intervention programmes effectively change parental conduct, and whether those changes reach athletes, remains scattered. This systematic review examined the effectiveness of parental intervention programmes in youth sport, positioning athlete outcomes as primary endpoints alongside parental behavior and mental health outcomes. Search was conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCO up to May 2025. Quantitative and qualitative designs were included, as the systematic search identified 2188 records, of which 14 studies met eligibility criteria, regarding parents or caregivers of youth athletes involved in sport-based intervention programmes (PROSPERO: CRD420250651529). Methodological quality was appraised using JBI Critical Appraisal Tools. Quantitative and mixed-methods findings were synthesized using a Level of Evidence framework, and qualitative findings were synthesized through Thematic Synthesis. Findings were considered "Inconclusive" for both parental behavior and mental health (59% consistency) and athlete well-being and stress (70% consistency). Thematic synthesis identified three analytical themes: Developing Sport Parenting Competence: Knowledge, Self-Awareness, and Confidence; Relational and Behavioral Change in the Parent-Athlete Dyad; Athlete Growth: Social Skills, Psychological Well-Being, and Coping Development, which gather outcomes such as gains in knowledge and awareness, relational and behavioral change in the relationship, and developmental and well-being gains in athletes. Parental intervention programs show promise in producing relational change in parents, with emerging evidence that these changes reach athletes through a relational pathway. Rigorous controlled trials and dyadic designs are needed to establish causal mechanisms and inform evidence-based programme development.

abstract: Subtle language changes occur early in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Early detection of these changes therefore represents a potential tool for the early detection of individuals who could develop the disease. Knowledge on connected speech (CS) in Subjective Cognitive Decline (SCD, a preclinical stage of AD for at least some individuals, characterized by cognitive complaints without objective cognitive deficits), remains limited. In this study, we used network analysis to examine the relationships between CS features extracted with Natural Language Processing techniques. This method allowed us to determine whether the patterns emerging from the SCD CS network (i.e., a network modelling the relationships between CS features) differed from those observed in similar networks constructed for controls and individuals with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI, a prodromal stage of AD for many individuals, characterized by objective cognitive deficits but preserved daily functioning). We found minimal differences between individuals with SCD and controls and individuals with MCI in raw CS features. Nevertheless, our network analysis revealed a stronger relative subdivision of the SCD network into different dimensions (representing linguistic domains), as well as relative reductions in within-dimension density and between-dimension strength compared to the Control and MCI networks. There were also relative differences in how the CS features forming the Semantic conciseness and Lexical and syntactic complexity dimensions associated with other features in the SCD network. Results suggest that network analysis might be more sensitive than other methods to subtle CS differences in SCD and that this population might use distinct CS production mechanisms.

abstract: Although virtual navigation tasks are widely used to investigate human spatial navigation, the processes underlying behavior across tasks remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we administered four virtual navigation tasks assessing spatial learning, path integration, and wayfinding in a single cohort. Participants additionally completed four event segmentation tasks to examine links with episodic memory. Across tasks, spatial cues such as landmarks or the arena center improved performance, with better outcomes when navigating near these cues and when goals were nearby. Despite these shared effects, between-task correlations were sparse. Significant associations emerged between the two path integration tasks, whereas reliance on spatial cues showed little correspondence. However, principal component analysis identified two behavioral dimensions: one aligned with self-reported preference for scene-based navigation, the other with reduced route-based navigation. Episodic memory showed no association with navigation. Virtual navigation tasks thus capture partially distinct processes, and dimensionality reduction helps disentangle navigation mechanisms.

abstract: This pilot study introduced and assessed a novel web-based spot-the-difference paradigm for investigating social information processing in naturalistic visual scenes. The task systematically manipulated both the presence versus absence of social elements (i.e., social figures) and the location of the target difference (social vs. nonsocial regions). Participants identified differences via mouse clicks while their eye movements and mouse trajectories were recorded simultaneously throughout the task. In Study 1, behavioral and eye-tracking data supported the task's sensitivity to social salience, as evidenced by differences in accuracy and reaction times for social versus nonsocial target differences, along with consistently greater gaze fixation on social regions regardless of where the target difference appeared. In comparison, mouse-tracking data reflected more goal-oriented behavior, with cursor trajectories more frequently falling within regions containing the target difference. Study 2 further showed that this paradigm was sensitive to individual differences in autistic traits. Participants with higher autistic trait scores exhibited slower responses specifically in social contexts, irrespective of the location of the target difference, suggesting increased cognitive demands during social information processing. However, their gaze and mouse movement patterns remained comparable to those with lower autistic trait scores. Collectively, these findings suggest that this paradigm may provide a scalable and flexible approach for studying social cognition beyond traditional laboratory settings and may help capture the dynamic unfolding of social information processing through integrated multimodal data.

abstract: Over the past three decades, psychology has documented the recurrence of specific themes in stories across cultures (e.g., love, alliances, monsters, and imaginary worlds) and linked them to identifiable motivational mechanisms (e.g., mate choice, cooperation, threat detection, and exploration). Yet this body of work has remained fragmented, organized around individual themes rather than integrated into a unified account of what makes narrative content psychologically engaging. Here, we propose the Motivational-Ingredient Framework. We identify a set of motivational ingredients: core narrative features, each defined by the specific motivational mechanism it activates. Drawing on evolutionary psychology, affective neuroscience, and the study of human motivation, we compile a comprehensive table of ingredients grounded in the current understanding of human motivational architecture. This framework offers a theory-driven, cross-culturally applicable foundation for the empirical study of narrative content, with implications for fields ranging from media psychology and computational humanities to education and public policy.
