abstract: The expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) and digitally mediated learning has intensified debate about flexibility, access, and quality assurance in higher education. This study examines stakeholder perceptions of the non-recognition of fully online doctoral education in India, focusing on career barriers, psychological burnout, acceptance of Education 4.0, institutional resistance, and support for policy reform. Using a cross-sectional questionnaire dataset of 832 respondents, the study applies descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), group comparisons, and ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. The findings indicate comparatively high mean scores for perceived career barriers and Education 4.0 acceptance. Group comparisons did not identify statistically significant differences across the categories examined. The overall regression model was statistically significant (F(7, 824) = 64.28, p < 0.001; R² = 0.353; adjusted R² = 0.348). Institutional resistance was positively associated with policy-reform support, whereas career barriers showed a smaller negative association. Education 4.0 acceptance also showed a positive association with reform support. These findings represent statistical relationships within the sample and do not establish causal effects. The study contributes to discussions on Indian higher-education policy by outlining considerations for a quality-assured framework that addresses research supervision, assessment, academic integrity, institutional accountability, and equitable access to doctoral education.

Background:

STEM education has an important role to play in the Society 5.0 era, but students with disabilities still face various barriers to access, participation, representation, and learning support. Technological advancements offer opportunities to reduce these barriers, but their effectiveness depends on the integration of technology with inclusive pedagogy, accessible instructional design, and institutional support. Methods This study used a systematic literature review (SLR) based on the PRISMA guidelines. The literature was obtained from SCOPUS, ERIC, IEEE Xplorer, and Emerald. Of the 292 articles, eight met the inclusion criteria. Article quality was assessed using the QualSyst quality assessment tool based on Kmet et al. (2004), with five quality indicators adapted from a previously published study, while the agreement among the five raters was assessed using Fleiss’ Kappa. Results Technology-assisted inclusive STEM education is implemented in a contextual and adaptive manner through virtual reality, digital storytelling, tactile diagrams, tactile manipulatives, audio-based augmented reality, and adaptive digital resources. Its integration with inclusive pedagogy includes scaffolding, structured activities, personalization, and accessible representations and interactions, with support from teachers, mentors, specialists, and multidisciplinary collaboration. This approach is linked to increased engagement, participation, confidence, autonomy, and STEM competencies. Conclusions Technology-assisted inclusive STEM education is contextual, adaptive, and sustainable. Inclusion does not depend on any specific technology, but rather on its adaptation and integration with inclusive pedagogy, accessible instructional design, and institutional and professional support. Technology, pedagogy, accessibility, and implementation support interact to expand participation and develop the STEM competencies of students with disabilities.

abstract: Objectives: This study aims to develops the curriculum into theoretical and workplace arround entrustable professional activities (EPAs)for advanced practice nurses (APNs) in China, so as to advance the implementation of competency‑oriented nursing education. Background: Globally, a master's degree has become essential educational preparation for APNs. Competence is central to advanced nursing education, but how to measure it? As a common standard and bridge between school education and clinical training, EPAs are increasingly used in APN programs. Traditional curricula lack competency-oriented evaluation of teaching effectiveness, while EPAs can drive APN education by designing curricula based on workplace needs and competencies. Methods: For the competency training of APN, a three-step model was developed to guide competency-based theoretical and workplace curriculum construction and teaching implementation. It includes standardized procedures for the identification, systematic formulation and optimization of EPAs.The modified Delphi method were employed in the curriculum development process. Results: The EPAs concept proved to be a valuable tool for developing competency-based theoretical and workplace teaching framework for APN education. In terms of workplace curriculum, a refined EPAs framework covering 5 domains and 20 EPAs indicators were established, with well-defined corresponding core competencies, entrustment levels, milestones and assessment methods. In terms of theoretical curriculum, compriseing 4 public compulsory courses, 4 APN core courses and 15 professional courses, with clarified course categories, course objectives, corresponding to EPAs titles and teaching methods. This model realizes the individualized and flexible teaching philosophy of competency-based medical education in real-world APN training. Conclusions: This EPA‑oriented model is feasible for Chinese APN education. The EPAs and matched theoretical‑workplace teaching facilitate competency‑focused APN training. It bridges education‑clinical gaps and realizes the individualized flexibility of competency‑based education for APN talent cultivation.

abstract:
Background

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients undergoing hemodialysis (HD) often face challenges in self-management, treatment adherence, and fluid control. Video-based education has shown promise in improving these outcomes, but evidence comparing interactive versus conventional approaches is limited.

Aim

To compare the effects of interactive and conventional video education on patient activation, treatment adherence, and interdialytic weight gain (IDWG) in patients receiving HD.

Design

A randomized clinical trial was conducted.

Methods

In this three-arm randomized clinical trial, 126 HD patients were randomized to interactive video education, conventional video education, or usual care (42 per group). A total of 123 (41 per group) participants completed the study. The intervention comprised ten 30-minute video modules and a one-hour consolidation workshop. Patient activation (PAM-13), adherence (ESRD-AQ), and interdialytic weight gain (IDWG) were assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and 1- and 3-month follow-ups.

Results

Baseline characteristics were comparable across groups. Significant group × time interactions were observed for all outcomes. Compared with Conventional Video and Usual Care, the Interactive Video group achieved greater and more sustained improvements in patient activation, treatment adherence, and IDWG over the 3-month follow-up. Immediately post-intervention, PAM-13 scores were 9.66 and 19.17 points higher than those of the Conventional Video and Usual Care groups, respectively, while IDWG was 0.34 kg lower than in the Usual Care group. Treatment adherence also improved significantly, with the Interactive Video intervention consistently outperforming Conventional Video education at all follow-up assessments.

Conclusion

Interactive video-based education significantly improved patient activation, treatment adherence, and weight management in HD patients, with greater and more sustained benefits than conventional video education or usual care. These findings highlight the added value of interactivity beyond video education alone.

Implications for patient care

Incorporating interactive digital education into routine dialysis care may improve self-management and clinical outcomes.

abstract: We report a robust, metal-free heterogeneous photocatalytic protocol for the direct decarboxylative fluorination of aliphatic carboxylic acids utilizing graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4). Operating under visible light, this strategy exhibits good substrate generality, particularly for activated aliphatic carboxylic acids and facilitates the late-stage functionalization of complex pharmaceutical scaffolds. The operationally simple photocatalyst can be recycled over seven consecutive cycles while maintaining high catalytic efficacy. Crucially, a continuous-flow, gram-scale synthesis validates its practical scalability. Mechanistic studies confirm a closed-loop photoredox pathway, establishing a versatile platform for C(sp3)-F bond construction.

abstract:
Introduction

Diagnostic radiographers perform examinations to support care for people from prison in acute hospitals, yet it remains unclear whether diagnostic radiography education in the UK adequately prepares students and practising radiographers to support this population. This study examined current education and provision of training, perceived preparedness and educational needs among diagnostic radiography students, HEI educators and practising diagnostic radiographers in the UK.

Methods

This exploratory cross-sectional study used an online structured questionnaire completed by diagnostic radiography students, practising diagnostic radiographers and higher education educators in the UK. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics. An inductive qualitative content analysis was completed for the open-ended responses, and categories were compared across participant groups to identify convergence and divergence.

Results

Forty participants completed the questionnaire: 11 students, 8 educators and 21 practising diagnostic radiographers. Only two practising radiographers reported receiving relevant training during their radiography education. No student reported receiving specific programme education, although one received relevant information during clinical placement and no educator reported relevant curriculum content. Further education was supported by nine students, seven educators and 16 practising radiographers. Fifteen practising radiographers reported that their departments lacked relevant policies. Four overarching categories concerned safety and procedural knowledge; communication and psychosocial care; confidence and preparedness; and integrated education and specific organisational guidance.

Conclusion

Education and training provision was limited across all three groups, while organisational guidance varied. Participants identified safety and procedural knowledge and communication and psychosocial care as educational priorities, with confidence, preparedness and equitable care as intended outcomes.

Implication for practice

Proportionately integrating relevant content through academic teaching, simulation and supervised clinical learning, alongside CPD and departmental guidance, may strengthen safe, equitable and consistent imaging for people from prison.

abstract: Single-crystalline metals, with their distinctive symmetries, are the ideal medium for high-order molecular arrangement and the diminishing of grain boundaries and defect sites coupled with high anisotropy. However, conventional synthesis via bulk growth or epitaxial deposition remains complex, costly, and difficult to scale. Here, we report a simple and inexpensive strategy as an alternative to conventional strategies for manufacturing single-crystalline metal foils. Miraculously, by miniaturization of grain boundaries and promoting surface energy minimization during the rotation of the crystal lattice followed by the consumption of neighboring grains, high-quality and large-scale single-crystalline metal foils (Cu(111), Ni(111)) were obtained via vertically suspended chemical vapor deposition (CVD) annealing of polycrystalline metal foils. This discovery offers a potential strategy for manipulating and producing large-scale metal foils that may be used for industrial-scale applications.

abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic had profound consequences for subjective well-being. Yet these consequences may have varied by educational attainment. This study aims to investigate whether patterns of happiness change during the COVID-19 pandemic differed between working-age adults with and without higher education. Using nationally representative panel data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) and focusing on the 2018 and 2020 waves (N = 13,203), this research employs a difference-in-differences design to compare changes in self-reported happiness between individuals with and without higher education. By centering higher education as a key stratifying factor, this study extends the higher education literature on how large-scale crises affect happiness. The findings reveal that individuals with higher education experienced a significantly less pronounced decline in self-reported happiness (β = 0.186, p = 0.003) during the public health crisis, and this apparent higher-education advantage in pandemic-related happiness is highly conditional on socioeconomic and psychosocial circumstances. The results underscore the need for policymakers to address educational disparities when developing mental health and social support strategies for future large-scale crises.

abstract:
Background

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate and evaluate patient-facing medical materials. Through persona prompting, LLMs can be instructed to simulate responses from individuals with different demographic and experiential backgrounds, offering a scalable approach for approximating patient feedback. However, it remains unclear how closely these simulated persona-based responses reflect real patient perspectives, and whether this alignment is consistent across demographic subgroups.

Objective

This study assessed whether contemporary LLMs can simulate diverse patient perspectives on hospital discharge summaries when prompted with personas defined by education, gender, and health care use. We further examined whether persona-based simulation performance was equitable across subgroups by comparing LLM-generated responses with responses from a general-population human cohort under a standardized evaluation framework.

Methods

We evaluated 4 contemporary LLMs, GPT-4.1, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Opus 4.6, against responses from 99 participants recruited through Prolific (Prolific Academic Ltd). Participants answered 10 questions for discharge summaries that varied in length and medical complexity. Questions included information-based items assessing factual comprehension and perception-based items assessing subjective understanding. Model-human alignment was measured using modal mean absolute error and expected absolute ordinal distance. We also conducted a chain-of-thought sensitivity analysis for cases with the greatest divergence between LLM-generated persona and matched human responses.

Results

Across LLMs, persona responses aligned more closely with human responses on information-based items than on perception-based items. Education was the most consistent stratification axis: every model aligned more closely with the high-education subgroup than with the low-education subgroup on information items, suggesting that LLMs capture broad factual-comprehension differences associated with educational background. Perception items, in which subjective understanding and uncertainty dominate human responses, were simulated less reliably. Alignment also depended on discharge summary characteristics, with short but clinically complex summaries producing the largest divergence. Gender-related differences were smaller and inconsistent in direction, reflecting item-level modal flips rather than systematic distributional bias. Chain-of-thought improved alignment on some factual items but did not recover the full range of less common human responses. Across models, LLMs underselected "I don't know" and "Not provided" responses relative to humans, indicating a tendency to commit to determinate answers even when human participants expressed uncertainty.

Conclusions

Contemporary LLMs can approximate common response patterns within demographic subgroups, particularly for factual comprehension and education-based personas. However, they are less reliable for capturing heterogeneous and perception-based patient responses. Equity performance varied substantially across models, making model selection an important design consideration. Persona-based LLM simulation should be used as an assistive screening tool for patient materials and should complement, not replace, human evaluation with subgroup validation.

abstract: Background Prenatal education is an important component of antenatal care that can address knowledge gaps, reduce fear and anxiety associated with childbirth, and support informed decision-making. However, standardized approaches may not meet the diverse informational needs of pregnant patients. Methods We conducted a prospective, cross-sectional survey of pregnant patients receiving care from October 2024 to December 2025. Eligible participants were ≥ 32 weeks’ gestation, ≥ 19 years old, and English- or Spanish-speaking. A 24-item survey assessed preferred educational formats, topics of interest, timing of education, perceived counseling gaps, and prior childbirth experience. Demographic and obstetric characteristics were collected. Results Among 198 participants, 84 (42.4%) had a high school education or less, and 114 (57.6%) had a college education or higher. Patients with lower educational attainment were more likely to have Medicaid insurance, higher gravidity and parity, prior cesarean delivery, social work involvement, and missed prenatal visits (all p < 0.05). Racial and ethnic composition differed significantly between groups (p < 0.0001). Interest in additional prenatal education was similar regardless of education level (48.2% vs 48.7%, p = 0.9). However, educational preferences differed by group: among patients with previous childbirth experience, those with lower educational attainment more frequently reported wanting additional information on normal pregnancy changes (p = 0.03) and labor induction (p = 0.001), even after adjustment for covariates. Preferred educational formats did not differ by education level (p = 0.9). Conclusions Interest in prenatal education is high across educational backgrounds, but informational priorities vary by educational attainment. Individualizing prenatal counseling content while maintaining accessible educational delivery

abstract: Ensuring the quality and credibility of medical education systems increasingly depends on robust accreditation mechanisms, yet the performance of accreditation bodies themselves often remains insufficiently evaluated. Addressing this gap, this study developed and validated the first national meta-accreditation standards for Iran's Ministry of Health and Medical Education. Using a rigorous mixed-methods design, the study integrated insights from semi-structured interviews with 13 national experts, a comparative review of six international recognition systems, expert panel consensus, and a national survey of 90 stakeholders. From an initial pool of 184 standards, systematic refinement led to a final set of 51 standards. Stakeholder evaluation demonstrated strong consensus across practicality, necessity, and transparency (76-94%), with all standards exceeding the predefined 70% agreement threshold. The resulting framework is structured across three domains: structure and formality, accreditation processes, and accountability and quality improvement. By aligning national needs with international benchmarks, these standards enhance transparency, consistency, and trust in accreditation systems. The high level of expert agreement and methodological rigor underscore the framework's readiness for implementation and its potential as a model for strengthening meta-accreditation in similar centralized health education systems.

abstract:
Background and purpose

Pathogenic aggregation and propagation of seed-competent TAU assemblies drive tauopathies. MAPT P301 mutations accelerate aggregation and enhance seed competence, yet pharmacological strategies selectively targeting these pathogenic species remain limited. We investigated whether the clinically approved catechol-O-methyltransferase inhibitors tolcapone (TOL) and entacapone (ENT) preferentially modulate mutant TAU aggregation and seeding.

Experimental approach

TOL and ENT effects on TAU aggregation were evaluated via cell-free assays, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), and in silico docking. Functional consequences of compound-modified fibrils were assessed in mutant TAU-expressing SH-SY5Y cells. Translational relevance was examined in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived neurons exposed to pathogenic K18 fibrils, followed by post-seeding compound treatment.

Key results

Both compounds dose-dependently inhibited TAU aggregation, exhibiting greater potency, stronger SPR binding affinities, and more favourable computed interaction energies for P301S mutant versus wild-type TAU. Fibrils formed with TOL or ENT induced less downstream TAU oligomerization and phosphorylation in SH-SY5Y cells, with TOL showing superior protection. In hiPSC-derived neurons, post-seeding treatment with either compound decreased fibril-induced, sarkosyl-insoluble, TAU aggregation and phosphorylation without overt cytotoxicity.

Conclusion and implications

TOL and ENT preferentially reduced the aggregation and seeding of pathogenic P301 mutant TAU in the experimental models examined. These findings provide proof-of-concept support for mutation-focused pharmacological approaches and identify catechol scaffolds as starting points for developing more potent and safer TAU-directed compounds. Further studies are required to define the relevant molecular interactions, confirm the neuronal findings across additional hiPSC lines and determine whether effective CNS exposure can be achieved in vivo.

abstract: Statement: Competency-based education (CBE) has become a prevalent framework in health professions education, emphasizing observable outcomes, learner progression, and accountability to patient needs. This scoping umbrella review examined how simulation-based education (SBE) is being used to support and implement CBE across health care professions and disciplines. Across 44 reviews, SBE was used to support knowledge, skills, clinical reasoning, communication, teamwork, and confidence. High-fidelity simulation, virtual reality, standardized patients, and hybrid modalities were commonly used to support deliberate practice and competency-focused learning. Despite this alignment, SBE was frequently implemented as a discrete educational modality rather than as a longitudinally integrated component of competency-based curricula, with inconsistent reporting of competency frameworks, theory-informed design, debriefing approaches, and programmatic assessment strategies. This review synthesizes key findings, gaps, and recommendations and proposes a simulation-grounded CBE framework to guide the intentional integration of SBE within competency-based health care curricula.

abstract:
Introduction

Physical education majors have a dual identity as current learners and future educators. Their digital literacy is not only related to their adaptation to digital learning environments but also directly influences the development of their future competence in physical education teaching, training organization, and management practice. Therefore, it is necessary to systematically identify and strengthen educational support for their digital literacy development. However, existing studies have mainly focused on digital literacy levels or single influencing factors, with insufficient attention paid to the educational support structure underlying the formation of digital literacy. In particular, standardized measurement tools tailored to the context of physical education remain limited. This study aimed to construct a Digital Literacy Education Support model for physical education majors in China and to develop and validate a corresponding scale.

Methods

Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 22 physical education majors and 12 university teachers and counselors. The interview data were analyzed using grounded theory through three-stage coding, which identified five main categories: personal traits, symbiotic environment, school environment, social environment, and policy and institutional system. Based on these categories, an educational support model was constructed. Subsequently, an initial item pool was developed through literature analysis and expert review, and item analysis, exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and reliability and validity testing were conducted using pilot and formal survey data.

Results

The results showed that exploratory factor analysis supported a five-factor structure, explaining 58.119% of the total variance. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated good model fit (χ 2/df = 2.725, RMSEA = 0.037, CFI = 0.968, TLI = 0.965, IFI = 0.968). Cronbach's alpha coefficients, split-half reliability, and test-retest reliability for all dimensions met recommended psychometric standards, and the scale demonstrated good convergent and discriminant validity.

Discussion

The findings suggest that the development of digital literacy among physical education majors is shaped by the joint effects of multilevel support involving individual, relational, school, social, and institutional conditions. The developed 30-item scale shows good reliability and validity and can provide a theoretical basis and practical tool for universities to diagnose and improve educational support for digital literacy among physical education majors.

abstract:
Objective

Publications of medical education research networks have been associated with higher rigor and higher-level outcomes. We sought to determine whether they also receive more citations than comparable papers.

Methods

We compared citation rates for pediatric education articles published from studies by the Association of Pediatric Program Directors Longitudinal Educational Assessment Research Network (APPD LEARN) with other pediatric education papers, non-pediatric education papers, non-education pediatric papers, and non-education non-pediatric papers, controlling for journal, issue, and numbers of co-authors using a Poisson model.

Results

We matched 50 APPD LEARN papers with 79 other pediatric education articles, 472 non-pediatric non-education articles, and 200 non-pediatric education articles. APPD LEARN articles had a significantly higher citation rate than other pediatric education articles in the same issues (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.53, 95% CI 1.37-1.72, p<.001). Higher number of authors was also associated with higher citation rates (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.38, 95% CI 1.35-1.41, p<.001). Non-Pediatric education articles were more highly cited than Pediatric education articles (marginal mean difference 10.6, 95% CI 9.7 - 11.4, p<.001) and Pediatric non-education articles were more highly cited than non-Pediatric non-education articles (marginal mean difference 1.7, 95% CI 1.1 - 2.3, p<.001).

Discussion

Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that network-based medical education papers receive more citations than comparable non-network-based papers.

abstract: Social accountability (SA) is a defining institutional mandate in health professions education (HPE), yet how educational approaches associated with SA are experienced in practice remains insufficiently understood. Rather than examining what these approaches aim to achieve, this study explores how they are encountered, interpreted, and made meaningful by those directly involved. We conducted an interpretive descriptive study using rich picture interviews combined with semi-structured interviews with 46 participants, including learners, clinical teachers, community organization members, patient partners, and leaders in SA. Participants depicted and discussed their experiences with educational approaches related to SA. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Five interrelated themes were identified. Participants described (a) an evolving reorientation in how they understood and positioned themselves in relation to responsibility, (b) the limits of abstraction, where experiential encounters revealed dissonance between lived realities and curricular representations, (c) reflexivity as uneven and pedagogically mediated, requiring dialogue, continuity, and psychological safety, (d) institutional conditions as shaping what can be questioned or enacted, including hierarchy, role modeling, and competing priorities, and (e) social accountability as a collective and relational practice, in which participation, reciprocity, and whose perspectives shape educational processes mattered. Across these themes, the presence of an educational approach did not itself determine how socially accountable education was experienced or made meaningful. Meaning was shaped through the interplay between what encounters made visible, opportunities to interpret and question those experiences, the institutional conditions in which they occurred, and whose perspectives were able to shape the educational process. Advancing SA in HPE therefore requires attention not only to which educational approaches are included, but to how they are experienced, facilitated, and negotiated within educational and community relationships.

abstract:
Objectives

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate health education materials, but their suitability for patient-facing human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) education remains insufficiently evaluated. We assessed the information quality, understandability, actionability, readability, text structure and source transparency of HIV patient education materials generated by six LLMs or artificial intelligence platforms.

Methods

In this cross-sectional study, 100 common HIV patient education questions across 10 domains were submitted once in English to ChatGPT 5.4-Thinking, DeepSeek-V3.2, Doubao, ERNIE Bot 5.0 Preview, Ant Afu and Gemini 3.1 Pro, yielding 600 responses. Responses were evaluated using Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials (PEMAT-P), EQ IP-36, DISCERN, Global Quality Score (GQS), artificial intelligence response quality metric (AIRM), Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) benchmarks and seven readability indices. Platform comparisons used paired Friedman tests with Wilcoxon-Holm post hoc analyses; topic analyses used question-level aggregation followed by Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn-Holm comparisons.

Results

Significant family-adjusted differences were observed across platforms for all prespecified text-structure, quality/understandability/actionability and readability outcomes. At the topic level, five of six text-structure outcomes, PEMAT-P Understandability, PEMAT-P Actionability, the exploratory PEMAT-P composite score and all seven readability indices differed significantly after family adjustment, whereas EQ IP-36, DISCERN, GQS, AIRM and JAMA did not. Overall actionability was limited and readability demands were high.

Conclusions

LLM-generated HIV patient education materials showed substantial cross-platform and topic-level heterogeneity. These findings support the use of LLMs as expert-reviewed drafting tools rather than independent patient education sources. Direct factual accuracy, guideline concordance, hallucination and clinical safety were not assessed.

abstract: One aspect of the Hispanic Health Paradox is the longstanding observation that Latin American immigrants in the United States often experience equal or better health outcomes than U.S.-born counterparts despite greater socioeconomic disadvantage. This advantage extends to their infants and is most pronounced among mothers with the least education. Whether such patterns reflect selective migration remains unclear. This study evaluates the role of educational selectivity in explaining nativity disparities in infant health. Using U.S. natality data among immigrants from Mexico, Cuba, El Salvador, Guatemala, the Dominican Republic, Colombia, Honduras, and Venezuela (2012-2023), linked with internationally harmonized educational data, we assess preterm birth disparities using two measures of maternal education: absolute and relative attainment. Immigrants at the bottom of the U.S. education distribution often rank much higher in their origin countries, consistent with positive selection. For most births to Latin American mothers (except Colombian and Venezuelan), measuring education relative to origin-country distributions reverses immigrant advantages. At equivalent relative education ranks, immigrant mothers face comparable or higher risks of preterm birth than U.S.-born Hispanic mothers. These findings offer a new perspective on the Hispanic Health Paradox, highlighting the importance of relative education in understanding the association between maternal education and infant health.

abstract: Massive parental labor migration in China has created distinct developmental experiences for adolescents varied in rural or urban residency and parental migration status, yet limited research has examined heterogeneity in positive development across these diverse groups. This study investigated developmental trajectories of positive youth development (PYD), their key predictors, and associated mental health outcomes among 3331 Chinese adolescents (M<sub>age</sub> = 11.91 years; 55.2% boys) across three waves from 2017 to 2019. Multigroup latent growth curve models were estimated for rural-to-urban migrant (27.5%), rural left-behind (15.0%), rural local (10.7%), and urban local (46.7%) adolescents. The four adolescent groups differed significantly in initial PYD levels. Migrant and left-behind adolescents demonstrated significant linear growth in PYD, while local adolescent groups showed stable levels; however, PYD slopes did not differ significantly across groups. Social mobility belief, parent-child communication, and positive school environment were independently and interactively related to initial PYD levels, with varying effects across groups. Increases in PYD were associated with decreases in depression and externalizing problem behaviors across all groups. These findings provide longitudinal evidence of positive development across diverse adolescent groups, offering insights into context-specific developmental processes shaped by macro-level contexts. Group variations highlight the need for context-sensitive strategies to promote adolescents' positive development amid rural-to-urban migration.

abstract:
Background

Self-efficacy and learning motivation are widely recognized as key psychological factors influencing students' engagement and learning outcomes. However, evidence regarding their measurement and relationship among vocational college students remains fragmented.

Purpose

This systematic review synthesizes recent empirical studies on self-efficacy and learning motivation among vocational college students, focusing on research trends, measurement approaches, and reported relationships between the two constructs.

Methods

Following PRISMA-informed procedures, studies published in English-language peer-reviewed journals from January 2022 to early August 2026 were identified through five databases (Web of Science, Scopus, APA PsycINFO, PubMed, and ERIC). After screening and eligibility assessment, 12 studies were included for coding and synthesis. Findings were analyzed descriptively and thematically to summarize study characteristics, measurement instruments, and patterns of association.

Results

The findings showed considerable variation in the measurement of both self-efficacy and learning motivation. Despite this heterogeneity, the included studies generally reported a positive relationship between the two constructs, although the strength and form of the relationship varied across studies and motivational dimensions. Overall, the evidence supports a broadly consistent positive association between self-efficacy and learning motivation among vocational college students, while conceptual and methodological heterogeneity limits direct comparison across studies. Future research should improve construct and measurement consistency and employ longitudinal or experimental designs to clarify the relationship between self-efficacy and learning motivation.

abstract: The 2015 Fundão dam collapse, the largest socio-environmental disaster in Brazilian history, resulted in severe human, ecological, and socioeconomic losses across the Rio Doce Basin (IBAMA, 2015). Previous studies indicate that mining activities and the disaster were absent from regional school practices, a phenomenon conceptualized as "Pedagogical Silence" (Antunes-Rocha et al., 2021; Antunes-Rocha & Santos, 2024). In response, the Rio Doce School Program was established to provide continuing education for local public-school teachers. This postdoctoral study investigated the contributions of the specialization course offered by the Program to countryside school communities affected by the disaster (IBAMA, 2015). Driven by the theoretical-methodological framework of Countryside Education (Educação do Campo) alongside the premises of social justice and social sustainability (Sartoretto & Bergström, 2026), the research sought to understand the Program's contributions to overcoming Pedagogical Silence. Analytical parameters derived from the convergence of these theoretical matrices were applied to fourteen final monographs written by participating teachers. The findings demonstrate a strong synergy among the Program, Countryside Education, and principles of justice and sustainability, highlighting community mobilization toward the critical inclusion of the disaster into pedagogical projects, thereby indicating that the Program makes significant contributions to reflexive teacher education.

abstract:
Background

A focus on nursing student trauma has increased since the COVID-19 pandemic. Scholars have turned to trauma-informed approaches to understand how nursing students can be better supported in their education and mitigate the effects of past, current, and future trauma exposure.

Aim

To examine the current published literature on how trauma-informed approaches to nursing education are described in the literature.

Design

We conducted a scoping review following the Joanna Briggs Institute framework. We used the PRISMA-ScR guidelines for reporting of findings.

Methods

We performed searches in June 2024 and then again in June 2025 in Medline via OVID, CINAHL via EBSCO, ERIC, PsycInfo, Education Research Complete, and Scopus. We included literature published in English in any year that focused on nursing students and/or nurse educators, included a definition of a trauma-informed approach (TIA) and involved any education context.

Results

35 sources were included, published between 2020 and 2025. Study types included 11 descriptions of implementing a TIA and 6 unstructured reviews supporting its implementation. 10 sources were primary research. Findings included descriptive categories of definitions of a TIA, sources of nursing students' exposure to trauma (in their education, personal lives, and specifically COVID-19), and the purpose of a TIA (success in education and the creation of a future workforce).

Conclusions

TIA to support student learning and develop the future nursing workforce are increasingly prevalent and recommended in the nursing education literature. Terminology and definitions of TIA varied but often shared commonalities, with some specifically addressing structural inequities. Differences between definitions that highlight structural inequities specifically need to be examined for how they differ from more common definitions. The student perspective on resilience and TIA effectiveness is needed. Conceptualizations of TIA must also address how they might reinforce power structures within educational institutions, thereby avoiding the reproduction of inequities.

abstract:
Background

Creativity and problem-solving are essential to contemporary nursing, but newly recruited nurses have limited opportunities to develop these competencies through traditional lecture-based education. This pilot study developed and evaluated a nursing innovation course that used the Bridge-in, Objectives, Preassessment, Participatory Learning, Postassessment and Summary (BOPPPS) model, with Problem-Based Learning (PBL) embedded in the participatory phase.

Methods

An uncontrolled single-group pretest-posttest pilot design was used. Sixty newly recruited nurses in one tertiary hospital attended the course as a required component of standardised training, while participation in the research evaluation was voluntary. The course combined short lectures, clinical cases, small-group PBL and innovation project design. Creativity and general self-efficacy were assessed before and after the course; self-efficacy was measured using a locally modified five-response-category GSES. Course evaluations and documented project outputs were also collected.

Results

Complete data from all 60 participants were analysed. Creativity increased from 20.50 ± 4.15 to 23.63 ± 3.32 (mean difference 3.13, 95% CI 1.69-4.58; p < 0.001; Cohen's dz = 0.56), and self-efficacy increased from 38.78 ± 8.64 to 42.48 ± 6.10 (mean difference 3.70, 95% CI 0.84-6.56; p = 0.012; Cohen's dz = 0.33).

Conclusions

Participation was associated with higher post-course creativity and self-efficacy, and the course appeared feasible and acceptable. The uncontrolled design and mentor-supported setting preclude attributing score changes or outputs to the course alone; controlled multicentre studies are needed.

Implications for nursing practice

The BOPPPS-PBL structure may inform innovation-focused content in nurse orientation, nurse continuing education and newly recruited nurse training when educators also provide facilitator preparation, protected learning time and context-appropriate mentoring.

abstract: Iron-chromium redox flow battery (ICRFB) has attracted increasing attention for large-scale energy storage in recent years because of their low cost, abundant raw materials, and high safety. As the primary sites for electrochemical reactions, electrodes directly affect battery efficiency and operational stability. This review summarizes recent progress in electrode materials for ICRFB and discusses different categories of electrode materials, with particular emphasis on the characteristics and applications of woven and nonwoven electrodes. Multiscale modification strategies for improving electrode performance are also systematically reviewed, including approaches that regulate surface chemistry, active sites, conductivity, pore structure, and mass transport behavior. In addition, the applications of advanced characterization techniques, such as synchrotron-based methods and neutron imaging, in electrode analysis are summarized. These techniques provide deeper insights into the structure-performance relationships of electrode materials and offer guidance for future electrode design and optimization. Finally, this review outlines future development directions for ICRFB electrode materials. By integrating material design with structural optimization, this work provides useful guidance for the development of next-generation electrodes for redox flow batteries.

abstract: Background: Professional ethical principles are fundamental to nursing practice, and ethics education is therefore embedded as a continuous component throughout nursing education. Objective: This study aims to present a bibliometric and scientific mapping analysis of nursing ethics education research. Methods: Web of Science and Scopus databases were searched for the keywords "ethic* education," "nurs*," and similar terms, and 514 documents published between 1964 and 2024 were analyzed. Bibliometric indicators were analyzed using the Bibliometrix package in the R programming language. Results: The analyzed publications were authored by 1,459 researchers and disseminated across 238 journals. The United States emerged as the most productive country, contributing 104 publications. An overall annual growth rate of 5.03% was observed, indicating a steady increase in scholarly interest in nursing ethics education. Conclusions: Research on ethics education in nursing demonstrates sustained academic attention alongside evolving thematic and methodological trends. Emerging technologies present new opportunities to diversify pedagogical approaches and strengthen the integration of ethics into nursing curricula. Implications for Nursing: Ethics education plays an important role in the formation of nurses' professional identity and in strengthening the patient-centered clinical decision-making process. Therefore, ethical values must be integrated into curricula and professional development programs at all levels.

abstract: Background Educational differences in fitness/leisure participation may reflect unequal access to time, resources, and supportive environments. Among adults reporting participation in 2020, we examined whether a 2022 report of no participation differed by completed education. The same-item responses were interpreted as a two-wave report pair, not exact cessation. Methods This preregistered observational analysis used linked 2020 and 2022 China Family Panel Studies data. Eligible respondents were aged ≥ 25 years, directly self-reported in both waves, had complete mandatory data, and reported any past-12-month fitness/leisure participation in 2020. Original, non-imputed completed education entered a prespecified linear model. An unweighted modified-Poisson model with covariance clustered by baseline primary sampling unit (PSU) standardized the probability of a 2022 “never” report at 6 and 12 education years. No population weighting or attrition correction was applied. Results Among 4,639 respondents in 176 PSUs, model-standardized probabilities of a 2022 “never” report were 47.2% (95% confidence interval [CI], 44.2%–50.1%) at 6 education years and 28.8% (95% CI, 26.9%–30.7%) at 12 years. The absolute probability difference (12 minus 6 years) was − 18.4 percentage points (95% CI, − 21.1 to − 15.6; P<.001), and the complementary probability ratio was 0.610 (95% CI, 0.569–0.654). Logistic-link and cluster/influence checks were directionally concordant. Five prespecified analyses stopped under the preregistered numerical rule; robustness to the age threshold, education functional form, baseline frequency, and four-state specification remains unestablished. Conclusions In this selected linked analytic sample, the model-standardized probability of reporting no fitness/leisure participation in 2022 was lower at 12 than at 6 completed education years. The finding supports population-representative investigation of modifiable barriers among adults with fewer completed years of education. The association is noncausal and not population-representative; the report pair does not measure total physical activity or establish exact cessation.

abstract:
Background

The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) has generated growing interest in its use to support teaching and learning in nursing education. This scoping review aimed to map the existing literature on AI-supported teaching approaches in nursing education, examine how learning outcome domains are addressed, and identify gaps in the current evidence base.

Method

A scoping review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute Framework and PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. Eight databases were searched: ProQuest Central, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, ERIC, and PubMed.

Results

Thirty-eight studies published were included. Three themes emerged: AI tools and applications in nursing education, learning outcome domains and assessment approaches, and current limitations and future directions.

Conclusion

AI-supported teaching approaches show promise in nursing education by supporting knowledge and skill development. However, further research using robust designs and clear pedagogical frameworks is needed to inform sustainable educational practice.

abstract: We respond to Chen's commentary on our recent article, "Personality and emotional intelligence among health professions students: the roles of perceived group cohesion, perceived team emotional intelligence, and attitudes toward interprofessional education." We address methodological and interpretive questions concerning covariate coding, variable centering, the Group Cohesion (GC) × Attitudes Toward Interprofessional Education (ATIPE) interaction, and the perceived team emotional intelligence (TEI)-only indirect pathway. Sensitivity analyses supported the main findings of the original article, including the serial mediation effects, the negative GC × ATIPE interaction, and the moderated mediation effects. We further clarify that the interaction reflects attenuation rather than amplification, and that the TEI-only pathway attenuated after attitudes toward interprofessional education were included as a predictor. Overall, this reply reinforces the robustness of the original findings while refining their interpretation.

abstract:
Rationale

Sexual harassment is common among healthcare workers and is associated with poor mental health, job dissatisfaction, and workforce attrition. Education and training may help prevent sexual harassment, but their effectiveness in healthcare settings has not been systematically evaluated.

Objectives

To assess the effectiveness of education and training interventions on knowledge and skills for managing sexual harassment, and to assess their impact on the incidence of sexual harassment towards healthcare workers in healthcare settings.

Search methods

We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, AMED, CINAHL, Scopus, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO ICTRP, together with reference checking and contact with study authors, to identify eligible studies. The latest search date was March 2025.

Eligibility criteria

We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) involving healthcare workers comparing education or training interventions with control (no intervention, waiting list, placebo, or minimal intervention) or different types of education or training to prevent sexual harassment in healthcare settings.

Outcomes

Our critical outcomes were knowledge and skills in managing sexual harassment and the incidence of all types of sexual harassment perpetrated by patients, visitors, coworkers, and management. Important outcomes were anxiety, depression, burnout, sick leave, staff turnover, disability, and perception of the organisational climate related to harassment.

Risk of bias

We used the Cochrane RoB 2 tool to assess risk of bias.

Synthesis methods

We synthesised results for each outcome using random-effects model meta-analysis. We used GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence for each outcome.

Included studies

We included two studies from Taiwan with a total of 170 nurses. Most participants were young women with little work experience. The intervention group received education to prevent sexual harassment, and the comparison group received a different type of education to prevent sexual harassment. We found no studies that had a comparison group without any active educational or training components.

Synthesis of results

Education and training interventions to prevent sexual harassment compared to control (no intervention, waiting list, placebo, or minimal intervention) in healthcare workers No studies addressed this comparison. Education and training interventions to prevent sexual harassment compared to other education and training interventions for healthcare workers We found two studies reporting on education and training interventions to prevent sexual harassment compared to other education and training interventions in healthcare workers. Educational interventions to prevent sexual harassment probably increase sexual harassment prevention knowledge slightly ('sexual harassment prevention', mean difference (MD) 4.74, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.21 to 8.28; P = 0.71; I2 = 0%; 2 RCTs, 168 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and may increase management skills slightly ('coping behaviour', MD 6.36, 95% CI -6.84 to 19.56; P = 0.43; I2 = 0%; 2 RCTs, 168 participants; low-certainty evidence) and ('prevention strategy', MD 11.70, 95% CI 2.56 to 20.85; P = 0.22; I2 = 33%; 2 RCTs, 168 participants; low-certainty evidence). No study evaluated the incidence of sexual harassment, anxiety, depression, burnout, sick leave, staff turnover, disability, or perception of the organisational climate related to harassment. Adverse effects were not measured or reported in the included studies. The certainty of the evidence was moderate to low. We judged the overall risk of bias as low, and we identified no inconsistency or publication bias. However, imprecision was more of a concern given the low number of participants and relatively broad CIs around the effect estimates.

Authors' conclusions

Healthcare workers may benefit from education and training compared to another type of education and training. The benefits were modest and were measured as increased knowledge ('sexual harassment prevention') and management skills ('coping behaviour' and 'prevention strategy'). The certainty of the evidence is moderate to low, and future studies could make the findings more robust. There is a need for future studies investigating other types of outcomes such as anxiety, depression, burnout, sick leave, staff turnover, disability, and perception of the organisational climate related to harassment. It would also be valuable to assess a wider range of healthcare workers, as we only found studies in nurses. No studies addressed the effects of education and training compared to control groups (no intervention, waiting list, placebo, or minimal intervention). The decision to offer sexual harassment education and training to healthcare workers is supported by the existing evidence. However, other contextual factors may also be considered, as well as healthcare workers' preferences to participate in educational activities.

abstract: Malaria negatively impacts childhood development and education outcomes. However, evidence on the effects of malaria control on education outcomes is limited. Since 2013, Senegal has scaled up routine monthly administration of malaria chemoprevention to young children during the peak malaria transmission season (i.e., seasonal malaria chemoprevention [SMC]) as a critical malaria control intervention. We conducted a district-level ecological analysis to determine whether large-scale implementation of SMC is associated with improved education outcomes. Using generalized additive mixed models applied to routine malaria intervention and education indicator data for the 2013-2019 period, we show that in comparison with non-SMC districts, districts that had received multiple SMC rounds had improved education outcomes, specifically enrollment, dropout and repetition rates, as well as pass rates of children completing primary school. Our findings highlight the broader benefits of SMC beyond malaria prevention and underscore its role in advancing educational attainment and human development goals in malaria-endemic settings.

abstract:
Background

Despite decades of attention to interprofessional education (IPE) in dental education, many programs still operationalize IPE as episodic exposure rather than as a durable, assessable competence embedded in clinical workflows. This gap limits the translation of IPE into interprofessional collaborative practice (IPCP), particularly for medically complex patients and populations most affected by fragmented care.

Objective

To move IPE from ceremonial participation to structural integration across predoctoral dental education and clinical training environments, by developing consensus recommendations from Working Group 4 of the Reimagining Dental Education Summit (Harvard School of Dental Medicine, June 11-13, 2026).

Consensus process

Working Group 4 consisted of nine dental education leaders and experts (two co-chairs, one summit scholar, and six members). Recommendations were developed using a structured "future-back" methodology in working sessions, iterative drafting, and plenary report-out. Evidence inputs included competency frameworks (IPEC), accreditation standards (CODA), staged integration frameworks, implementation tools, and exemplars of integrated care delivery (e.g., federally qualified health centers [FQHCs] and integrated health systems). Consensus was achieved through iterative discussion and a nominal group technique to reach unanimous agreement on final recommendations and proposed evaluation metrics.

Recommendations

The group recommends: (1) defining IPE competence as measurable, dentistry and oral health-specific outcomes; (2) prioritizing strategic partnerships beyond medicine (e.g., pharmacy, nursing, social work, nutrition, occupational/physical therapy); (3) anchoring IPE in IPCP settings such as FQHCs and integrated systems; (4) building an alumni/outcomes follow-up system to assess whether IPE training changes practice behaviors; and (5) strengthening communication and referral processes, including closed-loop referrals, even when electronic health records are not shared.

Conclusions

Structural IPE requires outcome-based performance expectations, practice-linked implementation models, and accountability mechanisms that measure behavior change and care-process improvement for both the learner and the patient, during training and after graduation. These consensus recommendations offer a practical roadmap for dental education programs, accreditors, and partners seeking to operationalize integrated oral health care.

abstract: Medical education increasingly calls for clinicians who are reflective, adaptable, and collaborative, not merely knowledgeable. This conceptual Perspective, rather than an empirical study, proposes the Four-Bridge Framework (4BF), developed by the authors, to consider how flexible clinical learning spaces may support transformative learning. Rather than assuming that space alone transforms learners, the framework suggests that space may contribute to conditions in which experience, dialogue, reflection, and agency are more likely to unfold, in interaction with educators, organizational culture, and learners' readiness. Drawing on a narrative synthesis of the literature, we describe four bridges: between experience and reflection, the individual and others, learning and experimentation, and reflection and action, and propose a heuristic mapping of these onto Mezirow's ten phases of transformative learning. From this, we outline design principles, low-resource adaptations, and contextual considerations. The 4BF is intended to contribute to medical education theory by offering a learning-theoretic account of how spatial features may matter, and to practice by offering educators and planners a structured basis for designing and evaluating clinical learning spaces. As a proposed framework, it has not yet been empirically validated, and we outline a research agenda for testing it.

abstract: Hepatitis remains a major global health challenge and an important contributor to liver fibrosis, cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and liver-related mortality worldwide. Early diagnosis, effective treatment selection, and accurate prognostic stratification remain critical unmet needs in clinical hepatology. Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning and deep learning, has emerged as a promising approach to addressing these challenges through the integration and analysis of large-scale, heterogeneous biomedical datasets. This narrative review synthesizes advances in artificial intelligence applications in hepatitis research and clinical practice published over the past decade, organized across three clinical domains: diagnosis, treatment optimization, and prognosis prediction. In the diagnostic domain, artificial intelligence-based approaches have been applied to medical imaging, digital pathology, and multi-omics data to enhance the detection, classification, and staging of liver disease. In the therapeutic domain, machine learning models have been increasingly deployed to support drug discovery, optimize therapeutic regimens, and predict individual treatment responses. In the prognostic domain, artificial intelligence-driven models have shown promising performance in predicting disease progression, survival outcomes, and clinical complications. Nevertheless, key limitations persist, including data heterogeneity, limited external generalizability, and barriers to clinical translation. Future progress will depend on prospective multicenter evaluation, use of interoperable multimodal data, development of transparent models that account for uncertainty, and evidence that artificial intelligence improves clinical decisions and patient outcomes rather than performance metrics alone.

abstract:
Background:

Virtual laboratories have become a standard infrastructure in physics teaching, yet their pedagogical value depends on the learning model that frames them. Inquiry and collaborative learning are routinely invoked together, but no synthesis has treated them as the joint pedagogical framework for virtual laboratories in physics education or examined how the three are configured in practice. Methods Scopus was searched on July 9, 2026, for English-language journal articles published between 2017 and 2026, reporting primary studies in formal physics education that used a virtual laboratory, interactive simulation, or digital experimental environment within an inquiry and/or collaborative framework and reported at least one learning outcome. The Reporting follows Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020. Quality was appraised from full texts using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool version 2018, and the findings were synthesized through a six-phase thematic analysis. Results In total, 925 records were returned. Of the 110 reports sought, 23 were not retrieved and 87 were assessed in full text, giving 58 studies in 59 reports from 22 countries, most often in higher education (n = 27) and upper secondary school (n = 22), with quasi-experimental designs being dominant (n = 21). Combining real and virtual laboratories consistently outperformed either single mode, while virtual laboratories alone matched physical laboratories on conceptual mastery and surpassed them on abstract concepts and inquiry self-efficacy. Guidance, moderated by prior knowledge, determines whether exploratory freedom aids learning or adds cognitive load. Conceptual outcomes were measured in 45 studies (76.3%), but collaboration was designed explicitly in only nine reports (15.3%) and measured in five (8.5%). Conclusions The advantage of virtual laboratories comes from the quality of the pedagogical design around them, and not from technology. Collaboration is the component least often designed and measured, so the evidence base remains one about inquiry with virtual laboratories that happen to be delivered in groups.

abstract:
Background

Pressures on the global nursing education workforce and a growing shortage of clinical educators in surgical settings have placed preceptorship models at the heart of education. Viewing nursing education as a "revenue-generating commodity" raises concerns regarding the erosion of academic identity and the risk of disciplinary expertise being reduced to a technical craft.

Aim

This study aimed to describe the effects of the mentorship model in surgical nursing education on academic identity, pedagogical processes, and workforce sustainability, based on the perceptions of academicians and clinical mentor nurses.

Design

A study using a qualitative descriptive design was conducted to gather in-depth perspectives from stakeholders in academic and clinical fields.

Method

Data were collected through semi-structured individual interviews; audio recordings were transcribed verbatim and analyzed using a self-reflective thematic analysis framework. The study involved 10 academics from the Department of Surgical Nursing and 10 preceptor nurses who supervise students in surgical clinics (Total N = 20).

Findings

The analysis revealed four main themes: a shift in academic identity, highlighting the transition of academics from clinical expertise to administrative coordination; pedagogical tension, pointing to the risk of surgical nursing education devolving into the mere transfer of technical skills-or a "watch-and-do" model; a sustainability paradox, describing the invisible labor undertaken by clinical preceptors and the accompanying sense of burnout; and institutional disconnect, revealing-through the participants' own words-the gap between theory and clinical reality.

Conclusions

The findings indicate that participants perceive a significant risk regarding the sustainability of the current preceptorship model. Key implications arising from these findings include the development of defined collaboration protocols between the university and the hospital, the recognition of the educational contributions made by clinical preceptor nurses, and the piloting of clinical-academic hybrid staffing models.

abstract: Despite substantial advances in HIV prevention and treatment, sexually transmitted infections (STIs) remain an increasing public health concern among young people, while stigma toward people living with HIV (PLHIV) continues to represent a major psychosocial barrier. This study examined whether knowledge about HIV and other STIs, compared with self-reported exposure to sexual health education, was associated with stigma toward PLHIV among Spanish university students. A cross-sectional study was conducted with 728 university students from several Spanish universities. Participants completed an anonymous self-administered questionnaire assessing sociodemographic characteristics, exposure to sexual health education, knowledge of HIV and other STIs, and stigma toward PLHIV. Descriptive analyses, correlation analyses, nonparametric group comparisons, and hierarchical linear regression models were performed. A Poisson regression model was also estimated as a sensitivity analysis. Participants demonstrated good knowledge of the main routes of HIV transmission but showed substantial gaps regarding the HIV window period and several aspects of STI transmission and treatment. Although stigma was generally low in everyday social interactions, it remained high in situations involving intimacy and close physical contact. Knowledge of HIV and other STIs was moderately and negatively associated with stigma (r = - .46, p < .001). Students exposed to sexual health education demonstrated higher levels of knowledge but did not differ in stigma from those who had not received such education. In the hierarchical regression analyses, knowledge emerged as the strongest predictor of stigma, explaining an additional 14.5% of the variance beyond sociodemographic characteristics and exposure to sexual health education. The Poisson regression model yielded consistent results. Greater knowledge about HIV and other STIs was independently associated with lower stigma toward PLHIV, whereas exposure to sexual health education was not associated with stigmatizing attitudes. These findings highlight the need for educational interventions that not only provide accurate and comprehensive sexual health information but also explicitly address HIV-related stigma, misconceptions about transmission, and attitudes toward intimacy and close physical contact with PLHIV.

abstract: Lifestyle interventions can provide meaningful clinical benefits in the prevention and management of diabetes, but achieving these benefits requires structured education and ongoing support. For people living with diabetes, diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES) offers an established, person-centered approach to building the knowledge, skills, and confidence needed to make lifestyle changes part of daily life with the potential to reduce medications, particularly when glycemia improves with the lifestyle interventions.

abstract: Professional identity formation (PIF) is the process through which medical students integrate professional values, norms, and behaviours into their developing professional identity. Although PIF is increasingly recognised as an educational goal in undergraduate medical education (UGME), intervention research remains heterogeneous in educational approaches, theoretical foundations, outcome measurement, and geographic distribution. This scoping review mapped educational interventions designed to support PIF in UGME, their theoretical foundations, outcome and measurement approaches, and geographic and income-group distribution. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and ERIC were searched for English-language studies published from 2010 to 2025, supplemented by grey literature and citation searching. Studies addressing PIF-focused educational interventions among undergraduate medical students were eligible. Two reviewers independently screened records, with disagreements resolved through discussion or adjudication by a third reviewer. Data were charted using a piloted form and narratively synthesised using an inductively derived seven-category intervention taxonomy. Fifty-two studies from 21 countries were included. Interventions comprised clinical exposure (n=13, 25.0%), humanities/arts (n=11, 21.2%), reflective/narrative approaches (n=9, 17.3%), mentorship (n=7, 13.5%), mixed interventions (n=5, 9.6%), simulation (n=4, 7.7%), and peer learning (n=3, 5.8%). Identity development was the predominant outcome (n=32, 61.5%). Theoretical or conceptual frameworks were reported in 44 studies (84.6%), whereas eight (15.4%) reported none. Validated instruments were used in only three studies (5.8%). Forty-nine studies (94.2%) originated from high-income countries, two (3.8%) from lower-middle-income countries, and one (1.9%) from an upper-middle-income country. Four studies reported null or near-null effects. PIF intervention research remains theoretically heterogeneous, measurement-limited, and geographically concentrated. Greater use of validated, culturally responsive measures and longitudinal, context-sensitive research, particularly in low- and middle-income settings, is needed.

abstract:
Introduction:

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in clinical practice and medical education, yet uncertainty remains regarding appropriate use, oversight, and potential effects on clinical reasoning and patient safety. This study examined current LLM use patterns, attitudes, perceived risks, and priorities for responsible integration among individuals engaged in trauma care, clinical guidance development, and medical education.

Methods:

Participants attending the third Design for Implementation: The Future of Trauma Clinical Guidance and Research Conference (DFI) completed surveys examining LLM use, attitudes, perceived inhibitors to personal use, and clinical applications. During facilitated sessions, participants used open-ended note-taking guides to document their perspectives regarding LLM use in clinical practice, education, and guidance development. Survey data were analyzed descriptively, and qualitative responses were analyzed using rapid qualitative content analysis.

Results:

77 participants completed the pre-conference survey; 62 clinicians provided data regarding clinical LLM use and attitudes. Among clinicians, 15% reported daily LLM use, whereas 26% reported never using LLMs. Respondents expressed strongest agreement with the need for regular quality auditing of LLM-supported clinical decisions. Among 52 post-conference survey respondents, 96% somewhat or strongly agreed that clinical training curricula should include education on LLM use. Barriers to LLM use included time required to verify accuracy, concern about patient harm, and insufficient training in appropriate prompting. Qualitative data came from 23 note-taking documents administered during the conference. Both positive and negative perspectives arose regarding AI use, centering on topics including efficiency gains, deskilling and never-skilling, governance and oversight, accuracy and hallucination, patient safety, and education.

Discussion:

DFI participants recognized efficiency and informational benefits of LLMs while identifying important concerns related to accuracy, patient safety, skill development, and governance. Findings support a need for institutional guidance, education in responsible LLM use, and evaluation of the incorporation of these technologies into clinical practice and health professions education.

abstract: Background Sexual and reproductive health (SRH) education is important for marriage preparation, but standardized premarital education may not address individual couples' concerns, information needs, and preferred learning approaches. This qualitative study, informed by a constructivist orientation, explored SRH educational needs, perceived educational challenges, and preferred educational strategies among engaged couples attending premarital counseling services in northern Iran. Methods Conducted in premarital counseling centers, the study used purposive sampling with maximum variation. Data were collected through 23 in-depth interviews with engaged individuals, one mini focus group with four engaged individuals representing two couples, and five interviews with key informants. Semi-structured interviews and the focus group were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Conventional inductive content analysis was used. The Health Belief Model served as a sensitizing framework rather than a predetermined coding framework. Trustworthiness was addressed through triangulation, peer debriefing, member checking, reflexive journaling, an audit trail, and double-coding of transcripts. Results Four main categories and 16 subcategories were identified. Participants described SRH education needs extending beyond basic reproductive information to sexual health, contraception, understanding partner differences, problem-solving, communication, mutual understanding, trust, commitment, and responsibility. Educational challenges included cultural sensitivity, limited access to credible information, insufficient continuity of governmental educational services, poor provider client interactions, and limited providers' SRH knowledge. Participants preferred technology-based, interactive, and continuing education. They also described a perceived mismatch between changing expectations and existing educational practices, including generational differences, traditional-modern discourse tensions, and perceived constraints surrounding sexual health education. Views differed on formal and contraceptive education. [9] Conclusions Engaged couples described SRH education as a multidimensional need involving knowledge, communication, relationship skills, credible information, and supportive educational interactions. Findings suggest premarital SRH education may benefit from interactive, accessible, multi-channel approaches that extend beyond a single premarital encounter.

abstract: Previous studies on the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) catalyzed by Pt(II)-based molecular catalysts have often demonstrated a second-order dependence of the HER rate on the catalyst concentration, suggesting the importance of stabilizing dinuclear platinum intermediates. However, some Pt(II)-based HER catalysts instead exhibit a first-order dependence, and the key factors governing this selection have received limited attention. Here, we discovered a new class of Pt(II)-based HER photocatalysts, abbreviated as [PtCl2(pBp)]2+, [Pt2Cl4(OpBp)]4+, and [Pt2Cl4(UpBp)]4+. Specifically, pBp2+ is a pyridinium-functionalized bipyridine, while OpBp4+ and UpBp4+ are dinucleating ligands wherein two pBp2+ fragments are doubly or singly bridged by phenylene moieties, respectively. Remarkably, all these photocatalysts exhibit two successive pBp2+-based 1-electron reductions with a potential separation of 290-320 mV. These complexes serve as efficient photocatalysts for the aqueous-based HER at pH 5.0 in the presence of EDTA. Importantly, the HER rate exhibits a second-order dependence at lower concentrations, indicating that a 2-electron-reduced species is generated via a rate-determining disproportionation reaction (2Cat- → Cat + Cat2-) and serves as a key intermediate for HER (Cat2- + 2H+ → Cat + H2). Conversely, a first-order dependence is observed at higher concentrations, where the rate-determining step shifts to the photoinduced electron transfer process. Notably, the Cat2- intermediate exists as a minor component (e.g., 0.2%) due to the large comproportionation constants. Nevertheless, this low-abundance species dictates the overall reaction rate because its HER pathway possesses a ca. 0.3 eV higher thermodynamic driving force than that doubly driven by the Cat-/Cat couple, rendering the process kinetically highly favorable.

abstract:
Aim

This study aimed to evaluate the effect of telephone-based education and counselling on stoma adjustment and complication severity in individuals with a colostomy.

Methods

A randomised controlled trial was conducted with patients assigned to the telephone-based education and counselling group (education group) or the control group receiving routine stoma care. Data were collected over a three-month follow-up period using validated measures of stoma adjustment and complication severity.

Results

Baseline characteristics were comparable between the groups. At three months, the education group had significantly higher acceptance and total stoma adjustment scores and significantly lower complication severity scores than the control group. No significant between-group differences were found in anxious preoccupation, social engagement, or anger scores.

Conclusion

At three months, participants receiving telephone-based education and counselling had higher stoma adjustment scores and lower complication severity scores than those receiving routine care. Integrating structured nurse-led telephone follow-up into routine practice may strengthen continuity of post-discharge care.
