abstract: This study examines Sanya's tourism image disparities across cognitive, spatial, and affective dimensions in Press Generated Content (PGC), Tourist Generated Content (TGC), and Official Generated Content (OGC) (2013-2022), comparing pre-pandemic (2013-2019) and COVID-19 (2020-2022) periods. Results show: cognitive consistency in "tourism/hotels" but TGC focusing on "coastal + food" vs. PGC/OGC emphasizing policy elements; spatial misalignment between policy-driven spaces and tourists' preferred spaces, revealing a systematic dissonance between institutional promotion and on-the-ground practices; affective dominance of "enjoyment/romance" but TGC expressing unmet needs and OGC suppressing negatives. Systematic cognitive divergence exists between official and tourist narratives. The Aitchison distance measuring this divergence jumps from 19.574 in the pre-pandemic phase (2013-2019) to 40.648 during the pandemic-impacted phase (2020-2022), demonstrating that structural gaps between the two narrative systems become more pronounced amid the public health crisis. Targeted strategies are accordingly proposed to narrow such narrative discrepancies.

abstract: Universities in Western -European migration societies are increasingly challenged to address historical and structural forms of inequality, colonial continuities, and institutional discrimination. While higher education institutions promote diversity and internationalization in their strategic rhetoric, minoritized students and international scholars—particularly Black, Indigenous, People of Color (BIPoC), and scholars with foreign qualifications—continue to face systemic barriers, administrative gatekeeping, and symbolic devaluation. This conceptual paper examines the ambivalences of recognition and empowerment within higher education. “Using the Bachelor’s program ‘Pedagogy and Social Work in the Migration Society’ (PHM) at Carl von Ossietzky University of Oldenburg as an illustrative institutional case, we develop a conceptual analysis of how competency-based recognition practices can challenge deficit-oriented approaches to foreign qualifications.” We argue that institutional recognition is inherently ambivalent: while it can enable academic and professional access, it may simultaneously reproduce nationally coded and Eurocentric hierarchies of legitimate knowledge. Furthermore, we outline a Community-Based Participatory Research (CBPR) framework as a transformative epistemological intervention to deconstruct power asymmetries and foster collective agency. We conclude with multi-level policy and structural recommendations for higher education transformation.

abstract: BackgroundEmerging artificial intelligence-based technologies are increasingly influencing teaching and learning practices in healthcare education, offering new opportunities for student engagement, learning, and skill development.ObjectiveThe purpose of this study was to explore utilization of artificial intelligence in audiology and speech-language pathology education based on insights from students. Further, to explore their awareness, use, perceived benefits, barriers, and attitudes toward the integration of artificial intelligence.MethodA cross-sectional online survey of 17 questions was distributed to 483 audiology and speech-language pathology students enrolled in undergraduate, postgraduate and doctoral programmes across multiple institutions in India through social media platforms. The questionnaire was developed following a review of previously published studies examining students' perceptions of the implications of artificial intelligence in education. Descriptive analysis was used to analyse the findings.ResultsA total of 286 students participated in the study (mean age = 21.73 ± 2.33 years), of whom 82.2% were females. Most participants (96.9%) were aware of artificial intelligence technologies, and 89.9% indicated using artificial intelligence tools for educational purposes. Regarding the future role of artificial intelligence in education, 75.1% disagreed that it could replace human lecturers. Students primarily used it for assignments and exam preparation, while limited institutional acceptance was a major barrier to its implementation.ConclusionsStudents expressed an optimistic view regarding the application of artificial intelligence in education. Students reported concerns about inaccurate artificial intelligence-generated information, while limited acceptance, inadequate knowledge, and ethical concerns hindered its effective integration into education.

abstract:
Background

Assessment feedback is essential in nursing education, supporting students' academic and professional development. While extensive literature exists on feedback in clinical placements, there is limited evidence on academic assessment feedback approaches within the theoretical component of nursing education.

Aim

This scoping review explores existing practices, feedback models and their effectiveness in theoretical nursing education.

Methods

The review is guided by Arksey and O'Malley's (2005) five-stage framework and reported in line with PRISMA-ScR. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across CINAHL and Medline databases, supplemented by Google Scholar and reference list screening, in March 2025. Inclusion criteria included peer-reviewed articles published in English language on academic assessment feedback in nursing education. Identified studies were managed using Covidence and data were synthesised using qualitative content analysis.

Results

A total of n = 261 studies were identified, n = 7 studies met the review criteria following full screening. Findings show a predominant focus on formative feedback, provided using approaches such as written annotations, audio podcasts and Immediate Feedback Assessment Technique (IF-AT). There are inconsistencies in the feedback approaches and a limited application of structured feedback models among educators. Evidence on summative feedback approaches remains limited.

Conclusion

Assessment feedback in theoretical nursing education is characterised by a strong emphasis on formative feedback. However, the practice lacks consistency and standardisation. The integration of structured, evidence-informed feedback models and enhancement of feedback literacy may improve consistency, quality and academic development value of assessment feedback.

abstract:
Introduction

Effective collaboration between classroom teachers and health professionals is essential for supporting school students' learning and wellbeing, yet evidence indicates that such collaboration is often fragmented in practice. While interprofessional education (IPE) is intended to prepare graduates for collaborative practice across complex contexts by enabling learners from different disciplines to learn with, from, and about each other, the extent to which IPE initiatives have included collaborative learning between pre-service health professions and education students is unclear.

Method

A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute methodology to map IPE initiatives involving pre-service health professions and education students. A systematic search of six databases was conducted, with two reviewers independently screening studies for eligibility. A collaboratively developed data charting framework was applied to extract and analyse data from the included studies.

Results

Thirty-one publications describing 19 distinct IPE initiatives were identified in the eligible literature. Initiatives varied considerably in scale, ranging from small placement programs to large cohort workshops delivered face-to-face, online or in blended formats. Common pedagogical approaches included case-based discussions, simulations, and collaborative projects. Across initiatives, reported outcomes primarily reflected perceived or self-reported improvements in interprofessional knowledge, attitudes, and collaborative skills, and knowledge relevant to supporting school students. However, despite these reported positive outcomes, the review identified constraints to implementation across interpersonal, pedagogical, curriculum, and institutional levels.

Discussion

While interpersonal and pedagogical challenges influenced the design and delivery of IPE initiatives, curriculum-level demands (crowded and accreditation-driven programs) and institutional conditions (siloed faculties, governance arrangements, and resource and scheduling limitations) also shaped how IPE could be implemented. Together, these findings highlight challenges embedding and sustaining cross-sector IPE within higher education. Addressing these challenges will be important if universities are to embed IPE between health professions and education students as a core component of pre-service preparation.

abstract: As Korea’s digital talent development agenda advanced, the 2022 curriculum revision incorporated basic AI literacy into schooling, while the Ministry of Education and local education offices expanded AI convergence education programs for in-service teachers through graduate schools of education. Despite substantial policy support, qualitative research on teachers’ experiences remains limited. This study examines how in-service teachers navigate AI teaching and learning across university and school settings. Drawing on interviews with teachers enrolled in an AI convergence education program in the Seoul metropolitan area and an instructor in the same program, the study identifies a persistent gap between policy ambitions and classroom practice. Teachers enrolled largely in response to practical pressures to engage with AI in schools, although their expectations varied by professional experience and position. Participants also reported limited practical guidance on AI ethics and insufficient support for translating AI knowledge into subject-specific teaching. While faculty expertise in AI-related disciplines strengthened participants’ understanding of AI, it offered fewer opportunities to explore how AI could be meaningfully integrated into classroom instruction. The study conceptualizes this challenge as pedagogical translation and calls for clearer definitions of AI education and stronger connections between graduate teacher education and school practice.

abstract: Despite growing interest in integrating “psychedelic knowledge” into medical and health professions training, the term remains inconsistently conceptualised and operationalised across the literature. This scoping review investigates how psychedelic knowledge is represented, justified and translated within medical education scholarship. Using the Mak and Thomas (2022) methodological framework, we systematically searched five databases: ERIC, Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO and Scopus. We identified 28 studies addressing psychedelic education across undergraduate medical education, graduate medical education, continuing professional education and mixed educational contexts. Through descriptive mapping and interpretive analysis, we developed an empirically emergent taxonomy that classifies psychedelic knowledge into four conceptual categories: (1) Attitudinal Knowledge, (2) Preparatory Knowledge, (3) Technical Knowledge and (4) Experiential–Relational–Formational Knowledge. While psychedelic education was commonly justified by linking present educational conditions with anticipated workforce needs, regulatory change, implementation readiness, and future clinical practice, we observed substantial variability in learner populations, educational aims, pedagogical approaches, and the forms of knowledge represented. The literature was predominantly recent and survey-based, with educational justifications most commonly reflecting a transitional orientation between present educational needs and anticipated future developments, and relatively few studies describing or evaluating structured educational programmes. This conceptual pluralism, while reflecting the multidisciplinary character of psychedelic knowledge scholarship in medical education, complicates curriculum development, comparative evaluation and assessment by combining distinct educational objects under a single label. Our findings offer a conceptual map of how psychedelic knowledge is currently situated within medical education and provide a taxonomy to support greater clarity, coherence and intentionality in the design, implementation and assessment of psychedelic education.

abstract:
Background

A ketogenic diet (KD) is increasingly investigated as a nutritional approach for improving glycemic control and metabolic health. However, relatively few studies have examined fish-rich ketogenic interventions. Fish consumption may substantially increase circulating trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), while habitual fish intake is generally associated with favourable cardiometabolic outcomes. The metabolic significance of a short-term diet-induced increase in TMAO therefore remains unclear. This study aimed to characterize changes in circulating TMAO and related metabolites, glycemic and insulin-related biomarkers, oxidative stress markers, and lipid profiles during a fish-rich, calorie-restricted KD in healthy adults.

Methods

Nine men and five women (mean age 45 ± 3 years) participated in a 2-week, single-arm, within-subject pre-post dietary intervention. TMAO and related metabolites, selected glycemic and insulin-related biomarkers, oxidative stress markers, and lipid-profile parameters were assessed before and after the intervention. Participants followed individualized fish-rich ketogenic meal plans providing an approximately 500 kcal/day energy deficit.

Results

Following the intervention, circulating TMAO and betaine concentrations increased significantly, whereas carnitine and glycerophosphocholine (GPC) concentrations decreased. Favourable changes were observed in fasting glucose, insulin, C-peptide, leptin, and resistin. HDL cholesterol decreased significantly, while total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides remained unchanged. No evidence of increased oxidative stress was observed. The direct estimate of insulin sensitivity (HOMA-%S) did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons.

Conclusions

A 2-week, calorie-restricted, fish-rich ketogenic intervention was associated with a marked increase in circulating TMAO together with favourable changes in selected glycemic, insulin-related, and adipokine biomarkers, without evidence of increased oxidative stress. HDL cholesterol decreased, whereas other lipid-profile parameters remained largely unchanged. Because caloric restriction, ketogenic macronutrient composition, high fish intake, and reductions in body weight and adiposity occurred simultaneously, the independent contribution of TMAO to these metabolic changes cannot be determined. These findings should therefore be considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating.

abstract: Decades of theoretical work in education research and developmental psychology suggest that students’ time in higher education is a critical period in their personal and moral development. Indeed, many institutions of higher education explicitly seek to promote students’ character growth. Yet empirical evidence regarding such growth during higher education remains limited. The present study (N = 473,627 undergraduates at 414 United States colleges anduniversities) used mixed-effects models to examine students’ character growth across four years in higher education and to test whether such growth is moderated academic major, institutional characteristics, or students’ engagement in their campus communities. Results indicated that students do experience significant growth during their years in higher education. However, academic major and institutional type accounted for little variation. Instead, specific forms of community engagement, including participation in student organizations, mentorship and conversations about social and cultural issues, emerged as clear moderators. Alongside these theoretical implications, the findings have practical significance. The factors that appear to play the largest roles in shaping students’ growth are precisely those that staff, faculty, and administrators can influence, for example by prioritizing mentorship and promoting organizational involvement and dialogue across differences.
